Rather than join the queue, I walk down the street and stumble onto a smaller, somewhat hidden site: The Globe Museum. Tucked inside Vienna's 17th-Century Palais Mollard, it's the only public museum on Earth dedicated entirely to globes, and one of Vienna's greatest surprises. Different worlds I soon realise that I've wandered into another world – or more accurately, many of them. Just steps from some of the city's most celebrated, crowded attractions, Vienna's Globe Museum displays more than 220 rare and antique spheres, most created before 1850, ranging from towering Coronelli globes to tiny, foldable pocket orbs. Beautiful and surreal, the museum's extensive collection goes beyond geography to reveal how humanity has mapped and imagined the Earth and heavens above. It's a chronicle of human curiosity, and – quite literally – the story of our world. "Globes show the change in our imagination of our planet," says Nikolaus Schobesberger, the director of museum. "And this is the only place in the world where you can see so many of them at the same time." Visitors start by travelling through the Golden Cabinet, a lavish room with centuries-old frescoes depicting scenes from Greek mythology. It's the backdrop for a stunning array of globe-related instruments, like telluriums, which illustrate the Earth's orbit around the Sun, and armillary spheres, which use a framework of rings to visualise the movements of celestial bodies. As I reach the museum's four main galleries, I realise the whole place is pin-drop quiet. I shuffle slowly from one glass case to another, holding my breath to not disturb the stillness, even though I'm alone with centuries-old objects. I find myself marvelling at two spherical worlds suspended in time. One is terrestrial, with oceans awash in vivid blues and squiggly brown coastlines. The other is celestial, where mythological creatures and constellations spill across a tea stain-coloured backdrop. Barely bigger than beach balls, these two time capsules were made by the same craftsman 10 years apart in the mid-1500s and preserve a world as it was still coming into focus. In one, Europe, the Mediterranean and Africa's coasts are filled with place names, while North America fades into the uncharted Arctic. Asia is distorted, a hypothetical southern continent stands in for Australia and Antarctica and the Pacific is populated by sea monsters instead of islands. In the other, Renaissance astrological observations exist alongside Pegasus taking flight and Perseus brandishing Medusa's severed head. "They're some of the oldest globes we have in our collection," says Schobesberger. Moving from one globe to the next, I notice how these relics extend beyond geography and depict what people once believed. Many fill the space of unexplored oceans with dragons, while some confidently depict my home state of California as an island. Some pieces also preserve colonial-era prejudices with elaborately painted scenes depicting Indigenous people as cannibals. On one, African coastlines are dotted with Spanish and Portuguese flags, showing "ownership". "They're a part of this colonial thinking. And so, they're beautiful art, but you also have to think about the time they were created," Schobesberger says, explaining that every globe is as much a record of what people knew as what they didn't. That's why he believes the museum resonates with all types of people, not just historians or cartography enthusiasts. One of Schobesberger's favourite objects is a lunar globe from 1961. The front portion of the Moon is meticulously mapped. The back, however, is a stark white strip, intentionally left blank because the far side of the Moon had not yet been seen. An updated lunar globe made two years later, also on display, contains the missing portion. I can't help but circle back to a showstopper in the front hall, a replica of the Behaim Globe – completed by Martin Behaim in 1492, the year Christopher Columbus sailed west – which shows a world without the Americas. There's simply an expanse of ocean between Europe and Asia. "A globe is such a great thing because it's a small-scale model of our planet, so you can tell stories about the world on it," he says. "Climate, geology, topography, trade routes, everything." From curios to cultural cornerstones Walking through the museum, visitors can see the globe's own journey unfold. The earliest examples were luxury objects reserved for aristocrats and wealthy merchants. Over time, globes lost their exclusivity, shrunk in size and became more affordable and popular. They entered schools, appeared in living rooms and even became playthings for children. Today, they are so commonplace that my son even won his desktop globe in a classroom raffle. I entered the museum expecting to view globes as historic artefacts, but I'm surprised by how alive they still feel. Even with Google Earth at my fingertips, these tactile objects invite curiosity and imagination in a way that a screen doesn't. "It's not just that the globe is a scientific instrument. It's also an object which lets you dream of foreign countries," says Schobesberger. Globes in pop culture Beginning 24 September 2026, the museum's newest exhibition, Globes in Everyday Life, Art and Culture, will explore how globes evolved from a status symbol to a familiar fixture. It also showcases the globe's enduring place in pop culture, from architecture to art and film, like Charlie Chaplin's famous dance with an inflatable globe in The Great Dictator. "The main idea was to show that globes are almost everywhere as a part of everyday life," Schobesberger says. Schobesberger's own fascination began as a young child, when he became captivated by the ships, sea monsters and mythical creatures that filled the blank spaces of historical maps and globes. He began to draw his own world maps when he was just six years old. "You can think about what's possible on the other side of the world, even when you're sitting here in Europe," he says. "Nothing else can capture the imagination quite like it." More like this: That sentiment resonates with author JF Penn, who stumbled onto the Globe Museum while researching her novel Spear of Destiny, based on a relic housed in Vienna's Imperial Treasury. Like me, she ended up lingering far longer than planned. "I particularly loved the oversized antique globes with the patina of age and use," she says. "I considered how many fingertips have turned them over generations and wondered if they thought of travelling to these far-off places that I do." Even after visitors leave Palais Mollard, the search continues. Across Vienna, some 50 globes are perched on rooftops and facades, hidden in plain sight. The museum even charts them on a virtual map in its new exhibit, encouraging people to look upward as they wander the city. When I finally step back outside, the sky is dark and the streets are even more crowded. Earlier in the day, I had been seeking a quieter corner of Vienna. Instead, I was given a whole new way of seeing the world – a place that's constantly being redrawn and reimagined. --

item.title: The smoky plant goo that Finns can't stop eating
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 4.88
Pine tar: The surprising, smoky goo that Finns can't stop eating Once used to waterproof boats and treat infections, this smoky plant byproduct is now used to flavour everything from schnapps to bread. But how does it taste? I've been in the sub-Arctic city of Oulu, Finland for only a few hours when I'm caught under a torrent of late summer rain. I take refuge in a cafe and order a coffee and sugar-dusted pannukakku (a thick pancake). The waiter asks me, "What flavour? We have almond, tar, blueberry..." I'm certain I've misunderstood: "Did you say tar?" He nods nonchalantly. Welcome to Oulu, the northern Finnish city where terva (pine tar, usually translated in English simply as "tar") is on the menu. Produced by heating pine wood without oxygen, this thick, dark substance flavours everything from lager to ice cream, lending a distinct, rich smokiness. "It's an intense flavour, so a little goes a long way," says Matti Moller of the Arctic Food Lab, an initiative showcasing northern Finland's culinary culture. "But it's brilliant to experiment with in everything from fish to desserts." To Finns, pine tar's aroma has long been associated with wooden boats, summer cottages and sauna scents. So what's the recent culinary appeal? I've decided to find out. From sealant to meal Yet just two centuries ago, Oulu had a very different reputation. Encircled by dense pine forests and the winding channels of the Oulujoki delta, it was famed as the tar capital of the world. "Oulu has been a major trading hub since the 15th Century thanks to its position on the Oulu River," says local guide Sirpa Törmä. "By the 1860s, it had become the world's largest tar-exporting port." Essential for waterproofing wooden sailing ships, tar was produced by smouldering wood in tar pits across villages along the river, then transported in narrow boats to Oulu's harbour for global export. Thanks to its antibacterial properties, tar had also long been used as a natural wound treatment all over Finland. "As the well-known saying goes: 'If sauna, spirits and tar do not help, the disease is fatal,'" explains Ritva Kylli, a food historian at the University of Oulu. But how did it make its way to the Finnish palate? Tar-as-flavour made its debut on pharmacy shelves. Archives at the National Library of Finland reveal that tar-flavoured medicinal lozenges date back to the early 1900s, and Oulu's local papers advertised tervakaramellit ('tar sweets') as early as 1902. "These were medicinal lozenges sold in apothecary shops for coughs and respiratory diseases," says Kylli. Even if not every Finn enjoys the taste of tar, virtually everyone has tried the iconic black terva pastille. The nation's most famous brand is Terva Leijona (Tar Lion), sold to this day. Launched in 1933, the pastilles were created by Oulu pharmacist YW Jalander after watching locals inhale smoky tar fumes for their health. Facing low profits, he invented a tar essence (tervaessanssi) and infused it into liquorice pastilles, which he sold through his confectionary company, Merijal. Terva Leijona eventually changed hands, but it is still made using his recipe. As popular as they were, tar didn't make the leap from pastille to gourmet treat until the end of the 20th Century, says Kylli, as living standards rose and interest in regional heritage cuisine grew across the country: "[It] seems to be connected to a growing interest in the cultural memory of Oulu's tar economy, a trend spreading beyond northern historical trade routes to all of Finland," she says. "It was reimagined into a distinctive heritage flavour." 'It can be addictive' Matti tells me he buys tar chocolate and syrup a few times a year. "The taste is unique – sweet, smoky, medicinal and completely unmistakable," he says as we walk across the picturesque island of Pikisaari, connected to Oulu's city centre by a short bridge. "Why do we love it? Perhaps we're tasting our roots, the Finnish forest and our heritage." The Oulu region, as the historic heart of the pine tar culture, has also become the symbolic centre of pine tar cuisine, with a high concentration of restaurants, cafes and bakeries that produce terva foods. At Pekka Heikkinen, a family bakery in Kajaani founded in 1913, owner Kaisa Marin bakes traditional bread and pastries. "Tar boats used to sail right past our bakery to Oulu," she explains. "When pine tar food innovations emerged in the '90s, it was natural to start baking tar-flavoured bread." For Marin, the connection is deeply personal: "My grandmother washed my hair with tar shampoo in the sauna, and our cabin's boat was sealed with tar. To me, the scent is cosy, nostalgic and rooted in home. I love it!" She always keeps thinly sliced tar bread in the freezer, ready to fry in butter when guests arrive. Though not for everyone, she warns it can be addictive. "My uncle, a master confectioner, created a rich tar chocolate that we bake every Christmas. We've even made cakes with pine tar and spruce needles." Rina Hirviniemi, owner of the cosy Kahvila Kiikku, also bakes tar bread at least once a week, usually pairing it with gravlax. "In summer, I serve vanilla ice cream with tar syrup, and in winter, we grill with tar outside," she says. "I like keeping tar products on hand, though I don't put them on the menu – I have an eye for people I can recommend it to." So what does it taste like? Convinced, I decide to – literally – bite. According to Marin, ice cream is the best starting point for tar newcomers, so I head to Market Square's ice cream van. Cone in hand, I sit by Toripolliisi, the brawny bronze police statue keeping watch over the square, and take my first hesitant taste. A smoky-sweet aroma rushes from nose to palate – the unexpected whiff of bacon. Yet, it's surprisingly sweet. Intrigued, I can't stop eating. Bite by bite, it completely wins me over. Just as Marin predicted, I find myself becoming addicted. I head next to ChocoSomnia, an Oulu chocolate maker. "We make tar pralines, chocolate bars and tar coffee. We get curious first-timers, but also loyal regulars," says co-owner Mika Lähteenmäki. Sampling a square of dark chocolate infused with pine tar and cranberry, I'm struck by the balance of smoky depth, rich cocoa bitterness and soft berry sweetness; the very taste of a pine forest in midsummer. I can't stop there. My local friend leads me to a supermarket for Terva Leijona pastilles. Like impatient children, we tear open the box and pop the tiny black sweets. Instead of subtle sweetness, an intense, smoky rush clears my airways. My friend introduces me to two of his mates, and I discover that local usage varies widely: some drizzle tar syrup on bacon, others serve tar schnapps before nights out. For others still, tar candies reign supreme. While most Finns buy ready-made tar products, today's skilled chefs craft them from scratch. This is what brought me to Lasaretti, a restaurant tucked into the riverfront oasis of Oulu's Hupisaaret Park. Today, head chef Laurance Robinson is serving smoked whitefish pasta with tar pearls, pickled fennel and red onion. "I can't build a tar pit, so I buy flavouring from Kujala's farm to make my syrup for sweet and savoury dishes," he says. "Balancing its strong, pungent taste took time." Resembling caviar, the tar pearls burst in my mouth against the whitefish, sharp fennel, and sweet archipelago bread. It is pure umami with subtle smokiness. More like this: Originally from the Isle of Man, Robinson cooked across Europe before settling in Finland. "I'll never forget my first taste of tar in 2011 – a sauna soda from my future father-in-law. It tasted like an ashtray at first, but the smokiness mellowed. Later, when I had the freedom to experiment, I said, 'I want to be the tar chef.'" His tar pavlova recently won best dessert at an Oulu culinary contest. "I wonder how far I can push it." Watching passersby drift through the sunny park, I marvel at how tar shifted from a maritime necessity to the flavour of local identity. "You know what," says my friend. "I've had a horrible headache since morning, but after eating this dish, it's completely gone." I can't promise it cures headaches, but in every sense, tar remains a uniquely Finnish ingredient that still works its quiet magic. --

item.title: Caramelized Onions
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.46
Making caramelized onions is an art, not a science—but this recipe gives you a reliable roadmap. Slowly cooking sliced yellow or white onions in butter transforms them from sharp and crisp to soft, savory-sweet, and deeply browned. How far you take them depends on the job: Stop at golden brown for softer, jammy onions, or keep going until deep brown with slightly crisp edges for an intensely caramelized burger topping. The key is a wide pan and a little patience. Plenty of surface area helps moisture evaporate efficiently, while moderate heat lets the onions soften and brown gradually, without burning. Make a batch now and thank yourself later. You can even double it for practically the same amount of work and time. Caramelized onions keep for up to a week in the refrigerator and even longer in the freezer. Use them as the foundation for French onion soup, spoon them over scrambled eggs, tuck them into sandwiches, or stir them into dips and pasta. Caramelized onion FAQ How long does it take to caramelize onions? For deeply caramelized onions, plan on 45 minutes to an hour. You can stop earlier if a recipe calls for blond or golden-brown onions; color and texture are better indicators of doneness than the clock. Need a more hands-off version? Try caramelizing onions in the oven → What should caramelized onions look like? Fully caramelized onions should be deeply browned, substantially reduced, and very soft but not mushy. Some crisp edges are fine, but blackened bits can taste bitter. Why aren’t my onions caramelizing? They may simply need more time. Onions release plenty of moisture in the early stages of caramelizing. Significant browning won’t begin until much of that water has cooked off. A crowded pan can slow this process; use a wide pan with plenty of surface area to speed things along. Once the onions begin browning, keep the heat moderate so they caramelize gradually without burning. How do you keep caramelized onions from burning? Stir regularly and lower the heat if they’re browning too quickly. If the bottom of the pan starts to burn, add a splash of water or broth and scrape up the browned bits. Can you freeze caramelized onions? Yes. Let caramelized onions cool completely, then freeze them in small portions so you can defrost only what you need. Add them straight to soups, stews, and sauces, or thaw them before using in eggs, sandwiches, and other dishes. Got any recipes that use caramelized onions? We thought you’d never ask. Recipe information - Total Time 1 hour 15 minutes - Yield Makes about ½ cup Ingredients 2 2 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Halve 2 large onions (about 1 lb.) through root ends. Using the tip of your knife, cut a V-shaped notch around each root to remove (this will ensure that all slices separate when you cut the onion). Place 1 onion half on a cutting board so root end is facing you, then thinly slice lengthwise (¼"–⅛" thick), starting at one side and working all the way to the other (your knife will run through root halfway through; you are not starting or ending at root end). Repeat with remaining onion halves. Step 2Heat 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large saucepan or high-sided skillet over medium until melted and sizzling. Add a couple of large handfuls of onion slices and cook, stirring constantly, until softened and starting to turn translucent, 1–2 minutes. Add remaining onion slices a few handfuls at a time, repeating cooking process after each addition. As soon as all of the onions have been cooked, season with a pinch of kosher salt. Step 3Reduce heat to medium-low and continue to cook onions, stirring every few minutes and reducing heat a little if sticking or getting too brown in any one place, until blond, 15–20 minutes more. Step 4For onions that are both softer and more caramelized (for a patty melt or onion dip), continue to cook, stirring often and adding a splash of low-sodium chicken broth or water if the bottom of pan starts to burn, until unmistakably golden brown, 15–20 minutes more. Step 5For extra-dark onions (the kind that make for a great burger topping), continue to cook, stirring often, until slightly crisp and starting to almost blacken around the edges, 10–15 minutes more. Step 6Let onions cool in pan before using. Do Ahead: Onions can be caramelized 1 week ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Editor’s note: This caramelized onion recipe was originally published on August 3, 2017; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more of our favorite onion-forward recipes →

item.title: Garlic Confit
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.09
Garlic confit transforms pungent raw cloves into a sweet, tender, jammy condiment by cooking them slowly in a bath of oil. A French technique classically used to preserve meat in its own rendered fat, confit can also be done, as it is here, with a neutral oil. Most of the cooking time is hands-off. For an aromatic variation, add a few sprigs of rosemary or thyme, a bay leaf, black peppercorns, or crushed red pepper flakes before the pan goes into the oven (see Herby Garlic Confit). And don’t overlook the oil. Garlic confit gives you two kitchen workhorses in one: Mash the cloves into potatoes or hummus, smear them onto toast, or mix them with softened butter for steak. Use the deeply savory garlic oil in salad dressings, marinades, or anywhere you want a mellow hit of garlic. Garlic confit FAQ What is the best oil for garlic confit? Most vegetable oils will work here. We prefer a neutral oil, such as grapeseed or safflower, which lets the garlic flavor shine. Extra-virgin olive oil is another good option, though its flavor can be overpowering here, and it tends to break down more quickly than a neutral variety. Avoid delicate oils, as well as canola, which develop off-flavors during the long cooking process. How do I peel all this garlic? You have a couple of options. The most reliable methods we’ve found include adding the separated cloves to a metal mixing bowl, covering it with a second mixing bowl to form a sort of sphere, then shaking the contraption rapidly up and down. The friction will slough off the skins, leaving the cloves intact. If that feels like too much work, you can also soak the separated garlic cloves in hot water for 1 minute. The skins will slip right off. Last, you could use a dedicated silicone garlic peeler: How do you know when garlic confit is done? Look for cloves that are completely tender. They should be golden, jammy, and soft enough to mash into a creamy purée using just a fork. Keep in mind that ovens vary; start checking the garlic before the full cooking time if yours tends to run hot. How do you store garlic confit? Transfer the cooled garlic and oil to an airtight container and keep refrigerated at or below 38°F for up to 2 weeks. Garlic stored in oil should not be kept at room temperature. Can you freeze garlic confit? Yes. For convenient portions, freeze the garlic cloves and infused oil together in an ice cube tray—or purée them first if you plan to add them to soups, stews, or spreads. Transfer the frozen portions to an airtight freezer container. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator, or add the frozen portion directly to a hot pot. Recipe information - Total Time 2 hours 10 minutes plus chilling - Yield Makes about 1½ cups Ingredients 3 1½ Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Preheat oven to 250°. Combine 3 heads of garlic, cloves separated and peeled, and 1½ cups grapeseed oil in a small ovenproof saucepan (add more oil if cloves aren’t submerged). Cover and bake until cloves are golden and tender, about 2 hours. Let cool, then transfer garlic and oil to an airtight container and chill. Do Ahead: Garlic can be cooked 2 weeks ahead. Keep chilled. Bring to room temperature before using. Safety note: In most cases, confited garlic is perfectly safe to eat, but storing garlic in oil does carry a risk of botulism, a foodborne illness caused by bacteria that thrive in low-oxygen, low-acid, low-sugar environments. The cooking process greatly reduces that risk, as does storing the cooked garlic and oil at a temperature below 38° and consuming them within 2 weeks. For longer storage, or for storing at room temperature, look for methods using a pressure canner. Editor’s note: This garlic confit recipe was originally published in our January 2016 issue; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more of our most garlicky recipes →

item.title: Google employees are already testing the next Gemini Flash AI model
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.55
Google just released a new AI model this month. Its employees are already testing the next one. Some staff have begun using a preview version of Gemini 3.8 Flash, highlighting the breakneck pace of the AI race as Google pushes out new models just weeks apart to keep up with OpenAI and Anthropic. The new model — dubbed "Gemini 3.8 Flash Preview" — was made available to staff on Google's internal coding platform, Jetski, according to images Business Insider obtained. One employee testing the new model said it already felt noticeably better than 3.7 Flash, but emphasized it was too early for a full review. Google declined to comment. With 3.5 Pro still missing and Anthropic and OpenAI sprinting ahead in the AI race, Google no longer has a frontier model. Instead, it has doubled down on its "Flash" models, which offer greater speed and lower costs for users, at a time when customers are keeping a closer eye on their AI bill. Google refers to these models as its "workhorse models" for coding and running agents, which often consume tokens faster than chatbots. Agentic assistants designed to help with everyday tasks are proving to be the next hot thing among the AI companies. Google launched its Gemini Spark agent earlier this year, and Meta is testing its "Hatch" agent internally. Google has been improving its Flash models at a rapid clip. Gemini 3.6 Flash rolled out in July, and 3.7 Flash followed just three weeks later. During the company's Q2 earnings call, CEO Sundar Pichai said the company would aim for an almost monthly release cadence. The employee preview suggests a public rollout of Gemini 3.8 Flash may not be far away, but it's not a guarantee. Some keen-eyed AI sleuthers are convinced they have spotted Gemini 3.8 Flash on Arena AI, a website for benchmarking models that Google has previously used to test upcoming releases. Have something to share? Contact this reporter via email at hlangley@businessinsider.com or Signal at 628-228-1836. Use a personal email address and a non-work device; here's our guide to sharing information securely.

item.title: These states have produced the most Miss USA winners
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.94
The United States has the most winners in Miss Universe history, but which states reign supreme when it comes to Miss USA? One state had a five-year winning streak and produced two future Miss Universe winners. Meanwhile, 18 states still haven't won the crown. They'll get a chance to change their record at the 75th annual Miss USA pageant in Miami on August 27. Until then, let's take a look back at the most successful states in the history of the Miss USA pageant. Texas has won the Miss USA crown 10 times. Texas has a storied history in the world of pageants. Two Miss Texas winners who won Miss USA went on to win Miss Universe: Chelsi Smith and R'Bonney Gabriel. Miss Texas 2008 Crystle Stewart, who also won Miss USA, served as CEO and president of the Miss USA and Miss Teen USA pageants from 2020 to 2023. Texas won five Miss USA pageants in a row from 1985 to 1989, a streak nicknamed the "Texas Aces." The full list of Miss Texas titleholders who won Miss USA is: - 1977: Kimberly Tomes - 1985: Laura Martinez Herring - 1986: Christy Fichtner - 1987: Michelle Royer - 1988: Courtney Gibbs - 1989: Gretchen Polhemus - 1995: Chelsi Smith - 2001: Kandace Krueger - 2008: Crystle Stewart - 2022: R'Bonney Gabriel California, which has taken the Miss USA crown six times, is catching up. California has won a Miss USA title in every decade except the 2000s. Its most recent winner was Alyssa Campanella, who took the crown in 2011. The full list of Miss California titleholders who won Miss USA is: - 1959: Terry Huntingdon - 1966: Maria Remenyi - 1975: Summer Bartholomew - 1983: Julie Hayek - 1992: Shannon Marketic - 2011: Alyssa Campanella Hawaii assumed its fifth Miss USA title after Miss USA 2023 Noelia Voigt resigned, a first in the pageant's history. Miss Hawaii 1962 Macel Wilson became the first woman from Hawaii to enter the Miss USA competition, as well as the first Asian American and first woman of color to win the crown. Miss Hawaii 1997 Brook Lee won both Miss USA and Miss Universe. The state assumed its fifth title after Miss USA 2023 Noelia Voigt stepped down three months before her reign came to an end due to the leadership of Laylah Rose, who was CEO of Miss USA at the time. Miss Hawaii Savannah Gankiewicz, who had won first runner-up at the pageant, took Voigt's place. The full list of Miss Hawaii titleholders who were named Miss USA is: - 1962: Macel Wilson - 1972: Tanya Wilson - 1978: Judi Andersen - 1997: Brook Lee - 2023: Savannah Gankiewicz Multiple states have four winners, including Michigan. Carole Gist was both the first Miss Michigan and the first African American woman to win the Miss USA crown. In 2010, Miss Michigan Rima Fakih made history as the first Arab American woman to take the title. Former Miss Michigan Kenya Moore, who won Miss USA in 1993, has become one of the most famous contestants in the pageant's history after starring in "The Real Housewives of Atlanta" from 2012 to 2025. The most recent Miss Michigan to win Miss USA is Alma Cooper, a US Army officer who took the crown in 2024. The full list of Miss Michigan titleholders who won Miss USA is: - 1990: Carole Gist - 1993: Kenya Moore - 2010: Rima Fakih - 2024: Alma Cooper The District of Columbia's recent Miss USA titles came in quick succession. The District of Columbia doesn't have representation in the Senate, but it sure does well on the Miss USA stage. In 2016, Deshauna Barber won Miss District of Columbia, and Kára McCullough placed first runner-up. Barber went on to win Miss USA, while McCullough won Miss District of Columbia in 2017. That year, Barber crowned McCullough the new Miss USA. It was the first time a place had won back-to-back Miss USA titles since the Texas Aces' reign. The full list of Miss District of Columbia titleholders who won Miss USA is: - 1964: Bobbi Johnson - 2002: Shauntay Hinton - 2016: Deshauna Barber - 2017: Kára McCullough Illinois has also taken the Miss USA title four times, but all its wins came before 1975. Illinois is also one of only four states to win back-to-back Miss USA titles. The full list of Miss Illinois titleholders who won Miss USA is: - 1953: Myrna Hansen - 1963: Marite Ozers - 1973: Amanda Jones - 1974: Karen Morrison New York has the honor of winning the very first Miss USA pageant. Miss New York 1952 Jackie Loughery was named the very first Miss USA. She also represented the USA at the first-ever Miss Universe pageant that same year, placing in the top 10. New York assumed its third Miss USA crown in 1995, when Shanna Moakler inherited the title after Chelsi Smith won Miss Universe 1995. The full list of Miss New York titleholders who won Miss USA is: - 1952: Jackie Loughery - 1979: Mary Therese Friel - 1995: Shanna Moakler - 1999: Kimberly Ann Pressler All four of North Carolina's wins have been during the 2000s. North Carolina has really hit its stride on the pageant stage in recent years. The state's most recent Miss USA title came when Morgan Romano assumed the 2022 crown after R'Bonney Gabriel won America's ninth Miss Universe title. The full list of Miss North Carolina titleholders who won Miss USA is: - 2005: Chelsea Cooley - 2009: Kristen Dalton - 2019: Cheslie Kryst - 2022: Morgan Romano

item.title: A Ukrainian air-defense sergeant says missiles aren't his most challenging shortage. It's the gear that finds enemy targets.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.43
The hardest shortage facing one Ukrainian shoulder-fired air-defense unit isn't necessarily missiles, its battery sergeant told Business Insider. It's some of the equipment that helps crews find targets and keep their systems running. The soldier, who uses the call sign Yankee, serves in a front-line unit equipped with man-portable air-defense systems, or MANPADS, which fire shoulder-launched missiles able to engage low-flying aircraft, as well as cruise missiles and drones. Weapons like these, which include the US Stinger, Polish Piorun, and Soviet-designed Igla, have been a key part of Ukraine's short-range air defense in front-line areas, protecting troops and operations from attacks. Yankee said that for him, at least, one of the hardest things "is finding resources. Secondary resources, not the weaponry, but electronic warfare stuff." He said some of the devices that help his team detect threats and keep its equipment working are "hard to get." What is hardest to find is "mostly electronics." "I'm talking more about devices that locate the drones and warn you," Yankee said. "I'm talking about stuff like EcoFlows, batteries, big batteries, because we have a shortage of them, just in general, just a mass shortage." Ukrainian soldiers are increasingly using drone detectors, including small handheld or vehicle-mounted models, to warn of certain incoming enemy drones by detecting their radio frequencies. EcoFlows are portable power stations that can power or recharge essential gear such as radios and communications equipment, Starlink terminals, laptops and tablets, drone equipment, electronic warfare systems, and sensors. These, and batteries in general, are especially important because soldiers are often far from power outlets, and Russian attacks often shut down energy infrastructure. Running a portable generator would be much louder and might reveal their positions. Electronic warfare systems are also vital for Ukraine as it tries to disrupt Russia's communications and jam its drones. Despite their importance, this equipment isn't always easy for units to obtain in sufficient quantities. Some of the gear is much newer and less readily available than supplies like ammunition. And while demand is high, some equipment still isn't being produced in large quantities. In some cases, there are also distribution bottlenecks that affect availability. Unlike many Western militaries, Ukraine's military doesn't have a highly centralized system for weapons procurement. Units often buy or receive gear themselves, including through crowdfunding. There are advantages to this setup for rapid innovation because units engage manufacturers directly, but the system can also result in uneven distribution, leaving some units facing shortages. Ukrainian foundations, units, and other groups that are involved in sourcing and crowdfunding equipment for troops often ask for gear like batteries and detectors, with some describing them as items that air defenders regularly need. MANPADS and the units that operate them are important for Ukraine. Units, service members, and officials have reported missiles taking down Russian drones, helicopters, and aircraft, and Western analysts have credited MANPADS with making penetrating low-altitude Russian fixed-wing and helicopter sorties too costly for Russia to continue. A report last year from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US think tank, said that Ukraine's integration of MANPADS operators into its air defense teams forced Russian pilots to choose between flying high and being targeted by ground-based air defenses or flying low and facing MANPAD missiles. These short-range defenses relieved the pressure on Ukraine's ground-based systems, allowing them to "survive and eventually recover." Yankee's unit provides air defense for infantry who need to get to the zero line, the far edge of the front line, and, as a result, "we participate in battle," he said. He said that conditions there can be so dangerous that moving just 300 meters can take 7 days of waiting for safe conditions and protection. Moving even that short distance, he said, "can be like a question of life and death." Yankee spoke with Business Insider at Operation Legio, a Norway-led multinational program that trains and equips Ukrainian forces, including at a purpose-built camp in Poland. He said he was learning NATO standards and tactics, combining Western practices with his existing battle-won skills before returning to Ukraine. Yankee said he uses the Stinger and Igla systems. Ukrainian soldiers have, at times since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, reported shortages of MANPADS missiles, saying those shortages allowed Russian forces to be bolder because they knew the Ukrainians couldn't try to stop as many of their attacks. But Ukraine's military has not suffered critical shortages of them the way it has with larger, surface-to-air missiles, and allies have announced new deliveries throughout the war. Not everything is consistent across the force though. Ukraine's military disseminates weapons and ammunition according to operational need, so one unit could be well supplied for critical missions while another comes up short.

item.title: Why is Meta calling out TikTok and YouTube with a flurry of new ads? It's a game of 'reputational jujitsu.'
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.29
Meta has a message for the public: Don't forget about TikTok and YouTube. After Meta's surprise settlement of up to $18 billion in a teen addiction lawsuit on Wednesday, the company is going on the offensive to shape the narrative with a series of ads on social media and in print newspapers. The advertisements, which Meta began running as a paid ad on its own platforms starting Wednesday, call for the two rival social media platforms to "join us in supporting teens." The ad links out to Meta's website announcing the settlement agreement. "We want to ensure teens benefit from this new industry standard, but we cannot do it alone," the blog post reads. "These protections will only be truly effective if we work with our peers — TikTok and YouTube — to put the same measures in place." It's true that Meta's Instagram and Facebook apps aren't the only social media apps under scrutiny for how teens use them. It's also true that Meta's messaging is a useful public relations strategy in the wake of a year fraught with legal battles. Mark Borkowski, a UK-based public-relations consultant, called Meta's advertisements an attempt at "reputational jujitsu." We asked PR pros, including Borkowski, what they made of Meta's latest move. A potential win-win for Meta "This is actually quite a clever move from Meta," Sam Gauchier, a brand and communications consultant, told Business Insider. "They've put TikTok and YouTube in a position where almost any response benefits them." If TikTok and YouTube follow suit, Meta can take credit for the public pressure it exerted on the two platforms, Gauchier said. If the platforms don't, Meta could benefit from appearing to be the good guy. "On paper, Meta's taking a 'shared responsibility' approach," comms consultant Michael Draznin said. "It's designed so Meta keeps a perceived industry leadership role either way." Motivation is in the eye of the beholder A key part of Meta's settlement agreement is implementing limits for how teens use apps like Instagram. Teens will be limited to 2 hours a day on Meta's apps, have access blocked at night, and get adjusted notifications. The apps will also add more parental controls. If teens are barred from using Instagram for hours on end, where will they go instead? Borkowski said that Meta has a "clear commercial interest in ensuring competitors inherit the same costs and constraints." Ad dollars could flow to TikTok and YouTube instead, Forrester principal analyst Kate Winick said. Meta said that teens account for less than 1% of its overall revenue and that, on average, US teens spend about 1 hour a day on Instagram. Meta will also pay an additional $5.3 billion — on top of the baseline $12.7 billion — if TikTok and YouTube agree to implement product changes for teens and make their own settlements of $5.3 billion each. Still, perception is the name of the game in PR. "Had they first taken accountability, shown real humility and started to make progress on their agreements, I think a stronger public push for the rest of the industry — not just singling out TikTok and YouTube — could have helped them rebuild a bit of trust with parents and the public," PR consultant Sarah Gooding said. "Instead, their letter came off as self-serving and insincere." It's going to be a marathon, not a sprint This isn't the first time Meta's reputation has been in hot water. It often takes time, and ultimately, substantial changes to shift public opinion about a brand. Borkowski said that "the proof will be in the pudding" in how much Facebook and Instagram actually change. Meta's strategy isn't a surefire path to redemption. "Could it backfire? Of course," Forrester's Winick said. "We're talking here about a company that has an immense amount of public sentiment already against it." That said, calling for industry changes — especially by putting rivals in the spotlight — could force social media companies to get on the same page. Winick said that Meta's biggest PR win will come "if they can make consumers stop and think and say, 'You know what? It's not just Instagram that's the problem.'"

item.title: Miss Virginia wins Miss USA 2026, becoming the first mother to take the crown
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.65
A new Miss USA has been crowned. Miss Virginia Justus Kelley was named the winner of the 75th Miss USA pageant on Thursday at the Adrienne Arsht Center for the Performing Arts in Miami, becoming Virginia's first winner since 1970. She was crowned by Miss USA 2025 Audrey Eckert. Kelley, 31, is a foster mom of two, a nonprofit founder, and a children's book author. She's also the first married woman, first mother, and first woman in her 30s to win Miss USA. The pageant only began allowing married women and mothers to compete in 2023, and 2024 was the first year that all women 18 and over were eligible. The previous cutoff age was 28. Kelley will represent the United States at the Miss Universe pageant in Puerto Rico in November. A historic pageant Fifty-one women competed for the Miss USA crown, taking part in swimsuit, evening gown, and interview rounds during the preliminary competition earlier this week in Miami. The top 20 competed in an onstage swimsuit round, while the top 10 also competed in an evening gown round. Those who made the top five were asked to answer a final question. For Kelley, that question was: "For 75 years, Miss USA has reflected the changing face of American women. If you become the 75th Miss USA, what do you hope your year will say about women in America today?" "We are here tonight celebrating the 75th anniversary of Miss USA, but we also have an opportunity to make history tonight," Kelley responded. "I'm 31 years old, I'm married to my college sweetheart of nine years, and we are proud foster parents of two adorable siblings that absolutely have my heart." "What my year as Miss USA would mean and look like is no longer questioning if we have to choose between our ambitious careers, our families, and our wildest dreams," she continued. "I'm standing on this stage embracing every part of who I am, and I believe that I can be your next Miss USA." She addressed her history-making win at a press conference after the pageant, saying it was "a huge honor." "I look at this like a responsibility to know that I was trusted to be the first," she said about being the first mother and married woman to win the title, adding that she "won't be the last." Kelley, a big fan of thrifting, also dressed in secondhand clothing for the pageant. "I had gone into the competition weekend wearing an all-thrifted wardrobe for each phase," she said. "I loved one of my first USA state pageants, walking in with a really special suit that I found in Goodwill, and as soon as I walked in, the judges said, 'Oh, you look stunning,' and I said, 'Thank you, $9.99 at Goodwill.'" Though she fell in love with the thrill of "the hunt" while thrifting, she said she realized it was a way to show people you "don't have to spend a million dollars" to be up on the pageant stage. A new category, a new judge This year, the Miss USA contestants were also judged on a brand-new category called "commercial appeal," which evaluated how they might attract sponsorships. "When it comes to commercial appeal, Miss USA shouldn't only look incredible wearing that crown, they should make the rest of the world want to work with the woman wearing it," Miss USA host and actor Ian Ziering said about the category during the live show. Ziering's co-host, Miss USA 1993 Kenya Moore, added that the pageant was "putting emphasis" on the winner's "ability to connect with a camera, with major brands, with beauty campaigns, and more" by adding the new criteria. "Commercial appeal" was judged based on a portfolio of non-pageant images that were submitted to this year's judges, who were present for all rounds of the competition, including the preliminary rounds. On Tuesday, Miss USA announced on its Instagram page that the audience would also have a say in the top 10 during the finals. "Your vote can have a real impact on who advances," the Instagram caption read. Fans watching from home were given a 12-minute window to cast their votes on a website. They were combined with the judges' scores, though it was unclear how much weight the fan votes held. By the end of the 12 minutes, Miss Montana was leading, but she didn't make it to the top 10. A new reign Miss USA has undergone several changes following a tumultuous few years. The pageant has had three different leaders since 2020 amid scandals that included rigging accusations, lawsuits, and queens relinquishing their crowns. This year's final show was originally supposed to air on The CW, but, as Business Insider first reported, the network dropped the Miss USA and Miss Teen USA finals from its schedule on August 20. "After careful consideration and conversations with the Miss USA Organization, The CW Network has decided to forego next week's broadcasts of the Miss USA and Miss Teen USA pageants," a spokesperson for the network said in a statement. In an Instagram story posted the same day, the Miss USA organization said it had identified a "contractual issue with our production arrangements that could not be resolved within the necessary timeframe." "Since then, our team has worked diligently to explore options that would allow us to continue with a live broadcast on The CW," it added. "Unfortunately, we were unable to reach mutually agreeable terms for this year's event." The final competition for both pageants was available to watch live on the Queen Beauty Network, a streaming service focused on the pageant industry, as it was in 2025.

item.title: I used Claude to solve a problem that data centers helped cause for my photography business. It's saved me thousands.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.61
This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Allen Cooley, photographer, director, and founder of Allen Cooley Photography, a commercial, beauty, and portrait studio based in Atlanta, Georgia. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. I've been working professionally as a photographer since about 2006, and for most of my career, I barely had to think about the price of hard drives. They were a basic cost of doing business. Now, I have to be strategic about every drive I buy. I started noticing a spike in hard drive prices toward the end of 2025. When I went back through my receipts, I found that I'd paid $400 for a 4-terabyte drive in 2022. Today, a comparable drive costs around $1,200. When I tallied up what I'd paid in 2025 for drives, it was over $20,000. That's why I stopped buying them entirely this year. Luckily, I've accumulated hundreds of hard drives over my career. Every new job, I'd simply buy a few more. So, 20 years and thousands of jobs later, I've become something of a hard-drive hoarder — and that habit is finally paying off. How I used AI to solve my problem Commercial photography requires a lot of storage. I usually need three or four portable drives for a job, and sometimes as many as five or six. And because a client might come back three years later to renew the assets, I have to keep the files long after a shoot is over. On a recent campaign that involved both video and still photography, buying that amount of new drives would have cost me $4,000 to $5,000. That was money I didn't want to spend. So, I used Claude to help me build a program that catalogs what's stored across my drives. Now, I can search for a file, find every drive that contains a copy, and figure out what I can safely delete to free up space. Instead of manually organizing hundreds of drives, I can essentially have a conversation with my archive. It's saved me days, if not weeks, worth of work. The irony isn't lost on me: I believe demand from the data centers powering AI is one reason storage has gotten so expensive, and then I turn around and use Claude to help me avoid spending thousands of dollars on new drives. I don't know how long I can avoid buying more drives How long I can keep avoiding new hard drives depends on how much work comes in. If I'm shooting only still photography, I can probably keep this going for a while. Video is different. I'm primarily hired to shoot video and stills together, and those jobs require so much storage that eventually I'll need more drives. Also, my business is down about 30% from its peak in 2023. Last year was particularly rough, and this year has been roughly flat compared with last year. I don't blame all of that on the advertising industry. Earlier in my career, I worked 10- or 13-hour days, answered emails at midnight and on weekends, and made myself extraordinarily accessible. Now I have two young daughters, and I'm more likely to spend my time at a soccer game or taking one of them somewhere. So when I look at that decline, I know some of it reflects a choice I've made to spend less time working. Still, I'm watching the industry closely. The cost of doing business has gone up while, in my experience, companies and agencies are reallocating their budgets or spending less on some traditional photography and advertising work. I also don't expect hard-drive prices simply to return to what I was used to paying. My guess is that eventually another manufacturer could step in to serve consumers who need cheaper storage. Until then, I'm going to keep being resourceful with what I have. If work picks up, I'll probably have to start buying drives again. If it doesn't, I can make these hundreds of old drives last a lot longer.

item.title: Texas Gov. Greg Abbott says China isn't behind the anti-data-center debate
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.65
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott isn't buying the Chinese psy-op theory. In a Fox News interview on Friday, the Texas governor pushed back against the notion that China is influencing the data center debate in the United States. "I haven't done it because of anything said by China, I've done it by listening to and working with constituents and seeing real problems they're facing in their communities," Abbott said of his recent moratorium on data center construction in Texas. "None of that has anything to do with China," he added. X said on Thursday that it uncovered a 200,000-strong Chinese bot farm and that a couple hundred of those accounts posted disparaging content about data centers "in a manner that could manipulate a legitimate debate about American AI and energy policy." The disclosure prompted a fresh wave of I-told-you-sos from the members of the tech industry, who say vast numbers of Americans are being duped by cheap, AI-produced Chinese propaganda, and that anti-data-center sentiment in the United States was, as a result, illegitimate. What X didn't disclose, said Darren Linvill, a researcher at Clemson University, is that many of those bots had zero engagement and were likely quickly deactivated by X before they could garner a following. On Fox News on Friday, host Will Cain raised X's disclosure and asked Abbott whether "real concerns" about data centers in the United States were "being driven by China." Abbott said that China is certainly attempting to influence data center sentiment, but added that his recent pivot against the compute factories was the result of legitimate concerns raised by Texans in communities where they're being built. "We know what the power demand was going to be for the state of Texas, which was five times the current ability to provide power," Abbot said. Once a staunch supporter of data center construction in Texas, Abbott has recently pivoted. Abbott introduced new standards for AI data center projects in Texas, including directing the state's utility commission and grid operator to protect residents from associated infrastructure costs. He also suggested a ban on data center development in rural Texas and said that projects must undergo an audit before moving forward. Abbott said earlier this month that his administration had halted some 1,800 AI data center projects in the state. AI data centers are an existential issue for AI companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and Microsoft, which rely on them to power their products. All across the country, however, Americans are rallying to fight against AI data centers, which can cost billions to build and span hundreds of acres. Many are concerned about how the sprawling facilities will affect the environment, utility prices, water resources, and noise levels. Some just don't like AI. The effectiveness of any Chinese campaign, which has been pushed by right-wing commentators, tech bros, and Shark Tank investor Kevin O'Leary, who is developing a data center in Utah, was disputed by several researchers who study misinformation campaigns. Samuel Woolley, a researcher at the University of Pittsburgh, said the only reports he's seen about Chinese AI data center propaganda have come directly from Big Tech companies, which he said have a "vested interest" in data center development in the United States. X is owned by Elon Musk, whose companies need AI data centers to survive. "We have to take research that's potentially political with a pinch of salt," he said.

item.title: I gave birth in both Puerto Rico and New York. There were several striking differences.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.02
When I moved from Brooklyn to Puerto Rico two years ago, with my husband and then-3-year-old son, we were firmly "one and done." Life with a toddler in New York City was too hard; we spent weekends at chain-link fence-enclosed playgrounds that were either shadeless and sweltering in the summer or freezing and depressing in the winter, struggled to find affordable childcare, and didn't have the village it takes to raise a kid. Moving to Puerto Rico changed our tune. The near-constant sunshine, excellent and affordable bilingual schools, easy access to beaches, and welcoming people who instantly became our community had us considering a second. Fast forward to April 2026, and we welcomed a baby girl in San Juan. My first child, now 5, was born in Southampton, New York, in August 2021. From the moment I started looking for an OB-GYN in San Juan, my experience being pregnant and giving birth in New York and Puerto Rico was strikingly different. Here are some of the biggest contrasts I noticed. In Puerto Rico, I had a hard time finding an OB-GYN open to new patients, and my appointments took forever I kept hearing from friends and fellow parents from my son's school that they were taking entire mornings or afternoons off work for standard doctor appointments — multi-hour waits were that common. I didn't believe it until I regularly found myself waiting three hours to see my obstetrician. In Southampton, I considered a 30-minute wait a bad day. A potential reason is Puerto Rico's severe doctor shortage. Lower reimbursement rates and wages than on the mainland have contributed to a long-running physician exodus, with many doctors leaving for better pay and working conditions. Those who remain can end up juggling a lot of patients and overscheduling themselves to keep up, leading to the long wait times I (and many others) experience. On top of that, it took me quite some time and a lot of searching to find an OB-GYN who was taking new patients in the first place. Things I took for granted in New York had to be purchased from the hospital pharmacy in Puerto Rico In Southampton, I just showed up to give birth — I didn't really have to think about pillows, epidurals, or diapers. In San Juan, patients must purchase these items from the on-site pharmacy. Pillows were $8 a pop, so I brought my own from home. I also brought my own blankets instead of buying them. I ended up buying a mandatory baby care kit (containing things like a T-shirt, swaddle blanket, and diapers) and a delivery kit (with a hairnet and scrubs for my husband) for $35 and $25, respectively. I was offered a bedpan for another $15 but declined. Had I had a boy I wanted circumcised, I would've had to purchase a circumcision tray for $100. I had to buy my epidural in advance — and getting it was a whole process In Southampton, I didn't fill out any forms before arriving at the hospital, asked for the epidural once I got there, and received it with no fuss. As far as I remember, it was fully covered by our insurance. In San Juan, I went through pre-admission, in which I filled out tons of paperwork a week before my due date. Part of pre-admission included purchasing an epidural. Many fellow moms who had given birth at the same hospital warned me that it sometimes runs out of epidurals, and to make sure they know I want one (and boy, did I want one!) well in advance. Thus, I purchased an epidural from the billing department for $1,000. I then had to make an appointment with a member of the hospital's anesthesia provider group, present them with the paid invoice, and answer dozens of questions related to my medical history. Once in labor, the anesthesiologist came to my bedside and gave me a presentation — including diagrams — explaining in great detail how the epidural works and asking for consent before administering it. My husband was well-fed and got a full bed to sleep in for a small extra fee In Southampton, I received a private room with an ensuite bathroom without having asked for it — lucky for me, the maternity ward at the hospital there doesn't have any other kind. My husband slept in a chair and complains about how uncomfortable it was to this day (I don't remember there being enough room for another bed). And while I received three full meals a day, my husband wasn't provided any food — he was begrudingly given a cup of coffee when asked. That said, on our last night at the hospital, we were provided a celebratory steak dinner for two, which was sweet. In San Juan, I was given a list of different hospital rooms to choose from during pre-admission, ranging from shared ones with limited visitor allowances to private suites with mini fridges and extra space. Each room cost a different amount — the nicer ones weren't covered by insurance and had to be prepaid — and came with different amenities. The one we chose, for example, came with full meals for the patient's partner, and so my husband received a tray of food every time I did. It was also spacious enough to allow him to sleep on a full bed, which cost an additional $10 per night and could be folded and tucked away when not in use. Ultimately, I had a positive experience giving birth in Puerto Rico It was certainly interesting to give birth in separate parts of the United States, and my experience is just my own. Every hospital and every birth experience is different, even if two people are having a baby in the same city. Despite long waits and some surprising quirks, my pregnancy care and delivery in Puerto Rico went smoothly, and I have no complaints.

item.title: 38 Best Restaurants in Los Angeles, According to a Longtime Local
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.89
Los Angeles doesn't have any one true center, and that's kind of the point. Neighborhoods here have grown up on their own terms: Chinatown, Sawtelle, Fairfax, Melrose Hill, DTLA, a strip mall in East Hollywood—each has quietly become its own destination. You don't come to LA for one great meal; you come for 50, scattered across a map that makes no sense and somehow works anyway. What ties it together isn't cuisine or price, it's specificity. A former cathedral turned into a modern American dining room. A Taiwanese night market condensed into a Silver Lake storefront. A taco truck at La Brea and Venice that's been perfecting one thing for decades. Every place on this list knows exactly what it is, and none of them are trying to be anywhere but exactly where they are. Looking for the best restaurants in LA? Here's where to start. Read our complete Los Angeles travel guide here, which includes: How we choose the best restaurants in Los Angeles Every restaurant on this list has been selected independently by Condé Nast Traveler editors and reviewed by a local contributor who has visited that restaurant. Our editors consider both high-end and affordable eateries, and weigh stand-out dishes, location, and service—as well as inclusivity and sustainability credentials. We update this list as new restaurants open and existing ones evolve. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Venice Price range: $$ Dish to order: Kanpachi al Pastor with pineapple butter Enrique Olvera's crew is doing coastal Mexican right on Abbot Kinney, and the room has that same effortless, sun-bleached confidence as the food; you half expect to see Baja out the window instead of Venice traffic. It doesn't try too hard, which is rare for this stretch of the block. This is Olvera's Pacific Coast fantasy—heirloom tortillas, uni-topped ceviche, prawns you'll think about for days—landed a few blocks from the boardwalk. Come for a date, a splurge, or anyone you're trying to impress with good taste. On the night we were there, we couldn’t help but notice that the staff was mostly Latinx, which means that every dish—Botanas, Aguachile, Flan de Naranja—was pronounced and explained without difficulty. Address: 1025 Abbot Kinney Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90291 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Melrose Hill Price range: $ Dish to order: The fried fish sandwich (beer-battered Pacific striped bass with American cheese, kewpie mayo, dill pickles) This is Anna Sonenshein and Niki Vahle's crowd, built over years of pop-ups before they had walls. The corner space is flooded with sunlight, all bone-colored tile and warm wood, with dry-aging fish hanging behind a porthole kitchen window that makes the whole room feel a little maritime. Sonenshein and Vahle went from a pandemic pop-up to California's 2026 Michelin Guide Most Promising Young Chef Award without losing the fried fish sandwich that built their following. It's the rare restaurant that's equally right for a solo lunch or a proper seafood dinner: unfussy, confident, exactly what it wants to be. Come dinner it shifts into something moodier, akin to a mysterious European wine bar run by seasoned fishmongers. It’s the kind of place Steve Zissou from The Life Aquatic might frequent. Address: 5035 Melrose Ave, Los Angeles, CA 90038 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Sawtelle Price range: $$ Dish to order: Steak tartare in a stone pot (yukhoedeopbap) Sawtelle finally got the swanky neighborhood bistro it's been missing, featuring dark wood, warm low light, and a full bar up front; it feels more Beverly Hills than strip mall. And this is a kitchen with serious pedigree; alumni of Marea, Daniel, French Laundry, and Jean-Georges putting real technique behind Korean comfort food that never feels precious. Come for the bluefin tuna bibimbap and stay for the hotteok à la mode, a caramelized cinnamon crepe with toasted sunflower and pumpkin seeds, and a scoop of vanilla ice cream. The service was warm and gracious from the start of our visit, our server walked us through the more unfamiliar dishes without a hint of condescension and steered us toward pours we wouldn't have picked ourselves, both wine and cocktail. The Mulberry already feels like a neighborhood staple. Address: 1800 Sawtelle Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90069 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Victor Heights, between Echo Park and Chinatown Price range: $$ Dish to order: Onion bread with liptauer spread Enter through Alpine Courtyard's brick-lined garden, past banana trees and bougainvillea, before finding Baby Bistro tucked into a restored bungalow with an Arts and Crafts feel and a lovely outdoor porch. It's the kind of low-key charm that makes you forget you're minutes from the 110. Chef Miles Thompson's résumé runs through Michael's and stages in Europe, and it shows in food that's confident enough to keep dishes down to two or three ingredients on the menu. Order the whole thing between two, as it's designed to be shared. It's a tiny, unshowy room doing some of the most thoughtful cooking in the city right now. Address: 1027 Alpine St, Building B, Los Angeles, CA 90012 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Beverlywood Price range: $$$ Dish to order: Spaghetti all'Assassina with spiny lobster, preserved tomato, and sea urchin This isn't a scene restaurant, it's a destination for people who already know who Marcus Jernmark (Stockholm's Restaurant Frantzén, Singapore's Zen) is, or are curious to find out. Jernmark is threading Nordic technique (fermenting, curing, importing his own cloudberries and vendace roe) through California's best small farms, and somehow it never feels like a gimmick. This is someone cooking exactly what he wants, named for his daughter, in a room built by his wife; it's personal in a way most $150 tasting menus aren't. For wine, skip the idea of a formal pairing and let the by-the-glass list do the work instead. The list is heavy on small California producers like Scar of the Sea and Littorai, and is built for grazing through courses rather than committing to one bottle. Address: 9575 West Pico Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90035 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Fairfax District Price range: $$ Dish to order: Oxtail Pepperpot Lucia is theatrical from the first step, more 1950s Havana glamour than anything Fairfax usually offers. The shell-domed booths and smoked kitchen window make it feel like a set piece as much as a restaurant. And they're doing something no one else in LA is: modern Afro-Caribbean food at a genuine fine-dining level, from jerk ribeye to saltfish croquettes, in a room built to feel transportive rather than themed. Order the Oxtail Old Fashioned, made with bourbon washed with oxtail, sweet potato, and sugar cane; it sounds like a stunt and turns out to be pretty great. Melina Meza's whole program leans on Caribbean rum, so it's worth asking your server for something rum-forward and off the printed list too. Address: 351 N Fairfax Ave, Los Angeles, CA 90036 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Chinatown Price range: $$ Dish to order: Ragù of wild mushroom with tofu gnudi, marinated eggplant, spring garlic. Mandarin Plaza doesn't scream "hot new restaurant,” and that suits locals just fine. To find the place you walk through this unassuming Chinatown courtyard and land in a room that's warm and considered; it feels like someone's love letter to the neighborhood. This is Anthony Wang cooking his own family's dinner table through a decade of fine-dining training: mapo tofu next to duck fat rice next to a $68 prix fixe that never feels precious. It's Chinese American food finally getting to be the whole story, instead of a footnote. Address: 978 N Broadway, Los Angeles, CA 90012 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: East Hollywood Price range: $$ Dish to order: Shawarma with laffa, tahini salad, chili crunch, and beet amba A younger sibling to Bestia and Bavel, this relaxed Middle Eastern restaurant located on Fountain Avenue makes a lively first impression. Inside, the space is what you might expect from a retro- modern Moroccan room, with saffron colored banquettes and a curvilinear bar. It all feels effortlessly glamorous and welcoming, which is exactly what you want from a Hollywood restaurant that doesn't take itself too seriously. Indeed, don’t be surprised to spot diners eating with their hands, dunking falafels in the tangy hummus without a care in the world. The kebabs and shawarma rule this place, and the generous portions come with the works: laffa, tahini salad, chill crunch, and beet amba. The roasted vegetables are having a moment here, and most dishes cost less than $26 yet still taste worthy of a special occasion. This is Middle Eastern cuisine that honors tradition while speaking fluent LA. Address: 4845 Fountain Ave, Los Angeles, CA 90029 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: South Central Price range: $ Dish to order: Rockfish ceviche The hottest seafood counter in town is a bright food kiosk inside LA's Mercado La Paloma, and is celebrated for its contemporary approach to Mexican seafood kissed by the flavors of the Yucatán. Chef Gilberto Cetina’s restaurant always has a line for pristine Santa Barbara sea urchin and bay scallops dressed in dots of avocado puree, and sharp ceviche de rockot (rockfish) over a swirl of salsa. Bring the heat up a notch with flavorful house salsas including a spicy salsa kut. Don’t miss the octopus-in-its-own-ink taco, a Yucatán favorite, and get it all on the eight-course tasting menu. —Bill Esparza Address: 3655 S Grand Ave c9, Los Angeles, CA 90007 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Downtown LA Price range: $$ Dish to order: Branzino with Thai broth You're dining inside a former cathedral, how's that for making an entrance? The space is ornate, and the architecture is timeless, so it immediately sets expectations sky-high—and somehow Redbird manages to meet them without feeling stuffy about it. At Redbird, Angeleno Chef Neal Fraser showcases modern American cuisine that is refined yet approachable and highlights the multicultural influences of his native city. Standout dishes like the branzino with Thai broth and ricotta cavatelli with morels and English peas show technique without showing off. An extensive cocktail menu by Tobin Shea features well-balanced, bespoke renditions of the classics. The Cardinal Punch, made with bourbon, amaro, roasted orange, clove, lemon and orange essence, is like a strong punch in the face, in a good way. Address: 114 E 2nd St, Los Angeles, CA 90012 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Silverlake Price range: $$ Dish to order: Pan con tomate with Beylik Farm momotaro tomatoes The 1,300-square-foot space perfectly captures Spanish conviviality with its warm, boisterous atmosphere. This 50-seat indoor-outdoor destination feels like you're being transported to the Mediterranean. Spanish-influenced small plates that are perfect for sharing and grazing. Everything is designed to pair with wine and encourage long conversations. Don't miss the pan con tomate with Beylik Farm momotaro tomatoes, Patatas Bravas with thrice-cooked Weiser Family Farms potatoes, or the Matrimonio featuring Siesta Co. anchovies. Natural wines, vermouth, and sherry curated by Beverage Director Pierluc Dallaire, alongside classic Spanish wines. The program showcases thoughtful Spanish selections that pair perfectly with the tapas. This is what Silver Lake dining is all about. Address: 1710 Silver Lake Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90026 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: West Hollywood Price range: $$$ Dish to order: The 25+ dish tasting menu with wine pairings Walking into Somni (meaning ‘dream,’ in Catalan) feels like entering a piece of performance art—or something you might have dreamed up. Everything from the lighting to the table settings is designed to prepare you for something extraordinary. It's theater, but the kind where you're genuinely excited for the show to start. This is molecular gastronomy—chef Aitor Zabala hails from Barcelona and had a stint at El Bulli—with a sense of humor and genuine deliciousness. Expect techniques you've never seen, presentations that defy physics, and flavors that somehow make perfect sense despite seeming impossible. The wine pairings are essential because they're not just matching flavors but creating narrative arcs that complement each course. Trust the sommeliers; they're orchestrating the entire experience. You're coming for dinner as entertainment: A multi-sensory experience that you'll be talking about for months. It's expensive, but so is a show at Walt Disney Concert Hall. Address: 9045 Nemo St, Los Angeles, CA 90069 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Eagle Rock Price range: $$ Dish to order: Cornbread and pork chops Chef Brian Dunsmoor's "American heritage cooking" philosophy is written all over the rustic-meets-refined interior; you can smell the wood smoke before you even sit down; the space feels like someone took a hunting lodge and gave it just enough polish to make city folks comfortable. The menu here changes often, but signature dishes like the cornbread, pork chops, and ribeye are highly praised. Everything tastes like it was cooked over an actual fire because it was. Lots of natural wines and American bottles that actually make sense with wood-fired anything. The food is damn delicious and represents something rare: American cooking that honors tradition, without getting trapped by it. Address: 3501 Eagle Rock Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90065 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Santa Monica Price range: $ Dish to order: The donut ice cream sandwich for dessert It's got that effortless beachside elegance that only works in Santa Monica—bright, airy, and sophisticated without trying too hard. The kind of place that makes you want to order a glass of wine at 3:00 p.m. and call it research. Italian classics executed with California sensibility—lighter, brighter, but still satisfying. The seafood dishes make the most of the proximity to the ocean. Italian wines that transport you somewhere warmer, plus cocktails that lean into the coastal location. The Negroni variations are particularly strong here. You're coming for Italian comfort food that doesn't leave you needing a nap. Perfect for long lunches that turn into early dinners. Address: 3150 Ocean Park Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90405 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Little Tokyo Price range: $$$ Dish to order: The 22-course tasting menu The entrance to this sushi spot is so understated you might walk past it, which is kind of the point. Inside, it's all clean lines and natural materials, the type of space that immediately puts you in a contemplative mood. And with only eight seats at the counter, this is an intimate experience where the food takes center stage. The experience might be entirely unique each time you go, but expect somewhere around 22 dishes, some hot and others cold, plus soup, outstanding nigiri, and a handful of desserts. The flavors are clean and the technique impeccable. The sake list is impressive so don’t pretend you know it all and simply let them guide you through prefectures and styles you've never tried. You're coming for an education in omakase, with expert execution, flawless presentation, and a price point to match. Address: 738 E 3rd St, Los Angeles, CA 90013 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Downtown LA Price range: $$ Dish to order: The nine-course tasting menu The format here is tasting menu only, and if you’ve been to Baroo in the past, don’t be surprised to discover some familiar dishes that harken back to their humble beginnings in an East Hollywood strip mall. Standout menu items may include a soy-braised black cod, but also, this is Korean cooking filtered through a deeply personal lens; expect fermentation, unusual textures, and flavors you can't quite put a finger on. On the whole, you're coming for a completely singular dining experience that couldn't exist anywhere else. The look is sleek and somewhat industrial (think concrete floors and bare walls) and the seats to be had are at the chef's counter, though there are a handful of tables for groups of diners. It's minimalist in the way that signals maximum focus, nothing here is accidental. Address: 905 E 2nd St #109, Los Angeles, CA 90012 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Thai Town Price range: $ Dish to order: Green curry with mussels It's a kitschy, homey Thai spot in the heart of Thai Town may be slightly no-frills, but it's got a lot of heart—not to mention heat. There are over 300 dishes on the Jitlada menu, so it definitely takes some navigating. One thing you can be sure of, though, is that pretty much all of them are scorchers. Highlights include the Southern dry curry, spicy eggplant, green curry with mussels, fried morning glories, and crispy catfish salad. The showstopper of all of them is the seabass, served whole and studded with loads of punchy ginger. You'll want something to cool your palate, like a sweet Thai tea or a Singha beer. That and a bowl of rice, which actually cools the palate. The staff is loving and attentive and will make you feel right at home. Owner Sarintip "Jazz" Singsanong is the Thai auntie you always wished you had. Address: 5233 Sunset Blvd., Los Angeles, CA 90027 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Melrose Price range: $$ Dish to order: Something from the mozzarella bar You've probably heard about famed California-cuisine pioneer Nancy Silverton's Michelin-starred Mozza—with to-die-for pasta and a mozzarella bar that's rich in burrata. The lighting is dim and moody. The crowd (and staff) is nicely dressed and perfectly coiffed. The music volume is just the right decibel of loud. It's buzzy, and there's a pulsating energy in the air; it might just be that everyone came in hungry, and expectations are high. It's unlikely that anyone walked off the street and got a table, and as such, it's clear that coming for a meal here is a bit of an event. There are plenty of Gen X-ers and Millennials, mostly in groups rather than on dates. (And few Gen Z-ers, with their parents probably footing the bill.) In addition to the pasta and antipasti, there's perfectly grilled and seasoned fish, and decadent desserts. This iconic LA restaurant shows no signs of slowing down. Address: 6602 Melrose Avenue, Los Angeles, CA 90038 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Pico-Robertson Price range: $ Dish to order: The signature Tokyo-style Neapolitan William Joo started Pizzeria Sei in 2022 out of a tiny Pico-Robertson storefront (a deceptively simple eight-seat counter, one wood-fired oven, barely a kitchen behind it) and it quickly became one of the hardest reservations on the Westside. That original spot didn't disappear; it's now Sei Pizza Bar, a neighborhood-focused offshoot still slinging takeout and dine-in. But the real destination is Joo's new flagship in Palms, a full sit-down space that opened in June 2026 with room to actually stretch: a bigger kitchen, a broader wine program, and two new pizza styles—a fried montanara and a thin, wafer-crisp Roman scrocchiarella—alongside the signature Tokyo-style Neapolitan. The soul of the place hasn't changed. Joo, who trained at Providence, Ronan, and Angelini Osteria before going out on his own, still treats every pie as a study in technique over trend—think long fermentation and a distinctive crimped crust that goes airy in the center and lightly charred at the edges. The beer selection is small but thoughtful and the natural wine list is built specifically not to compete with what's coming out of the oven. This is pizza that respects the craft, now just with the space to prove it.
