Address: 8781 W Pico Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90035 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Hollywood Price range: $$ Dish to order: Burgundy escargot in butter and garlic If you're hankering for a slice of Paris, this tiny Hollywood bistro fits the bill. Nary a table, the room features a row of stools by a ledge on the wall, and more stools at the marble topped bar. French music plays on the stereo and conversation is lively and unrestrained. Chef Ludo Lefebvre, who trained with Alain Passard, Pierre Gagnaire, Marc Meneau, does classic French food like few others in LA. The Burgundy escargot in butter and garlic is as delicious as you'd hope, as are the steak frites and the croque madame. This is a great spot if you're dining alone, or if you and a friend think nothing of waiting an hour for a seat at the bar. Because space is tight and seats are stools, it's also not the kind of place that you'll want to linger over coffee and dessert. However, as far as Hollywood restaurants go, it's fairly affordable, the food is tasty, and the vibe is magnifique. Address: 718 N Highland Ave, Los Angeles, CA 90038 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Downtown LA Price range: $$$ Dish to order: Nonna's Tagliatelle Bolgonese Rossblu is a wonderland of Danish interiors, burning wood smells, and food served on a patio that makes the city feel far, far away. The crowd is decidedly in-the-know professionals looking for the next "it" Italian spot in DTLA. Handmade pastas fill a menu that will make you leave the Angeleno diet in the rear-view (and feel a thousand-times better for it.) Order a sparkling red Lambrusco and enjoy a Californian take on Bolognese classics, including a lighter take on eggplant parm called Valbruna's Eggplant; Tortellini en Brodo; and, natch, Nonna's Tagliatelle Bolgonese. Be sure to stop by on weekends for their especially noteworthy brunch served on their sun soaked patio. Did we mention there was bocce ball? There was bocce ball. Address: 1124 San Julian St, Los Angeles, CA 90015 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: South La Brea Price range: $$ Dish to order: The kimchi fried rice with beef short rib They don’t make buildings like this anymore. Which is probably what Charlie Chaplin said when he walked in, looked up from the indoor fountain and into the clock tower of this grand 1920s-era space, and turned it into his studio. It’s soaring, airy and welcoming, and it seems everyone wants to eat here on Sunday. Not for the faint of heart, in the best way. The question is, how are you going to decide what to indulge in: the short rib breakfast burrito? The potato pancake with smoked salmon and kaluga caviar? The chorizo toast? The kimchi fried rice with beef short rib? It's by far the richest, boldest, most satisfying brunch on the West Coast from a chef committed to making you happy and full. You’re here to eat and eat well, so plan accordingly. Either plan a hike just afterward to recalibrate, or a nap. Address: 624 South La Brea Ave, Los Angeles, 90036 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Culver City Price range: $$ Dish to order: Chicken confit with heirloom grits and roasted strawberries It seems appropriate, perhaps unexpected, that Jordan Kahn's home inventive cooking in LA is tucked in a tiny, almost monastic all-day café. Unlike so many esoteric chef-y menus that leave longing for a slice on the way home, Kahn's layering of texture is as radical and abstract as it is comforting and totally satisfying—and built on the notion of a slow reveal. Chicken confit, for example, looks more like a heap at first glance, until you start digging your way through the heirloom grits and roasted strawberries. Definitely do not miss the Icelandic rye bread with cultured butter and preserves, or the rice porridge dish that's topped with caramelized broccoli, crispy puffed rice, and burnt onion. Trust me, just like the descriptors at a museum, the piece is more beautiful than words can describe. Address: 3578 Hayden Ave, Los Angeles, CA 90232 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Koreatown Price range: $$ Dish to order: The most authentic mole outside of Oaxaca The vibrant colors, sounds, and scents of Oaxaca come to life upon walking into Guelaguetza. On any given night, banda musicians will be strumming their instruments while you sip on lesser-known mezcals from the region alongside a mixed bag of Angelenos, including locals longing for an authentic taste of their mother country. From the outside, you might mistake Guelaguetza, which retrofitted a freestanding Chinese pagoda structure into a Oaxacan institution, for any number of Gringo-style Mexican restaurants on charmless boulevards serving obscenely large portions of nachos/enchiladas/burritos rendered interchangeable blanketed under molten cheddar. Of course, you'd be wrong. Instead, what you get from this James Beard Classics-award-winner is some of the most authentic memelas, tlayudas, and moles outside of Oaxaca. The space itself, which is filled with families and live music and a riot of pinks, turquoises and yellows, will make you forget you're on Olympic Boulevard. Address: 3014 W Olympic Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90006 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: La Brea Price range: $$ Dish to order: The best bun cha (Vietnamese cold noodle salad) you'll find in LA The vibe is light, bright, and casual. This is by far the best bun cha (Vietnamese cold noodle salad) you'll find in LA. Like the best street stalls in Hanoi, the pork has that wonderfully caramelized char that gives you that hit of umami—a perfect counterpoint to the bowl of cold rice noodles, lettuce, herbs, and pickles that's all topped with a sweet and savory fish sauce dressing. Other hits include the clam and green papaya salad, filet mignon pho, and bun bo hue, which is a lemongrass beef noodle soup with pork patty, beef shank and aromatics. There's a small list of microbrews and Vietnamese beers, as well as wines by the glass, and because it's Cali, kombucha on tap. Address: 145 N La Brea Ave, Los Angeles, CA 90036 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Palms Price range: $$$ Dish to order: The 13-course kaiseki menu The minimal wood-paneled interior replicates the style and tranquility of a Japanese ryokan in the middle of LA. The 13-course kaiseki menu, which is also available in a vegetarian version, is almost too beautiful to eat. Each dish is a love letter to the season. So while chef Niki Nakayama does stick to a mostly traditional format of kaiseki, but it also can't help but be informed by its native Californian ingredients. You'll be equally as impressed with her classic presentation of sashimi as you will the spaghettini with abalone, pickled cod roe, and Burgundian truffles. Wine and beverage pairings are thoughtful and graceful as the meal itself, absolutely worth splurging on. Pacing and service are thoughtful and deliberate throughout the three-hour experience. Address: 3455 Overland Ave, Los Angeles, CA 90034 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: West Adams Price range: $$ Dish to order: Fall-off-the-bone tender braised oxtail The decidedly warm and unfussy nature of Alta is apparent the second you walk in. Terracotta tiles and honeyed woods nod to the Spanish Revival homes that are iconic to the Mid City and West Adams area. There are 12 counter seats and built-in booths, giving the space the feeling of a classic diner that's been made modern. Out back, there’s a charming patio lit with string light. Corbin’s SoCal comfort food includes dishes inspired by his grandmother’s cooking, like fall-off-the-bone tender braised oxtail and a vegan version of collard greens; served whole and on the rib and made with smoked oil, they'll totally fool you into thinking there’s ham hock hidden somewhere in there. Don’t skip the coconut cake, either. This is a great spot for a meal with friends out on the patio, or a second or third date with someone you're into. It's just buttoned up enough to be impressive, but not so stuffy that you'd be uncomfortable having a good laugh—or stealing a kiss. Address: 5359 W Adams Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90016 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Mid-Wilshire, Beverly Hills, and Downtown Los Angeles Price range: $$$ Dish to order: The galbi marinade One of the larger, more polished KBBQ spots in LA, Genwa has a lively, communal atmosphere. One of the first things you'll notices is the aroma of delicious marinated meats sizzling over live fire. The place is no frills in terms of design, but it's clean, and really, really delicious. Genwa has one of the highest quality selections of meat in LA, and in a format that even KBBQ virgins can handle. The galbi marinade is on point as is the cornucopia of banchan. Skip the cocktails and go straight for the soju and a frosty mug of Hite. Genwa is great for a celebratory group gathering, or for bringing family members from out of town on their first KBBQ adventure. Address: 5115 Wilshire Blvd Ste A, Los Angeles, CA 90036 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Fairfax District Price range: $$ Dish to order: Sweet and sour Goan pork curry Badmaash is fronted by a neon sign with Hindi script and a street art wall reflective of the neighborhood. Although the interior is quite sparse, what the restaurant downplays in design it makes up for in big flavors. Brothers Nakul and Arjun Mahendro tap into their father Pawan’s recipes to showcase dishes from his home state of Punjab, India, as well as other regional specialties including sweet and sour Goan pork curry, Madras-style coconut curry clams, and dahi poori stuffed with chickpeas, mint, and tamarind. There are also plenty of modern, playful takes like chicken tikka poutine (which recalls the Mahendros' Toronto upbringing). An eclectic wine list plays the field, with selections ranging from sparkling Lambrusco from Italy's Emilia Romagna region to a crisp Portuguese whites. On the beer side, think radlers and rice ales, as well as Kingfisher, a classic Indian lager. Address: 418 N Fairfax Ave, Los Angeles, CA 90036 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Arts District, DTLA Price range: $ Dish to order: Gluten-free karaage Like most vendors at the ultra-hip ROW DTLA development, there's an effortlessly cool vibe at Pikunico, a fast-casual spot by Kuniko Yagi, formerly of Hinoki and the Bird and Sona. Yagi makes a delectable gluten-free karaage, a classic Japanese spin on fried chicken. Try it solo, or enjoy it like we do: as a sandwich, served on turmeric bread with spread, sprouts, and pickles. Speedy service caters to a grab-and-go lunchtime crowd. And if you’re not in the mood for fried chicken, you can always opt for her delicious homemade Japanese style curry, which also happens to be plant-based. Address: 767 S Alameda St Ste 122, Los Angeles, CA 90021 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Culver City Price range: $ Dish to order: Bean and cheese burritos Tito's is a no-frills, stripped down taco stand, and it cranks any hour its open (which is most of them). The energy is buzzing, and it's truly the intersection of LA. Look, this may not be the most authentic Mexican street food, but these hard shelled tacos and bean and cheese burritos are certainly the most authentic So-Cal interpretation of a taco—almost as iconic as a double-double from In-N-Out. Taste one and you'll see why; this is comfort food at its best. Staff are on rapid fire, so know your order by the time you get to the front of the line or prepare for some 'tude, and rightfully so. You definitely don't want to mess up the well-choreographed flow it takes to keep Tito's going. This is the ideal pre- or post-airport meal. Address: 11222 Washington Pl, Culver City, CA 90230 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Highland Park Price range: $$ Dish to order: Cappellacci Hippo is warm and inviting, with beautiful bow-truss ceilings and warm wood touches. There may be a wait for a table, but don’t sweat it. The meal—and wine!—are well worth it. California/Mediterranean dishes are the play here, with market produce taking various forms, including crudos, salads, housemate pastas, and gorgeous grilled meats and fish. It’s pretty difficult to place a bad order at Hippo, but whatever you do, don’t miss out on the cappellacci, a pasta from Emilia-Romagna that gets its name from its hat-like shape. Served stuffed like a chubby tortellini with seasonal squash and then topped with brown butter, amaretti, and sage, the dish warrants doing something novel for an LA restaurant: refusing to share. Rossoff is known for his impeccable palate, and the wine list at Hippo has some unique picks, including orange wines and selections from lesser-known regions like Lebanon and the Azores. Address: 5916 1/2 N Figueroa St, Los Angeles, CA 90042 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: West Adams, Highland Park, Ojai, Studio City Price range: $$ Dish to order: The fish sandwich Highly Likely has the bright, airy, vibrant vibes of some of Australia's best all-day cafés. You'll find all the California takes on breakfast classics on the menu here. All of them are great, but standouts include the fish sandwich, made with locally caught, tempura-battered fish and kosho tartar sauce, or the Japanese porridge bowl with housemade pickles, dashi broth, Okinawa potatoes, mushrooms, greens, miso granola, and a soft boiled egg. While Highly Likely is squarely a café, it also has wines that skew natural, as well as beer, kombucha, cider, and other brewed goodies. This spot is sunny and casual and just what you need no matter the occasion, whether that be a morning-after date or a decamp with colleagues. Address: 4310 W Jefferson Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90016 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Arts District, DTLA Price range: $$ Dish to order: Taiwanese steamed fish Kato, located in downtown LA's Row district, brings the energy of Jon Yao's Michelin-starred kitchen to an intimate dining experience. This tasting menu restaurant gracefully weaves together the flavors and ideas of Taiwan and Los Angeles, drawing heavily on Yao's Asian American nostalgia. The focus is on seafood, with dishes that constantly evolve while maintaining the restaurant's distinctive identity rooted in Taiwanese influences. Though the menu changes regularly, you'll consistently find preparations that showcase Yao's heritage and his interpretation of flavors from his upbringing. In 2019, Kato earned a Michelin star and established itself as one of LA's must-visit destinations for diners seeking an elevated exploration of Taiwanese American cuisine. Address: 777 S Alameda St Bldg 1, Suite 114, Los Angeles, CA 90021 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Fairfax Price range: $$ Dish to order: Spicy Chomper, a sausage-and-pepperoni pizza While its space is certainly design forward, there’s nothing overly fussy about Ronan. The industrial-modern details are warmed up by a stunning, live-edge communal table and the imported Neapolitan pizza oven. The space seats 70, and because of its reputation as a neighborhood restaurant, there's always a nice buzz going, especially out on the patio. When it comes to what you're getting, heed some words to the wise—two words: Spicy. Chomper. These sausage-and-pepperoni slices are a must. There's also a mind-blowing, anchovy-and-garlic laden caesar salad. The wine by the bottle list is extensive, with some excellent picks from Emilia-Romagna, Trentino, Adelaide, Austria and Georgia (the country!). If you’re drinking by the glass, you’re limited to only a couple of white or red choices. Address: 7315 Melrose Ave, Los Angeles, CA 90046 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Highland Park Price range: $$ Dish to order: The thousand layer pancake If you want to visit the Taipei night markets without having to hop on a plane, tuck into Joy, a charming, casual counter-service neighborhood spot helmed by Vivian Ku. Instead of street stalls, you’ll be greeted by the same cozy vibe you’ll find at Ku’s sister restaurant in Silver Lake, with warm brick walls, maple church pew benches, lots of natural light flowing in from the oversize windows, and delicate touches of Chinoiserie throughout. Don't miss the perfect thousand layer pancake (a flattened, savory croissant-type creation stuffed with cheese and egg), the slack season noodles with rich pork broth, or traditional Taiwanese shave ice with red beans, taro balls, boba, and grass jelly. Address: 5100 York Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90042 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Hollywood Price range: $$$ Dish to order: Rigatonicini with oxtail ragu It's hard not to feel like you've just walked into what promises to be the best night of your life—well, perhaps of your week–the moment you step inside Mother Wolf, set within the 1931 art deco Hollywood Citizen News building. The massive Romanesque dining room is ornate and opulent (yet keeps a safe distance from kitschy Vegas vibes), the crowd is boisterous, the food is delicious and plentiful. Chef Evan Funke brings his usual passion and fatto a mano (made by hand) dedication to Mother Wolf, his ode to Rome in the heart of Hollywood. The rigatonicini with oxtail ragu is nothing short of a revelation. Tender and flaky, the branzino is grilled to perfection. The pizza is airy, light and crispy. The torta di ricotta with figs and raspberries is to die for. Address: 1545 Wilcox Ave, Los Angeles, CA 90028 - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Hollywood Price range: $$$ Dish to order: The seasonal tasting menu One of LA's longest-standing fine dining restaurants reopened in May 2023 with a sophisticated new look, and a Green Michelin star to add to its accolades. Walking in from busy Melrose Ave, diners are gently transported to an underwater world thanks to hand-finished Venetian plaster walls in an ombre effect of tidal greens and blues, carpeting that evokes wave ripples, and a hand-blown glass installation (Sea Clouds by Jeremy Maxwell Wintrebert) above the dining room that could be reminiscent of air bubbles floating to the surface. An advocate of sustainable seafood, chef Michael Cimarusti's ever-evolving tasting menu proudly showcases the herbs and flowers his team grows in the rooftop garden, which is also home to two beehives. It's hard not to be impressed by the care and attention he puts into every dish, which might start with a include a vermilion rockfish with porcini and sea fennel or a delicate swordfish with lipstick pepper, charred vegetable jus, and mint. Address: 5955 Melrose Ave, Los Angeles, CA 90038

item.title: 39 Best Hotels in Tokyo for Ryokan Stays and High-Rise Views
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.89
The world's largest metropolis, Tokyo is renowned for its incredible restaurants, exceptional shopping, one-of-a-kind skyline, and plethora of gorgeous hotels. There are so many accommodation options in this glittering Japanese city—whether you're interested in a classic ryokan that lets you connect with the city's history, or a modern high-rise that feels straight out of a sci-fi movie. Whatever your budget, there are great finds to be scored, from over-the-top five-star properties for special occasions to affordable spots for solo travelers. Taking into account the vast scope of hotels and Airbnbs available—and the city’s soaring accommodation costs relative to its other offerings—choosing the best of the best is no easy feat. Some fan-favorite brands already have multiple Tokyo flagships in their portfolio, and new construction just keeps coming as the country continues to be a tourism darling. But fear not, we did the research for you. No matter what you're heading to the Japanese capital for—delicious food, a futuristic cityscape, pop-culture highlights, or historic landmarks—there's a wonderful property just waiting for you to check in. Read on for our editors' picks of the 39 best hotels in Tokyo right now. Top picks: - Best for families: Mimaru Tokyo Asakusa Station - Best for romance: The Peninsula Tokyo - Best value: Hamacho Hotel Tokyo - Best for views: Four Seasons Hotel Tokyo at Otemachi - Read Full ReviewYou notice the building before you notice the hotel: nine stories wrapped in corrugated, rust-colored balconies, each filled with greenery, giving the structure a scalloped silhouette. It's the work of architect Kiyoaki Takeda,who came up with the design by walking the neighborhood and cataloguing the potted plants that residents keep on sidewalks. In lieu of a lobby, there’s Pizza Tane, a 20-seat pizzeria, and you check in at a reception desk beside it. With just 14 rooms across nine floors—two per floor at most—there are few chances to cross paths with other guests. Every room gets floor-to-ceiling windows and plenty of natural light, custom-dyed paper lamps, and plants both on the balconies and inside—some of them donated by neighbors. Head up to the pocket-sized rooftop, where a few tables and chairs sit beside a surprisingly lush herb garden, where they’re even growing eggplants and olives. Guests can also use the mellow co-working space above Parklet for free. —Melinda Joe - Read Full ReviewTravelers come here for a boutique-scale Hyatt in the most useful location in Tokyo, newly reimagined by André Fu. When the hotel opened in 2002 on the lower floors of the Pacific Century Place office tower, its 57 rooms made it an outlier in a city that equates luxury with height. Yabu Pushelberg's original interiors worked around the architectural constraints—the massive columns among them. Two decades and a year-long renovation later, Fu treated the building's quirks as inspiration rather than a problem, turning structural necessity into a set piece. The effect is faintly Alice in Wonderland. Round the lobby, and a miniature rock garden appears through the window before the space opens onto a bright lounge under triple-height ceilings, where natural oak and grey marble meet washi panelling. It’s Art Deco filtered through a contemporary Japanese lens. The crowd is a mix of business travelers, families, and canoodling couples. —M.J. - Read Full ReviewDon’t expect a big five-star entrance where heels and voices ricochet off marble floors and up a grand staircase. The Four Seasons takes it down a notch at its location in quiet Marunouchi, where interiors stress a lounge-like atmosphere that's luxuriously intimate—the hotel has just 57 guest rooms. Sure, you'll catch a hint of polish here and there, but the overall vibe leans on cushy upholstered chairs, plush sofas, thick area rugs, and smooth wooden floors. The brand has little intention of matching Tokyo’s energy, and instead, lets it all go—this booking is about sitting back and relaxing. For a Four Seasons, the design feels cut from a more relaxed cloth—but with the same level of service. Other hotels will bring more flavor, but this property is at the very least consistent. —M.J. - Read Full ReviewThe Royal Park Hotel Ginza 6-chome is a playful newcomer to Tokyo's most polished shopping district. Bold, graphic interiors take cues from the Kabukiza Theater around the corner—muted greens and persimmon oranges drawn from the theater's iconic curtain carry through the 273 rooms—while the yellow-and-green entrance nods to the ginkgo trees lining the surrounding streets. Rooms deliver serious comfort at a price point well below Ginza's luxury competition, with exceptionally comfortable beds across all categories, including the cheerfully appointed suites. The real differentiator, though, is Kobikicho Club: an authentic "snack" bar hidden behind a mirrored door in the lobby, where the karaoke continues until 1 a.m. —M.J. - Read Full ReviewSet across the 38th to 43rd floors of the Akasaka Trust Tower, 1 Hotel Tokyo is a sanctuary above the city’s neon-lit chaos. This 211-key property combines the brand’s signature nature-inspired, calming interiors with subtle local touches, from revived Japanese crafts to upcycled moss artwork. Wellness is central, with in-room meditation beds, spa-like bathrooms featuring Bamford toiletries, and a plant-ringed indoor pool. The service style at 1 Hotel Tokyo is easygoing and never stuffy. It seems like team members, dressed in hip, minimalist Uniqlo-esque gear, have been briefed to keep their manner friendly, helpful, yet laid-back. Sustainability runs through every detail: no single-use plastics, recycled glassware, water-saving showers, and the 1 Less Thing initiative, which encourages guests to leave behind one item for charity. —Adam Turner - Read Full ReviewIn the early aughts the Park Hyatt Tokyo and its indelible Kenzo Tange–inspired tiered tower so inspired Sofia Coppola that she wrote an Oscar-winning screenplay around it. And that air of enchantment is as effervescent as ever after the hotel’s 19-month closure and thorough renovation. The graceful reinvention of this cinematic legend in Tokyo’s Shinjuku should please the most loyal of patrons, including Coppola, with its simultaneously reverent and refreshing take on masterful designer John Morford’s initial vision—a noticeable ramp up of contemporary residential-esque luxury that retains its subtly moody, slightly traditional, forest-imbued je ne sais quoi, not to mention many of the original artworks that now hang with new commissions from those same Japanese talents. —Kathryn Romeyn - Read Full ReviewThe lobby is a vast, bubble-era set piece—soaring double-height ceilings gridded with geometric lights, warm wood paneling, and a glowing staircase. At 3 p.m., pilots and cabin crew roll carry-ons past families at the check-in counter, business travelers make a beeline for the Club Lounge upstairs, and women linger over afternoon tea in the Atrium Lounge. Renovated rooms lean into subdued Japanese modernism: origami-inspired geometric patterns, custom carpets with a cherry blossom motif in grey with soft pink and indigo, and touches like a wine-colored cast-iron teapot or tea. The address is technically Akasaka, but you're on the Roppongi side of it, a short walk to that neighborhood's restaurants and bars, and around the corner from the US Embassy (should diplomatic business arise). Suntory Hall is two minutes away, which makes this the obvious choice on a concert night. Toranomon Hills and Azabudai Hills are both walkable for shopping and dining. —M.J. - Read Full ReviewAn event venue and planning service first and foremost, Trunk’s incredible popularity as a hotel venue has encouraged its founder to expand throughout Japan’s capital, first with Trunk(Hotel) Cat Street, set within the street- and outdoor-wear mecca just beyond the epicenter of roaring Shibuya, then Trunk(House)—an incredible, single-room hotel located along the cobblestone alleys of Kagurazaka. “Copenhagen-chic” is the prevailing style throughout the hotel. If you’re opting for an entry-level room, pay the extra coins for a view of the park instead of the backstreets—the square footage is limited; the views of the sky and trees lend a feeling of spaciousness. Take special note of the more colorful pieces of art on the various walls—all created by artists with special needs through a not-for-profit initiative and available for purchase. —Brandon Presser - Read Full ReviewAt the fresh-faced Hotel Groove, rooms come with colorful carpets and wooden paneling to elevate the offering beyond paint-by-numbers accommodations. It's a great pick for those who aim to spend minimal time in their rooms, but want comfortable—if predictable—digs for a good sleep at the end of a busy day. A boon to older travelers or those with special needs who need extra space to move around, Hotel Groove’s sleeping quarters—beyond the entry-level superior rooms—are reasonably large compared to other properties in this price range. Floor-to-ceiling windows create an even greater sense of grandeur, and decor is functional but with a few pops of texture and color to distance the vibe from cookie-cutter hotel blocks. At the higher end are suites designed by noted Japanese artists, not to mention some traditional-style accommodations (tatami and futons), too. Coin laundry is a surprise perk for long-staying travelers. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewThe Kitano is a family-run operation that takes service seriously, but lets personality shine through in the delivery. A minute's walk from Nagatacho station, the hotel sits in the heart of Chiyoda—Tokyo’s political nerve center and home to the National Diet Building and the Prime Minister's residence, with the leafy grounds of the Imperial Palace just beyond. The lobby is airy but warm, with sand-colored stone, natural wood, and modern Japanese details like latticed screens and gold-leaf artwork behind the reception desk. Upstairs, corridors wrap around a striking double-height bamboo atrium—real moso bamboo is planted at the building's core. The crowd skews well-traveled and unhurried, mostly European and Japanese guests, many with families in tow. The 70 rooms take their design cue from Japan's four seasons, each floor dressed in a different palette: cherry blossoms for spring, cool blue waves for summer, warm coppers with maple-leaf motifs for autumn, and snow rabbits for winter. But the property really distinguishes itself through its service. The meticulousness feels personal rather than corporate. Early arrivals are greeted with tea, and the head concierge, himself a former tea master, sets the tone for a team that takes hospitality seriously. —M.J. - Read Full ReviewThe world of Muji is headquartered at its Ginza shop, a venue of department store proportions cluttered in equal measures with objects and people. The lobby of the hotel doubles as the store's highest floor, where there's a charming café and communal reading room. From there, an elevator shuttles you up to your refreshingly spare room, perched in a distinctly quieter area of the building. The entry-level rooms at Muji Hotel come with only a whisper of design; everything's as simple as can be within the confines of minimal square footage. It's like Barbie's dream Tokyo apartment, where everything's teeny-tiny and low-slung—but the toilet still has all the expected bells and whistles. Come to live in the wonderful world of Muji for a few days. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewThis winner for small wallets outpaces its competitors in both the decor and wellness categories. Guests here are international travelers on the hunt for exceptional value sans credit card point deals. Most are first-time travelers to Japan who want to be in the center of the action and fully immerse themselves in the country's visual culture. This tower of tiny rooms is a smart place to start since the decor is inspired by traditional ryokans found mostly in rural Japan. The friendly staff will gladly guide you to the hundreds of restaurants littered throughout Shinjuku, Tokyo’s most electric, all-night neighborhood. Truly tight budgets shouldn’t wince at the hotel’s entry-level product—although the rooms are closet-sized, clever attention has been paid to maximizing the efficiency of the layout and giving the rooms a distinct Japanese touch: a low-slung bed, modern blond-wood furniture, and a small tatami area. Larger rooms allowed the designers more space to really go all-in on the ryokan sensibilities within the bones of a city-center business hotel. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewWhen it opened in 2005 in the Shiodome area, Conrad Tokyo neatly fit in among the pantheon of international luxury brands. More than two decades later, it remains as eye-catching as ever. Smack in the middle of the ground floor, a glossy red sculpture marks the moodily lit entrance and hasn’t lost its dramatic effect. Up on the 28th floor, a tall lobby soars with bold, black lines, which are warmed with light boxes dangling from the ceiling. It's a business hotel, but it's dressed to impress. The King Room Bay View hides nothing: windows do, in fact, frame Tokyo Bay. But even better, the panoramic view also includes the lush Hamariku Gardens, which flourish at the foot of the hotel. Modern furnishings borrow local motifs, whether they're the bedside lamps that vibe with Japanese lanterns or the Sumi-e cherry blossoms painted above the bed and woven across the floor’s lightly patterned carpet. —Keith Flanagan - Read Full ReviewFufu Tokyo Ginza is an urban oasis in every sense, with 34 suites boasting private gardens and natural hot spring baths sourced from Atami, all perched above the Ginza 1-chome intersection with direct metro access below. It's a rare property that makes the center of Tokyo feel genuinely still. The design is contemporary Japanese minimalism—shoji sliding doors, washi paper lamps, seasonal ikebana, a green tea–inspired scent threading through the common spaces—but with enough warmth to keep things from feeling austere. The first urban property from Fufu Japan, a brand known for intimate onsen retreats in quieter corners of the country, the Tokyo outpost, which opened in November 2025 inside the Hulic Ginza Building, takes the brand's signature stillness and drops it into one of the most electric neighborhoods in the country. Step onto your leafy private balcony and you're gazing out over Chuo-dori, the glittering boulevard that transforms into a car-free pedestrian paradise on weekends. Located in Ginza—Tokyo's answer to Fifth Avenue, and then some—the area surrounding the hotel is lined with flagship fashion houses, jewelers, and upscale dining options. —M.J. - Read Full ReviewAccor's first luxury hotel in Tokyo, the Fairmont is a serene perch above Tokyo Bay where warm tones, plush textiles, and wide, softly lit corridors create a soothing, sophisticated atmosphere. Thoughtful Japanese art and design details surface throughout, right down to the delicate botanical paper-cut installations in the elevators. Fairmont's first foray into Japan takes up floors 35 to 43 of the Maki & Associates–designed Blue Front Shibaura South Tower. With 217 rooms, the shining stars of the property are the Fairmont Gold Suites, which occupy the southwest corners of each guest room floor. From the living room, views sweep across Tokyo Bay to the east and out over the city's sprawl to the south and west, with Tokyo Tower front and center and, on a clear day, Mount Fuji in the distance. The bedrooms face the tower directly, and waking up to raise the blackout shades on that view is a delight. —M.J. - Read Full ReviewHoshinoya Tokyo is a serious, serene vertical ryokan hidden within the city’s corporate heart. Behind a massive cypress door, tatami floors, hushed rituals, and a deep sense of reverence replace Tokyo’s neon dazzle. Rooms are minimalist sanctuaries dressed in washi screens and ikebana florals and come with custom kimonos by designer Jotaro Saito, while communal lounges on every floor encourage slow tea sipping and quiet reflection. Dining is traditional and guest-exclusive, from restorative Japanese bento breakfasts to multi-course dinners that resurrect fading regional recipes. The highlight is the rooftop onsen (Tokyo’s rare true hot spring) fed by mineral-rich waters from nearly 5,000 feet underground. Service is exemplary omotenashi: graceful, intuitive, and—if you follow all the rules—warm. It’s not about views but instead, stillness, ritual, and retreat. An immersion into old Japan, improbably stacked 17 stories high. —Nicole Trilivas - Read Full ReviewIn Tokyo's Takanawa Gateway City—a well-connected development in Minato City—this new JW Marriott outpost is a surprisingly tranquil sanctuary for busy travelers. For JW Marriott fans, and particularly those who care about their Marriott Bonvoy points, the brand's entry into Japan is an exciting one. In keeping with the brand's global ethos, they focus on pure comfort, slinky settings, and at-your-service attendance, with the privacy and serenity that most Tokyo visitors will crave after soaking up the city's energy. Moody, low-lit hallways guide visitors to the rooms, the defining feature of which is a huge window looking out upon the sprawl of the city. Wood paneling from the doors to the armoire to the ceiling lends a warmth to the space, punctuated by glossy acrylic and velvet in tones of gray. The room has a global feel—nothing too distinctly Tokyo—though the chance to see Mount Fuji peeking through the clouds from some rooms will certainly ground you in the destination. The breakfast buffet, lavish in volume but also variety, should be your first sign that you will eat well here. Come dinner, Kakō offers seasonal ingredients in a tasting menu format, while Saki is an eight-seat experience led by Michelin-starred chefs. —Megan Spurrell - Read Full ReviewFor a serene walk through history, Hotel Gajoen Tokyo is an artful sanctuary that embodies local culture at every turn with over 2,500 pieces of Japanese art. You’ll embark on a sensorial journey from the moment you enter—think murals for your eyes, waterfalls for your ears, and culinary wonders for your taste buds. The peaceful serenity of the rest of the hotel extends into its guest rooms, which offer an oasis from city life. The rooms are more muted in color, allowing for a calming transition into me time. A pleasant surprise is the in-room steam sauna, which is offered in all accommodations, regardless of room type. Coupled with the whirlpool bath, city views, and spacious square footage, you’ll be whisked away into private luxury. With seven restaurants and a pastry shop, there is no shortage of choice for food here—traditional Japanese, Chinese, New American, and Italian included. It's located in Meguro City, a bit less touristy of an area that allows for a more local experience. And as long as you’re up for about a 10-minute walk uphill to the subway, it’s a quick train ride to most other parts of the city. —Taylor Mead - Read Full ReviewRising to the upper floors of the Nihonbashi Mitsui Tower, the 38th-floor lobby of the Mandarin Oriental is like a gallery to the capital’s best angles. It’s the same in the rooms: No matter the category, the view is paramount from your tranquil retreat in the sky, as the frenetic financial district eases down below and, on cloudless days, Mount Fuji glistens in the distance. Comfort is prime here, too. Beds are as supple as the sheets are slippery. And if you can’t find a perfect pillow on the extensive “pillow menu,” it’s not the feathers—it’s you. Room service can get expensive, but the menu itself is so long and varied (from macaroni and cheese to okayo don) that it’s worth a look. And yet, there are so many dining options on the property—from an actual pizza bar to haute Cantonese to a silver-lined French restaurant—that every in-house venue deserves a gander. For example, Sushi Shin by Miyakawa is perhaps the city’s most atmospheric sushi restaurant: A nine-seat L-shaped counter, made from a 350-year-old cypress tree, sits next to a floor-to-ceiling window that perfectly frames Tokyo Skytree. Dip sushi as the sun dips, too, and the city lights up by nightfall. If you care to step outside, the location is convenient. It’s just around the corner from famous kimono shops and department stores, and Ginza is a short stroll away. —K.F. - Read Full ReviewA ryokan-style hotel complete with mineral-rich onsen water set in the heart of Tokyo’s coolest neighborhood—need we say more? We will. Like the quaint Japanese inns found deep in the countryside, Yuen Bettei Daita leans hard into traditional wellness, and has become a favorite among international visitors and staycationing Tokyoites alike. The multi-course menus in the restaurant Tsukikage pay tribute to a panoply of seasonal ingredients. Plus, you're smack dab in the middle of Shimokitazawa, largely considered to be Tokyo’s most fun cluster of city blocks and a global hub of streetwear fashion. Expect a scatter of traditional and modern construction replete with chic espresso shops, vintage clothing stores, and plenty of curry parlors and ramen joints. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewOnly a few blocks away from Omotesando-dori, the city’s most coveted thoroughfare of luxury retail, the Aoyama Grand attracts a mod mix of young professionals in its various international dining venues. Upstairs, hotel guests are an assortment of domestic and international travelers who prefer more intimate digs in a trendy ‘hood to taking up residence in one of the more corporate quarters of the city. The loft-style rooms don’t shy away from bold furniture, light fixtures, and wall art. And out the floor-to-ceiling windows are views of one of the coolest neighborhoods in the world. Inside tip: Skip the six interior rooms, which face a light well rather than having windows looking out over the urban sprawl. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewExpect nothing but ultra-polished old-school Japanese hospitality. Retro luxury is alive and well at the Okura, and for a fraction of the cost of some of the city’s other high-end players. The mid-mod lobby is practically a museum dedicated to Japan’s post-war flourish in the 1960s, when the whole world witnessed the country’s ascent to the modern global stage. Now the Okura’s at it again with a phalanx of next-gen businessmen lounging on the lobby’s Eames- and Juhl-inspired furniture. Even if you’re not staying on-property, it’s worth checking out the hotel's diverse eating options from hallowed kaiseki multi-course meals to more playful teppanyaki options. Fun fact: the property lays claim to inventing teppanyaki—hot plate cooking with a pinch of chef acrobatics designed to delight visiting dignitaries during the 1964 Olympics. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewSmack dab in the middle of Shibuya’s Dogenzaka area, IHG’s Hotel Indigo Tokyo Shibuya is changing the face of the neighborhood from seedy hotels to trendier digs. Design details are a bit prescriptive, but no one seems to mind as the location is unbeatable and the cleanliness of the brand-new build earns an A+ from us. You can’t go wrong with any of the rooms here—they’re all lofted high enough in their tower to offer views of Shibuya and beyond below. Take your pick of your favorite angle: direct eyeshot over the Scramble Crossing, the busiest pedestrian crossing in the world; Mount Fuji in the distance, visible on a clear day; or simply the endless sprawl of the metropolis. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewA budget-friendly hotel disguised as a luxury stay, the Gate Hotel’s glass tower rises up over a bustling intersection in Ginza, offering those quintessential Lost in Translation views. The first thing you’ll notice when you step off the elevator is a lively Champagne bar inhabiting the lounge-style lobby on the building’s fourth floor, filled with a mix of hotel guests and local business folk enjoying an after-work coupe. The front desk around the corner may seem like an afterthought, but au contraire—service is as polished and capable as any of the city’s five-star offerings. Spic and span rooms come with a brightly colored accent pillow to enliven otherwise dim, nightlife-inspired decor. Light sleepers may want to request to avoid rooms facing the train tracks—though the double-glazed windows do an effective job of blocking out noise. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewA Tetris tower with lush greenery sprouting off the balconies, Hamacho is a plot twist for those who think cheap hotels in Tokyo are relegated to capsules and by-the-hour hotels. This new multi-use concept, proffering teensy hotel rooms and long-term living spaces, is breathing new life into an old-town neighborhood with more wooden roofs than steel-and-glass buildings. If you're opting for the smallest rooms, make sure you don't bring a large suitcase—there won't be space—but no one does chic efficiency better than Tokyoites. Spend a little more for a larger room and you'll get a shrub-lined terrace, city views, and plenty of sunlight. Clean design and perfect housekeeping keep the rooms feeling spare but luxe. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewLike the bulk of luxury brand hotels in Tokyo, the 164-room Andaz Tokyo commands a series of floors at the top of a shared skyscraper—except, unlike most skyscrapers, Toranomon Hills happens to be among the tallest. Check-in reflects this higher perspective as guests arrive on the 51st-floor Andaz Lounge. Instead of starting the process behind a counter, check-in happens in the lounge, offering a relaxed introduction that's more like a casual conversation than a stiff transaction. Blessed with edgy architecture, the rooms take shape along the skyscraper's rounded corner. The result? A panorama of floor-to-ceiling windows curving like an IMAX screen around the room’s focal point. Midcentury-inspired interiors boast moss-green carpeting, maroon leather chairs, white walls, and handsome walnut or color-blocked surfaces. —K.F. - Read Full ReviewPocketed between Shibuya and Harajuku, just off of the ultra-trendy Cat Street, Trunk(Hotel) is marked by a façade of glass, black steel, and stone, softened by the timber decks and ferns that line the wraparound terraces on each of the four floors. It’s a showstopper, for sure, but one that feels part of the neighborhood. Inside, a subdued vibe takes over common areas—all of which feel like a lounge, equally suited for a MacBook, a latte, or a cocktail. The Living Suite includes a lofted space for additional guests (up to four), while the interiors are all crafted by Japanese designers. There are only 15 rooms spread across two buildings here—meaning there’s more to this place than beds: The lobby café and bar slings just as many lattes as cocktails, and the main restaurant, Trunk(Kitchen), brings local flavor to international staples (burrata, for example, from a shop in Shibuya). —K.F. - Read Full ReviewThere’s an unspoken playbook for most luxury hotels in Tokyo: loft your rooms at the top of an office tower so guests can have unobstructed views of the sprawling city. The OMO5 Tokyo Gotanda has done exactly that, only its entry-level pricing is about one-sixth of the cost of a stay at one of Tokyo’s international luxury brands. Of course, the rooms are smaller and have fewer of the fancy bells and whistles, but you’ll still find eager service here, not to mention bold, big swings with the expressive decor. Also, while many of the city’s luxury hotels are relegated to more corporate neighborhoods, this property has sprouted up on the cooler west side of the city, only a stone’s throw from trending hubs like Meguro. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewPart of Hyatt’s Unbound Collection, the Hotel Toranomon Hills has the business traveler in mind, but that shouldn’t deter leisure tourists either. One of the biggest selling points is a dedicated hangout area modeled after an airport lounge. There’s plenty of complimentary coffee and snacks, but the best part is the resting room and shower facilities. If you arrive before check-in (or have a late departing flight), you can wash off the jet lag upon landing and start your day. Like flipping through a Danish design magazine, the hotel’s decor is pared back without being overly spartan. We do, however, recommend upgrading to a premium room—it’s worth the extra spend to indulge in a little more space, better views, and a few extra Scandi-style flourishes that’ll go great with the view of Tokyo Tower outside. —B.P. and T.M. - Read Full ReviewReady for some numbers? This five-star hotel commands the top nine floors of one of Tokyo's tallest buildings—and windows place you at eye-level with Tokyo’s second-tallest structure, Tokyo Tower. Inside is no less humble, and the restaurants and bars feel rich and handsome with dark finishes, plush chairs, and slick sights. There are two main views on offer—the Tokyo Tower view and the Mount Fuji view. Generally, Japanese guests want Fuji (really only visible on clear days with low humidity—it’s far), while visitors are keen to glimpse the city’s orange version of the Eiffel Tower (a few feet taller than the real thing, for those who are keeping track). Suites are double the size of the rooms and feel like a proper apartment in the sky; a great choice if you’re planning on sticking around for a while. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewThe collection of Mitsui Garden Hotels has a strong reputation in Japan for providing quality accommodations at prices that don’t break the bank—the Ginza-Gochome property earns bonus points for its great location and Edo-style baths inside. Most Tokyo hotels cater to a mix of business and leisure travelers—there are mostly tourists here; savvy visitors who like their lodging to have a distinct sense of place. Although most of the furniture is agnostic in style, the old-school nods to Japan feel welcome and never gaudy. Mitsui Gardens is a budget-friendly concept from Mitsui Fudosan, a well-established Japanese hospitality brand that has a keen eye for serving luxury travelers as well. Standard rooms have limited views from the windows, but the trade-off is the quietness in an otherwise busy neighborhood. Go for the Deluxe Twin room, which fuses East and West design—think a quaint tatami sitting area, low-slung beds, but a souped-up entertainment center and ultra-modern bathrooms. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewWith the opening of the Otemachi sister hotel to the longstanding Marunouchi property, the Four Seasons has reestablished itself as a major force to be reckoned with when choosing among the finest places to stay around town. Otemachi sits more in a financial hub than a proper neighborhood, but it’s a stone’s throw from bustling Ginza and temple-ridden Asakusa—and the gridded streets make it abundantly easy to navigate on foot. In the same space, find guests and ladies who lunch, sipping high tea, dining on Instagrammable snacks, and enjoying the unobstructed views of Mount Fuji across the lush gardens down below. Head farther into the property to find a passageway to some of the best dining in the city, and upstairs for rooms so plush—yet also somehow embracing Japanese austerity—that you’ll never want to leave. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewPaper walls, tatami floors, and oversized bathing suites are par for the course in this ryokan in the heart of the city; a fun way to combine the tenets of Japanese hospitality with the spirit of a city hotel—one that doesn’t hold you captive, but lets you explore your surrounds guilt-free, then retreat to your throwback digs. The clever idea: to take a few low-floor rooms in an aging hotel and completely reimagine them as a traditional Japanese inn similar to one that you’d usually find on the hillside of a quaint rural village. The secret perk of staying in one of the 16 Hanakohro rooms is unfettered access to the campus’s collection of executive lounges—one in all three of the towers—each filled with coffee bars, a snack carousel, and plenty of private seating nooks. Within the confines of the ryokan is a fourth lounge where guests can enjoy their oversized Japanese breakfasts and sample complimentary spirits—sake and umeshu—in the early evenings. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewThe decadent Bulgari Hotel Tokyo crowns the cloud-brushing apex of the 45-story Tokyo Midtown Yaesu tower, just opposite Tokyo Station. Against a backdrop of sultry black granite with pops of jewel tones, the deluxe hotel smoothly blends contemporary Italian design with Japanese craftsmanship and a glamorous sprinkling of Bulgari heritage. Picture hand-blown Murano lights suspended from temple-like wood ceilings; traditional Japanese textile motifs recreated in Venetian mosaic tiling; and, adorning the walls, photographs of celebrities visiting the Roman flagship in the 1950s, plus vintage advertising and jewelry sketches. The 98 guest rooms balance Japanese touches (woven bamboo wall vases, modern sliding screens, gold-flecked bed throws by Kyoto kimono textile masters Hosoo) with warm saffron fabric headboards, natural elm wood, and sexy black-granite bathrooms. —Danielle Demetriou - Read Full ReviewMimaru has established itself as the indispensable apartment-hotel brand that’s perfect for vacationing families or for those with dietary restrictions who need to prepare some of their own meals. Consider this entry on our list as an endorsement of all of the Mimaru locations across Japan’s capital—pick the location that most suits your travel tastes, be it this location among Tokyo’s old temples, Ginza’s fashionable department stores, or bustling Shinjuku. Tasteful Tokyo apartment decor prioritizes streamlined design, but this hotel is located on the doorstep of Tokyo’s most popular temple, Senso-ji, and its delightful shopping street, Nakamise-dori, which features snack and souvenir stalls that date back over a century. And with multiple bedrooms and bunk beds, there are plenty of configurations for visiting families or large groups of friends. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewOne of Tokyo’s most iconic pieces of art is not in fact in one of its museums—it’s in the lobby of the Peninsula Tokyo. The Lying Dragon Gate (which looks like a giant wooden eye) attracts legions of curious outsiders who sneak in for a glance. And when they walk through the lobby, they are immediately ensconced in the coziness of the entry’s dark wood and heavy fabrics. Rather than splurging on a suite upgrade at a middle-tier hotel, it’s worth eking into the entry-level rooms here, which never skimp on the Peninsula’s signature luxuries: plush interiors, lavish toiletries, and, most importantly, plenty of space. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewJapan’s capital is many things—sprawling, neon-lit, nocturnal—but one word not often used to describe it is relaxing. Something guests will forget about while floating 34 floors above ground, inhaling and exhaling with a meditation teacher in a white space, distracted only by vivid sunset views. Aman has, of course, long been a byword for a certain kind of crisp, zen wellness. The lobby still turns heads, with its towering ceiling, abstract blooms, and kimono-clad musician plucking the strings of a koto. The bedrooms always seem more akin to mindfulness spaces, with their aromatic hinoki wood, sliding screens, and staggered levels. The food and the service are impeccable—of course they are—but the spa is the real scene-stealer, a place of complete sensory purity that hovers unperturbed over the fizzing city. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewIt’s not easy being the Aman's new little sister, whose minimalist temples set the benchmark for escapist luxury. Yet when Janu Tokyo, the inaugural flagship, launched in Japan last year, it quickly made its mark with a playful, sociable spirit and—something of an anomaly in the Aman cosmos—splashes of color in the interior. The hotel, whose name means “soul” in Sanskrit, rises up to the 13th floor of a tower in the heart of Azabudai Hills, a major new urban development in Tokyo. It’s home to a culinary constellation of food and drink venues, including relaxed Janu Mercato, an Italian restaurant, and intimate sushi spot Iigura. A vast, four-level spa spans over 43,000 square feet, and 122 guest rooms with serenely minimalist decor hint at Aman's DNA. —D.D. - Read Full ReviewThe legendary property, so named as it’s the closest hotel to the Imperial Palace, lures wealthy Japanese guests with its demure luxury gloss; now, international travelers have gotten wise and are starting to book in as well. Back in the early 2010s, the Palace Hotel doubled down on its commitment to quality and completely demolished its historical property that was erected in the early 1960s, in time for the first Tokyo Olympics. A glimmering new luxury stay was born anew, with all the contemporary touches but maintaining its sedate charm born 50 years prior. When you think of modern Japanese design, it’s not these rooms—the decor at the Palace, while less than two decades old, feels like a retro nod to an earlier vocabulary of modernity. Muted beige and a palette of floral colors are a subtle nod to the ample views of the Imperial Gardens below. —B.P. FAQ: What is the best area of Tokyo to stay in? Pairing a luxury hotel with the right neighborhood can be a conundrum in Tokyo, where many modern high-end properties occupy the upper floors of skyscrapers in business districts—a model the Park Hyatt Tokyo popularized in Nishi-Shinjuku in the 1990s, since replicated across the city's corporate precincts. Consider Central Tokyo like a clock face along the JR Yamanote loop. For a fashion-forward base, look to the lower-left quadrant—around seven to nine o'clock—near Shibuya, including Jingumae, Daikanyama, Nakameguro, and Shimokitazawa. If history is more your speed, aim for two o'clock: Asakusa and the surrounding Shitamachi ("lower town") districts, which retain an older Edo-era street sensibility. Around three o'clock, Ginza and Marunouchi combine polished shopping with a strong cluster of luxury hotels, while nearby Toranomon has emerged as an enclave of design-driven high-rises. For serious food lovers, geography matters. The Ginza area places you within walking distance of many of the city's most acclaimed restaurants and cocktail bars. Shibuya and Shinjuku offer broader hotel options with easy access to lively dining districts, from yokocho alleys to natural wine spots in Ebisu, Daikanyama, and Nakameguro. For a more atmospheric base, Asakusa puts you close to emerging scenes in Kuramae and Kiyosumi-Shirakawa, known for specialty coffee and small independent eateries. How long should you stay in Tokyo? Four nights is the minimum needed to move beyond Tokyo's headline sights and begin to grasp its scale and texture. The city is made for unhurried wandering—lingering over dinner, ducking into a tiny specialty shop, spending an afternoon in a single neighborhood. Up close, it feels less like a sprawling metropolis than a patchwork of distinct enclaves. If Tokyo is part of your broader Japan itinerary, consider adding another day or two at the end of your trip. By then, you'll be more attuned to the country's rhythms and better equipped to go deeper, whether that means drinking at an eight-seater bar, finding time for proper omiyage (souvenir) shopping, or revisiting an area that deserves a second look. How do you get around Tokyo? A map of Tokyo’s metro system may seem intimidating with its dozens of interconnected subway lines—some managed by the government, others privately operated—but traveling aboard is now a breeze with the tap-to-use Suica and Pasmo cards available on your smartphone. English signage is abundant and trains are virtually always on time. For taxis between inconvenient points, or for when your luggage becomes too cumbersome (shopping is an inevitability in Japan!), there are ranks at all of the city’s major train stations, and your hotel can easily hail you a car—plus, they all accept credit cards. App users should prioritize GO for a ride-share vehicle. Note that passengers should never touch a taxi’s door; your driver will push a trigger that both releases and closes the hinges as you enter and exit. When is the best time to visit Tokyo? Tokyo’s busiest season is late March to early April, when cherry blossoms draw visitors from around the world and hotel rates can double. Book hotels at least four to six months in advance—earlier for top properties. Golden Week (late April–early May) and Obon (mid-August) also see heavy domestic travel, while Lunar New Year (late January–February) brings increased international traffic. Autumn foliage in November is another high-demand period. For better value, consider February or early December, when rates soften and the city feels calmer. Note that many independent restaurants close from around December 28 to January 5, though hotels often host festive New Year programming. How do you travel with luggage in Tokyo? Traveling with luggage in Japan is remarkably easy. Most hotels can arrange door-to-door luggage delivery (takkyubin), sending suitcases to your next hotel or the airport, often overnight. Forms are available at the front desk, and the service is efficient, reliable, and reasonably priced—allowing you to navigate trains comfortably and considerately. If you plan on taking the Shinkansen with very large bags (over 63 inches total dimensions), you must reserve a seat with access to the rear luggage space when booking. The reservation is free, but space is limited; boarding without one may result in a 1,000 yen (around $6) fee. How we choose the best hotels in Tokyo Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. item.title: The Timeless Boot That Deserves a Spot in Your Suitcase This Fall
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.62
What exactly is a Chelsea boot, you ask? Well, it’s the little ankle boot that seems to have figured out all of our travel wardrobes: sleek enough for dinner, sturdy enough for a day of wandering, and easy enough to slip on when you’re running through the airport. With its close-cut shape, elastic side panels, and pull-on design, these stylish booties look equally at home on a rainy sidewalk in London as they do hopping from art gallery to dive bar in New York City. A brief history of the Chelsea boot Chelsea boots are hardly a new discovery. The style has been around for more than 150 years, first developed in England by Queen Victoria’s shoemaker, Josepth Sparkles-Hall. His mission? To create an elastic-sided design that made the boots easier to pull on and off, and that he did—even the Queen herself wore them. Commonly known as the “paddock” boot, the style was soon adopted by equestrians and countryside folk worldwide. Its name arrived later, when the boot became associated with London’s cool Chelsea neighborhood; by the 1960s, the Beatles and the Rolling Stones had transformed the practical boot into a rock-and-roll staple. While there have been many renditions of the Chelsea boot, from hot new prints to chunky platform versions, its functional features and signature silhouette has remained. My introduction to the Chelsea boot came from my mother and her Dr. Marten’s. She has always been a sucker for ’90s NYC style, with most of her outfits consisting of the classic downtown vibe: effortlessly cool and a little bit edgy. A New York rocker at heart, she was the first person to tell me that Chelsea boots are iconic. I would borrow her pairs through my angsty teenage years, and somewhere along the way, they became a staple in my own wardrobe. Why Chelsea boots are a travel staple I pack a pair of these bad boys everywhere—and that’s the beauty of a Chelsea; there’s a version of them for any trip you can dream up (minus a beach vacation). Whether your next vacation involves walking, unpredictable weather, dinner somewhere fabulous, or simply wanting your jeans to look a little cooler, there’s a Chelsea boot ready to come along. The dozens of pairs I've had over the years have followed me around the world, from the timeless Dr. Martens 2976 Chelsea (one of my favorites) to Blundstone’s classic pull-ons that I bought in Australia, and at this point, more Sam Edelman iterations than I can count. The versatility of the Chelsea boot is exactly why travelers all over the world trust them. They can be the dependable pair you walk miles in, or the goes-with-anything shoe that makes a simple travel outfit feel like a look. And unlike so many shoes that promise to do both, the Chelsea boot has the history and rockstar lore to back it up. The Chelsea boots I’m eyeing There are lots of excellent Chelsea boots out there right now. Classic leather, lug soles, chunky platforms, sleek low-profile versions, and weather-ready pairs from brands I love and trust. Below, I’ve rounded up a dozen travel-friendly Chelsea boots worth packing this season—many of which I’ve got my eye on.

item.title: How I Travel: Jannik Sinner Can Fall Asleep Anywhere—Especially on a Great Hotel Couch
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.62
Jannik Sinner is with me on a cruise. Not words I ever thought I’d say. But there he was, sitting across from me as our ship, the spanking-new Explora III, proceeded to dock in Marseille. Later, we would ride the elevator together, chatting about Formula One, and even play paddle on the same court (not at the same time; I could never). We weren’t traveling together, exactly, but we weren’t exactly not traveling together, either. Sinner, who is the luxury cruise company’s global brand ambassador and helps shape its athletic and wellness routines for guests, was fresh off his Wimbledon win—and not too far removed from what would be his quest for a second US Open title. His life as the men’s world No. 1 singles tennis player, he says, is spent on the road, so a different vantage point from the sea is both welcome—and calming. “It’s so nice to be far away from everything—hidden in a way,” he says. Sinner chatted with Condé Nast Traveler about traveling by sea, his go-to comfort food on the road, and how much he longs for time at his parents’ home in South Tyrol in the Dolomites. He also explains why, if you see him dashing through an airport terminal, you should probably resist the urge to stop him for a selfie. The one region in Italy he hasn't traveled enough in—and wants to go to: In Italy, it’s hard to go wrong, because we have everything: the sea, we have mountains, we have hills. But I think Tuscany, specifically the Tuscan Hills is a little bit underrated. It's very beautiful, with a lot of sunshine, a lot of nature, and a lot of peace. I've been there once, but I would love to go back some more. The trip he could never tire of: Has to be to my parents’ home [in the German-speaking province of South Tyrol] in northern Italy, to be honest, because I left home when I was around 13 years of age. So every time I come back to see my parents or family, it's something really, really special. It's what always helps me rest and recover as well. I don’t go a lot. Maybe two or three times a year and, yeah, it's never enough. A comfort meal he orders after a long day of playing tennis: We need a lot of carbohydrates, so I would say pasta… Probably a rigatoni, which is my favorite pasta shape, with some tomato sauce, and some salad as well. When I’m on a break from playing, and I go home to my parents, it’s a wiener schnitzel, this Austrian dish which is a crispy fried veal cutlet. That’s my comfort food. The items that always make it to his carry-on: An iPad for downloading movies or a television series, AirPods because I like to listen to music, and that's it really. I'm actually a good sleeper, so during flights I sleep a lot and the time goes way faster. The one thing I wish I could carry on my travels is my mattress! For us tennis players it's very difficult because we are constantly changing beds, as well as mattresses; every tournament we sleep somewhere new. So I would say having the same bed or mattress would be so good. What he thinks of journeying by sea: I mean [the Explora III is] very, very elegant. And the quality of the food… I've eaten here now for a couple of days, and it's really, really good. I think this basically is like an amazing hotel. A hotel that moves around the world. Yesterday we were in Genova, and today we are in Marseille. You know—as tennis players—we get so much attention all the time, and are always under pressure to perform. And of course everyone handles it differently, but I always like to step away from the limelight. Back when I was young I would've never thought about escaping to the middle of the sea, but it's somewhere where I feel like you're kind of untouchable, and you can switch off your phone. And that to me is priceless. Where we'd find him hiding on a ship: Well, there’s the amazing paddle court upstairs on deck 14. But being on a ship like this, I might get away to one of the swimming pools or perhaps a jacuzzi. Favorite feature of a hotel: Quiet and calm. I don’t like a hotel that’s too busy and full of people. And I’m kind of strict about that. We play so much tennis a year and recovery periods are so important, even if it’s a short one. To perform well, you need to be more rested. Any travel rituals we should know about?: It’s more a wellness ritual. After a tennis match it’s always an ice bath for me, which I know is not that relaxing but it's important. And then of course the jacuzzi, which releases tension and relaxes the muscles. Longevity is always top of mind as a player, and it's something you know you can work towards. There’s so many new tools, and you see new routines on social media all the time that you think you might try out. A sport (other than tennis) he enjoys traveling for?: It has to be Formula One. I'm a big F1 fan, so I like to, if I have the time, go to races. Because my schedule is very busy, it's tough to do, but I do enjoy watching a race. The qualifying race in Monaco would be really cool, especially since I live there—it's a bucket-list race and qualifying is always the most exciting part. I haven't been there in person yet, but it's on my list. His favorite hotel (or cruise) amenity: I'm someone who needs a great couch in my room. I'm a big couch lover, and sometimes I fall asleep at the couch and don't move to my bed even though it's three or four meters away. So that's definitely something that makes me very happy to have. It makes me feel “at home” in a certain way. Rapid-fire time: Arriving at the airport early or just in time? Just in time. Late enough that I nearly miss my flight. Aisle seat or window seat? Window always, so I can rest my head. Restaurant or room service? It depends on scenarios, to be honest, but I like restaurants a little bit more. Gets you out of the room. Carry-on or checked luggage? I need to go with checked because we carry so much stuff, but I would love to travel only with with carry-on—my backpack, and that's it. That's a dream.

item.title: Long Live the Hard Rock—Inside the Kitsch, Memorabilia, and Excess That Lives On
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.10
I was about nine years old when my dad first took me to the Hard Rock Cafe in New York, and I still remember being completely taken with the walls. My dad and I gushed over everything together: That's Eddie Van Halen's suit—look, Jeff Ament's bass! There's no way that's Jimi Hendrix's actual handwriting. Of course, it's his signature, messy, cursive—a write-up of the classic track, Midnight Lightning. How about those massive, towering stage boots and custom bass guitars? Yep, they were used and worn by none other than Gene Simmons himself. My dad was a rock ‘n’ roll traveler then, in the way some are food travelers today. Concerts determined where he went, and he had stories about bands the way others have stories about family vacations. We bonded deeply through music—so when we walked into a Hard Rock in any city, it wasn't simply a chain to me. Instead, it was a portal—filled with scents of hairspray, greasy burgers, and a touch of booze—that cosmically actualized the music so intrinsic to our relationship. If you've ever walked into a Hard Rock Cafe, you already know the lore: memorabilia displayed behind glass with plaques like artifacts, cult-favorite souvenir T-shirts stacked in the Rock shop, and music playing live or streaming on every television. Some might mistake these spaces as tourist traps—and sure enough, you'll find your out-of-towners here. But I’ve always associated Hard Rock's hubs with a different kind of traveler: the nostalgia-forward, music-obsessed folk who collect the pins, know the songs, and are willing to embrace a little kitsch in pursuit of something travel can sometimes take itself too seriously to deliver: fun. That simple pleasure is the throughline of Hard Rock's evolution. For more than five decades, the brand has grown without sanding down the personality that made its original spaces memorable. What began as one London restaurant is now a global hospitality and entertainment empire, spanning cafes, hotels, casinos, resorts, and live venues in cities across the globe. And it's still building outward: In 2027, Hard Rock is expected to bring its most recognizable piece of architecture yet to the Las Vegas Strip, with a brand new guitar-shaped hotel rising where The Mirage once stood. Hard Rock Cafe's journey began in London in 1971, when two homesick Americans, Isaac Tigrett and Peter Morton, brought the comforts of a classic American diner to the British capital. What later became its most enduring calling card—the memorabilia—arrived almost by accident. In 1979, Eric Clapton reportedly sent the cafe a guitar in exchange for the right to reserve his favorite barstool; Pete Townshend swiftly followed with a guitar of his own, scrawling, “Mine’s as good as his! Love, Pete.” That friendly bit of rockstar one-upmanship became the first note in what would grow into a vast global archive of more than 88,000 historic pieces. As crowds gathered and the idea caught fire, Hard Rock began taking its particular mix of burgers, band tees, and music history around the world, eventually opening its first Asian cafe in Tokyo in 1983. Its next major chapter came in 2007, when the Seminole Tribe of Florida acquired Hard Rock International following a competitive bidding process led by Jim Allen, now chairman of Hard Rock International and CEO of Seminole Gaming, a role he has held for nearly two decades.The deal marked a historic first: according to Allen, it was the first time a Native American tribe had acquired an international company of Hard Rock’s scale. More importantly, it set Hard Rock on an entirely new trajectory. Under Seminole ownership, the company expanded beyond its restaurant roots, evolving into a full-fledged entertainment brand spanning hotels, integrated resorts, casinos, retail, and live-music venues. In the years since, its reach has nearly doubled from 46 countries to more than 80 today. One of Hard Rock's greatest goals over the past two decades, according to Allen, has been to be more intentional about its curation—to create a museum-like experience. From building location-specific collections around local music history to adding QR codes that allow guests to learn more about a piece, turning the company’s vast inventory into something more than decor. “When you can look at artifacts—in this case memorabilia—that represent individual celebrities or individual songs, or certain periods in life that reflect very favorably on positive times, that’s something that’s very valuable in the perception of brand,” Allen says. That evolution is important because it gives the brand’s history a physical, almost theatrical presence. And if you can appreciate a little glitz and historical lore in all its buzz and excess, the effect can be surprisingly transportive. My own Hard Rock infatuation came full circle on a 2022 mother-daughter trip. We were seeing Incubus's (epic) live performance at the Hard Rock's Atlantic City hotel, and while waiting in line, my mother—another rockstar-at-heart—turned to me and said: “This is probably the only ‘museum’ you could ever get me to." There, we realized it had been almost exactly a decade since we first traveled together to Hollywood, Florida, to see Bon Jovi play live at the iconic Seminole Hard Rock Hotel and Casino—long before its Guitar Hotel changed the skyline. My dad, who first introduced me to the Hard Rock world via its Cafes—had passed away in 2010, and in the years after, the Florida property had become part of a different family tradition—my mom’s side of the family loves to gamble, so beginning around 2012, we started traveling there together, often twice a year. And while the hotel was certainly a different kind of spectacle—tamer and more refined than its Cafe counterparts—there was always another corner left to discover, or a new extension to look forward to on the next visit. At a time when I was too young to gamble, I spent nights wandering around, reading up on all the iconic artifacts, from Madonna’s Like a Virgin dress or Elvis Presley’s signature blue pajamas and motorcycle from the ’70s. It was my very own bizarre rendition of Night(s) at the Museum. It's no secret that Hard Rock creates these sorts of long-lasting memories for travelers all over the globe. If you spend enough time at a Hard Rock location, you'll often find a superfan or few that check off these spaces on their travels. “It's absolutely worth popping into a Hard Rock wherever you go, if they have one,” a solo traveler once told me over drinks at the Hard Rock Cafe bar in Amsterdam. “Part of the fun is just how different they all are.” It's true, when it comes to consistency—Hard Rock has it down pat: You know the logo, you know there will be music, and you have a pretty good idea that there will be a guitar or two on the wall. But what you can't know is what the place will mean in that particular city—or what you'll happen to remember from being there. One of the Hard Rock's staying powers comes from making that familiarity feel rooted in the destination. “There is only one universal language—and that is music,” Allen says. So when the company enters a new destination, the team begins with digging local: “We look at the culture of the specific country, location, and city that we’re in, as well as the music history of that particular region.” he says. That research shapes the memorabilia, local performers and, at the cafes, even parts of the menus. A property in Davos will look different from one in Punta Cana or New York; in Las Vegas, Allen says the collection will include artists associated with Nevada and the city, alongside big celebrity names, like Beyoncé, Bruce Springsteen, and Taylor Swift. On a recent visit to both the Hard Rock Cafe and hotel locations in New York, I found it oddly comforting that the Cafe remains the maximalist portal I remember: The wall of stacked guitars—against which my late father and I posed for countless over-priced photos—still remains as if it was built yesterday. I hadn't been here in years, but it all was all too familiar; a sight of one table even pulled me right back to a memory of us two sharing chicken wings while a Pink Floyd track played real loud. (It's one of my earliest memories of knowing the band, now one of my favorites.) Today, neon-blue lights still frame the bar; TVs stream an old Creed music video; tourists stop mid-meal to photograph whatever they recognize; and local musicians continue to perform live. Five blocks away on 48th street, Hard Rock Hotel New York, which opened in 2022, feels like the next generation—brighter, more airy, and refined, with Beyoncé and Jay-Z’s custom outfits by the elevator bank, sweeping views from its rooftop bar, RT60, home to tasty cocktails worth lingering over. “When I first started [working here], I assumed it was mostly about music and memorabilia,” says David Salcfas, the hotel's general manager. “Those things are certainly important, but over time I've realized Hard Rock, as an entity, creates something far more personal, more wholesome." I know the feeling, although I first encountered it over a cafe booth rather than a hotel bar. The hotels may have made the experience bigger, and in many cases more refined, but it’s the Cafes that still give me that old jolt. I can walk in for a comfort burger, look up at the walls, and suddenly I’m nine years old again, standing beside my dad and reading the stories behind the artifacts. That collision of food, kitsch, and memorabilia is the portal I grew up with—and, even now, my favorite kind of time travel. Our team's favorite Hard Rock memories “I grew up in South Florida, so for years the Seminole Hard Rock in Hollywood was something I’d see while driving around the area.
