But when the 450-foot Guitar Hotel went up in 2019, it became impossible to miss—especially because, well, South Florida is nothing if not flat. Now that I live in New York, seeing those guitar strings of light from the plane when I fly back into Fort Lauderdale feels strangely heartwarming. It’s so very Florida, in the best way. And when I run into a Hard Rock somewhere else, like I recently did in Niagara Falls, it still feels like a little piece of home.” —Madison Flager, commerce director “When Hard Rock Cafe arrived in Bombay in 2006, it landed in a converted textile mill and quickly became a key part of the city’s social life. I remember its tall blue cocktails turning up in blurry photos, Nirvana tribute nights by bands from Ohio that we’d never heard of but lined up to see, and local bands getting a stage, too. Most of all, it was a place that let a motley crew of college kids, models, and happy-hour work crowds be their wilder selves under the watchful gaze of Alice Cooper’s leather. It gave us permission to grow up, with all the messiness that came with it. I recently learned that Hard Rock’s Indian franchises have all closed, and it really does feel like the end of an era.” —Arati Menon, global digital director “My Hard Rock memory goes back to a family vacation in Gatlinburg around 2002. During lunch, a familiar song came on and every server stopped, put down their trays, climbed onto the tables, and started dancing. I remember being completely amazed: you were allowed to do that? Years later, I started collecting the little guitar pins from Hard Rock locations around the world, even when I wasn’t actually eating there. I eventually stopped, but the pins are still sitting in a bin at my parents’ house in Florida—and somehow that feels exactly right.” —Taylor Eisenhauer, editorial operations manager

item.title: Dive Into These European Airbnbs With Pools, From Italy to Greece
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.07
Jumping into one on a hot day, a nighttime dip under a blanket of stars, or a few leisurely laps to get you started in the morning; whatever your preference, access to a swimming pool on holiday is a welcome treat. The best hotels will have their own, yes, but Airbnb offers the chance for unfettered access to your own private lagoon, for blissful secluded swims whenever you please. I’ve picked out the most fabulous homestays with pools to book into on your next European trip, ready to dive into and lounge beside throughout your visit. We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor. Our top picks: - Best for couples: The Hoam House, Styria, Austria - Best for families: Finca Las Brisas, Jávea, Spain - Best for big groups: Villa des Rêves, Normandy, France - Best for a room with a view: Dalmatia Vibe, Čelina, Croatia - Number of guests: 7 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 baths Why we love it: Views, terrace, proximity to SplitFloor-to-ceiling glass wall-to-wall views blend seamlessly into the shimmering Adriatic at this ultra-sleek coastal haven in Čelina. With a prime location above a picturesque pebble beach, the three-bedroom villa has a crisp, contemporary design and a secluded location with bags of Mediterranean charm. The open-plan living space opens onto a sun-soaked terrace where a heated infinity pool overlooks idyllic views of the sea. Plus, you’re just a 10-minute hop from the historic town of Omiš and an easy drive from Split, so you’re spoilt for choice whether you’re after island-hopping adventures or long days relaxing on the beach. Location: Čelina, Croatia What to do nearby: Split, Omiš, island hopping - Number of guests: 12 Bed and bath: 6 bedrooms, 8 baths Why we love it: Air-conditioned suites, cinema room, two kitchens, padel courtGlorious 1930s architecture meets five-star luxury at this grand estate in Villers-sur-Mer, which is just moments from the pretty seaside resort town of Deauville. It’s a sprawling fever dream, with 37,674 square feet of landscaped gardens and room for 12 guests. If you want a weekend where you rarely stray too far, this is a great choice—it has five air-conditioned suites, its own cinema room, and two fully equipped kitchens. Head outside and there’s more delights: a year-round heated pool, bubbling hot tub, and Normandy’s only private lit padel court for evening challenges with friends. With options to book private chefs, yoga instructors, and the arrival of daily continental breakfasts, it’s a lavish bolthole in a prime position for exploring Normandy’s glorious coast. Location: Normandy, France What to do nearby: Deauville, Normandy's coast - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Alpine views, fitness studio, alpacasPretty alpine views, a great gulp of fresh air, and cool loft-style design come together at this unique mountain sanctuary, perched up and away in the clouds near the vibrant city of Graz. Inside is achingly minimalist, like an art studio—the perfect place to unwind after workout sessions in the shared fitness studio. The showstopper, however, is the heated outdoor pool, which transforms into a steamy panoramic hot tub during the snowy winter months. Then there’s the resident herd of friendly alpacas roaming nearby—put it together and you have a delightfully whimsical, offbeat Austrian getaway for four. Location: Styria, Austria What to do nearby: Graz, Alps - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Terrace, office space, barbecue, gardenSweeping mountain vistas make a theatrical backdrop for this tranquil Spanish retreat in Jávea. This is real indoor-outdoor living, with three bedrooms and plenty of creature comforts coupled with lush, sun-baked outdoor spaces and ritzy seagrass umbrellas. Should you be able to muster up the strength, there’s an office space for any important emails, while evenings mean big group barbecues on the shady terrace and a few lazy laps in the glittering pool. When it’s time to settle in with a book, take your pick from two open terraces and a quiet, secluded garden with wondrous views. All that and you’re just a few minutes’ drive from the vibrant Costa Blanca coastline. Location: Jávea, Spain What to do nearby: Costa Blanca coastline - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Rustic interiors, view of the Alps and Côte d’AzurVisit in January or February, and the mimosa forests that surround Tanneron will be in bloom, blanketing the quintessential French village in burnished gold. This Airbnb is surely the best bolthole from which to explore the many walking paths in the area. Once a stone shepherd’s home, it’s now one of the most serene, thoughtfully decorated retreats around. Inside, beautiful rustic interiors amp up the coziness, with rich, warm caramel tones befitting its mimosa-dusted surroundings—and beyond the windows, expansive views over the Côte d’Azur and the snow-capped Alps. Location: Tanneron, France What to do nearby: Walking paths, Côte d’Azur - Number of guests: 3 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 2 baths Why we love it: Terrace, sea views, glass infinity poolThere are infinity pools, and then there are glass-walled infinity pools cut right into a cliff face overlooking Lefkada’s most gorgeous golden beaches. That’s what you get with a stay here. This villa is huge, with a spacious terrace from which to enjoy Greece’s famous sunsets (and sunrises, for morning people). It’s modern-as-you-like, built only in 2021 and outfitted in cool minimal tones and no-frills furniture—the focus is kept squarely on those sparkly sea views. It’s just a five-minute stroll to bouncy Kathisma Beach, with its variety of restaurants, bars and shops to explore. Location: Kathisma Beach, Greece What to do nearby: Lefkada, Kathisma Beach - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Panoramic views, olive trees, waterfallBe warned—to get to this Airbnb, you’ll have to take a walk while the hosts escort your cases via tractor. But when you set off, you’ll see just why you’d book here. Panoramic views over the Mediterranean Sea and wave upon wave of olive trees hug the landscapes surrounding this peaceful Tuscan farmhouse, with pretty vistas on offer from every room in the house. Cool off when you arrive in the plunge pool, or just sit up beside a lounger and enjoy the ambience courtesy of the trickling waterfall. The village of Metato is sleepy and quaint, but you’re well-placed for buzzier adventures—Pisa, Florence, Lucca, plus the imposing marble quarries of Cararra, Pietrasanta, Viareggio are all under an hour away. Location: Metato, Italy What to do nearby: Pisa, Florence, Lucca, Cararra, Pietrasanta, Viareggio - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Nearby trails, breakfast, gardenPull on your hiking boots and get ready for an outdoorsy weekend; your suite here is surrounded by some of Portugal's loveliest wild nature, with a wealth of pretty trails right at your doorstep. This one-time Algarvian farm is now home to three charming guest suites, and this is the largest of the lot, with 452 square feet decked out in breezy neutrals warmed up with smidges of caramel. Wake up every morning to breakfast cooked for you, then peter out to the natural pool, which is set among a fragrant Mediterranean garden. When it’s time to head out, the historic center of Loulé is just five minutes away in the car, and you’ll be walking along windswept coastlines in under half an hour. Peckish? The hosts live on site, providing a changing menu of snacks, salads, sharing plates, and refreshments each day. Location: Loulé, Portugal What to do nearby: Walking trails, historic center of Loulé, coastline - Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Antiques, garden, on-site hostsAfter years spent renovating their spectacular 16th-century French château, owners Alison and Costas decided to open up a string of cozy cottages in the grounds to guests. This one—the smallest—sleeps just two; there’s a big en suite bedroom packed with carefully curated antiques and a shared kitchen and sitting room a few footsteps away. The swimming pool is the focal point of the fairytale gardens: It’s a blissfully peaceful spot to unfurl between days exploring the nearby Provençal towns of Uzès and Châteauneuf-du-Pape. Alison is often found pottering around the grounds—so she’s always on hand to dish out local restaurant recommendations and day-trip tips. Location: Saint-Victor-la-Coste, France What to do nearby: Provençal towns of Uzès and Châteauneuf-du-Pape - Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Cave home, hot tub, airport transferAll of the other boltholes on this list have a pool, but only this traditional Grecian cave home possesses one inside the property itself—and a heated one with a hot tub to boot. Enter this cozy space, once the village’s bakery, and you’ll be snugly wrapped in a spot renovated sensitively to honor the unique local architecture. The palette throughout mimics that of the sea (and the pool), and there’s a generous outdoor space with a barbecue. A daily breakfast is provided—to eat at the table while perched on a swinging seat—and the hosts can offer airport transfers, car and bike rentals, catamaran excursions, horseback riding, and massages upon request. Location: Vothonas, Greece What to do nearby: Catamaran excursions, horseback riding - Number of guests: 7 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Private garden, excellent location, daily housekeepingDown a quiet cobbled street in the heart of Porto’s Old Town, this two-bedroom villa comes with all the finger-clicking perks of a hotel (daily housekeeping, breakfast deliveries, and a private chef to summon), but the total freedom to do your own thing. Colorful art and jaunty cushions brighten up crisp white linens in the bedrooms, and there’s a huge sofa and TV loaded with Netflix in the sitting room. However, this property’s real coup is the private garden and swimming pool—a little urban oasis, hidden in plain sight—and a perfect spot to while away a post-sightseeing afternoon. Location: Porto, Portugal What to do nearby: Porto's Old Town - Number of guests: 16+ Bed and bath: 12 bedrooms, 12 baths Why we love it: Art, balconies, terraceWith their faded frescoes, colorful antique tiles, beautiful furniture, and walls lined with Renaissance paintings, most of the rooms at this splendid Amalfi Coast villa feel more like museum pieces. Some of the bedrooms open onto balconies with dizzying views of the rocky shoreline, and there’s plenty of space to enjoy sundowner spritzes and suppers on the vine-covered terrace. The pool is the real scene-stealer here—teetering on the cliff edge, it looks straight out over the tumble of pastel-colored houses spilling down Positano’s lemon-scented hillside (it’ll certainly help if you have a head for heights). Location: Positano, Italy What to do nearby: Amalfi Coast - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 baths Why we love it: Terrace, hidden thermal pool in an underground caveIt took owner Giovanni seven years to restore this two-story, loft-like space in San Miniato, an extraordinarily pretty hilltop Tuscan town. The result is a rental for serious aesthetes—and a beguiling mash-up of medieval and modern. Vintage brushed lamps hang from Renaissance brick arches, midcentury furniture in the industrial-style kitchen, and a 16th-century cobblestone terrace accessed via steel-edged sliding doors. Even more remarkable is the property’s most unexpected detail. In the master bedroom, there’s a trap door; pry it open, and you’ll stumble across a hidden thermal pool, squirreled away in a secret underground cave. Location: Tuscany, Italy What to do nearby: White truffle festival, Tuscan hills - Number of guests: 7 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 baths Why we love it: Solarium, garden, shaded lounge in the backyardIt's hard to believe you can stay in this historic villa in southern Italy's countryside. Float among the trees in this expansive pool, then take a leisurely afternoon nap inside the cool, stone-walled bedrooms (there are three, two with doubles and one with a queen, and three bathrooms). There's a solarium, a garden to check out, and a cheery yellow lounge in a shaded part of the backyard. Location: Ceglie Messapica, Italy What to do nearby: Southern Italy - Number of guests: 8 Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 baths Why we love it: Hot tub, coastline, deep bathtubJust a short drive from Crikvenica’s azure coastline and long, sandy beaches, this spacious cottage offers charm and style in ample measure. The master bedroom has a deep tub—always a welcome treat—and the home itself couldn’t be prettier, with pastel blue shutters and wobbly sandstone brickwork finished with ruby trailing leaves. The pool area benefits from a shady spot most of the day, allowing for maximum time soaking up the views, with the odd dip into the pool to cool off in between. Inside, a large hot tub invites you to recline with a glass of fizz. Location: Crikvenica, Croatia What to do nearby: Coastline, beaches - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Heated pool, smart TV, vineyard views, outdoor showerWarm, earthy Travertine stone features throughout this picturesque French villa, creating a comfy countryside feel that perfectly complements the secluded rural location. But that’s not to say you’ll be without modern comforts—the brand-new space is decked out with all mod cons, including a smart TV, strong Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth speakers. Take a dip in the pool—it’s heated, so great for night swims—and enjoy the views over vineyards and towards the sea; the Testa di Ventilegne, Caldarello Tower and, on good days, the Sardinian coast are all within sight. When you’re done, refresh yourself in the outdoor shower and set up on the covered terrace (no sunburns here) for a lazy afternoon. Location: Figari, France What to do nearby: French countryside - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 baths Why we love it: Mountain views, fireplace, infrared shower, beer tapLuxury is the order of the day here in Austria, where this sweeping 1,772-square-foot chalet pays homage to the beauty of natural materials with impressive effect. Wood, the dominant element, features heavily throughout, while slate and concrete ebb and flow, adding welcome contrast. Inside, a statement freestanding fireplace will warm you up as you return from a ski session—and, of course, there are infrared seats and an infrared shower to ease aching muscles. A beer tap, liquor fountain, and teppanyaki grill ensure evenings go without a hitch in the kitchen. Head outdoors, and you’ll find a covered outdoor kitchen with a barbecue, luxurious heated seats, and a huge swimming pool for lazy laps surrounded by those picture-perfect mountain views. Location: Brand bei Bludenz, Austria What to do nearby: Alps - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Floor-to-ceiling windows, spiral staircase, heat and ACSmall but perfectly formed, this pointed chalet is the ideal spot for a romantic spell exploring Turkey’s lush Sapanca region. Floor-to-ceiling glass windows look out over the heated pool, which glows atmospherically after dark, inviting you in for a midnight swim among the trees. A spiral staircase leads you up to bed, and you can order breakfast from the nearby market, bringing your goodies right to your door. A heating system and an air conditioner keep conditions just right year-round. Location: Sapanca, Turkey What to do nearby: Sapanca region, nearby market

item.title: 41 Best Airbnbs in Italy, From Chic Tuscan Farmhouses to Canalside Lofts in Venice
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.06
Finding the best Airbnbs in Italy is no easy job—there’s an almost absurd number of beautiful places to choose from, whether you’re after a weathered stone farmhouse surrounded by olive trees, a colorful apartment above a village piazza, a cliffside villa overlooking the Mediterranean, or a centuries-old home where the original tile and shutters have somehow survived. The best ones aren’t just pretty places to sleep, either. They give you a little window into the day-to-day life of locals in Italy. After traveling through Italy in the off-season, including chasing trains between the five towns of Cinque Terre and visiting friends in Puglia, some of my favorite memories are the most low-key: lingering over coffee, wandering into a tiny market, coming home to our rental with a bag of tomatoes and bread, and then opening every window in the house as the evening breeze rolled in. That is how to do Italy best: A wander through the local neighborhood, a glass of wine on the terrace, and nowhere you need to be until tomorrow. Below I’ve rounded up the best Airbnbs in Italy by region, with stays that make that fantasy feel wonderfully attainable. Think terra-cotta roofs, lemon trees, private pools, balconies above cobblestoned streets, citrus groves, and terraces made for lingering long after dinner. From Lake Como to the Amalfi Coast and all the underrated gems in between, these are the Italian vacation rentals worth building an entire trip around. We’ve selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews. Our top picks: - Best for history lovers: Hidden apartment in a Renaissance church - Best for couples: Romantic 16th-century Puglia estate - Best for adventurers: Group-friendly chalet in the Dolomites - Best for wine tastings: Dreamy Monte San Pietro stay near sweeping vineyards - Best for artsy folk: Milan apartment with a film library - Number of guests: 11 Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 3 baths Why we love it: Three-floor balcony, modern kitchen, free parkingWhether you’re planning a destination family reunion or want to gather your friends for the most epic birthday weekend ever, this massive waterside villa should be bookmarked immediately. The house (once home to Como’s village doctor) has enough room for 11 guests, not to mention some of the best lake views I’ve ever seen. As for the decor, it’s rustic Italian at its best: think antique wall sconces, ornate armoires, whimsical bathroom tiles, and artwork on nearly every wall. City: Fagetto Lario Things to do nearby: Lido di Faggeto Miamilaryo, Presswine of Palanzo museum, Ristorante Pizzeria Tipi Tipici - Number of guests: 3 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Gorgeous lake views, outdoor garden, goats on-propertyLocated on the west side of the lake about an hour from Como, this two-story one-bedroom home offers the best of every world: a modern kitchen and chic design, rustic features like wood-beam ceilings, outdoor living areas, and private access to Lake Como, not to mention views over the lake from every room and two goats as neighbors. Note, it's a bit of a hike here (about 150 stairs), and while there's a cable system to ferry up your luggage, you'll have to make your own way to the home. City: Menaggio Things to do nearby: Punta Gaeta, Bar Trattoria Pizzeria La’Cupera, Prato Stella - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1.5 baths Why we love it: Lake access, ivy-covered exterior, heated floors in the bathroomThis is one of the most unusual Airbnb apartments I've seen thanks to the curved stone ceiling featured throughout—but don't think the 13th-century build comes without modern amenities. Expect an industrial kitchen, spacious living area, cozy bedroom, lakefront outdoor space with sun loungers and dining areas, and even baby gear, like a high chair and pack-and-play, available on request. City: Blevio Things to do nearby: Il Colombaio hiking trail, Il Pratone hiking trail, Sasso del Lupo park, Grotta dei Miti - Number of guests: 10 Bed and bath: 6 bedrooms, 4.5 baths Why we love it: Private parking, garden with sun loungers, kayaks and bikes providedRenting your own villa on Lake Como is peak luxury, and this six-bedroom rental really ups the ante. Aside from its classic stone façade and private beach access, the property boasts sunny interiors with wood wainscoting and multiple balconies overlooking the lake. The home is also close to several restaurants and cafés in the charming village of Vassena. City: Vassena Things to do nearby: La Bolla hiking trail, Monte Castel di Leves hiking trail, Pachina Gigante, Parco Bellavista - Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Free parking, washing machine, private balcony, pet-friendlyI could have sworn this apartment was created by Asteroid City’s set designers, but the quirky space was actually dressed by a group of young Salento artists. They certainly nailed the whole Wes Anderson aesthetic, however, from the pastel pistachio walls to the perfectly symmetrical furniture placement. The home is situated in the small town of Casamassella, which is removed from the heavily touristed trails but still within a 10-minute drive of Otranto and its famously gorgeous beaches. City: Casamassella Things to do nearby: Castello di Casamassella, Abbazia di San Nicola di Casole, Belvedere Fazi, Grotta Turchese, Cavernette - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Indoor fireplace, private balcony, backyard, Bluetooth sound system, hammockThis gem is one of the highest ranked on my Italian bucket list: a romantic, 16th-century Arezzo estate that marries Renaissance grandeur with antique-luxe design. Tucked in the old town center right next to Casa Vasari, this noble building—once owned by the aristocratic Ubertini family—has brilliantly reimagined its ancient kitchens into an elegant, hyper-charming guesthouse where every detail stands out. The interior is a culmination of cinematic romance, dripping in pastel pink and crimson tones, gilded historical paintings, traditional carpets, and cozy stone wall alcoves filled with bookshelves. Just a few steps from all the city's main attractions, the sanctuary unfolds into three unique, plush bedrooms that act as both beacons of comfort and beautiful odes to Italy's storied past. City: Arezzo Things to do nearby: Church of San Domenico, the Duomo, Stadio Comunale Città di Arezzo, Il Castelo di Rigutinelli - Number of guests: 8 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 baths Why we love it: Courtyard and garden views,Visited and adored by Traveler contributor Lucrezia Worthington, this dreamy base is an easy train from Florence to Brindisi (and within a 30-minute drive from there). Set between Ostuni and Ceglie Messapica and surrounded by silvery olive groves, the home is a former Masseriola, or rural farmhouse, dating back to the 18th century. When the current owners first purchased the property, they added a few touches to the main villa, including a charming little conservatory with a dining table where the light filters in from sunrise to sunset. Inside, there’s a living room, kitchen, two bedrooms, and two bathrooms, while outside, a stone staircase leads up to the rooftop for views that stretch across the valley. Worthington's favorite bedroom is the one toward the back of the property with a door that leads directly to the garden. It’s cozy, with blue drapes hanging over the bed, and has enough storage space to hang up the essentials. Here, you'll have access to all the simple delights of Ostuni: from endless stretches of olive groves to the coastline of Monopoli and Savelletri for glittery, impromptu swims. Read a full review of the property. City: Ostuni Things to do nearby: Ceglie Messapica, Cisternino, Alberobello, Martina Franca, Locorotondo, Grottaglie (with its beautiful ceramics) - Number of guests: 7 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3.5 baths Why we love it: Hardwood floors, marble fireplace in the main bedroom, washer/dryerI can’t imagine a better place to rest up between sightseeing jaunts than this soothing apartment in San Marco. The three oversized bedrooms are filled with potted plants and cool linen curtains, allowing the stunning architectural details of the home—like beamed ceilings and dark wood window frames—to shine. The spa-like bathrooms, modern slip of a kitchen, and roomy dining room only help make this feel like a true home away from home. City: Venice Things to do nearby: Teatro La Fenice, Piazza San Marco, Rialto Bridge, Museo Fortuny, Basilica di Santa Maria della Salute - Number of guests: 7 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Canal views, central location, fully equipped kitchen, sofa bed, food and wine tours (upon request)Located in the north of Venice, this gem lies in one of the city's most lively, dynamic neighborhoods: Cannaregio. It's design-forward in a subtle, chic way—with brick walls, marble floors, and pops of earth tones in all the right places. It's home to two spacious bedrooms: one with a king and single bed and the other with one king bed. While you might want to stay home, cook a nice meal, and enjoy your waterfront views, it's the property's access that makes it so special. Walk along the picturesque canals and enjoy quick access to the city's top restaurants, including Al Timon (for steak), or Paradiso Perduto (for fresh seafood and live music). According to previous guests, it's also located above a lively collection of wine bars. City: Venice Things to do nearby: Madonna Dell'Orto (a ferry stop), Guglie, Rialto Bridge, Ponte dei Tre Archi, St. Marks Square - Number of guests: 3 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bath Why we love it: Walkable location, iconic architectural design, AC and heating, fully equipped kitchenNestled within the 11th-century walls of Chiesa di San Giovanni Elemosinario—the only church to survive Rialto’s devastating 1514 fire—this breathtaking apartment weaves millennium-old history into an ultra-exclusive and memorable Venetian stay. Guests cross a grand entrance adorned with ceiling masterpieces by Renaissance powerhouses like Titian and Pordenone to enter the living space which weaves in history with modern comforts: glass floors reveal original 10th-century stone foundations, exposed walls showcase bricks still charred from the 16th-century blaze, and the ceiling boasts an extraordinary hyper-dense canopy of ancient, tightly packed wooden beams unique to this historic sanctuary. It's a sublime choice for small groups or families looking to soak in all the impressive, artful glory that Venice has always offered. City: Venice Things to do nearby: Rialto Bridge, La Porto d'Acqua, Palazzo Soranzo, Campo di San Silvestro - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bath Why we love it: Floor-to-ceiling glass doors, eclectic decor, proximity to the Duomo, pet-friendly, elevatorThe real accent walls in this home are the floor-to-ceiling glass panels in the kitchen and dining room that showcase views over Florence and its surrounding hills. The color-filled two-bedroom is a little outside the city center in a largely residential district, but you're still only 15 minutes from the Museo di San Marco, Galleria dell'Accademia, and more. Once you've finished exploring for the day, relax on the private terrace. City: Florence Things to do nearby: Galleria dell'Accademia, Piazza San Marco, Cattedrale di Santa Maria del Fiore, Basilica di Santa Croce di Firenze, Orto Botanico Giardino dei Semplici, Galleria degli Uffizi - Number of guests: 7 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: City views, abundance of plants, group-friendly, dishwasherWhat a view: This three-bedroom Airbnb offers an unparalleled look at Florence's San Frediano in Cestello church. In fact, the building itself was a former Carmelite monastery in the 15th century—this particular apartment is on the third floor, so pray for strength on the steps. (One of the bedrooms is also in the loft, so prep for more steps.) There's air conditioning, a washer/dryer, and a decent-sized kitchen inside. Outside, you're just a 10-minute walk from Palazzo Pitti and 15 minutes from the Uffizi Gallery. City: Florence Things to do nearby: Pitti Palace, Ponte alla Carraia, Ponte Santa Trinita, Ponte Vecchio, Piazza della Repubblica, Piazza di Santa Maria Novella - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 2.5 baths Why we love it: Private terrace, air conditioning, elevator building, washing machineAssociate commerce editor Meaghan Kenny stayed at this Florence one-bedroom in summer 2023, and adored the private terrace and central location (it's within walking distance of the Duomo and the Ponte Vecchio). “At the end of each long day clocking up to 20,000 steps while wandering around the city, I was grateful to have such a relaxing place to unwind. I'd recommend this Florence Airbnb to any solo traveler, couple, or family with one or two young kids. It's bright and airy, and quickly feels like home.” Read a full review of the property. City: Florence Things to do nearby: Palazzo Strozzi, Cattedrale di Santa Maria del Fiore, Museo Nazionale del Bargello, Palazzo Vecchio, Ponte Vecchio - Number of guests: 6 guests Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 baths Why we love it: Central location, view of Ponte Vecchio, recently renovatedSenior commerce editor Hannah Chubb loved having her family of six stay at this luxury Airbnb in Florence in the days leading up to her Tuscan wedding. “The apartment could have been a shack and we would have been thrilled to stay there with that view,” she says, of the windows looking out into the Ponte Vecchio and Uffizi Gallery. Thankfully, you'll have all the comfort you need—in the heart of Florence, no less—with three plush bedrooms, air conditioning, and an elevator to lug up those suitcases. Read a full review of the property. Neighborhood: Via de Bare Things to do nearby: Santa Maria del Fiore Cathedral, Uffizi Gallery, Boboli Gardens - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Ocean views, AC, sun loungers, barbecue, heated towel rackYes, this is a picture of the quaint kitchen at this two-bedroom cliffside villa in Conca dei Marini—but trust us, the private terrace here that looks over the sea with 180-degree views of the coast is simply magical. (Many guests mention spending nights cooking in the kitchen or grilling out on the terrace.) The interiors are bright, fresh, and plant-filled, with tons of cozy nooks and crannies to laze the day away in. City: Conca dei Marini Things to do nearby: Torre del Capo di Conca, Grotta dello Smeraldo, Fiordo di Furore, Castello Lauritano - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Terrace overlooking the Amalfi Coast with lush plants and vines, tons of lights, indoor fireplace, AC and heatingI'd book this Airbnb for the terrace alone. Sure, the views of the Mediterranean are nice, but the terrace itself has lounge chairs, a dining area, a water feature, a plant-covered trellis, and more, which all make relaxing that much easier. Inside, there's beautiful tile work, two sumptuous bedrooms, and a light-filled kitchen that overlooks the aforementioned terrace. Plus, if you can pull yourself away from home, you're within walking distance of Positano's best restaurants and shopping, and just 10 minutes from the beach. City: Positano Things to do nearby: Spiaggia Grande, Fornillo Spiaggia, Fotopoint Positano, Roman Archaeological Museum - Number of guests: 3 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Beach view, AC and heating, balcony, unique location in the Old TownWith wide windows and natural wood furnishings, this seaside apartment feels like the idyllic dreamscape. Peep the vintage-inspired sun room that speaks to the more local side of Amalfi Coast, rather than the overly-crowded touristy parts of the destination. To really live like a local here, be willing to walk down cobblestone streets to restaurants and shops. And from the terrace, get used to a bit of noise from life around you: church bells, motorbikes, families chattering—it’s all part of the experience. City: Salerno Things to do nearby: Giardino della Minerva, Castello di Arechi, Devil’s Arch, Croce di Saragnano - Number of guests: 12 Bed and bath: 6 bedrooms, 6 baths Why we love it: Private pool, outdoor seating, spacious design, countryside viewsOn a trip with a group of friends, travel bookings editor Jamie Spain nabbed this villa for a stay on one of the most recognizable and beautiful coastlines in the world, the Amalfi Coast. Her group settled on Villa Orologio: the ultimate base to take in the sights, stroll down cobblestone streets, and eat as much gelato as possible. According to Spain, rolling up the hill to this six-bedroom villa felt like her group was stuck in a movie (perhaps Under the Tuscan Sun, or the Italian stretch of Normal People). Perched almost on top of a hill and overlooking the village of Sant'Agata sui Due Golfi, about a 25-minute drive from Sorrento, the view from this vacation rental felt all-encompassing, from the village to the nearby mountains to the Gulf of Naples in the distance. Spend your time on the property enjoying breakfast, dinner, and the company of your crew—perhaps seated around the large table under the awning on the terrace or on the lounge chairs around the private pool. Read a full review of the property. City: Sant’Agata sui Due Golfi Things to do nearby: Sorrento, Massa Lubrense, Capri (accessible via boat trip) - Number of guests: 5 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 baths Why we love it: In-unit laundry, portable Wi-Fi, free street parking, pet-friendly, AC and heatingBuilt in the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Modica's Old Town, this Sicilian apartment has original stone floors from the 18th century. Despite its history, the home is filled with modern amenities, including a washer/dryer, air conditioning, and Wi-Fi. The host also offers a portable Wi-Fi device for trips to the coastal beaches, about 20 to 30 minutes away by car. Architecturally stunning, it has its own private cobblestoned backyard, large living spaces with impossibly high ceilings, and two bedrooms—one with a single bed, the other with a double. While farther away from major Sicilian cities (Palermo is a three-hour drive, Catania about an hour and a half), you can fly into the Comiso airport about 20 minutes away. City: Modica Things to do nearby: Parco Urbano Padre Basile, Belvedere Pizzo, Belvedere di San Benedetto, Castello dei Conti - Number of guests: 5 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Hot tub, arched stone entryway, sunny yellow kitchen, portable fans, indoor fireplaceThis 19th-century farmhouse (appropriately named “The Poet’s House”) is like a portal to the Sicily that time forgot. This space in Ragusa practically begs its guests to unplug, breathe in the sea breezes, and brainstorm their next great novel—preferably from the hot tub in the inner courtyard. And whenever writer’s block strikes, the hosts will happily arrange wine tastings at a local vineyard, Sicilian cooking classes, e-bike tours, and beyond. City: Costa Things to do nearby: Ragusa, Santa Croce Camarina, Castle of Donnafugata, Villa Criscione - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bath Why we love it: Unique design, waterfront location, vintage furnishings, bathtubVisited by Traveler contributor Megan Rose Murray, it's safe to say there's nothing quite like this dream of an Airbnb. Sitting on a seemingly forgotten beach along northwest Sicily’s Alcamo coastline is an early 20th-century tuna fishery turned centuries-old watchtower. The building is split into four apartments, all of which you can book separately or group together (which Murray did). One spans two spacious bedrooms, while another has its own kitchenette, and the largest includes a living room. The owners want guests to think of it as a “private residence” and enthusiastically welcome you to share the common spaces, including a dining room, lounge, and kitchen. Once you wrap your head around the arrangement that this isn’t a totally private house, it's easy to settle in and make yourself at home. Though the building is clearly old (it was built in 1913), its shutters are a curiously contemporary shade of blue, sitting brightly next to the terra-cotta roof. This flash of color feels like a playful wink—there’s something just a little Wes Anderson about it. Read a full review of the property. City: Alcamo Things to do nearby: Castellammare del Golfo, Tonnara di Scopello, hilltop town of Erice - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bath Why we love it: Vineyard and valley views, infinity pool, fireplace, king-size bed, outdoor space, easy access to UmbriaFor travelers in need of a good dose of nature, a stay at this Arezzo farmhouse will get the job done. Situated in the middle of Chianti wine country, there's a large yard with a picnic table, infinity pool, and lounge chairs to spend time in. Inside, you'll find stone walls, terra-cotta floors, and exposed wood-beam ceilings, alongside modern amenities like air conditioning and room-darkening shades. It's the perfect size for a small family, with a king bed in one room and two singles in another, along with one bathroom to share. City: Arezzo Things to do nearby: Chiusa di Monaci, Parco di Villa Severi, Torre di Gnicche, Parco Archeologico Etrusco di Castelsecco - Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Shared pool and tennis courts, barbecue grill, indoor fireplace, floor-to-ceiling windowsThis one-bedroom also made it onto Traveler's list of the coolest Airbnb tree houses—and for good reason. Located just 20 minutes outside of Florence in Galluzzo, its interior design is as quirky as its metal exterior, with a marble kitchen sink, wraparound terrace, antique wood-burning stove, and walls covered in chalkboard paint. Surrounded by olive groves, guests also get access to the main house's pool and tennis courts. City: Galluzzo Things to do nearby: Villa Romana, Porta Romana, La Limonaia di Villa Savonarola, Monte Fattucchia hiking trail - Number of guests: 16+ Bed and bath: 7 bedrooms, 5.5 baths Why we love it: Surrounding olive groves, saltwater pool, wood-fired pizza oven, indoor fireplace, outdoor showerDo not let the price tag scare you away: This Airbnb fits more than 16 in its seven bedrooms—ideal for family reunions in the Italian countryside, about an hour's drive south of Florence in Montevarchi. The 17th-century farmhouse also has a saltwater swimming pool, two fireplaces, a stone amphitheater, and 45 acres of garden and olive groves to explore. The best perk here, according to Traveler contributor Jayna Maleri, is actually the cook, Maria, who has been working with the villa for years. She can whip up pizzas in one of the villa's two pizza ovens, teach pasta-making classes, and more. (Hiring a cook comes at an additional cost, so message the host to work out pricing beforehand.) Bonus: That aforementioned amphitheater has also hosted many a destination wedding; you can find inspo for your dream nuptials on the home's Instagram. City: Montevarchi Things to do nearby: Semboloni Winery, Castello di Montegonzi, Luppoleto Toscano, Tenuta Scrafana - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Moroccan tiles, shutters and blackout curtains for sleeping in, proximity to the metro, backyardOne of our favorite colorful Airbnbs, this one-bedroom apartment in the Ponte Venezia neighborhood leans into the use of these green Moroccan tiles, which cover a statement wall in the kitchen, the deep green shower, and the bathroom sink backsplash. Elsewhere, the design is minimal to let the green shine. As for exploring beyond the apartment, it's a 15-minute walk from Milan's iconic Duomo, and just a 20-minute walk from the Milan Centrale train station. City: Milan Things to do nearby: Casa Galimberti, Giardini Indro Montanelli, Casa Museo Boschi di Stefano, Crazy Cat Café - Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Private patio, welcome gift of panettone and wine (per reviews), AC and heating, elevatorThis apartment’s atrium-style living room—complete with a glass ceiling and walls—means you can enjoy Milan’s atmosphere even when you’re inside. The sunroom is surrounded by an open terrace with flowers and a bistro table, while ivy provides plenty of privacy with just enough openings to still peep the skyline. The rest of the space is cozy and comfortable, but you’ll want to spend most of your time in the greenhouse-esque living room. City: Milan Things to do nearby: Duomo di Milano, Palazzo Reale di Milano, La Scala, Palazzo Clerici, Biblioteca Ambrosiana - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 2 baths Why we love it: Fireplace, plant-filled balcony, art and trinkets, near-perfect rating on AirbnbThose aren't books on the living room's bookshelves: It's an incredible DVD collection that may keep you glued to the couch. You won't have to sit still, though, since this one-bedroom apartment is in Milan's Brera neighborhood, about a 10-minute walk from the Duomo and just five minutes from the Castello Sforzesco. This spot is definitely on the homier side when it comes to decorations, with lots of wall accoutrements and knick-knacks, so if you're looking for a clean, hotel-like experience, book elsewhere. As for sleeping arrangements, there is one king bed and a sofa bed. City: Milan Things to do nearby: Castello Sforzesco, Pinacoteca di Brera, The Botanic Garden of Brera, Teatro alla Scala - Number of guests: 3 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Direct Trevi views, smart TV, indoor fireplace, free street parkingIt’s famously hard to get unobstructed views of Rome’s Trevi Fountain thanks to the overwhelming hordes of tourists fighting their way to snap photos. Bypass all of that suffocating effort and book this Rome Airbnb instead—it directly faces the fountain, so you can sit comfortably and look out over it 24/7. The interiors of this one-bed are simple and neutral (lest they distract from that view), and the host can help you book add-ons like airport transfers, cooking classes, and Vespa rentals. City: Rome Things to do nearby: Trevi Fountain, Pantheon, Piazza Navona, Tempio di Adriano, Galleria Sciarra, Palazzo Borghese - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Central location, over-the-top interiors, hot tub, room-darkening shadesItaly isn’t exactly a country that embraces minimalism, and that just makes us love it all the more. Just check out this one-bedroom suite in Rome’s historic center with wall-to-wall frescoes, gold decor, lush textiles, and crystal chandeliers that would put any royal palace to shame. (There’s even a hot tub in the bedroom. Casual.) The location is also fit for royalty: It’s situated between Piazza di Spagna and the Pantheon and is within easy walking distance of the Spanish Steps. City: Rome Things to do nearby: Spanish Steps, Mausoleum of Augustus, Museum of the Ara Pacis, Villa Medici, Piazza del Popolo, Villa Borghese, Trevi Fountain, Piazza Navona - Number of guests: 5 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bath Why we love it: City skyline view from a private outdoor terrace, AC and radiant heating, pet-friendlyIdeal for first-time visitors to Rome, this apartment is on the second floor (take note, there's no elevator) of a completely refurbished building and only a few steps away from the Roman Forum. It’s also between the lush parks of Villa Celimontana and Colle Oppio, perfect for daytime strolls outside of the busy city center streets. It fits up to five guests across two bedrooms (each with a double bed, plus a loft with a twin-size floor mattress), with pets allowed, so it might be perfect for a family trip, too. City: Rome Things to do nearby: Pantheon, Roman Forum, Piazza Navona, Trevi Fountain, Basilica of Saint Mary Major, the Colosseum, Vatican City, Castel Sant’Angelo - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bath Why we love it: Renovated bathrooms, art, abundance of books, pet-friendlyMany of Rome's best Airbnbs are decked out in antiques and art, but this two-bedroom one-ups the rest with a jaw-dropping library that's filled to the brim with books. (It serves as the second bedroom with a pull-out bed, if you want to sleep surrounded by tomes.) It's located in Trastevere, and there are views of the ochre, ivy-covered buildings that define the neighborhood—plus it's only on the second floor, so you won't have to haul your luggage (and yourself) up too many stairs. City: Rome Things to do nearby: Ponte Cestio, The Mouth of Truth, Roman Forum, the Colosseum - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Lush private garden, vintage-style bath, barbecue grill, free parkingIn the province of Treviso, this storybook home is well positioned for a visit to the region of Veneto, home to art, beaches, and mountains. It’s all about open spaces and airy rooms—on the first floor, guests can find a double bed and separate full bathroom with a tasteful vintage-style bathtub. Each room is more colorful than the next, with red and pink vibrant adornments that complement the lush green gardens outside (one at the back and one at the front of the house). It’s perfect for families or two couples—the home can comfortably accommodate four guests. City: Chiarano Things to do nearby: Sfriso Winery, Forest of Cessalto, Villa Benzon, Antonio Rigoni Winery - Number of guests: 14 Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 5 baths Why we love it: Vineyard and garden views, private outdoor pool, spacious design, kid-friendly amenitiesPart Saltburn fantasy, part slow-living Italian dream, this masterfully revived Stabiuzzo farmhouse—tucked just 19 miles outside Treviso—is a sun-filled, pale-yellow playground designed for living like the main character. The cinematic high begins at the threshold, where a sweeping, theatrical staircase sets a grand tone, unfolding into a sanctuary sculpted from local clay, raw timber, and smooth Piave River stones that ground the space in a deeply organic harmony. It is a stylish estate built for friends and families alike, where days dissolve into a blissful loop of dipping in the massive swimming pool, baking on the sun terrace, and sipping local prosecco in a blooming flower garden framed by endless vineyard views, before retreating to your own immaculate bedroom complete with a private en suite bathroom. City: Stabiuzzo Things to do nearby: La Castellana village, Cimadolmo, San Polo di Piave, Azienda Agricola Zago - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bath Why we love it: Garden with private terrace, vineyard access, private parking, fully equipped kitchenNestled within rolling Veneto vineyards, this serene countryside retreat offers a masterclass in slow, sun-drenched Italian living. Anchored by an expansive terrace, the property is strategically poised between the UNESCO-listed Prosecco hills, historic Venice, and the golden beaches of Jesolo, making it an idyllic launchpad for discovering boutique wineries, historic hamlets, and scenic bike paths. Previous guests proclaim this rental to be an oasis of calm—a pristine, secure haven where you can park in a private courtyard, lock up your mountain bikes, and zip to Valdobbiadene for a cellar tour in just 40 minutes. Marrying traditional countryside architecture with playful, design-forward details—like its whimsically vintage, dusty-rose bathroom—this estate boasts a seamless mix of rustic authenticity with the hospitality of a host who seemingly knows every hidden local festival in the valley. City: Vazzola Things to do nearby: Veneto vineyards, Lake Garda, vines of Valpolicella, Malanotte Village - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 baths Why we love it: Design-forward interiors, convenient location, fully equipped kitchen, ping-pong and foosball tablesSpread across two floors, this massive art-filled retreat is a peaceful haven in the heart of old-city Bologna, designed to make you feel like royalty waking up inside a museum. Lovingly renovated to honor the historic building's original bones, the soaring ceilings create a luminous, open-air concept where almost every room features double doors opening directly onto your very own private paradise: a beautifully landscaped courtyard and parterre garden complete with a tranquil pond and constant birdsong. Inside, the grand layout offers an absolutely huge, comfortable living space equipped with brilliant air conditioning for hot Euro summer days, seamlessly balancing its quiet seclusion with an incredibly vibrant local neighborhood. Another plus? Step outside, and you are within walking distance of Bologna's best bars, fashion boutiques, and traditional trattorias, while the city's main square—famed for its free summer public movies—is just moments away. City: Bologna Things to do nearby: Porta San Felice, Piazza Maggiore, Finestrella Canale di Reno, the Museo d’Arte Moderna di Bologna - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Mountain and valley views, outdoor dining table, hammock, garden, walk-in wardrobe, indoor fireplaceThis renovated farmhouse—immersed in the flowing green hills of Bologna—just might be the stay you've been waiting for. Perhaps the pastoral antidote to city life, the home conveniently sits just 25 minutes from the downtown city center. Inside, the ground floor centers around a spacious, fluid lounge and a dining area anchored by a kitchen with all of the right amenities, alongside a laundry room and full bath. Glass doors open directly onto a private garden sanctuary, where a hammock, summer barbecue, and alfresco dining table invite long, unhurried afternoons. Upstairs, the layout transitions into two large, sunny bedrooms—including a primary suite with a private bath and walk-in closet—each uniquely configured with a queen and a single bed to easily accommodate families or close-knit friend groups. It is a peaceful, quiet country retreat that refuses to compromise on location, keeping you minutes from beloved local restaurants and perfectly positioned for hyper-local trips to Lamborghini, Ferrari, traditional balsamic vinegar makers, and artisanal Parmigiano-Reggiano dairies. City: Ozzano dell'Emilia Things to do nearby: Osteria San Pietro, Piazza Maggiore, Ciclovia dei Gessi di Gaibola (a highly-rated cycling route), Mercatale, Casalecchio dei Conti - Number of guests: 8 Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 5 baths Why we love it: Bedroom terraces, vineyard views, spacious design, convenient locationIf you’ve been looking for an excuse to book an artsy, hyper-convenient Italian getaway, this midcentury hill lodge perched between Bologna and Modena is your ultimate home base. The air-conditioned estate is a blend of peace and panoramas with four sleek bedrooms—two opening directly onto a terrace overlooking the valley—and five bathrooms, all styled with picture-perfect vintage furniture. While you can effortlessly day-trip to Modena in 30 minutes, or reach Ferrara, Ravenna, Florence, and Venice within 90, the real allure lies right outside your door in Italy's premier culinary heartland. Surrounded by rolling vineyards and agricultural artisans, the lodge puts you within a 15-minute drive of an infinite number of world-class, traditional Bolognese trattorias, farmhouses, and local winemakers alike. Oh, how lucky to be a guest here! City: Monte San Pietro Things to do nearby: Trattoria Gilberto, Trattoria Vecchia Roma, Montemaggiore, Ca' la Ghironda Modern Art Museum - Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Balcony terrace with an outdoor shower, free parking, mountain view, central heatingAttached to the home of designer Harry Thaler, this minimalist loft is a dream come true for contemporary hotel aesthetes—all angular white walls and just a few well-placed pieces of furniture. The bare-bones interiors give way to spectacular views of the mountains, vineyards, and cottages of Algund, best enjoyed from the bedroom terrace (complete with an outdoor shower). City: Lagundo Things to do nearby: Freibad Lido Algund, Castello Foresta, I Troni di Trauttmansdorff Observatory - Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Outdoor pool, wood-burning fireplace, private garden, washer/dryer, AC and heatingWhen hosts Ilonka and Rob purchased a few old country houses to turn into rental properties, they made sure to retain the structural charms: travertine floors, large chestnut wood beams, exposed stonework, and sinks crafted from local quarried stone chief among them. This charming one-bedroom is perfect for a solo traveler or couple; it has a full-size kitchen, spacious living room with a fireplace, and a sweet backyard setup with a pool, vegetable garden, and lounge chairs. Past guests call the location “beautiful and tranquil,” and say the hosts are extremely welcoming and helpful. City: Prato Things to do nearby: Castello di Lippiano, Campeggio Luna Del Monte, Marzana historic site - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Proximity to the sea and city center, 19th-century Neapolitan furniture, AC and heating, private patio/balconyThis Neapolitan flat is in a central location, on the second floor of a charming historic building (with six steps up to an elevator). With velvet sofas and deco lamps and furniture, the apartment feels hip and spacious all at once. It can host up to six guests across the three bedrooms. The home, also named Ammore a Mare, or “love at the seaside,” gets points for being both very central and very quiet: It's close to the sea, an easy walk to restaurants and shops, but still tucked away in the elegant Chiaia neighborhood. City: Naples Things to do nearby: Galleria Borbonica, Palazzo Serra di Cassano, Acquario di Napoli, Villa Comunale, Mappatella Beach, Fontana del Gigante - Number of guests: 8 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Mountain views, private sauna, table tennis, two sofa beds, indoor fireplaceFor an idyllic stay in the Trentino-Alto Adige pocket of the Italian Alps, this two-story is a stunning and convenient pick. Light pours over the warm woods and unique textures of this abode—complete with a sleek and modern fireplace, a spiral staircase, and an outdoor patio with two eggshell chairs that look out on the sprawling mountain vistas. Whether you're headed to the iconic region for its sublime ski or summer season, this is a base that certainly won't disappoint. While the listing does state that it can host up to eight guests, there are only two bedrooms that are private—the other sleeping areas are in the living room on the main floor, where there are two sofa beds available for use. A plus? The property also has access to a shared outdoor area, which includes a pool and whirlpool, garden, playground, and outdoor shower. City: Renon (also known as Ritten) Things to do nearby: Renon Cable Car (with access to South Tyrol’s capital city, Bolzano), Earth Pyramids of Longomoso, Corno del Renon This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Caitlin Morton.

item.title: Can American Southern cuisine finally take hold in London?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.41
“A decade ago, I had customers who didn't know what brisket was!” Mursal Saiq, co-owner of Afghan-Texan barbecue outfit Cue Point tells me. Now, Austin barbecue restaurants InterStellar BBQ and la Barbecue are about to kick off a residency at The Ned. Texan barbecue is one area of Southern cuisine gaining meaningful traction across the city. Following an initial wave of Texan barbecue-inspired outfits like Texas Joes and Smokestak, a newer generation is emerging. “We meet diners from across Wales, London, Ireland, on any given day. We’ve seen that the UK market is interested in us, so it makes sense to bring our style of Texas barbecue over,” InterStellar BBQ owner and pitmaster John Bates tells me. “Folks in London are mad for barbecue right now!” “We’re rooted in classical Austin barbecue,” he adds. “So we’ll be serving the trinity tray of brisket, ribs, sausage, but we’re also nudging barbecue into the future with new ideas." “We also play around, adding ingredients like kimchi, for instance,” says Ali Clem, owner and pitmaster at la Barbecue. “Barbecue has been around for centuries, so it’s always been evolving.” The Big Smoke That spirit of experimentation is increasingly evident in London. At Cue Point, Mursal and co-founder Josh Moroney combine low-and-slow Texan barbecue with Afghan recipes. Traditional Texan brisket, delightfully but not overly sweet, comes with crisp Afghan naan and toasty cowboy butter, whilst a rainbow of lively toshi pickles brings crunch and acidity that cuts through the richness of the meat. The combinations don't feel cacophonous – a risk with fusion. “Many Texan barbecue rubs and sauces actually use spices found in our cooking,” Mursal explains. “Like cumin – that’s basically our national spice!” By drawing on Afghan recipes through Texan methodology, Mursal is preserving her identity on her own terms, whilst also catering for wider cultural and religious dietary requirements. “It's a barbecue for the many, not the few.” Hon’s BBQ moved into a slick canalside space in Hackney Wick this summer and also amalgamates culinary cultures. The pièce de résistance is the Sichuan peppercorn short rib – a gustatory firework display, bringing different notes of pepperiness and spice to beautifully cooked slices of meat that gently tumble from the bone like a stack of dominoes. “No one writes the rules of fusion,” says Hon, who built up his Texas barbecue expertise at InterStellar. But here the principles of Texas barbecue remain sacrosanct. “It’s the triangle of happiness,” he explains. “The correct balance between infusing a great flavour profile, the right level of smokiness and the right level of tenderness – not mushiness.” Over at Black Cactus, I taste layered spices in the Caribbean brisket croquettes (influenced by curry goat), whilst their pastrami croissant cleverly leverages the textural pleasure of flaky pastry whilst allowing the rosy meat to shine. On Saturdays, Texan roots are honoured with a generous platter including beef sausage tinged with fennel and paprika, and glistening melt-in-the-mouth slices of Wagyu ox cheek that resemble the cross-section of a crystal. Owners Josh Alcock and Matt Kears practised their craft alongside Texan barbecue experts like Schulze’s Pit Room and Burnt Bean. Beyond barbecue At All Roads, opened in Brixton earlier this year, Southern inflections come through in plates like expertly charred Creole shrimp with a heartening, resoundingly flavourful sauce (we don’t leave a single streak behind!) and succulent lamb ribs harnessing the sweetness and tartness of pomegranate. It feels distinctly London, rooted in its surrounding community while bringing a less narrow vision of Southern cuisine to the fore. “We wanted to create something brasserie-style, to showcase more of Southern cooking outside of barbecue,” says co-founder Malika Greene. Appalachia, which opened in June in the former Counter 71 space in Shoreditch, draws from this region (which covers some of the American South but stretches beyond it). I’m pleasantly surprised by the bold aromas of the Old Bay omelette for example, initially dubious as to whether it would offer sufficient wow factor for a main course. “We’re nodding to how Old Bay seasonings are paired with seafood in places like Maryland and beyond,” says co-owner Ryan Sheenan. Appalachia allows its London context into the cooking. “It’s nice to have a chef who’s cooked here bring that into what they do,” says Ryan, referring to head chef Ali Borer, formerly of Smoking Goat. “To bring in their skill and flair to put their own stamp on dishes whilst still referencing the region.” I sense this approach in dishes like the soulful butter-brined chicken and miso-infused grits, full of warmth and umami, or the uplifting cheddar and Jalapeño cornbread madeleines. The drivers and challenges Both John and Mursal credit institutional recognition as part of the growing interest in Southern food, with both InterStellar and La Barbecue awarded Michelin stars in 2024. Further, television, music and social media have opened up Southern culture to global audiences – from the high kicks of the pristinely manicured Dallas Cowboy Cheerleaders, to Beyoncé’s modern country anthems, to food-focused explorations like Deb Freeman’s recent documentary about Edna Lewis, a grand dame of Southern cooking. “People love drooling over these gigantic pieces of meat sliding off the bones on socials,” says Josh. But don’t always understand what it takes to achieve it.” “Time is a huge ingredient in our cooking,” says Ali. “The recipes take days.” “We’re not batch smoking, which is labour intensive, and tough in London,” says Josh. “An industrial area allows more freedom, but further out you lose more of the central London customer base.” The enormous smokers are expensive and difficult to accommodate within health, safety and fire regulations. As Black Cactus is currently housed within a brandy distillery, I see parallels with the technical apparatus required for distilling. Both processes require large-scale equipment, time, experience and obsessive attention to detail for an excellent result. There is also the cultural learning curve. “You’ll have customers demanding something that’s run out,” says Mursal. “We have to explain that you cannot make another brisket in an hour! That wouldn’t happen in the US because there’s an understanding of the nature of barbecue – that when it sells out, it sells out.” The skill involved can be similarly misunderstood. “When I started, some chefs would look down on this as a lower art form,” Mursal tells me. “But you have to learn how to form and adapt very particular chemical equations, the sound of fire at different stages. You’re working with nitrates, haemoglobin, figuring out whether to go slower or not.” Another challenge is how Southern food is perceived. “There are still biases about Southern cooking,” says Tom Zahir Browne, founder of Louisiana-focused hospitality project Decatur. Having lived in the US and travelled extensively, particularly around New Orleans, he felt that much of the representation when he returned here in 2013 was “a poor facsimile” of the food he had come to revere. For Safiya Robinson, who champions Southern Black foodways under the moniker Sisterwoman, the problem is acute around soul food. Of Jamaican, British and Black American heritage, she felt that “a lot of people didn’t extend their appreciation of gastronomy to Southern Black American food.” She adds, “there’s this belief that it’s just fried chicken, unhealthy, scraps, full of salt. My work around the philosophy of ‘intentional nourishment’ deconstructs this.” Her plant-based cooking foregrounds the breadth of this culinary tradition, with dishes like butter beans and hot pepper vinegar, grilled okra with ackee spicy mayo, and peach and hemp barbecue sauce alongside smoked jackfruit brisket. These misconceptions affect perceptions of price. Southern food can be perceived as low-value because its most recognisable dishes are associated with affordability, despite the skilled labour and quality, often farm-to-table produce involved.“We’re cooking fresh and from scratch,” Malika tells me. “That has to be accounted for!” Then there is the nebulous question of ‘authenticity’. What does it mean to attempt to reproduce a cuisine thousands of miles away from the culture and agriculture that birthed it? “This food is closely connected to its land, for example we don’t get collard greens en masse here, so we have to use spring greens instead,” Safiya highlights. “We also don’t have the community numbers to form an initial customer base, so you’re marketing to unfamiliar audiences from the start.” Ryan says Appalachia has been praised by diners from the region as more evocative of the Southern cooking they know than the stereotypical ‘all you can eat’ excess. He shares how one guest from Kentucky described dishes as reminiscent of acclaimed Southern chef and restaurateur Sean Brock. However, others have said it isn’t what they consider Appalachian. “When you develop from a regional cuisine, you’ll face interrogation,” he says. “Local pride is understandable, and we’re constantly and willingly learning. But we can’t cook like everybody’s grandma. We’re paying a tribute whilst creating something of our own.” “Cooking from a London perspective, multiculturalism translates into the output,” says Safiya, who, for instance, serves a sweet potato tart infusing Japanese fermentation techniques. “But the ambition is to think creatively about what I can offer, that stays true to the essence of the cuisine.” Cultural significance Despite the challenges, exploring these cuisines reveals important histories and customs. “This food has such a long line of history, with relationships to many different cultures,” says Malika. For example, the ‘house pot’ at All Roads reflects similarities between Southern and Caribbean slow-cooked dishes, whilst Mursal observes how “Southern barbecue wouldn’t have become what it is without the enslaved Africans who developed pits, or the contributions of Indigenous Americans.” Safiya tells me about her gumbo z’herbes, a custom of abstaining from meat throughout Lent, made with seven or nine greens to represent good luck and the number of friends one will make that year. Similarly, Malika learned Hoppin’ John is a New Year’s tradition for prosperity. Young Nola, which took up a permanent location in Shoreditch this summer, fuses New Orleans and West African dishes, two historically connected cuisines. By contrast, Safiya has a bread pudding that illustrates the connection between Britain and former Southern colonies. The European connection is also explored at Appalachia. Ryan notes the parallel (observed by Ali, who is from Wales) between Southern country ham and Carmarthen cured hams. European settlers adapted their recipes and techniques to the ingredients around them – learning how to use corn from Indigenous communities, whilst uncertain winters encouraged preservation, smoking, curing and pickling. “We want to capture some of that history in a way that makes sense for this city today.” What comes next? Safiya shares how “it’ll be great to see more places where we can experience these foods with a degree of ceremony – after all these cuisines developed through ceremonies and entertaining!” For Tom, aside from spots like Plaquemine Locke, there are still few restaurants that replicate classic Creole or Cajun cuisine, but we’re seeing modern iterations of this cooking. However, he points to Cardinal Rule in Manchester as an example of the Southern food niches he expects we’ll see more of in London. “A business focused on Southern biscuits would have been unthinkable to me a decade ago!” But Tom thinks London still has room for an elevated Southern dining room with plenty of covers. “And we might eventually see a big-name chef from the South deciding to take London on.” Mursal predicts models like more US-style barbecue drive-thrus. For now, noteworthy developments are happening away from the canonically Southern, like Afghan and East Asian recipes meeting the pit and Southern family recipes revisited with creative licence. Perhaps that is what makes this moment feel different. London has had its share of Southern kitsch – cloyingly sweet sauces, pools of melted cheese, theme park aesthetics and quantity prioritised over nuanced flavours. What is emerging now feels more considered. Rather than imitating what’s come before, newer ventures are cognisant of the depth of these cuisines, whilst engaging with them in the vernacular of London’s own culturally layered dining scene.

item.title: "If the industry won't give it to us, we’ll give it to ourselves”: how a Caribbean food festival in East London is changing our perception of jerk
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.97
“No Caribbean restaurant has ever been given a top culinary award in the UK,” Jackson Mclarty, founder of Black Eats LDN, mused recently. In the run-up to Jerk Fest, the UK's first food festival dedicated to the Jamaican art of jerk, this dilution, underrepresentation and misunderstanding of one of the Caribbean's most iconic dishes was front of mind. On a balmy summer weekend in Hackney Bridge, Black Eats LDN – the UK's first and only black-owned restaurant directory – brought together 6,000 hungry Londoners to crown the best jerk in the UK. After all, as Mclarty notes: “If the industry won't give it to us, we’ll give it to ourselves.” London's Caribbean diaspora is thriving. According to the 2021 UK Census, there are 345,405 people who identify as Black Caribbean in the capital. The biggest celebration of Caribbean culture, Notting Hill Carnival, is now famous world-over. But jerk, Jamaica's most famous dish, hasn't been given the reverence it deserves. Until now. Mclarty spent his formative teenage years in Jamaica, and revisited earlier this year following Hurricane Melissa. “This festival is personal for me," he commented. “I know what authentic jerk is and how it should be represented, and coming back to the UK without seeing that, I want to revive it and uphold the standard.” So Hackney Wick became, for the weekend, a little Jamaica – with street food vendors hawking their takes on the best jerk recipes to a live soundtrack of reggae and dancehall. At the heart of the festival, 11 vendors went toe-to-toe for three awards that celebrate the community's excellence: Best Jerk in the UK and Jerk Innovation, chosen by the attendees, and the Judge's Choice, chosen by a panel from Caribbean food culture. As for who won the top prizes? Best Jerk in the UK The thousands of Jerk Fest attendees crowned Yard 2 Yard the best in the country. The award-winning team are based out of Romford. Find them cooking until 9pm daily at Sandys 111. Jerk Innovation The guys at Quick Tingz say they're “inspired by soul food, rooted in Caribbean flavours”, and their recipes won them the title of best Jerk Innovation. The team currently caters from their base in North West London – keep an eye on their Instagram to see where they're popping at festivals and street food events throughout the year. Judge's Choice Whats On The Menu Ish was awarded by the expert Jerk Fest judging panel: find the Caribbean seafood specialists near Hackney Wick six days a week to judge for yourself.

item.title: 12 show-stopping Valencia Airbnbs to book before everyone else does in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.06
There are many reasons the charming seaside town of Valencia, Spain, is an ideal holiday destination. From exploring the cultural marvels of the historic centre and the City of Arts and Sciences to savouring authentic paella by the beach, there's something for all types of travellers. The city's laidback character and temperate climate inspire simple pleasures, like sipping horchata in an outdoor café or taking a walk through the lush Turia Garden. Staying at an Airbnb means you’ll be right at the centre of the action in this marvellous city – completely immersed in the city's diverse and dynamic culture. With so much to see and do, choosing the right place to stay can be overwhelming. An apartment in Ciutat Vella (Old Town) will keep you close to attractions like the 13th-century cathedral and the bustling Central Market, while a rental in Ruzafa means being close to trendy streets lined with restaurants and boutiques. Of course, there is also the colourful seaside charm of El Cabanyal. Thankfully, we're here to help. Whether you’re drawn to Valencia for its rich history, thriving culinary scene, or beautiful seaside, here are 9 outstanding Airbnbs in Valencia for an unforgettable stay in Spain's vibrant coastal city. Editor’s picks of the best Airbnbs in Valencia - For beach access: El Rincón de María Vicenta, El Cabanyal - For families: Ruzafa Loft, El Carmen - For big groups: Penthouse Mercado, Central Market - For interior design fans: Ruzafa Loft, El Carmen - For a room with a view: Sunny attic duplex, Ruzafa How we choose the best Airbnbs in Valencia We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor. All listings featured on Condé Nast Traveller are independently selected by our editors. If you book something through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This is our pick of the best Airbnbs in Valencia.

item.title: How London became the day party capital of the world
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.08
Like many people born in the early ’90s, I spent a large portion of my youth camping out in muddy fields, surviving on a few Nutri-Grain bars between long weekends of music with friends. I wouldn’t change a minute of it. I’ve always believed that nowhere does music festivals quite like the UK. The weather might be unpredictable, but there’s a particular camaraderie in trudging through ankle-deep mud to make it to the main stage, come rain or shine, that you simply can’t find elsewhere. These days, I’m a little longer in the tooth and expect a touch more finesse from my festival experiences. I’m no longer able to survive on fumes alone, and I’m certainly less inclined to partake in the infamous “roll throughs”. When I moved to London from Cornwall almost a decade ago, I quickly discovered a new favourite way to enjoy music with friends: the city’s seemingly endless roster of day festivals and raves. Spending an entire day dancing to my favourite artists, then being tucked up in bed by midnight with the next day still vaguely intact, felt like a win-win. As the years passed, I noticed more and more day parties cropping up across the city. It left me wondering: is this the result of our growing focus on health and wellbeing, or a response to London’s increasingly fragile nightlife scene, as bars and clubs continue to close across the capital? I spoke to some of the people at the heart of the city’s music scene to find out. If the night is disappearing, party by day This explosion of daytime partying might seem at odds with the increasingly common narrative around the “death of club culture” in London. The statistics certainly make for grim reading, with Mixmag reporting that a predicted 57 per cent of London’s pubs and clubs could close by 2030. So what’s behind the downturn in late-night venues? “It’s less about law and more an accumulation of challenges that have made operating late at night in London increasingly difficult,” says Luke Huxham, managing director of Broadwick Live. “Since Covid, the industry has faced rising operating costs, inconsistent licensing frameworks and planning decisions that allow residential development next to venues that were there first.” In some ways, the rise of day parties feels like a direct response. If it’s becoming harder to party all night, why not dance all day? “Partly it’s the industry adapting to how hard it’s become to operate late at night in London,” Luke agrees. “But partly it’s a shift in how people want to socialise, drinking less, craving new experiences and still wanting to dance even if late nights don’t fit their lives anymore.” It’s a shift I’ve noticed in myself and my peers, too. While Millennials might occasionally roll their eyes at Gen Z’s obsession with health and wellbeing, there’s something increasingly appealing about a party that doesn’t require sacrificing an entire weekend to recover from. DJ Moxie has been at the forefront of both London’s late-night and day party culture and recognises this wellbeing shift: “Nightlife and club culture bring so much to our city, but it’s not for everyone”, she says, “I think having the option to dance and still have a relatively early night is attractive for a lot of people.” It represents a significant departure from the all-nighters and unapologetic hedonism so deeply entwined with the history of clubbing and festival culture. But perhaps that’s exactly the point – London’s party culture isn’t disappearing, it’s just changing shape. How do you curate the environment to keep the energy of a nighttime rave? “You have to really think about how the spaces look and feel, from daytime into dusk and sunset into night, and storyboard that journey,” Simon Denby co-founder of Body Movements explains. “The space has to be lit very thoughtfully, as, for example, beams of light don’t work in the same way in daylight as they do in a dark club, without the haze over the dance floor.” For Luke Huxham, who has worked on events at some of London’s best-known venues, including Printworks and Drumsheds, it’s about creating an experience that evolves throughout the day. “Sound, lighting, stage design and the physical journey through the space all contribute to how the energy builds,” he explains. “Magazine Open-Air is a great example. We’ve got this incredible location on the Thames, surrounded by London’s skyline. Rather than shutting those things out, we’ve designed the experience to make them part of the event.” The future of London’s party scene Two forces seem to be driving the boom in London’s day-rave scene: the increasing difficulty and cost of operating late-night venues, and a broader shift in how people want to socialise. It’s a complicated dichotomy, but the conversations I’ve had with people at the heart of the scene leave me feeling optimistic. They aren’t suggesting that the rise of daytime partying has to come at the expense of nightlife.
