Instead, they see it as another way for communities to create the spaces they need and keep London’s music culture moving forward. “True ravers know day parties have always been around,” says London-born DJ and producer Maya Jane Coles, “I don’t think it takes away from nightlife at all – it just means there’s something for everyone at different times.” When I asked what they thought the future of London’s nightlife looked like, the responses were surprisingly hopeful: “My hopes are that we continue seeking joy in all corners of the world, especially in London, and nightlife thrives under a new wave of people who are dedicated to encouraging silliness, fun, and chaos,” says Glyn Fussell, co-founder of Mighty Hoopla. Luke agrees that the future doesn’t have to be either-or. “What’s exciting is that the definition of going out is becoming broader. Day parties are a part of that, but so are grassroots venues, community events, festivals and cultural spaces that make London what it is.” “London needs all of it,” he says, “and I hope we keep moving towards an ecosystem where all of that can coexist.” Perhaps that’s the real secret to London’s day-party boom. It isn’t that we’ve stopped wanting to party at night. We’ve simply found more ways to do it. And in a city that has always reinvented its relationship with music, maybe the future of nightlife looks less like an ending and more like the start of a new, very long, day. The best day parties to go to Body Movements, Southwark Park Body Movements Festival is described as a space for “queer [and] trans art to be discovered [and] applauded, queer exploration to be encouraged, and queer expression to flourish” and toted as the city's first outdoor queer arts and music celebration. Field Day, Brockwell Park Field Day has been a popular London day festival mainstay since it started out in 2007 with a lineup consistently comprised of rising stars alongside big-name headliners. Previously hosted in East London’s Victoria Park, the festival is now setting down new roots in the South. Rally, Southwark Park Held in leafy Southwark Park every August, Rally is a relative newcomer on London’s festival scene but has been heavily praised for its programming and production value. Mighty Hoopla, Brockwell Park One of the UK’s most inclusive pop festivals, Mighty Hoopla is a glitter-strewn celebration of alternative culture where new and established pop acts perform alongside cabaret shows and drag performers. Pxssy Palace, across London Pxssy Palace is a collective that celebrates Black, black, indigenous and people of colour who are women, queer, intersex, trans or non-binary. They regularly host club nights in diverse venues across the capital, as well as programming their own stage at Maiden Voyage festival. Maiden Voyage, Burgess Park Electronic music festival Maiden Voyage has been going from strength to strength over the years, from the team behind the famous Camden Jazz Cafe. Unfold, Canning Town A weekly Sunday rave held at Canning Town’s, Fold, Unfold is a celebration of electronic music and the queer community. The Cause, East London Docklands The Cause is up there as one of the best venues in London, and hosts not only late-night events but plenty of daytime raves too. It’s great for summer day parties with its recently developed outdoor staging. GALA, Peckham More than a decade since its debut in South London, Gala has grown into one of the mainstays of London’s festival scene. Usually at the beginning of the season, it’s a great way to kick off the summer and let loose a little.

item.title: My favourite Airbnb: an earthy-toned lodge on the hilltops in Milos with steps into the sea
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.07
The landscape on Milos is endlessly surprising; there’s more to this volcanic island in the Cyclades than its cerulean waters – though those are reason enough to visit. But it’s also home to gorgeous fauna and flora and raw, natural terrain. Wildflowers scatter the island in spring, and sage, thyme, oregano and lavender grow along its winding wild paths. That’s the scent I smell as we arrive at our Airbnb, which is based just outside the beautiful town of Trypiti. The scent permeates around me; it's almost distracting – so good I want to bottle it. We are welcomed by Nausicka, the owner of the homes that perch on this private nine-acre property. She shows us to our sea-view villa and tells us that each room is named after Greek herbs, trees and plants that grow on the land. I am wowed by the view beyond our glass doors where oat plants and red grass dance in front of the sea. Beyond our outdoor kitchen and terrace, two small deck chairs sit at the end of a curving path. They look more like sculptural pieces of art than actual seats, surrounded by a calming palette of brown and green. Immediately, I know I’ll feel at peace here. And there was that smell again, carried through the room with the breeze. The interiors are minimal, and the walls are made of local stone. It feels fitting here: why compete with such a perfect setting? I never want to be far from a swim, so I was pleased to know there was access to a private cove just a short walk beyond the winding path in front of our room. Stairs built into a cliff led right to the rocks; no beach beds in sight, just a sun-warmed stone platform to lay your towel next to a ladder directly into the sea. We were told the space was shared with guests from the neighbouring lodges, but no one came. We felt lucky to have it all to ourselves, so I devoured a book and listened to the ambient sounds of the waves knocking the rocks for hours on end. I nodded off watching sailboats meander by. Later, we climbed the stairs back to the room, sticky from the sea salt, and I headed straight for the outdoor shower, leaning my head up to the open blue sky, as I washed off the salt in my hair. Wrapped up in a towel, hair dripping wet, I do as everyone does on their holidays: make a beeline for a chair to dry in fresh air, swapping the classic balcony-and-bag-of-Lays for a chair on a cliff, a sea view and a crisp glass of local Greek wine. The southern side of the island is known for its sunsets, and it's easy to see why. At first, I don’t focus on the sky; instead, I focus on the changing colours of the plants and herbs, which light up and glow like little orbs. Browns turn to gold as they catch the light, and the sky turns pink as we walk back to our room with empty glasses. We don’t want to leave the room, and thankfully we don’t have to. Nausika tells us that a nearby taverna can deliver dinner. We lit candles and settled into our outdoor kitchen. In the morning, a breakfast basket arrived at our door – an additional cost but one worth every penny. I dig through my haul of fresh, local goods: the Greek yoghurt I had hoped for, fat juicy strawberries, peaches, homemade jam, boiled eggs and freshly squeezed juice. Checking out was bittersweet, but as we followed the island’s rocky roads, we felt sure we’d be back soon.

item.title: Turkish, Somali forces free vessel seized by pirates in Somalia
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.42
Turkey’s navy and Somali armed forces have freed a hijacked vessel in Somali waters and killed 14 alleged pirates following a battle that lasted several days, Somalia’s government said on Saturday. "During the 10-day operation, four boats used by the pirates were destroyed and 14 pirates were killed," said a Somali Defense Ministry statement. "The sustained military pressure finally forced the remaining pirates to abandon the ship." The MV LUTUF, a Cameroon-flagged vessel, was hijacked on August 17 off the coast of the Nugaal region of Puntland state. The joint Turkey-Somalia operation was carried out as part of a defense cooperation agreement between the two countries. The ministry did not provide details about any casualties or the well-being of the crew aboard the vessel but said, "The forces subsequently secured the MV LATUF, which has now safely resumed its journey." According to AFP news agency sources, at least eight members of the crew were on board, including one Turkish national. Resurgence of piracy along Somalia’s coast The Horn of Africa has seen a resurgence in piracy since April, according to figures from the International Maritime Organization, with at least 15 attacks off the coast of Somalia this year. At least five cargo ships were held hostage, the most recent of which was seized on August 20 off Yemen. These attacks are the highest since 2013. Piracy was rampant off the coast of Somaliain the 2000s. It peaked in 2011 before being curbed by international naval deployments and new protection measures for commercial shipping. The resurgence of piracy in the Horn of Africa is adding to mounting challenges for international shipping in the Middle East, where vessels are already navigating around the contested Strait of Hormuz and seeking to avoid Houthi attacks in the Red Sea. In recent years, pirate attacks have also increased along the West African coast, adding another layer of risk for commercial shipping. Edited by: Sean Sinico If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Influential humanists: These are the winners of the Goethe Medal 2026
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.87
Estonian classical music composer Arvo Pärt, Italian literary translator Anita Raja and Greek theater director and actor Prodromos Tsinikoris are the three recipients of the 2026 Goethe Medal, an annual award that honors international public figures who contribute to creating cultural bridges between Germany and partner countries. The annual award, presented this year on August 28 in Weimar, is one of the most prestigious awards in Germany for international cultural work. So what connects these three personalities to Germany's culture? A prolific German exile: Estonian composer Arvo Pärt Considered one of the most influential figures in contemporary classical music since the 1960s, the Estonian composer is renowned for his minimalist, contemplative compositional technique called "tintinnabula." With his iconic works including "Für Alina" (1976), "Fratres" (1977), "Tabula rasa" (1977) and "Spiegel im Spiegel" (1978), Pärt is one of the most performed living composers in the world. In 1980, the composer was forced to leave his home country, and his works were banned in the Soviet Union. After leaving then Soviet Estonia, Pärt settled in West Berlin with his family. He lived in Germany for nearly three decades. "Germany plays such an important part in my father's work," Michael Pärt told DW. The composer's son added that his renowned father found creative freedom through his collaborations with different German conductors and musicians. He was also inspired to compose works to German texts. Pärt's minimalist and spiritual works found a broad audience in the West thanks to the recordings of Manfred Eicher, founder of the Munich-based record label ECM. After Estonia gained independence in 1991, Pärt reestablished contacts with his home country and returned there permanently in 2010. The composer, who turned 90 in September 2025, now lives in the Estonian village of Laulasmaa, where the Arvo Pärt Centre opened in 2018. It is directed by his son, Michael Pärt, who will be traveling to Weimar to pick up the award on behalf of his father. One of the most significant translators from German into Italian: Anita Raja Born in Naples in 1953 to an Italian father and a German mother, Anita Raja studied literature in Rome, where she still lives. Specialized in the translation of modern German-language authors, Raja introduced East German author Christa Wolf to Italian readers with her translation of "Cassandra" in the early 1980s. "Anita Raja's translation is a translation from woman to woman. It's very empathetic, very powerful. It shows that there really was a surprisingly magical connection between the author and the translator," noted renowned Italian actor Sonia Bergamasco at a recent event marking the release of a new edition of the novel. Wolf became a widely celebrated author in Italy thanks to this first translation, and Raja then went on to translate many more of Wolf's novels. She has also translated the works of other major German-language writers, including Georg Büchner, Franz Kafka and Ingeborg Bachmann. All while translating literature, Raja also worked full-time as a librarian in Rome. She became the founding director of the Biblioteca Europea in Rome in 2005, heading it for more than 10 years. She turned the library into a model project focusing on the promotion of European cultures, languages and international cooperation. Prodromos Tsinikoris: Documentary theater as a bridge between cultures Born in the West German city of Wuppertal in 1981 as the son of Greek labor migrants, Prodromos Tsinikoris is one of the leading voices in contemporary Greek and European theater. As a theater director, actor and dramaturg, he creates documentary productions exploring the themes of migration, social inequality and historical perspectives. His audio walk "In the middle of the street" centers on homeless people during Greece's financial crisis. The documentary theater production "Clean City," co-created with Anestis Azas, focuses on the lives of migrant cleaners, juxtaposing their personal testimonies with the rhetoric of neo-fascist movements who want to "clean" Greece of its foreigners and refugees. In the play "96%" Tsinikoris deals with the Holocaust of the Jews of Thessaloniki and the looting of their property during the Nazi occupation. From 2015 to 2020, Tsinikoris directed the Experimental Stage at the National Theater in Athens. Today, he is co-curator of the International Forest Festival in Thessaloniki and teaches at the National Theater's directing school in Athens. Many of Tsinikoris' plays have been developed and presented in Germany. His work has also circulated broadly across Europe, particularly through documentary theater festivals and major public theaters. Edited by: Brenda Haas

item.title: Death toll from Nepal-Tibet floods rises to over 600
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.32
The latest death toll from the devastating flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border was reported on Saturday to be over 600, as frantic rescue operations to search for hundreds of missing people entered a fourth day. Figures from both countries put the number of missing close to 3,000, with 682 bodies recovered and reports of corpses swept as far downstream as India. According to Nepal's disaster agency, the death toll there now stands at 675, with 2,426 people — including foreigners — still missing. Across the border in Tibet, China's state news agency, Xinhua, has confirmed seven deaths and reported 554 missing individuals. A glacial collapse on Wednesday sent rock, ice, mud and debris surging through the Himalayan mountain river systems below. The flood swept through areas near the Chinese border, ravaging entire towns and damaging hydropower plants. What is the status of rescue efforts in Nepal? Rainy weather conditions are hindering aerial rescue operations in Nepal. Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told the media on Saturday that helicopter operations were on hold until the weather improved. Rescuers are battling thick layers of mud in the affected areas, which is making it difficult for helicopters to land and take off. Tunnels in the mountainous region are also a challenge, Basnet said. The army has located people trapped in a tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project in Nepal's Rasuwa District. Over 100 people are believed to be inside the tunnel filled with mud. Basnet said that rescuers were struggling to locate the entry points of the tunnel and had made use of baskets and ropes to reach some people. There are also limited places for helicopters to land in the area. On Friday, Nepal's Army shared visuals of some people being rescued from the tunnel. The survivors were seen stuck in the mud, while officials crawled through the sludge and held out their hands to them. On Saturday, Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal said a specialized tunnel rescue team had arrived from neighboring India and was ready to start work. Nepalese authorities said the bodies of many flood victims have also been found dozens of kilometers from the disaster zone in Chitwan District in southern Nepal, which borders India. Meanwhile, Indian authorities said they recovered the bodies of seven people who were swept downstream from Nepal and believe them to be flood victims. Nepal needs help in technical areas, says foreign minister Late on Friday, Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told the Reuters news agency that his country needed equipment, along with technical knowledge in tunnel rescue operations. Khanal also told Reuters that Nepal did not need help with search and rescue operations but needed assistance in opening transport and communication lines in places where bridges were destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storage of bodies for a longer timeframe. "We have already made requests for such specialized services and technical assistance in areas where we don't have enough expertise and technical know-how," Reuters quoted Khanal as saying. Nepal's Foreign Ministry had on Friday declined foreign involvement in search and rescue. Nepal's post-flood rebuilding estimated at $4-$5 billion In another Reuters interview, Nepal's Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle said that the Himalayan nation may need $4 billion (€3.5 billion) to $5 billion to rebuild after the flood. The estimate is equivalent to nearly a tenth of Nepal's economy. "The initial estimate is between $4-$5 billion. Just an estimate," Wagle told Reuters, adding that the bill would be much less than what was needed in reconstruction after the disastrous 2015 earthquake — Nepal's worst recorded disaster. "Loss and damage is being assessed," he said. What do we know about rescue operations in Tibet? In Gyirong, one of the hardest-hit areas in Tibet along the China-Nepal border, Beijing had temporarily halted its rescue efforts due to the risk of renewed flooding before announcing that the threat had waned. China's Xinhua agency reported on Saturday morning that two villagers had been rescued in the Gyirong area. The glacial collapse on Wednesday led to the formation of a barrier lake upstream due to debris dams. Experts warned that the lake had started to overflow. On Saturday, Chinese authorities announced that the lake had begun to shrink. China's state broadcaster, CCTV, cited the Ministry of Water Resources as saying that satellite imagery of the surface area of the lake in the Tsangpo River basin on Saturday morning showed a reduction of around 21,000 square meters compared to images from Thursday. Authorities have also identified a larger body of water at the bottom of the glacier collapse. "We estimate its area to be over 120,000 square meters, but its depth is currently unknown," Reuters quoted Chen Hongqi, a senior engineer at the Ministry of Natural Resources' Geological Disaster Technical Guidance Center, as saying. Reuters also reported an official of Nepal's Disaster Management Authority as saying that flood risks will remain until the two lakes have fully drained. Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko and Wesley Dockery If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Niger's defense ministry says soldiers attempted mutiny
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.30
Niger's Ministry of National Defense on Saturday said a group of soldiers shot at "sensitive" locations in Niamey in an apparent mutiny. Gunfire and explosions had been heard across Niger's capital in the early hours of Saturday morning. Attackers had targeted Diori Hamani International Airport, which also houses a military air base. They also attempted to breach the presidential palace, althoughthe presidential guard was able to push the attackers back. "Another cowardly attack on Base 101 and once again our defense and security forces ensured ... Situation under control," said lawmaker Bana Wagana Ibrahim, who serves on the Consultative Council. State broadcaster RTN said dozens of rebelling soldiers were arrested or killed. "The fighting lasted a few hours in several places, which allowed [security forces] to gradually control the situation, arrest and incapacitate these moody soldiers," the broadcaster said. Niger military 'gradually regaining control' The situation remained tense on Saturday evening as some mutineers remained camped out near the airport. The whereabouts of the leader of Niger's military junta Abdourahamane Tchiani, remained unclear. The military said it was "gradually regaining control" after mutineers took soldiers hostage at a base near the airport in Niamey, AFP news agency reported. Authorities urged the public to "remain calm and freely go about their business" in a statement read out on public television and signed by Defense Minister General Salifou Mody. The attack posed the latest threat to Niger's military junta, led by Tchiani, who seized power in a 2023 coup. Niger, like its Sahelian neighbors Mali and Burkina Faso, has for years been ruled by a military junta that has struggled to stem a jihadi insurgency. Junta requests support from Russia's Africa Corps Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropayev, told Russian media that the junta requested assistance from Russia's Africa Corps to help suppress the mutiny. The Africa Corps is based in the same Niamey airport that was attacked by the rebelling soldiers. Niger's northern neighbor Algeria, meanwhile, offered its "full solidarity and firm support, with a view to overcoming this ordeal and promoting a rapid return to stability." National TV signal reportedly cut after gunfire The shooting began around 1 a.m. local time (0000 GMT) and continued until daybreak. Locals said that the country's national television had gone off air. Tele Sahel's satellite and online programming was replaced with a black screen at 9 a.m. local time (0800 GMT), AFP reported. It was restored around one hour later. Niamey has been targeted by jihadists twice this year: once by the so-called "Islamic State in the Sahel" group (EIS) and again in June by their rivals from the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM). Edited by: Sean Sinico, Dmytro Hubenko and Wesley Dockery If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Tech giants urge global response to AI cybersecurity threats
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.25
More than 100 companies, including AI giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Perplexity, have signed an open letter calling for a global effort to strengthen AI-powered cybersecurity threats. "We have a limited window to strengthen cyber defenses," the letter read. "In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable." Other signatories to the open letter include Adobe, AMD, Cisco, Dell, Oracle, IBM and German tech giant SAP as well as Deutsche Telekom. Letter urges more funding, resources for cybersecurity The companies called for a broad response, ranging from end-user companies strengthening their own security protocols to "frontier AI companies" building new observability and security tools to cope with AI-powered threats. In particular, they also called on governments to pay for local and international responses to new threats to cybersecurity. "Fund cyber defense, starting with essential services that lack the staff or budget to act," the letter read. In the United States, the Trump administration has imposed deep cuts to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) last year, cutting staff by around a third. The letter also urged governments to "expedite the expansion of trusted access programs, especially for critical infrastructure supply chains, and broaden access to defensive capabilities for other defenders." AI agents reportedly go rogue Last month, OpenAI said two of its models escaped their test environment, gained access to the internet and attacked Hugging Face, a site that AI developers use to store and share code. The incident prompted Anthropic to check if its own models had also carried out similar attacks. It found three incidents in which a Claude model broke out of its testing environment and breached the systems of three organizations. In June, the "Five Eyes" intelligence community — consisting of the US, the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand — issued a rare joint statement warning that new AI models were "fundamentally transforming both offensive and defensive cyber capabilities." "The timeline is not years, it is months," the statement said. Edited by: Sean Sinico If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: The great lake divide: Collapse vs. comeback
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.13
Some of the world's largest lakes could shrink substantially within this century, with far-reaching consequences for ecosystems and roughly a quarter of the global population living in affected regions. Although restoration efforts have proved successful in some cases, many inland bodies of water face extreme challenges. Caspian Sea: A shrinking giant Despite its name, the Caspian Sea is actually a lake. Bordered by Iran, Russia, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan, it is the largest inland water body on Earth. But its surface area has been rapidly receding since the 1990s. This shift is partly due to the use of dams and water-management practices in the Volga River basin. But hotter conditions driven by burning fossil fuels to power societies is also a contributing factor. Rising temperatures increase evaporation rates. Scientific models project that water levels could fall up to 21 meters (68 feet) by 2100. Even a decline of 10 meters could leave large parts of the shallow northern basin dry, eliminating nearly one-third of the lake's current surface area. The consequences are already becoming apparent. Ports require increasingly extensive dredging, fish stocks and wetlands are coming under growing pressure and habitats used by the endangered Caspian seal are drying out. Scientists also warn that exposed lakebeds could release dust and pollutants. Joint conservation efforts among the five coastal states remain politically challenging. Lake Constance: A pollution turnaround Like much of Europe, Lake Constance has been impacted by high temperatures this summer. Bordered by Germany, Austria and Switzerland, the 63-kilometer-long (39-mile-long) lake has experienced high evaporation rates that have caused water levels to fall significantly in some places. In the late 1970s, however, low water levels were not the main concern. At the time, the lake was suffering from severe nutrient pollution and was at risk of ecological collapse. Massive algal blooms and oxygen depletion in deeper waters threatened fish populations and led to swimming bans. The expansion of wastewater treatment facilities and removal of phosphorus from sewage significantly reduced nutrient concentrations, led to the stabilization of lake trout, which had been at risk of disappearing. Local communities also benefited. Around 4 million people in the southern German state of Baden-Württemberg rely on Lake Constance for their drinking water. Yet the ecosystem is far from fully restored. Shoreline development, invasive species and climate change continue to pose major challenges. Restoring more of the lake's natural shoreline could help strengthen its resilience. Aral Sea: A disaster with glimmers of hope The Aral Sea in Central Asia has become one of the defining examples of how water extraction can devastate even the world's largest lakes. Only a few decades ago, it was the fourth-largest lake on Earth. During the Soviet era, vast amounts of water were diverted to irrigate cotton and rice fields, creating an environmental catastrophe whose effects continue today. By 2010, the surface area had shrunk by more than 50,000 square kilometers. Thirty fish species that once supported commercial operations have disappeared, and entire communities along the former shoreline have vanished with them. The Aralkum Desert has emerged where the water once shimmered, covering roughly 62,000 square kilometers. Today, dust and sandstorms carry salt and toxic residues from the former lakebed across surrounding regions, posing serious risks to human health. But the North Aral Sea has benefited from the Kok-Aral Dam, which raised water levels. Where a return of the lake is considered unrealistic, saxaul shrubs are being planted to stabilize the sand and contaminated dust. According to the Kazakh government, more than 1.8 million hectares have been planted since 2018. Muskegon Lake: The big clean up For decades, Muskegon Lake in the US state of Michigan was polluted by industrial waste and contaminated sediments. Extensive clean-up efforts by local environmental authorities removed contaminated soil and more than 110,000 tons of historic sawmill waste. As a result, 54 hectares of habitat along the shoreline and in surrounding areas were restored. In 2025, authorities finally removed Muskegon from the list of severely degraded lakes. According to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the restoration efforts now generate an estimated $28 million (€23 million) in additional recreational value annually and attract roughly 500,000 extra visitors each year. However, the lake is not entirely free of pollution. Authorities continue to warn against eating certain fish species because contaminant levels remain too high. Lake Chad: A region fighting for survival The vast Sahel forms the transition zone between the Sahara Desert to the north and the African savannas to the south. Stretching across the continent from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea, it is home to one of Africa's most distinctive ecosystems: Lake Chad. Shaped by sand, wind and harsh environmental conditions, the wetland ecosystem is a critical source of water for people and wildlife and supports livelihoods across the region. In the 1960s, during periods of high water, Lake Chad covered up to around 25,000 square kilometers, slightly more than the area of New Jersey. During severe droughts in the 1970s and 1980s, it temporarily lost more than 90% of that area. Since then, the lake has partially recovered. Its size now fluctuates considerably depending on rainfall and the season — ranging from roughly 12,000 to 20,000 square kilometers. Climate change, irrigation and deforestation continue to put pressure on the lake. According to aid organizations, its decline has contributed to a wider ecological crisis across the region and threatens the food security of millions of people. Some 30 million people depend on the resources of the Lake Chad basin. Hundreds of bird species migrate from Europe and Asia to Africa each winter, and many use Lake Chad as an important stopover site. Some waterways previously blocked by dams have been reopened. In May, the African Development Bank, the Lake Chad Basin Commission and five neighboring countries launched investment projects worth $10 million. The funding is intended to help preserve the lake both as a habitat and an economic lifeline for the region. This article was originally published in German.

item.title: Norway's King Harald dies at 89
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.07
Norway's King Harald, Europe's oldest living monarch, has died at 89, the royal court said on Friday. The monarch had been receiving treatment for a rare blood condition, hemolytic anemia, at Oslo University Hospital since mid-August. His son, Prince Haakon automatically becomes King Haakon VIII, with the Norwegian Royal Court also confirming on Thursday that his wife, Mette-Marit, will become queen. The Norwegian monarch is head of state, but has a largely ceremonial and representative role. What the palace said about King Harald's death "It is with deep sadness that we announce that His Majesty King Harald passed away today. King Harald passed away peacefully at Oslo University Hospital on Friday, August 28 at 6:35 a.m.," the palace said in a statement. Harald's condition worsened over the last few days, and his wife, Queen Sonja, and son, Haakon, canceled all their engagements to be at his bedside. Harald, who had been king since 1991, suffered a series of health problems in recent years and had increasingly scaled back his official duties. However, he repeatedly ruled out abdicating, saying the oath he had taken on becoming king "lasts for life." Hundreds of well-wishers gathered outside the royal palace in Oslo overnight, holding a vigil as the king's condition deteriorated. King's body moves from hospital to palace A motor procession carrying King Harald's casket left Oslo University Hospital for the royal palace, as per television images. Thousands of people have gathered outside the palace to pay their respects to the late king and bid him farewell. They laid down flowers, cards, cuddly toys and Norwegian flags. "He was the king of the people," mourner Kristoffer Hamre told AFP. The government has announced a period of national mourning, and flags were flown at half mast on Friday. "I think he has been such a down-to-earth king who has cared about all of us, and the words he always uses when he gives a speech are so wise and so valuable," Vigdis Haug, 65, told AFP. Will King Haakon VIII be crowned? Haakon VIII will take his oath of allegiance to the constitution in a ceremony scheduled for next Tuesday. He is due to deliver a short address that will be broadcast on TV, with parliament saying the address will focus on the monarch's limited power. Norway no longer stages a traditional coronation. "King Haakon will promise and swear to govern Norway in accordance with the Constitution and law of the land," President of the Storting [Norway's Parliament], Masud Gharahkhani, said in a statement. World leaders, royals pay tribute Britain's King Charles expressed his condolences for Harald's death, paying tribute to a "towering figure" who guided his country with "warmth and humility." Norway's prime minister, Jonas Gahr Stoere, said Harald demonstrated an "unwavering faith in the Norwegian people" and "helped us to see the best in ourselves – and in one another." Swedish King Carl XVI Gustaf said the late king had "been a good friend" and would be "mourned by many in our country." "I wish my dear Godson Haakon, who now succeeds his father as head of state, success and good fortune in the important role that lies ahead of him," he added. King Frederik and Queen Mary of Denmark praised Harald's "warm personality and rock-solid calm," saying he "combined duty and responsibility with presence and humanity. He was loved like few others and will be missed by many." European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described him as "a true European and a lifelong servant of his people." "In moments of joy and sorrow, he brought Norwegians together," she said. NATO chief Mark Rutte said Harald "showed himself to be a dedicated leader. His own military roots made him a champion of the Norwegian military and a long-time friend of NATO." How will King Harald be remembered? Born in 1937, Harald became Norway's first prince to be born in the country in more than 500 years. As a child, he fled Norway with his mother and sisters following the Nazi invasion in 1940, spending much of World War II in the United States. Harald succeeded his father, King Olav V, in January 1991 and went on to modernize the Norwegian monarchy during more than 35 years on the throne. He was widely praised for his response to the 2011 far-right terrorist attacks that killed 77 people and later drew attention for speeches stressing tolerance, diversity and LGBTQ+ equality. The king's death comes after a turbulent period for Norway's royal family. Crown Princess [nonw Queen] Mette-Marit has faced scrutiny over her past correspondence with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Hoiby, was sentenced in June to four years in prison after being convicted of two rapes and dozens of other offenses, including violence against a former partner. He has appealed the verdict. Edited by: Natalie Muller

item.title: Zimbabwe crash involving church minibus kills 27
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.91
At least 27 people were killed in a minibus crash in central Zimbabwe after the vehicle carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck, police said Saturday. Seven people were injured. Police spokesperson Paul Nyathi said members of a popular Indigenous African Christian denomination, known for wearing white robes, were traveling to a conference on Friday when their minibus collided with a truck on a major highway near the town of Chivhu, about 140 kilometers (87 miles) south of the capital, Harare. The foreign-registered haulage truck was overtaking another vehicle when it collided with the minibus. Both vehicles were carrying an "unspecified" number of passengers, Nyathi said in a statement. Footage shared on social media by public broadcaster ZBC showed the mangled minibus charred to a shell. Zimbabwe faces road safety crisis Authorities say 94% of road accidents occur due to human error. Many Zimbabweans rely on privately operated minibus taxis, known locally as kombis, for everyday transportation. The vehicles are often criticized for carrying more passengers than allowed. Zimbabwe’s roads are also riddled with potholes after years of underfunding and neglect, while driving standards can be poor. In April, at least 18 people were killed when a minibus burst into flames on a highway in southern Zimbabwe. Earlier that month, a woman and her five children were killed when their vehicle collided with a haulage truck on another highway linking Zimbabwe and South Africa. Road crashes kill about 300,000 people across Africa each year, accounting for roughly a quarter of the global road death toll, according to the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa. The continent has the world’s highest road fatality rate, the commission says. This is despite Africa’s 1.5 billion people accounting for only about 3% of the world’s vehicle fleet. Edited by: Wesley Dockery If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: South Korea leans toward military conscription for women
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.81
Nearly 60% of South Koreans are now in favor of young women serving mandatory military service alongside their male counterparts, according to a recent survey, representing a significant shift in the long-held taboo against women being obliged to defend the nation. Thousands of women already serve in the South Korean armed forces on a voluntary basis, but the debate over mandatory service has always been delicate. Now, for a series of reasons that include a falling birth rate and shrinking number of recruits as well as an insistence that social equality means that women should also serve, the issue has re-emerged ahead of a reform of the national defense plan scheduled to be released this autumn. Yet, there are still those who insist women should be kept away from the front lines and, instead, that South Korea should invest more in drones and other advanced technologies. "South Korea's male-centered conscription system has long been closely connected to traditional gender roles," said Hyobin Lee, a professor at Sogang University in Seoul. "Men were generally expected to protect the country and the family and to fight in wartime, while women were expected to take primary responsibility for childbirth, childcare and the household," she told DW. A second factor is the intensifying debate about gender equality, a debate in large part driven by young men, she said. Warfare moves beyond the physical "South Korean men generally perform their military service in their early 20s, which interrupts their education, employment or early career development," Lee said. "At the same time, gender equality has become an increasingly important social value, and women's opportunities in education and employment have expanded." "As a result, some younger men ask a very simple question: If society expects equality in rights and opportunities, why does one of the country's most significant civic obligations — military service — still fall only on men?" Another contributing factor is the change in the nature of the military itself, with a shift away from physically demanding combat roles that were perceived as being more suited to men and the emergence of a national defense more heavily reliant on technology. This includes unmanned systems, cyber capabilities, information and communications technology and others that do not require physical strength. What does the study show? According to the study, carried out by the Reform Institute, the policy research arm of the conservative-leaning Reform Party, and published on August 20, almost 60% of the respondents were in favor of changing the law to require women to undergo national service. Just 34% were opposed to the idea. Nearly 65% of men were in favor — a figure that rose to 71.7% among men in their 20s and 30s — with 54.5% of women across all age groups similarly supportive. At present, all able-bodied men are required to complete a minimum of 18 months and up to 21 months of service and can be called back into service in the event of a national emergency, such as war breaking out on the tense Korean Peninsula. The latest figures highlight, however, personnel shortages that have affected South Korea's armed forces. According to the Defense Ministry, around 332,000 men were eligible to perform mandatory military service in 2019. That number fell to 257,000 men in 2022 and is forecast to shrink to just 120,000 men in 2043. While Hyobin Lee is strongly in favor of equality throughout South Korean society, she fears that obliging women to serve the same military terms as men may turn out to be a negative because so many other elements in society still lag. Women's traditional responsibilities remain unchanged "Women in South Korea still bear a much greater share of the responsibilities associated with pregnancy, childbirth and childcare," she underlined. "Having a child can still lead to career interruption or withdrawal from the labor market, and women's responsibilities for caregiving have not declined to the same extent that their participation in education and employment has increased," Lee added. "If women were also required to complete military service, the cumulative burden across their life course could become even greater," she pointed out. "In a country that is already experiencing an extremely low birth rate, it is also possible that this additional compulsory obligation could further delay or discourage marriage and childbirth." Lee comes from a family with a strong military background, with a grandfather an admiral in the navy and her father serving in the same branch of the military. But she would have had reservations in completing mandatory service herself. "If someone chooses a military career, that is completely different from compulsory service," she said. "Eighteen months in your 20s is a very significant period in a person's life. It is a time when people are studying, beginning their careers, and making important personal choices. Having to put all of that on hold because the state requires it is a substantial burden," she said. "Personally, I would have found it extremely difficult to give up 18 months of my younger years in that way." Song Young-Chae, a Seoul-based academic and human rights activist, completed two years in the infantry as a younger man, when periods of service were longer. He is opposed to mandatory service for women. "The defense of the nation is traditionally the responsibility of men, and I do not believe that there is such an urgent need to conscript women into front-line service," he told DW. Need to invest in modern technology "I served along the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) with North Korea, and it was a hard posting," he added. "I believe that we should be investing far more in drones, robots and other advanced military technologies to protect our borders." The South Korean government set up a task force in 2025 to revise the nation's basic defense plan, with troop modernization and an overhaul of the conscription system — introduced in the 1950s — high on the agenda. In an interview with the Yonhap News Agency on August 9, Military Manpower Commissioner Hong So-young admitted that the nation faces a "demographic cliff" and that reforms are urgently required. Those include potentially reducing the number of people exempt from service and requiring foreign-born people who have taken South Korean nationality to also serve. Hong made no comment about mandatory service for Korean women, but said the system needs a "fundamental" overhaul. Edited by: Shamil Shams

item.title: Spain: Thieves steal Bronze Age gold in lightning raid on Villena Museum
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.75
Thieves on Thursday raided one of the world's greatest Bronze Age gold collections in the latest of a series of high-profile heists on European museums in recent months. The early morning raid on Villena Museum in eastern Spain lasted just a few minutes. A group of thieves described by one official as "super-fast and super-professional" made off with almost the entire Treasure of Villena collection, leaving behind only a few items. What happened in the heist? "The alarm at the Villena Museum went off around 5:20 a.m.," said a spokesman for the town council, adding that within four minutes, they had all left the building again in an extremely rapid and professional operation. The collection of Bronze Age gold, some of which we now know hailed from a meteorite, was a centerpiece at the small museum in the Alicante province. "They've taken most of the treasure," the mayor of Villena, Fulgencio Cerdan told journalists. "We are absolutely devastated, I'm even trembling. The truth is that for those of us from Villena, this destroys us. It's part of our heritage, our wealth." The thieves arrived in several vehicles and apparently entered the museum "through a window," according to the Spanish government's deputy representative in Alicante, Manuel Pineda. Mayor Cerdan said that only three silver vessels, a bracelet, an earring and one of four crowns in the collection — which the thieves appeared to have "dropped" while making their exit — remained behind. "All security systems were activated," according to the Villena spokesman, who insisted there had been "no failure" by the museum.
What is the Treasure of Villena? The Treasure of Villena is a collection of more than 50 mainly gold objects, discovered in 1963 by archaeologist Jose Maria Soler in a sunken vessel in a dried out riverbed. They are dated to between 1300 and 1000 BCE. The gold pieces include 11 bowls, three bottles and 28 bracelets. The collection has been exhibited beyond Villena in cities including Madrid, Alicante, Tokyo and Kyoto, and two sets of replicas were later made to showcase the collection without taking it away from the armored display at the Villena Archaeological Museum. The relics' historical value is incalculable, although thieves might struggle to sell them even on the black market after having famously lifted them from a well-known display. The mayor said the gold alone would be worth around €1.7 million or $2 million. According to the museum's website, specialist researchers consider it the most important collection of gold tableware from the Bronze Age. It also represents the earliest known example of iron use in Western Europe, two pieces crafted from a metal that recent studies showed hailed from a meteor. Several slick heists on European museums recently, most famously the Louvre Thursday's lightning dawn raid is the latest in a series on European museums in the last year. Most famously, the Louvre Museum was hit in broad daylight last October, escaping in less than 10 minutes with jewelry worth millions. This led to the director's eventual resignation and a protracted political scandal, as well as forcing part of the museum to close for an extended period. Italy's Culture Ministry announced on Sunday that four works of "extraordinary value" by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Sicily. Shortly before that, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse stolen from a museum near Parma. Again this involved a highly-organized group of thieves who were in and out in a matter of minutes. Edited by: Rana Taha If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Norway’s new King Haakon remembers ‘dear father’ Harald in first speech as sovereign
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.70
King Haakon VIII of Norway paid tribute to his late father, King Harald V, calling him "such a wonderful papa" in his first address to the nation as monarch. "Above all, you were a person who remained committed to your values and dedicated to your duties," Haakon said Saturday in a televised speech. "We greatly mourn his loss. At the same time, it gives us consolation and strength to know that there are so many who are grieving with us." Norway's King Harald died at 89, after more than three decades on the throne, during which time he became known as a reformer and a popular monarch. In a televised speech from the palace, Haakon praised his father as a "warm and devoted family man." Haakon became emotional while speaking about his widowed mother, Queen Sonja. He noted that his parents would have celebrated their 58th wedding anniversary on Saturday. Earlier on Saturday, Haakon met at the palace with leaders of the Church of Norway, parliament and the Supreme Court. He also received Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, who viewed the late king’s casket after it was brought to the palace from Oslo University Hospital on Friday evening. Flags flew at half-mast Saturday as mourners continued to gather at the palace, laying flowers alongside tributes left the previous day by more than 20,000 people. Haakon stresses he will do things 'his own way' Haakon said he would follow his own path, as his father did before him, while reaffirming the principles of Norway’s constitutional monarchy. He is due to swear an oath in parliament on Tuesday to uphold the country’s constitution and laws. "We believe in our system of self-governance — and in democracy. We believe in a society built on the rule of law, where every individual has equal worth," he said. Haakon automatically became king following his father’s death. Norway does not hold coronations, which were abolished by parliament in 1908. But, like his father and grandfather before him, Haakon could opt for a consecration ceremony at Trondheim Cathedral, where Norwegian monarchs were crowned between 1814 and 1906. The Norwegian prime minister told Reuters news agency that Haakon shared many of his father’s qualities, particularly his "ability to create an atmosphere of togetherness." Mourning and challenges for the royal family A national period of mourning has been declared, with no date yet set for Harald’s funeral. Churches across Norway will hold memorial services Sunday, including one in Asker, south of Oslo, which the royal family was scheduled to attend. Harald was widely regarded as a symbol of an open and tolerant Norway and praised for leading a modern, modest monarchy. The king had been hospitalized in Oslo since August 17 with hemolytic anemia, a condition that causes the rapid destruction of red blood cells and can lead to fatigue and shortness of breath. His health had deteriorated in recent years, forcing him to reduce his official duties. The royal family has also faced a series of challenges. Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, has come under scrutiny over her ties to the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. In June, her son from a previous relationship was sentenced to four years in prison for two rapes, a sentence he is appealing. Mette-Marit, 53, who has a serious lung disease, underwent a lung transplant in July. item.title: What 'The Odyssey' can teach us about climate chaos
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.68
Christopher Nolan's latest blockbuster has drawn tens of millions of viewers into a world of stormy seas and cities on fire. Minus the monsters, that world is based in reality. "The Odyssey" — a post-Trojan War survival story — is set during the Bronze Age collapse of civilization. A new study links that collapse to a severe climate shift. And the authors warn of "implications for the future." Scientists have long known about a mysterious and severe drought that struck more than 3,000 years ago, overlapping with the disintegration of kingdoms and states across the Mediterranean. Research published last month sheds light on the potential cause of that drought: A slow drying trend and a quicker natural cycle of dry weather stacked on top of each other. By the late Bronze Age, the West African monsoon system had been shrinking for thousands of years, turning a green Sahara into desert. Less rain over Africa meant less over the Mediterranean. That trend amplified when the region hit a dry spell caused by natural climate cycles from the Atlantic, which saw the region swing between decades-long wet and dry periods. Katherine Power, the Stockholm University scientist who led the study, said the environment at the time could explain the mass migration and conflicts of the Odyssey's era. For decades, scholars have speculated on the reason for the large-scale movement during this time — which is also referred to as the period of the so-called Sea Peoples. Archeologists argue that climate shifts could help explain the migration and political collapse at the end of the Bronze Age. The new findings add puzzle pieces. "We don't know necessarily why those people moved," Power said. "But if we can say, 'hey, the climate was getting worse and worse to survive,' that could be a potential reason." 'A perfect storm of calamities' And that, she says, is relevant to today. Europe's major rivers are at record lows, and drought is creating conditions for devastating wildfires as well as fueling historic crop-loss. That includes France's lowest maize harvest in 50 years. The same cycles of wetting and drying from the Atlantic are still at play, but they're now happening in the context of a world that's heating as a result of humans burning oil, gas and coal. "I think it is even more alarming and even more of a threat," Power said. But does what happened then give insights into what might happen now? Eric H. Cline, archeologist at George Washington University, who wrote a book on the roots of the Bronze Age crisis, said drought and disease were part of the "perfect storm of calamities" that led to societal downfall. He sees parallels to today. In an email to DW, he said "we should be very concerned" about climate change as a stressor for the collapse of civilization. "That fear is not too dramatic at all." He added that on his most optimistic days, he believes "we will come to our senses and sidestep that possibility at some point." Was there a trigger moment for the collapse? Power's research sought to explore what patterns might lie behind isolated Bronze Age drought events. They started by examining plant spores, ice cores, cave stones, and other natural records that pointed to drought. Then, she and co-author Stockholm paleoclimate scientist Qiong Zhang turned to modeling to get a broader picture. Their model looked at the whole planet, overlaid with a grid, each cell covering a roughly 125-kilometer (78-mile) area. A supercomputer then calculated the conditions in each of these cells, for every month, across thousands of years. That let the scientists look at the entire Mediterranean. "We're not now stuck with just one core or one cave," Power said. "We can see farther afield and build a whole picture." What they found was not a single event that dramatically and suddenly changed the climate. Instead, shorter cycles of wetting and drying lined up with a longer warming trend. "When we are looking for connections between climate changes and civilization changes, we often are looking for that big, huge, abrupt, catastrophic event," Power said, adding that it is "slow, gradual changes that push a society over a threshold.” She said it could have been a steady fall in water supply that led to a slow decline in crops, which prompted people to migrate, triggering conflict. "It doesn't take very much to push a society over the threshold that they're comfortable with," Power said. "What if you add something more to the mix? Maybe then that pushes you a bit farther, and you can't quite recover from that." Edited by: Tamsin Walker

item.title: The man behind Srebrenica: Ratko Mladic dies at 84
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.16
More than 30 years after the end of the 1992-1995 war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Srebrenica remains emblematic of its brutality. And no one is more closely linked to the genocide that took place in the small town in eastern Bosnia than Ratko Mladic, the former commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb army. Although the United Nations had declared Srebrenica a "safe area," Bosnian Serb forces attacked the town. Within just a few days in July 1995, they expelled women and children, then killed more than 8,300 unarmed Muslim boys and men in the nearby village of Potocari — on Mladic's direct orders, according to the verdict handed down by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) in The Hague 22 years later. At the time, Srebrenica was the largest massacre in Europe since World War II. The ICTY classified it as genocide. Mladic was also held responsible for other war crimes beyond the Srebrenica genocide. Under his command, the years-long siege of Sarajevo began at the start of the war. The city was shelled for more than 40 months, killing around 11,000 people, including more than 1,600 children. Mladic always claimed that he targeted only military objectives. But numerous reports and intercepted radio communications indicate that civilian facilities and residential areas were also deliberately attacked. Around 100,000 people were killed during the three-year war in Bosnia, while some 2.2 million were driven from their homes in cities and villages across the country half of its total population at the time. 'Butcher of the Balkans' In 2017, Mladic was sentenced to life in prison by the tribunal in The Hague. International media dubbed him "the Butcher of the Balkans." He was found responsible for some of the most serious war crimes and the genocide committed during the Bosnian war. Mladic consistently denied any responsibility. He saw himself as an avenger of the Serbs for centuries of Ottoman rule in the Balkans, and viewed Bosnia's Muslims, who today call themselves Bosniaks, as direct descendants of the Turks. In front of his soldiers, he referred to them simply as "the Turks" and showed no empathy. "Borders are always drawn with blood, and states are marked with graves," he is quoted as saying. Career in the Yugoslav army At the beginning of the Croatian war in June 1991, when Serbs living in Croatia rose up against the independence of the former Yugoslav republic with active support from Serbia, Mladic's role fundamentally changed. As a colonel in the Yugoslav army, he became commander of the 9th Corps in the Croatian city of Knin. His task was to organize Serb militias and support them in their fight against Croatian independence. Under Mladic's command, the Croatian cities of Sibenik and Zadar were bombarded, and Croatian civilians were driven from surrounding towns and villages. In May 1992, he took on the same role in Bosnia. By then promoted to general, Mladic became commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb forces, seeking to establish a territorial link between Serb-held areas in the east and west of the former Yugoslav republic. Flight, arrest and final verdict At the height of his career, Colonel General Ratko Mladic was a fervent Serbian nationalist. But he began his career as a committed communist. Born in eastern Bosnia in 1943, Mladic was just 2 years old when his father, a Partisan follower of Yugoslavia's longtime communist leader Josip Broz Titos, was killed by fascist Croatian Ustasha militia. The loss is often described as a formative influence, shaping his later worldview. As a young man, Mladic embarked on a military career, attending the Military Academy in Belgrade. He later graduated at the top of his class and quickly rose through the ranks of the Yugoslav army, which for many years was regarded as one of the most stable institutions in the multiethnic state. Serbian nationalist Before the end of the Bosnian war in late 1995, Mladic was indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. But he evaded arrest for years. Supported by networks within the Serbian military and political establishment, he lived largely undisturbed underground and was even seen in public. He was finally arrested in 2011, after 16 years on the run and mounting international pressure. The subsequent trial in The Hague lasted a total of 523 days. Nearly 600 witnesses testified, while numerous documents and other pieces of evidence were examined. Mladic was ultimately sentenced to life in prison, among other charges for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. In 2021, an appeals chamber upheld the verdict, making it final. Legally, this established his responsibility as one of the principal figures behind the crimes committed during the Bosnian war. War criminal who saw himself as a hero Internationally, the verdict was hailed as historic. UN officials saw it as a signal that accountability can still be pursued decades after crimes are committed. For many survivors and relatives of the victims, the verdict was a long overdue, but an important acknowledgment of their suffering. Mladic himself, however, remained defiant to the end. Throughout the trial, he maintained he was innocent, calling the charges against him "disgusting" and the tribunal "satanic." Many of his supporters in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs still see him as a hero. While he is regarded internationally as a war criminal, his admirers continue to portray him as a defender of Serbian interests and a hero — even painting his likeness on walls. While he was still on the run, Mladic threatened his pursuers, claiming he always carried a poison pill and that he would never be captured alive. But he never swallowed the pill during his decades in hiding, and later survived several strokes while in prison. Mladic died on August 27, 2026, at the prison hospital in The Hague at the age of 84. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Why Germany's military is betting on gamers
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.16
Gamescom, which runs from August 26-30 in Cologne, is promoted as the world's largest video game trade show. Last year, two-thirds of its non-industry visitors were male, with over 40% of them between the ages of 16 and 25. Those are precisely the young people the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, is trying to reach as it urgently seeks to expand its ranks. Germany's military aims to have 260,000 active-duty soldiers by 2035. The German government has supplied hundreds of billions of euros to modernize the country's armed forces. Defense has become a priority for Germany in the face of the current global security situation. Career advice in camouflage The Bundeswehr set up shop at Gamescom for the first time in 2016. It's been back every year since. A brand-new, olive-green Caracal off-road vehicle is one of the main attractions. Alongside it are laptops belonging to the Bundeswehr's Center for Cyber Operations — tasked with cyber defense, among other responsibilities. Under a watchful eye, visitors can try their hand at hacking. At another station, visitors can put on VR headsets to get a glimpse into the working life of a soldier aboard a naval vessel. Pilots, aircraft mechanics and air traffic controllers present their professions in a 3D experience. Elsewhere, several fit mountain infantry soldiers stand beside a pull-up bar, where visitors are invited to test their strength. New this year is a career lounge where interested visitors can have what the Bundeswehr is calling "career counseling sessions." The atmosphere is positive, with soldiers promoting their jobs without being pushy, taking time to answer questions from visitors — who have primarily come to Gamescom to have fun, meet friends and play the latest games. Do gamers make good soldiers? A representative study by Germany's Bitkom digital association found that one in five people found it likely that video and computer games teach skills that could be useful in wartime — training reaction speed and problem-solving, for instance. However, being a good gamer doesn't necessarily make for a good soldier. "We need people who are comfortable with technology," Lt. Gen. Robert Sieger, president of the Federal Office for Bundeswehr Personnel Management, told DW. "What we don't want are people who think we're playing an ego shooter or some kind of shooting game. That doesn't do justice to the seriousness of the situation at all. War isn't a game. As a soldier and a general, it is important to me that people understand the seriousness of what we do." For Sieger, educating people about the Bundeswehr and the range of careers it offers is a central reason for having a booth at Gamescom. "We're an integral part of our country's safety net. We have to simply be here and show what it means to stand up for the freedom of our country, be that as a soldier or a civilian." Criticism of Bundeswehr presence The Bundeswehr is represented alongside many other employers in the gaming trade show's Job Area, including Germany's federal police, retailer Edeka and software company DATEV. Gamescom is, however, still a video game trade show — and not everyone is comfortable with the Bundeswehr getting close to the gaming world. The German Peace Society — United War Resisters has criticized the Bundeswehr presence at Gamescom, along with booths operated by Germany's foreign intelligence service and defense companies such as Airbus and Rheinmetall. Peace campaigner Marius Pletsch says the Bundeswehr uses inappropriate slogans, designed to appeal specifically to gamers, and distorts the image of military service. "We think it's wrong to lure young people to the booth by appealing to their sense of adventure. We don't think the Bundeswehr should be represented at a trade show that is primarily about video games and leisure to boost its personnel numbers," he told DW. For two days, the peace organization will have a booth outside the trade show exhibition halls, providing information about conscientious objection to military service. Bundeswehr: Not just any job "Being a soldier isn't a normal job," the peace initiative said in a statement. Lt. Gen. Sieger uses similar terms, but puts it somewhat differently: "Being a soldier isn't a job like any other. We put our lives on the line for the security of our people." He reaches a different conclusion than the peace advocates, though. "It would be downright negligent for an organization responsible for our country's security not to be an inherent part of society," Sieger said. "As an inherent part of society and a modern employer, of course we have our rightful spot here in the Job Area, just as we have over recent years." What do young Gamescom visitors make of the Bundeswehr's presence? "Morally questionable, but a good employer," said Dennis, a 22-year-old computer science student, although he said the Bundeswehr wasn't for him. Dominik, 26, said he was pleased that the German military was represented at Gamescom. "You can actually have a pretty good conversation with them. They're all very nice," he said. He said he may even consider working for the Bundeswehr's cyber defense division. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: What's the difference between TPU vs. GPU?
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 6.54
What's the difference between TPU vs. GPU? Why so many acronyms? First, we had CPU and GPU. Then came AMD's Accelerated Processing Unit (APU, if you're nasty). And with the advent of the AI PC and smartphones, we've welcomed the NPU (Neural Processing Unit). But now, thanks to Google, we're getting yet another chip: the TPU. First internally deployed by Google back in 2015, the TPU, or Tensor Processing Unit, is the company's proprietary AI accelerator designed to handle all the complex mathematical calculations necessary for artificial intelligence and machine learning (ML) workloads. Designed for cloud-based applications, the TPU is used primarily for data centers. However, this term has recently popped up in the new Pixel 11 smartphone by way of its Google Tensor G6 chip, which the company says packs "50 percent more TPU compute." So which is it? The answer is confusingly both. In the Pixel 11 series smartphones, the TPU is basically Google's fancy-schmancy way to say NPU. This version of a TPU handles camera and image processing as well as local AI tasks. But the data center TPU is decidedly different from a smartphone version, a traditional NPU and a GPU, although there are a few similarities. In order to help keep your chipset lingo straight, we're here to formally introduce you to the real TPU and clear up some of the misconceptions. What the heck is a TPU? Great question. A TPU is a chip Google created to deal with cloud-based AI and machine learning tasks in the company's data centers. Known as an AI accelerator, a TPU is optimized to perform millions of mathematical calculations on the fly in AI models, something that NPUs and GPUs do as well. We've been talking a lot about AI and ML, which for many of us will call into play an NPU. As it should, since we've been beaten over the head with them ad nauseum thanks to Apple, the various PC and smartphone makers and the chip manufacturers. If you're unfamiliar, NPUs are the chips you'll find in all your modern smartphones, Macs and PCs. They do all the heavy lifting for your generative and agentic AI tasks, whether it's erasing an ex from a photo or using ChatGPT to build out a three-day travel itinerary. For the Pixel 11 phones, the TPU replaces the NPU, with Google claiming "up to 3.5 times faster AI processing while using up to 3.5 times less energy." GPUs are familiar to many of us, especially if you're a gamer or work with 3D models. Before AI, we wanted a powerful GPU to run graphically demanding games like Crysis 3 at the highest settings with blistering frame rates and buttery smooth rendering. Post-AI, GPUs still do that as well as handle AI training and crypto mining, hence why the best ones cost an arm, a leg and a firstborn. A jack-of-all-trades, a GPU can do many things well depending on how powerful it is. So what's the difference between TPU, NPU and GPU? The things that set these chipsets apart are largely use cases and scale. While TPUs are used for cloud-based AI running in Google data centers, NPUs, on-device TPUs and GPUs can be found in your smartphones and laptops. TPUs have the largest scale by far. Thanks to its specialized architecture, a TPU is employed in accelerating massive computations used in LLM (Large Language Models) and massive deep learning (DL) tasks. TPUs utilize a hardware layout called a systolic array that allows data to go from one unit to the next in a 2D grid of multipliers, which help eliminate potential bottlenecks. That means the calculation output becomes the input for the next unit without having to write back to memory, unlike GPUs, which are stuck juggling data between their compute units and their high-bandwidth memory. When servicing big AI companies such as Anthropic and Midjourney, which serve billions of AI requests daily, relying on a GPU-based solution can be costly in terms of bottlenecks, latency and power efficiency. Since a TPU isn't cycling back and forth to read and write memory, it's a better fit for training large-scale neural networks and other massive workloads. Living in our smartphones, IoT and laptops, NPUs and Google's on-device TPUs are relegated to the shallow end of the AI/ML pool. They're optimized for low-power tasks, which is why they're perfect for things like camera effects and real-time translation. A TPU can do an LLM, but it has to be a small and really well-defined local one. Which one is better? "Better" is relative. Each AI accelerator is best in a specific use case. NPUs and on-device TPUs are better for handling the smaller mainstream AI tasks. Their low power consumption means they won't be too much of a draw on your smartphone, laptop or smartwatch. However, it's got enough kick to do real-time translation, blur your background during a call or help you remember that obscure show you swore you saw back in the '90s. TPUs are the cost- and energy-efficient solution that helps run the AI/ML/DL show globally. Processing millions of mathematical calculations while training ML and DL models at massive scale means TPUs are purely for big data centers. With their innate flexibility, GPUs can take on both small- and large-scale AI workloads as well as run games, edit video and run simulations. If you want to run local LLMs, a beefy GPU is the way to go.

item.title: Why would you pay $359 for the most expensive Whoop membership?
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.89
Why would you pay $359 for the most expensive Whoop membership? The highest tier offers more data, but you may not need it. When you're purchasing a fitness wearable, one of the important considerations is the ongoing cost of its use. There are some products that don't require subscriptions to access key features for the devices, but many brands will levy monthly or annual charges to get the most data out of your wearable sensors. Whoop is one of those companies where owning a device means you'll likely be paying a recurring fee. And those annual costs aren't insignificant, especially for the most comprehensive plan. Here's what you get and why the investment might be valuable. What are your Whoop membership options? Whoop has three membership tiers. The company recently made its Advanced Labs blood test tools available without a subscription (though not without lab fees), which is a nice perk for anyone who wants to get additional insights on their own pace and budget rather than committing to a long-term plan. But on the whole, Whoop wearables are meant to be paired with a subscription. The least expensive option with the fewest features is Whoop One. While the company does offer some discounts for new and first-time customers, in general this plan costs $199 a year. Its feature set includes fitness and recovery insights, strain and sleep tracking, a strength trainer, estimations of VO2 maximums, integration with Natural Cycles and a personalized AI-powered coach. Whoop Peak is the middle choice at $239 a year. In addition to the features of the One plan, it offers the company's health monitor, stress monitor and healthspan features. Healthspan includes Whoop Age and Pace of Aging, two programs that promise to deliver insights centered around longevity and long-term health based on sleep, strain and fitness data. Then there's the big-ticket choice. With an annual fee of $359, Whoop Life combines all the tools of the other two tiers with blood pressure insights and its Heart Screener package. Customers also receive priority phone support, plus their device will have more upscale materials, including a 5.0 medical-grade sensor. Is Whoop Life membership worth the cost? First off, there is an important caveat: I am not a medical professional or a fitness expert. If you have particular needs in either of those areas, then be sure to confer with a qualified professional before making any big decisions. In fact, talk to a doctor if you have any questions or concerns about your physical health or the results you get from your wearable. The two biggest exclusive features of the Life plan are for tracking blood pressure and cardiovascular health. For instance, the more advanced monitor has the ability to take an electrocardiogram, or ECG, which can help detect signs of atrial fibrillation. Bear in mind that Whoop has offered limitations on who should use those different perks; for instance, the ECG tests aren't intended for users with a known arrhythmia other than AFib. However, if you have a family history of heart issues or concerns about your cardiovascular risks, then having a large amount of data history to draw on can offer peace of mind. That's tough to quantify with a dollar amount, but $359 a year might feel very worthwhile. If you don't have strong concerns about heart health or blood pressure, then it's likely that the Life plan is more data than you need. In fact, the Whoop One plan covers a whole lot of useful data and stats for the average user, so even the middle tier might feel like overkill, especially if you're just beginning your fitness journey or if you simply don't care about quantifying every aspect of your health.

item.title: How to use the new Siri app in iOS 27
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.77
How to use the new Siri app in iOS 27 Assuming your device is new enough to use it. Siri has been around since 2011, and for most of that time it's lagged behind assistants from Google, OpenAI and Anthropic. iOS 27 is Apple's attempt to close that gap, rebuilding the assistant with new AI capabilities and, for the first time, giving it a standalone app for conversational, chatbot-style use. Getting started with Siri AI on your iPhone is easy, as long as you meet a few requirements. This includes not only updating to iOS 27 first, but also checking to see if your device is compatible with Apple Intelligence. Setting up Siri AI on iOS 27 Even if you have an iPhone running iOS 27, it may not be compatible with Siri AI. Apple Intelligence and the new Siri features are limited to the iPhone 15 Pro and later. Older iPhones, the base iPhone 15 included, are stuck with classic-and-dumb Siri. You may also have some trouble using Siri AI depending on your region and language. For now, it only works in English. Users in the EU or China won't be able to access it either due to local regulations.
