Charlevoix, Quebec, Canada: Outdoor Activities In La Malbaie From Baie-Saint-Paul, explore the rest of the region by pushing east along the St. Lawrence Route, a coastal road that bends and climbs above the valley below. All roads eventually arrive at Fairmont Le Manoir Richelieu, a luxury hotel perched on the cliffs of Pointe-au-Pic. Adorned in the full Châteauesque regalia of a French country manor transplanted to a Canadian bluff, the hotel dates to 1899. A steamship company built the original property in hopes of luring Victorian travelers off its boats. It burned in 1928 and was rebuilt the following year in the grand style it still wears. The golf course, opened in 1925 by former U.S. President William Howard Taft, boasts riverfront vistas that make it one of Canada's most photographed fairways. (It’s open from May to October.) Golf might have helped the hotel land the G7 Summit in 2018, and lends credence to the persistent local legend that Winston Churchill and Franklin Roosevelt stayed here. (Their wartime Quebec Conferences were actually held at the Château Frontenac, in the city.) A treatment at the Moment Spa and dinner at Le Saint-Laurent, the river doing most of the scenery's work, make the case for why people have found reasons to end up on this cliff for well over a century. There’s also the quirk of a casino staring at you steps from the hotel’s entrance, to remind us that Quebec’s quiet luxury is, pleasantly, idiosyncratic. Some of the region’s history ends up on the cliff in a more literal sense. Cité-Mémoire Charlevoix, a free, open-air multimedia experience, turns the region’s history into a kind of cinematic dreamscape. In La Malbaie’s Pointe-au-Pic sector, projections bring historic characters, stories and landscapes to life on buildings, rock faces and other surfaces, while a companion app provides the voices and stories behind what you see. Charlevoix, Quebec, Canada: Embrace The Pace Anyone who arrives in Charlevoix with an activity-packed checklist and no downtime is doing it wrong. No trip to the region is complete without the freedom to explore the countryside, with the phone on silent and the watch tucked away. Permanent settlement began around 1675, and the region developed in relative geographic isolation. That Charlevoix has retained its cultural coherence to this day is even more special than the specifics — the nostalgia for Gilded Age cottages, circus-founder folklore, wine, cheese, and art. Together, it evokes a classic image of pastoral European charm, exported directly from an earlier era to the edge of the St. Lawrence River. It’s hard to put an accurate price tag on that experience, but it’s unsurprising that those who treasure it pay a lot. Power Corporation patriarch Paul Desmarais Sr. maintained an estate there until his death in 2013. Another local billionaire, Laliberté, invested $10 million Canadian for a 10 percent stake in Gauthier’s Le Massif development—two Charlevoix natives continuing to invest in the region that launched their careers. That a home to multiple billionaires doubles as a fantastic vacation spot is one of Canada’s best-kept secrets. “The Tafts went to Murray Bay for a hundred years and nobody marketed it,” said Jeremy Savory, founder of Millionaire Migrant. “Whereas Aspen, the Hamptons, Como, they got discovered, then priced, then crowded, and then everyone who went for the quiet went looking for the next quiet place. Charlevoix just skipped that.” Going so far out of the way to escape a fast-paced, modern world isn’t for everyone—and that’s the point. Le Germain's farm-to-suite philosophy and the Manoir's century of unbroken grandeur are two different bets on the same idea: that authenticity, cultivated carefully enough, becomes its own form of luxury.

item.title: Who Are The Americans That Are Increasingly Moving Overseas And Why?
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 3.91
No one knows exactly how many Americans live overseas, but the statistics are clear: interest in moving abroad is increasing, including among middle-class professionals, Californians, LGBTQ+ households, and, unsurprisingly, those with European ancestry. More Americans Are Moving Overseas An analysis by The Wall Street Journal in early 2026 estimates that anywhere between 4 and 9 million Americans are living abroad at the moment, stating that for the first time in America's 250 years of existence, more people have moved out than in. This great emigration has been documented elsewhere, and the Treasury Department's Federal Register section 6039G publishes its quarterly list of Americans who have chosen to repatriate. In the quarter ending June 30, 2026, 1,781 names were on the list, up from 1,462 in April. Half Of All Americans Who Live Overseas Are In Three Countries In 2024, the Social Security Administration (SSA) reported that around 760,000 Americans receive benefits while living abroad, totaling more than $7.5 billion in benefits. The top three countries are Canada, Japan, and Mexico, which account for over half of all beneficiaries. In Europe, Germany, the U.K., Italy, Portugal, and Spain are the highest recipients, while after Japan, the Philippines and South Korea rank highest in Asia. Americans Are Moving Overseas For A Variety Of Reasons For decades, having a U.S. passport meant you could move around the world unchecked, but as America tightens its entry rules, reciprocity is reshaping visa policies for Americans. Between 2025 and 2026, the U.S. lost visa-free access to seven nations, including Brazil. This led to the Henley Passport Index 2026 ranking the U.S. passport as the 10th most powerful in the world, behind 38 other countries, including Malaysia, Lithuania, Iceland, Slovakia, Canada, and the United Arab Emirates. Last year, it ranked at its lowest level in history, number 12, a fall from the 20 years before, when it consistently ranked within the top ten. Beyond this, others are interested in finding access to more affordable healthcare (particularly true for Americans of retirement age) or schooling. American families are increasingly treating the residency rights that come with golden visa programs, for instance, as part of an inheritance, an insurance policy for healthcare, education and the future freedom to move. Which Americans Are Moving Overseas? The market for Americans looking for golden visa programs is booming, but there are also other ways of moving, whether that be by applying for passports through citizenship-by-descent routes or opting for some of the world’s retirement visas. Those Who Can Apply For Citizenship-By-Descent Many Americans are eligible for citizenship by descent—estimates suggest this could be as many as 30 million, but those emigration windows are slowly closing, particularly across Europe, as governments update their immigration laws. Americans can claim Irish citizenship if they have an Irish-born grandparent or a parent who was already an Irish citizen before their birth. Applications take about one year to process and have been increasing markedly according to 2026 figures—11,601 registrations were completed in 2024, up from 7,726 in 2023. LGBTQ+ American Households Who Are Over 55 Are Interested In Moving Overseas In 2025, research by GetGoldenVisa showed that a ‘silent migration’ was seemingly happening among LGBTQ+ Americans. This consultancy data suggests that over a 20-month period, the fastest-growing cohort of departing Americans was of LGBTQ+ households aged 55 or older. For this demographic, choosing a new country can serve as an insurance policy for legal recognition. Affluent Californians The Los Angeles Times reports that Californians are pursuing golden visa programs at historic rates. California is home to the largest number of the world’s wealthiest people and has more billionaires than any other state. One of the drivers may be California’s proposed billionaire tax, which would impose a 5% one-time tax on Californians with net worth exceeding €1 billion. The big draws in Europe are Portugal and Malta’s golden visa program. New Zealand’s golden visa program offers a faster route than EU countries, however, and Dominic Jones, Managing Director of Greener Pastures New Zealand, says, “The U.S. is also our strongest market for New Zealand’s Active Investor Plus visa. Americans represent the largest proportion of our Greener Pastures invested clients as well as those we are currently supporting through the visa process.” Jones adds that “The billionaire tax debate is adding to the broader questions we’re hearing from wealthy Americans around taxation, policy certainty and where they want to live, invest and hold their assets long term.” Middle Class Americans Immigrant Invest, a Malta-based citizenship-by-investment consultancy, told Business Insider that salaried professionals and retirees now account for 25% of its U.S. consultation calls, up from around 15% in 2025. This includes doctors, academics, lawyers and tech workers, while the share of ultra-rich consultation calls has decreased. With the cost of investment programs remaining stable in recent years, Business Insider’s conclusion is that more Americans are looking to move. Many golden visa programs in the Caribbean offer a more affordable option—Príncipe, an island off the west coast of Africa, starts at $90,000, while Vanuatu in the South Pacific starts at $130,000. This view is supported by Jones of Greener Pastures, New Zealand, who says, “We’re seeing interest in New Zealand extend well beyond high-net-worth Americans,” particularly from middle-class Americans. Jones adds that these aren’t just wealthy investors looking at the Active Investor Plus visa (the golden visa program). Many of these Americans are professionals exploring pathways such as New Zealand’s Skilled Migrant visa. Jones concludes “that the desire for an international alternative is becoming much broader across the U.S. and is no longer limited to just the wealthy.” While More Americans Are Moving Overseas, Many More Are Interested In Doing So Henley & Partners’ 2026 Private Wealth Migration Report says that demand from U.S. clients doubled in 2025 compared with 2024, but many were U.S. residents considering future moves rather than current ones. It is clear that many Americans are thinking about different residency options to protect their futures; much more than ever used to be the case, when it used to be just high-net-worth individuals. Zaid Aldayriyeh, Founder of Citizenship Bay, says that “while renouncing U.S. citizenship remains uncommon, the Treasury report cited at the outset represents the final stage of a much longer decision-making process.” Citizenship Bay’s own consultancy data points to growing interest in building international optionality long before anyone considers expatriation. The firm's recent data found that 32% of Americans seeking second citizenship or residency cited having a ‘Plan B’ as their primary motivation; 69% of inquiries came from families; and inquiries into Italian citizenship increased by 56% following recent changes to European citizenship programs. This view is echoed by Jones, who states that “these conversations are about international optionality and having another place where they can invest, establish residency and create a long-term option for themselves and their families.” So instead of viewing the Treasury report simply as a count of Americans leaving the United States, Zaid says it reflects a broader shift in how affluent families are thinking about international mobility, long-term planning and protecting future options. The conclusion is that these golden visa investment programs offer the option to move, particularly those with low residency requirements, rather than a requirement to move. The picture that emerges from these datasets is not a mass exodus overseas but a broadening mindset, with countries becoming more of a residency Plan B for a growing class of Americans across varied income levels, taking insurance against perceived political, tax and healthcare risks. For many, these programs are about optionality and future flexibility rather than an immediate move. MORE FROM FORBES

item.title: Why National Parks Are Important For Wildlife, History And Local Economies
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 3.37
America’s National Parks have been called “the best idea we ever had” by the conservationist Wallace Stegner, a phrase that filmmaker Ken Burns used in his 2009 PBS series The National Parks: America’s Best Idea. It’s safe to say these parks are unique in the world, preserving such important areas. National parks are significant because they were established to preserve America’s history and to protect the scenic features of the American landscape from development. They are also critical in protecting wildlife and maintaining ecological balance, as well as clean air and water. They offer preserved landscapes, places for the American people to recreate: to hike, boat, swim and camp in some of the most majestic scenery in the world. However, the U.S. National Park System is facing pressures in governance, funding and climate change. For example, The Guardian reported that Yosemite National Park has experienced massive overcrowding. This is after the park announced that it would no longer have a reservation system in 2026 and the Trump administration cut millions from the NPS budget and also cut park staff significantly. This makes it even more important to understand why the parks are more than simply beautiful nature and how to be a good park visitor. A Brief History of the U.S. The National Park System The National Park system arose from a need to protect some of the most spectacular, beautiful, and scenic places in the U.S. The idea had been put forward as early as 1832, when artist George Catlin was exploring the Dakotas. Catlin proposed that the government should step in and preserve this landscape and others for future generations. He was among many such artists and explorers who voiced a similar idea. They were aware that as the United States expanded westward, the dramatic and unique landscapes they were encountering risked being despoiled by settlement. It wasn’t until 1861 that an explorer named Ferdinand Hayden, who led the government’s newly established geological survey, visited the headwaters of the Yellowstone River with biologists and zoologists to explore an area that had attracted hunters and trappers for the previous century. He recommended its preservation, and in 1872, under President Ulysses S. Grant, the first national park was established as Yellowstone National Park, decades before the economic value of tourism was known. Sequoia National Park was next in 1890, followed by Mt. Rainier National Park in 1899, Crater Lake National Park in 1902 and Yosemite National Park in 1890. There are now 63 major national parks, from Acadia National Park (1919) in Maine to Volcanoes National Park (1961) on the island of Hawaii. As of today, the national parks are still designed to protect these incredible places for current and future visitors. Education has also come to the forefront, and increasingly, scientists are monitoring these parks, which serve as baselines for the effects of climate change. This is especially important for sensitive environments like Virgin Islands National Park, where coral reefs are closely watched, and the remaining glaciers in Glacier National Park. The Importance Of The National Parks Extends Beyond Nature Our national parks protect some of our most precious landscapes and provide a sanctuary for plants, wildlife and historic areas. They also keep aspects of American history visible and real for visitors. The national parks are a significant economic driver, with admission fees that help fund their maintenance. That economic impact is also felt in the areas surrounding the park, as hotels, campgrounds, restaurants and shops in nearby towns benefit from serving visitors. Visitors to national parks in 2022 spent more than $42 billion in nearby communities of parks, creating and supporting jobs in tourism and transportation in neighboring communities. Overcrowding can be a serious issue in some of the most popular national parks, such as Grand Canyon National Park, Zion National Park and Great Smoky Mountains National Park. Some use reservation systems to control visitation, which would otherwise overwhelm the parks. However, some were cancelled by the Department of the Interior. Erosion and overuse are major problems in overcrowded areas. Since the Park Service has lost a significant percentage of its workforce over the last few years, The National Parks Conservation Association says the cuts have resulted in fewer ranger-led programs, postponed maintenance and drained resource protection. Conservation One of the most basic aspects of national parks is that they are safeguards for conservation. They offer protection for animals and plants that, in many cases, are rare and found nowhere else on the planet. In Great Smoky Mountains National Park, there are 30 species of salamanders, and some, like the red-cheeked salamander, are found nowhere else in the world. The park’s waterways help supply the water needs of millions of people in the Southeast. Like many parks, it provides a bulwark against commercial interests in agriculture, development and timber industries. National parks can play a role in protecting watersheds and old-growth forests. So much of what they do is to maintain the unique ecosystem they were established to protect a century ago. If these systems were allowed to be changed or compromised, it could have dire effects on a wide region. These parks provide a living laboratory for scientists to monitor, study, and preserve. As such, they offer a baseline for studying climate change. For the general public, they can function as classrooms without walls, places where we can learn about various ecosystems and our role in preserving them. History And Culture Our national parks are essential for maintaining historic landmarks, as well as indigenous heritage and culture. They accomplish this by collaborating with Tribal Nations on educational initiatives and with help from federal programs. For example, Yellowstone National Park is actually on the sacred lands of the Shoshone, Crow and Northern Cheyenne peoples. The national parks have established more than 250 co-stewardship agreements with Tribal Nations to manage federal lands and identify and protect sacred resources. Tribal nations also take part in decisions and policy-making related to local ecology. The protection of Native American sites, from cave dwellings to sacred landscapes such as those found in Canyon de Chelly and Mesa Verde, is also vital. That includes helping to maintain local cultural traditions. Communities National parks offer a vital outlet for visitors to stay physically and mentally healthy. There are endless walks and hikes on offer, and the sheer beauty of the landscapes can go a long way to calming and reducing stress. Beyond these benefits, there are myriad ways to have family fun in the national parks, from hiking and fishing to camping. The parks are ideal places to give kids space to play and enjoy the outdoors, and often foster family bonding. Ranger programs aimed at kids can open their eyes to the animals and plants around them, teach them why conservation matters, and inspire them to protect the earth. Economic Growth National parks are essential supporters of local economies and small businesses. They drive regional job growth through visitor spending and infrastructure investments. For example, 4.5 million visitors to Yellowstone National Park spent $623 million in the park and neighboring communities in 2023, supporting 8,560 jobs in the area, according to a National Park Service report. How Can Visitors Help Preserve National Parks The best way for visitors to support national parks is to practice responsible recreation and not be a “touron.” That includes Leave No Trace policies, which require you to pack out all trash, respect wildlife and stay on designated trails. You can take it a step further by reducing light pollution at your campsite by turning off unnecessary lighting. Visiting lesser-known parks, such as Isle Royale in Lake Superior, can help soften the impact of overtourism on better-known parks, such as Yellowstone. You can take it one step further by volunteering your time at national parks, pitching in to maintain trails, tidy campgrounds and serve as a docent at ranger stations. The National Park Service Volunteer Program is a great place to look for such opportunities. Donations are always welcome at the National Park Foundation and the National Parks Conservation Association. National parks cannot protect themselves but require consistent funding, savvy management and community support. Why Protecting National Parks Matters For Future Generations Forests and wetlands provide climate benefits by absorbing carbon dioxide, helping to create a cleaner planet for future generations. The same holds for protected watersheds, which can offer clean water for future generations. The parks also protect and preserve Native American history and sacred tribal lands. Our national parks are where Americans build stewardship — that sense of responsibility and care for the natural world that ideally leads to long-term protection. The federal government has continued to trim these budgets, cutting both seasonal and full-time positions. This affects visitor experience, as maintenance lags and visitor centers and roads suffer the impact. At the end of fiscal year 2025, about $24 billion was needed to repair aging infrastructure and restore much-needed programs. These budget constraints mean that smaller parks may face reduced operating hours or even closures. America’s national parks are an extraordinary resource, protecting some of the country's treasured landscapes, flora and fauna, and safeguarding its history, landmarks and Native American culture. They provide recreational opportunities for millions and safeguard fragile ecosystems, yet a lack of funding and political gamesmanship often undermines their mission. There is no question that protecting our national parks can benefit future generations. It’s a gift to protect and share the landscapes, ecosystems, and cultural heritage found in these parks. Maintaining biosystems for the future is critical, not just for their sake.

item.title: Burning Man 2026: The Most Outrageous Mutant Vehicles And Art Installations In The Black Rock Desert
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 2.62
Every year, Black Rock City appears on a dry lakebed in one of Nevada’s harshest areas, then disappears just as fast. There are no paved roads or permanent structures. Instead, glowing art moves through dust storms, ships show up on the horizon, and sculptures as large as small buildings fill the empty playa. Burning Man returns to Nevada’s Black Rock Desert in the first week of September and attracts estimated crowds of over 70,000 people. This year’s theme, Axis Mundi, looks at how people, communities, and nature are connected. The art features major Honoraria projects and hundreds of other works, many of which take months to create and use lighting, sound, fire, and engineering. Mutant vehicles are some of the most striking sights at Black Rock City. They look part machine and part ghost, moving slowly across the dry lakebed like relics from a lost civilization that never stopped building. A few years ago, I wrote about some of the most well-known vehicles and the people who made them. In 2026, the playa will see new creations alongside old favorites. Some are quieter this year, some are almost ridiculous, but all of them share a strange sense of purpose. These are carefully built obsessions, brought out into a harsh landscape that will wipe them away by the end of the week. Some of my favorites are coming back too, like El Pulpo Magnifico, Duane Flatmo's fire-breathing octopus, and the Monaco, a 40-foot ship with three masts that sails across dust instead of water. Instead of only admiring the wild designs, I wanted to find out what some of these teams are really building, who is behind the work, and why they would spend months making a complex machine that will only move slowly across a place meant to erase it. Some of these mutant vehicles and big installations have been captured by top Burning Man photographers, including longtime participant Scott London, whose photos are featured in the popular book Burning Man: Art on Fire. These are the projects and stories that caught my attention at Burning Man 2026. THE MUTANT VEHICLES SharkCar Design team: Sid Kurtz and crew, Tulalip, Washington SharkCar has one of the simplest ideas here and one of the biggest footprints. Burning Man lists it at 72 feet long and 17 feet tall, roughly the length of a large motor yacht. Red LED rope lighting traces the body from head to tail, so the shark keeps its unmistakable outline after dark as it moves across the playa. A shark this large has to be stored, transported, maintained and maneuvered through Black Rock City before anyone gets to enjoy the visual joke. Underneath the spectacle is a serious piece of mobile engineering built to move a sculpture larger than almost anything parked beside it. Designed by Jason Anderholm Chester began as a napkin sketch, created by Jason Anderholm, who went from electrician to showman. The frame was once a delivery truck, but now it’s a rearing horse with a driver’s platform, a mane made from welded motorcycle tires, glowing red eyes, and fire-shooting nostrils. A stripper pole on its back transforms it into a moving stage for acrobats. Design team: Camp Axolotl, San Miguel de Allende, Mexico ¡AXOLOTL! is almost 50 feet long and feels more like a moving stage than a typical art car. Inspired by Mexico’s endangered axolotl, Camp Axolotl turned this unique amphibian into a huge mobile space for music, performances, and gatherings as it travels through Black Rock City. There is a deeper story behind its playful look. The axolotl, which comes from the shrinking wetlands of Mexico City, is known for its rare ability to regrow limbs and other body parts. This has made it valuable in medical research. As its habitat disappears, the axolotl has also become a strong symbol of both environmental loss and survival. Abraxas Design team: Tim Clark and the Abraxas Dragon Team Abraxas has been a familiar sight at Burning Man since 2006. This dragon-shaped art car stands out for its music, performances, and unmistakable silhouette. Beyond the playa, the team has helped with disaster relief through the Grassroots Aid Partnership, including work after Hurricane Helene in North Carolina, and has supported the Moonlight Orphanage in Uganda. Abraxas has also shown up at events like Catharsis on the Mall in Washington, D.C., and the MAPS Psychedelic Science conference in Denver. Design team: Yaroslav Korets, Kurenivka, Wonders Workshop and Ukrainian collaborators in Kyiv, Odesa and the United States Blue Bull started as a painting nearly 80 years ago. The vehicle is inspired by Ukrainian artist Maria Prymachenko’s 1947 Blue Bull, one of the imaginative animals central to her work. At Burning Man, this artwork becomes a three-dimensional piece with a large body covered in bright blue UV-reactive fur, along with lighting and sound that make it stand out at night on the playa. The project was created through teamwork in Kyiv, Odesa, and the United States, which gives it a deeper meaning beyond just being a spectacle. The creators bring Prymachenko’s artistic style to a place she likely never imagined. Watching a giant blue bull move through the Nevada desert feels surreal, and with Ukrainian collaborators building it, the piece strongly shows cultural identity and resilience. Design team: Kyrsten Mate and Jon Sarriugarte and EOD Golden Mean takes its name from the golden ratio, a mathematical proportion that’s said to produce aesthetically pleasing art and architecture. Other inspirations for the project include the Giant Pink Sea Snail from Doctor Dolittle, giant mechanical elephant puppets by Royal de Luxe and Jules Verne’s imaginative creations. Jon Sarriugarte tells me, “My motivation to make things is to encourage others to create what they imagine. The Golden Mean snail car came from my wife Kyrsten Mate's dream. We sketched it on a napkin and made it over the summer with 6 of our friends and her dad. I'd like to see people make something they imagine and show people.” Design team: Cassidy Damore, Kristen Hoard, Dennis Damore, and Niko McManus Eileen is a pearl-white peacock with five big metal tail feathers that stand tall behind her lace-covered body. During the day, you can see all the fine details in the sculpture. At night, the feathers light up and the whole bird glows across the playa. The camp calls it a celebration of creativity and storytelling, but the story behind it is much more personal. “Building an art car is by far the dumbest, hardest, and most expensive thing I’ve ever done that had no purpose other than to make people happy,” Project Co-Lead Cassidy Damore tells me. “And it completely changed my life. It reignited my passion for building. I left my career in film and went back to school. I graduated with my second bachelor's in mechanical engineering in May.” The car is a tribute to Damore’s grandmother, Eileen Hoard. “It’s built on her ’97 Honda Civic,” Damore says. “She was a creative powerhouse who wrote a book on storytelling for children and started and taught at a preschool in Phoenix, Arizona.” This year, the family sold the car to a Burning Man camp in Kidsville. “More children than adults will be riding on her,” Damore says. “I can't think of a better home or purpose for her car than taking children around to all the magic on the playa.” Eileen’s daughter, Kristen Hoard, says the project grew into something bigger for the family. “Creating art together and sharing it with the Burning Man community has been one of the most meaningful experiences of our lives. Most importantly, the art car became a timeless tribute to my mother, Eileen, whose creative spirit continues to flow through our entire family. We were so happy that it eventually found a new home surrounded by children, a place my mom would have loved.” Design team: Engineered Artworks Elektra is a fire-breathing dragon built by Engineered Artworks, with wings stretching about 60 feet and wrapped in addressable, sequenced LEDs. The scale is theatrical even before the flames start. At night, the lighting turns the wings into a moving field of color while bursts of fire give the dragon the kind of oversized entrance Burning Man was made for. The Art Installations Design team: Lead artist Sean Orlando; fabrication by Engineered Artworks in partnership with Five Ton Crane Arts Collective and a crew of over 50 contributing artists; structural engineering by Tipping Structural, with Andrew O’Keefe of Figure 13 as lead technical designer. Sean Orlando’s Above & Below stands 50 feet tall on the playa. It starts with a house at ground level and winds up a twisting beanstalk to a Victorian cottage near the top. Made from steel, wood, found objects, and recycled materials, this piece is meant to be explored up close. Visitors are invited to climb through it. Since June, over 130 artists, fabricators, and volunteers have worked on the project at Seaport Studios in Richmond, California. For Orlando, the size of the piece is just one aspect. “Above & Below started as a very personal project, it's my version of a self-portrait, built around an inventor and his daughter who create a home for themselves inside a living beanstalk,” he told me. “It mirrors my experience building a world with my daughter filled with imagination, creativity, and community.” The world Orlando imagined takes place after the apocalypse, not in the middle of it. People are rebuilding with old artifacts, scraps, and whatever creativity they have left. He drew inspiration from fairy tales, unusual workshops, and sketches of impossible machines. Still, he does not want visitors to follow a set story. “I don't want to hand people a fixed meaning though, I want them to climb through it, find their own artifacts and clues, and leave with their own wonder-filled story.” Bringing this fantasy to life in the Black Rock Desert is a different challenge. The structure is modular, so it can be taken apart, loaded onto 48- and 53-foot flatbed trucks, and reassembled in just a few days at Black Rock City. It also needs to stand up to desert winds and dust while thousands of people explore it. “It has to come apart into truckable pieces that can be assembled in a matter of days, and still feel like a fairytale and not a jungle gym,” Orlando said. “Getting the engineering and the storytelling to hold together at the same time, on that timeline, that’s the real challenge.” Design team: Moonlight Collective and the Temple Build Crew, lead artist James Gwertzman; architect Annie Locke Scherer The Temple of the Moon is inspired by the Queen of the Night, a desert cactus flower that blooms for just one night before fading at sunrise. Its flowing, inward-curving shape wraps around a 30-foot central tower, forming a space where people can come together to reflect, remember, and gather. Gwertzman worked on the project with architect Annie Locke Scherer, the Moonlight Collective, and the Temple Build Crew. Burning Man calls the temple a sacred communal space before it is released by fire on Sunday night. The design reflects the cycles of the moon and the short life of the cactus flower, giving this important structure a unique and personal feel. Gwertzman tells me, “It’s magical to see this Temple take shape, having lived with it as a constant companion in my head for nearly a year. What makes it so special, though, is not the structure that we've built, but the community of more than 100 builders who have given up their time and energy to bring it to life. It's the love that binds this team together that makes this Temple sacred.” Designed by Alexander Rose Another key Axis Mundi structure this year is Cryptomeria, the pavilion that surrounds the Man. Alexander Rose designed it, drawing inspiration from Japan’s ancient Jōmon Sugi cedar tree. The pavilion has three levels, starting with roots and the natural world, moving through the human realm, and reaching toward the sky. Paths shaped like roots guide visitors inside, and a double spiral staircase leads upward. This pavilion directly reflects the year’s theme and serves as the physical center of Black Rock City. TITANIC Design team: Titanic’s End, led by Chris DN TITANIC could become one of the standout sights at Burning Man 2026. The San Francisco group Titanic’s End is creating a large wooden ship that looks like it has split in two and begun to sink into the desert. The way the two parts are arranged makes it seem as if the ship is vanishing under the playa. The wreck will also serve as a casual amphitheater for performances and watching the sunset. At night, lights shine on the wreck, and flames will shoot from the smokestacks. The group says their work raises questions about our trust in technology, how we use resources, and the belief that complicated human systems cannot fail. Still, the main impact may be the striking image itself. A shipwreck sinking into the Nevada desert is the kind of surprising scene Burning Man is known for. Artist: Philippe Maindron This piece is a metal model of the Eiffel Tower, first built for Paris’s 1889 Exposition Universelle, shown here at one-tenth its original size. In this version, the tower is split in two, as if it crashed into the desert after a wild journey. The lower part, with its four legs on the ground, stands for the fall of a lost civilization. The top, reaching up, suggests hope for a better future. A cable will connect the two parts, allowing a tightrope walker to cross from one side to the other. Artist: Gazelle Dasti Gazelle Dasti’s ZARVAN stands 23 feet tall on the playa, shaped as a large human head inspired by the ancient Persian deity linked to time. The sculpture features patterns from Persian rugs, hand-painted details, and a glowing crown inspired by traditional stained glass. These elements give it a look grounded in Persian art, which is different from the futuristic style usually seen at Burning Man. Inside, the experience is different. Periscopes behind the eyes let visitors see across Black Rock City, and speaking tubes through the ears allow people on opposite sides to talk to each other. Dasti is the first Persian woman to receive a Burning Man honorarium, which adds more meaning to a piece focused on time, perception, and cultural memory. Gazelle tells me, "As an Iranian woman with an engineering background, and recognized as the first Iranian woman to receive a Burning Man Honorarium for a large-scale steel sculpture, ZARVAN is deeply meaningful to me. Inspired by the Persian divinity of boundless time, she combines Persian heritage, art, and engineering. Her hand-painted Persian rug patterns, acoustic ears, and internal periscopes that let you see through her eyes invite people to experience time, perception, and connection, and simply come together as human beings.” What It Takes To Build The Impossible It’s easy to capture Burning Man’s wildest creations in photos, but the real stories behind them often reveal much more than the spectacle itself. This year, artists are turning an 80-year-old Ukrainian painting into a moving sculpture, building a 50-foot fairytale world you can climb, and creating a broken Eiffel Tower for a tightrope walker to cross high above the playa. This is why the best Burning Man projects are worth seeing for more than just their looks. They might be impractical, costly, and tough to build, but they let artists, builders, and engineers try things they wouldn’t get to do anywhere else. For one week in Black Rock City, a 72-foot shark, a giant blue bull, a sinking Titanic, and a fire-breathing dragon can all share the same space, and somehow, they all fit right in. item.title: Venice’s Palazzo Giovanelli Launches A New Chapter
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 2.55
The storied Palazzo Giovanelli reopened to guests this summer after a meticulous four-year restoration carried out under the supervision of Venice’s Superintendency of Fine Arts. Beyond its restoration, the historic Palazzo Giovanelli has been reimagined as a boutique, 33-room, five-star hotel that blends a rich Venetian heritage with contemporary luxury. Venice is one of the most popular tourist destinations in Italy, attracting millions of visitors each year. So it’s not surprising that the city has more than two dozen five-star hotels. However, while most are owned and/or managed by corporate brands, Palazzo Giovanelli stands out as one of a handful that are both family-owned and operated. A Legacy Restored and Renewed Overlooking the Grand Canal, the palace was originally built in the 16th century as a noble residence for the Coccina family. Over the years, the building changed hands from the Foscarini family to the Giovanellis, who held the palace for more than two centuries. Among the notable figures who have stayed at Palazzo Giovanelli are Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and aristocrats such as Marco Foscarini, who later became the 117th Doge of Venice. The Palazzo also hosted Frederik Christian, the future King of Denmark. About 15 years ago, Luciano Semenzato, the successful owner of an Italian railway construction company, discovered and acquired what had become an abandoned property. Born and bred nearby, this purchase represented more than a business venture. It was a passion project. The family first opened Palazzo Giovanelli as a four-star hotel in 2010. After the patriarch’s passing in 2014, the property was passed down to his daughter and son. In November 2025, the sibling owners decided to close the hotel and embark on a significant five-star transformation, adding contemporary luxuries and cutting-edge technology. “We feel like it is a natural continuation of our father’s vision,” they say. In partnership with interior design Studio Gascón, original frescoes attributed to Giovanni Battista Zelotti and polychrome marble details were restored. A secret passage in what was once the Doge’s apartment was opened, offering guests an immersion in the building’s history. The number of guest rooms and suites was reduced from 41 to 33. Refreshed guest rooms are light-filled and offer either Canal or interior garden views. “Our ambition was never simply to restore a historic building, but to reopen a living piece of Venice for a new generation of international travelers,” Angelica told me in an email. She is responsible for marketing; her brother, Oliviero, oversees operations. Nicolino Grigio is the hotel’s general manager. “This Palazzo holds deep emotional meaning for our family,” she explained. The reopening also signals the launch of two new on-site restaurants, likely to become culinary destinations; both are open to hotel and outside guests. Under the helm of Chef Ennio Interlenghi, the menu at “Armonico” is inspired by authentic Venetian flavors and traditions. The talented chef is known locally as the “Valentino della Cucina,” having previously worked as a fashion designer for Valentino, Max Mara, and FILA before discovering his passion for cooking. “Do Grifoni” is a contemporary cocktail lounge reflecting the social culture and aesthetics of the city’s nightlife. An Ideal Location On The Grand Canal Of course, Venice is perennially popular with tourists. The iconic destination woos visitors with its rich history, stunning architecture, and a unique network of bridges and canals linking neighborhoods across the Venetian lagoon. As one might expect (or have already experienced), the over-touristed historic center is typically filled with hordes of day trippers and other visitors, particularly in the central area dominated by St. Mark’s Square, St. Mark’s Basilica and the Doge’s Palace. By contrast, Palazzo Giovanelli is situated in the less dense San Stae neighborhood, between the Church of San Stae and Ca’ Pesaro, in the Santa Croce district. This location is more residential, with quieter streets and approachable local trattorias, but offers several architecturally significant palaces and one of the city's oldest churches, the 11th-century San Zan Degola. The hotel is only a 20-25-minute walk from the bustling heart of the city, and many travelers say that the “real” Venice is often best experienced by walking through its maze of narrow medieval streets and alleys. Palazzo Giovanelli: A Bespoke Venetian Retreat Under the stewardship of a family deeply rooted in Venice, Palazzo Giovanelli distinguishes itself by its unique blend of genuine Venetian hospitality and five-star luxury. With just 33 reimagined spaces, guests will appreciate its sophisticated but warm ambiance. “We hope to offer guests a more intimate way to experience Venice, one rooted in history, craftsmanship and a strong sense of place,” says Angelica. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION The Mozart Signature Suite (where Mozart stayed with his family during his visit to Venice) is approximately 1,290 square feet. It overlooks the Grand Canal and has a walk-out balcony. The Foscarini Signature Suite (which housed the Doge) is approximately 966 square feet and also offers Grand Canal views. Rates, which vary by room and season, start at €400 per night. A choice of a Continental breakfast or a "wellness" option (wholegrain bread, sugar-free preserves, organic honey, low-fat yogurt, fruit muesli) is included; an à la carte menu is also available at an extra charge. Guided tours of Palazzo Giovanelli are available to outside guests by appointment.

item.title: A Great Rebalancing Is Coming
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.75
The trade imbalances that have come to characterize the global economy are fundamentally untenable. China, Germany, and a handful of other economies run large, persistent trade surpluses, while the United States absorbs much of these surpluses by running the world’s largest trade deficit. Sooner or later, something must give. For an advanced, capital-rich economy such as that of the United States, an enduring trade deficit will bring with it either rising unemployment or rising debt, neither of which is sustainable. In theory, the major surplus and deficit economies could agree on a coordinated adjustment in which surplus countries would expand domestic demand and deficit countries would gradually reduce their dependence on debt-fueled consumption, allowing the imbalances to shrink without a sharp contraction in global demand. That would be the sensible solution. But because the major players disagree about the causes of the imbalances, they are unlikely to come to such a solution. China attributes them to excessive U.S. consumption and fiscal deficits; the United States blames foreign industrial, trade, and currency policies; and Europe has yet to settle on a coherent diagnosis. As a result, they all have proposed remedies that are at odds with one another. Beijing wants deficit countries to save more and prefers not to change China’s growth model. Washington wants surplus countries to reduce their surpluses by redistributing income to the household sector. European leaders continue to advocate for multilateral cooperation and rules-based trade. This makes the chances of a coordinated response slim. And as the economic analyst Martin Wolf wrote in the Financial Times earlier this year, if there is little prospect of preemptive action, “the second-best option is to prepare for a crisis.” Individual economies are now doing just that. History shows that trade imbalances of this scale almost always end painfully—and that the pain of the adjustment is not distributed evenly. High levels of debt combined with low productivity makes a country more likely to bear the burden of a trade adjustment, but economic and political power can also give it the tools to pass the burden off to others. Among the three main economic players today, China is the most vulnerable, the United States has the most capacity to reduce its exposure, and Europe possesses latent power but a dubious ability to use it. None of their maneuvers to protect themselves are likely to reduce the risk or overall cost of a crisis. The question is only who will feel the brunt of the losses when it arrives. HISTORY REPEATS ITSELF Large, persistent trade imbalances have cropped up periodically over the past century, and they are rarely benign. One such episode occurred during the 1920s, when a surge in American productivity was not accompanied by rising wages. Production soared past consumption, and the United States ran enormous trade surpluses. Europe ran the corresponding deficits, as many countries borrowed heavily abroad to rebuild economies devastated by war. Germany in particular borrowed extensively to finance both domestic growth and its reparations payments. American domestic debt also rose rapidly, much of it to fund consumption and asset speculation. As the imbalances persisted and U.S. manufacturing expanded at the expense of European manufacturing, protectionist pressures intensified. France devalued its currency in 1927, the United Kingdom abandoned the gold standard in 1931, and the same year Germany imposed import restrictions and rationed access to foreign currency. Even the United States, whose manufacturers and farmers complained that weak demand was threatening domestic production and employment, passed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act in 1930. The adjustment came in the form of a collapse in global trade during the Great Depression of the early and mid-1930s. Nearly every major economy suffered from the contraction, but they did not suffer equally. Those with large deficits, such as the United Kingdom, recovered more quickly and suffered less severe financial distress than the United States, which absorbed a disproportionate share of the costs. American exports fell faster than imports, domestic investment imploded, banks failed, and bankruptcies surged. Trade imbalances on a large scale almost always end painfully. The next major episode of persistent trade imbalances was the rare case in which the imbalances faded away without causing major disruption. During the 1950s and 1960s, the United States again ran very large surpluses while Europe and Japan ran corresponding deficits. Similar to the situation in the 1920s, these deficits financed the reconstruction of postwar economies as resources poured into infrastructure and manufacturing. But unlike in the earlier period, governments maintained strict controls over capital flows and imported capital mostly to fund investments that generated enough future income to service the associated liabilities. Because the investments were so productive, debt rose little relative to GDP. There was also minimal protectionist pressure, largely because Europe and Japan urgently needed imports and the United States actively encouraged reconstruction in both places. As a result of these unusual conditions, trade imbalances disappeared gradually without any countries bearing severe costs. Four more episodes of trade imbalances would follow, all of them ending in pain for the countries involved. One happened in Latin America during the 1970s. The oil shocks of that period, in which the global price of oil soared from roughly $2 per barrel at the beginning of the decade to around $30 per barrel by the end, generated massive petrodollar surpluses in the oil-exporting economies of the Middle East and other members of OPEC. Much of this was deposited in major international banks that, eager to find new customers, loaned the funds to Latin American and other developing economies, eventually leading to overvalued currencies and large trade deficits. By the early 1980s, rising global interest rates made their debt unsustainable. Debt crises resolved the trade imbalances but left the deficit countries with the overwhelming share of the adjustment costs: recession, inflation, austerity, and lost decades of growth. The next case developed during the late 1970s and 1980s. Japanese productivity growth outpaced Japanese wages during this period, and the country began running enormous trade surpluses. The same happened in Germany, allowing the country’s manufacturing sector to become increasingly competitive internationally. The United Kingdom and the United States ran deficits that accommodated both Japan’s and Germany’s surpluses. Japan in particular saw a spectacular surge in domestic debt during the 1980s, as extremely high levels of investment flowed into projects whose returns fell far below expectations. China has every incentive to maintain the largest possible trade surplus for as long as it can. Protectionist pressures rose steadily, culminating in the Plaza Accord of 1985, in which the world’s major economies agreed to appreciate the yen and the deutsche mark against the dollar in an effort to reduce trade imbalances. Yet a real resolution of the imbalances did not come until Japan’s economic downturn in the 1990s, which brought collapsing asset prices, persistent deflation, and years of stagnation. It is difficult to compare this to Germany’s experience, however, given that the 1990 unification of East and West Germany fundamentally altered the economy at precisely the same time. The Asian financial crisis of the 1990s in some ways resembled the Latin American trade imbalances of the 1970s. In the early part of the decade, foreign capital poured into a group of East Asian economies. These economies developed large trade deficits, which were balanced by surpluses in Japan, European countries, and, increasingly, China. Although their domestic and external debt rose rapidly, protectionism remained limited. Even so, when investor confidence broke in 1997, the adjustment was swift and brutal. Currency collapses, banking crises, and deep recessions struck the East Asian deficit countries, while the surplus countries bore few costs. Finally, between roughly 2002 and 2008, Germany accumulated large surpluses after implementing labor reforms that pushed wage growth down relative to productivity growth and caused huge increases in saving. It exported more and more to Greece, Portugal, Spain, and several other eurozone economies, which in turn accumulated deficits financed by rapidly rising debt. Because this dynamic emerged within the eurozone, where most members shared a common currency, countries could not impose protectionist measures and exchange-rate adjustment was impossible. When the 2008 global financial crisis triggered the eurozone crisis, the deficit countries experienced sovereign debt crises, unemployment, austerity, and prolonged stagnation that unwound the imbalances. COST ANALYSIS These events demonstrate that trade imbalances become dangerous when they are accompanied by rapidly rising debt and growing financial fragility in either surplus or deficit economies. If a country with a surplus uses its high savings to finance productive investment at home or abroad, the imbalance can persist for many years without causing serious economic disruption. But if instead its excess savings finance unproductive investment at home or drive high household consumption, asset bubbles, or persistent fiscal deficits in the economies of its trading partners, the whole system becomes increasingly shaky. Protectionism is generally not the cause of trade conflicts, but rather a symptom of imbalances that have endured for too long. Its absence does not make the eventual adjustment less painful. Yet when countries adopt protectionist policies, they can influence where the adjustment occurs and who bears the costs. Whether it is surplus or deficit economies that take on those costs may also depend on which side has the greater ability to use trade, financial, or exchange-rate policies to compel the other to adjust. Deficit countries more often bear the costs when they are politically weak and unable to finance themselves independently, defend their currencies, or restrict capital and trade flows without triggering a financial crisis—as Latin American countries were in the early 1980s, much of East Asia was in 1997, and southern Europe was after 2008. Surplus countries are at risk, meanwhile, when deficit countries have sufficiently strong economies and political systems to reduce their own deficits by restricting imports, limiting capital inflows, depreciating their currencies, or otherwise preventing the surplus countries from exporting their excess savings. This is what happened to the United States in the early 1930s and to Japan beginning in the 1990s. Their trade partners reduced their deficits by intervening to reduce imports and increase exports, forcing the U.S. and Japanese surplus-based growth models to unravel as investment collapsed and exports, profits, and asset prices fell. The main takeaway for governments today is twofold. First, the place where debt has risen furthest without a corresponding rise in productive capacity is most at risk when an adjustment to a trade imbalance eventually arrives. Second, the countries involved in imbalanced trade can take action to push adjustment costs onto others, but their success depends largely on economic power and their ability to wield it. THE CRISIS TO COME Today’s global trade imbalances are unusually large, and the coming adjustment is likely to be especially difficult. China looks most vulnerable. Its debt burden is already among the world’s highest; the country has experienced perhaps the fastest increase in debt relative to GDP in history. Much of this debt has funded investment that has generated progressively lower—even negative—economic returns, including excess residential real estate, underutilized infrastructure, and manufacturing capacity that far outstrips demand. This huge and growing debt burden creates enormous pressure on Beijing to take any steps necessary to avoid absorbing the bulk of the adjustment costs. China will almost certainly try to push as much of this burden as possible onto its trade partners. It has every incentive to maintain the largest possible trade surplus for as long as it can, allowing excess production to be absorbed abroad rather than forcing a sharp contraction in domestic production and employment. In doing so, China can spread the adjustment over many years as it gradually works down its debt, while its trading partners endure greater costs in the form of larger trade deficits, rising debt, deindustrialization, or weaker growth. If foreign protectionist measures or weaker external demand make this strategy impossible, however, China’s economy would face some combination of slower growth, rising unemployment, falling investment, and financial distress. Whether Beijing can offload the costs of adjustment depends on the willingness of the rest of the world to absorb them. Washington has little reason to continue allowing large, persistent trade deficits. As the world’s largest economy and by far its largest source of demand, the United States has the economic power to reduce its deficit and stop acting as the world’s consumer of last resort. And because U.S. trade policy is centralized within the executive branch—with the president able to impose tariffs, investment restrictions, and export controls under broad statutory authority—Washington has the political ability to exercise this power. If the United States uses industrial policy to expand domestic manufacturing capacity and, more important, takes greater control over its trade and capital flows using tariffs and other restrictive measures, China and other major surplus economies will not be able to maintain their surpluses with corresponding U.S. deficits. They will have to either reduce those surpluses with a painful contraction in domestic production or find new importers among countries that remain both willing and able to absorb them. The United States has the economic power to reduce its deficit. This leaves Europe in perhaps the most difficult position. The eurozone is the world’s third-largest economy and its second-largest source of demand, so Europe has economic power at its disposal. What is much less clear is whether it has the political ability to exercise this power, given its fragmented policymaking institutions and the often divergent interests of its member states. If the United States is able to reduce its trade deficit and expand its share of global manufacturing while China resists an equivalent contraction in its surpluses, a politically divided Europe could be forced to take on larger deficits almost by default. The costs could include deindustrialization, rising debt, and weaker growth. This process may have begun already. Once the major economies stop asking how to minimize the global costs of adjustment and begin asking instead how to minimize their own risk, the opportunity to find a relatively painless solution to the global trade imbalance will have passed. Beijing seems set on trying to preserve its surpluses for as long as possible. Washington is just as intent on reducing its deficits. If Europe can develop the political capacity to do the same, the burden of adjustment will increasingly fall onto the surplus economies, which would have to rely more on domestic demand and less on exports. If it cannot, Europe will absorb more and more of the global surpluses, and what appears today to be a trade conflict mainly between China and the United States may become a conflict between China and Europe—and a struggle between the two of them to avoid bearing steeper costs down the road. History makes clear that trade imbalances are always resolved eventually. What remains uncertain is how damaging the resolution will be—and for whom. item.title: A Book as Big as the War
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.80
World War II books have a habit of being as enormous as the conflict itself. The average war buff owns at least a couple of hefty tomes that could, in a pinch, stop a bullet or two, whether it’s Gerhard Weinberg’s classic A World at Arms (1,208 pages), Richard Overy’s Blood and Ruins (1,040 pages), or Antony Beevor’s The Second World War (880 pages). Even a relatively svelte volume like John Ellis’ One Day In a Very Long War runs over 400 pages. The third world war could be fought by using World War II books as artillery shells. Jonathan Parshall’s 1942: Crux of War is a 17-year labor of love—as well as dogged perseverance and inveterate curiosity—that, at 1,280 pages, can easily hold its own among the big boys. The book is a sprawling, blow-by-blow account of a single year, but one that was the linchpin of everything to follow. As Parshall notes, 1942 encompassed the crux of the entire war—12 months in which everything started out catastrophically for the Allies and (nearly) ended up swimmingly. That was the year that featured the battles of Midway, Guadalcanal, El Alamein, and Stalingrad, all of them crushing victories for the anti-fascist coalition. World War II books have a habit of being as enormous as the conflict itself. The average war buff owns at least a couple of hefty tomes that could, in a pinch, stop a bullet or two, whether it’s Gerhard Weinberg’s classic A World at Arms (1,208 pages), Richard Overy’s Blood and Ruins (1,040 pages), or Antony Beevor’s The Second World War (880 pages). Even a relatively svelte volume like John Ellis’ One Day In a Very Long War runs over 400 pages. The third world war could be fought by using World War II books as artillery shells. Jonathan Parshall’s 1942: Crux of War is a 17-year labor of love—as well as dogged perseverance and inveterate curiosity—that, at 1,280 pages, can easily hold its own among the big boys. The book is a sprawling, blow-by-blow account of a single year, but one that was the linchpin of everything to follow. As Parshall notes, 1942 encompassed the crux of the entire war—12 months in which everything started out catastrophically for the Allies and (nearly) ended up swimmingly. That was the year that featured the battles of Midway, Guadalcanal, El Alamein, and Stalingrad, all of them crushing victories for the anti-fascist coalition. As Winston Churchill said after British church bells rang for the first time after victory at El Alamein in November 1942, “This is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning.” Parshall tells the story of every action in every theater of war with careful detail and an eye to answering the question, how did we get here from there? The biggest virtue of Parshall’s book is that he can write empathically from the viewpoint of the time, not with the benefit of eight decades of hindsight. It’s easy, if discomfiting, to look back on the rebar remains of Hiroshima or on bombed-out Berlin and believe that Allied victory in World War II was a foregone conclusion. But as Parshall stresses throughout, “It sure wasn’t obvious at the time.” There are probably a million books on World War II, catering to every taste and fancy. There are books on single battles, or extended campaigns. There are one-volume histories, two-volume couplets, and some lovely trilogies. There are wonderful books on the naval war, the strategic bombing campaign, and the Battle of the Atlantic, from both sides. There are books focused on economics, war production, and even food. And memoirs galore, of course. What makes Parshall’s book special is his ability to tell the story of the whole war at a time when the conflict still seemed to hang in the balance. The first three years of the war were an unmitigated disaster for the Allies, from Poland to Norway, France, the Low Countries, the Balkans, Greece, and North Africa. Then came the invasion of Russia, the mass surrender of Soviet forces, and the Germans at the gates of Moscow—plus the U-boat offensive in the Atlantic. And then it got worse. The Japanese attack on U.S. Pacific possessions at Pearl Harbor and the Philippines, coupled with a lightning attack on British colonies in Hong Kong and Malaya, were hammer blows both to the troops on the ground and, above all, the leaders in London. When British forces in Singapore, Britain’s greatest fortress, fell to an invading Japanese army with one-third as many men in early 1942, Britain’s warlords were despairing. The head of the British Army, “General [Alan] Brooke confided to his diary that he ‘certainly never expected that we should fall to pieces as fast as we are, and to see Hong Kong and Singapore go in less than three months plus a failure in the Western Desert is far from reassuring.’ Noting Britain’s previous powers of recovery, he wondered ‘whether we shall again bring off a comeback?,’” Parshall writes. The comeback that they did pull off—the British as well as the Americans and the Soviets—make up the rest of the 1,200-odd pages of this very thorough and thoroughly enjoyable book. Parshall cracks his knuckles and sets to work with a month-by-month chronicle of the crucial year, with a detailed analysis of every theater of war. There is a lot of old-school military history (Parshall’s vocation by training) with corps, divisions, and brigades marching over maps or holding river lines. Woe betides the reader who confuses the 22nd Panzer with the 24th Panzer or the Australian 7th Division with the British 7th Armoured Brigade. To his credit, for a historian who was weaned to his craft by a fascination with the Pacific theater, and whose previous great work was on its pivotal battle, Parshall gives every theater its due—even if there are plenty of cruiser-on-cruiser battles and a good few pages on the Battle of Midway. But the beauty of Parshall’s book lies elsewhere. Parshall prefaces each monthly bulletin with a big-picture essay; taken together, these would make for a great book in their own right. They range from detailed analyses of the economics of tank or aircraft production, to the difficulties the United States faced in mobilizing slack industrial capacity for total war; from managing a cumbersome U.S.-U.K. command system, to the transformation of the Red Army from cannon fodder to deep battle specialists. Parshall ties all the theaters of war together in a way largely unparalleled in World War II history. He offers a vision that is certainly lost in narrow biographies of battles, but which also fails to cohere even in the best supposedly comprehensive histories. To pluck one example at random: When, on a lark in the spring of 1942, the Imperial Japanese Navy launched a nonsensical raid into the Indian Ocean and raised havoc with British naval forces and merchant shipping, the Royal Navy’s response was to leave a strong naval force in East Africa. That starved the already-beleaguered Mediterranean Fleet of ships precisely at a time when it was actually losing the naval war against Italy, which had nasty implications for the war in North Africa, as Gen. Erwin Rommel and Germany’s Afrika Korps nearly took Egypt. For a book about events 80-some years ago, there sure is a lot of suspense. That takes us back to Parshall’s original point: For the statesmen, generals, soldiers, sailors, and airmen of the time, there was a lot of suspense. Victory was a slogan, not a given. There was nothing deterministic about it. I think this might be my desert island book—and not just because, in a pinch, it could be a serviceable shelter.
