item.title: Why Are Yields on U.S. Treasury Bonds Rising?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.78
Why Are Yields on U.S. Treasury Bonds Rising? The fluctuations could have huge impacts on the U.S. and global economy. The yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond—effectively, the rate of interest on U.S. government debt—peaked last week at 5.33 percent, its highest level in 19 years. This may be the product of the normal laws of supply and demand. But the fluctuations in the vast market for U.S. debt have effects that are profound for both the U.S. and global economies—and, in this case, for U.S. politics, as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has now assumed responsibility for trying to bring that interest rate down. Why exactly are yields rising? How is Bessent’s background as a bond trader informing his actions as treasury secretary? And is the Treasury Department’s intervention in bond markets encroaching on the Federal Reserve’s turf? The yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond—effectively, the rate of interest on U.S. government debt—peaked last week at 5.33 percent, its highest level in 19 years. This may be the product of the normal laws of supply and demand. But the fluctuations in the vast market for U.S. debt have effects that are profound for both the U.S. and global economies—and, in this case, for U.S. politics, as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has now assumed responsibility for trying to bring that interest rate down. Why exactly are yields rising? How is Bessent’s background as a bond trader informing his actions as treasury secretary? And is the Treasury Department’s intervention in bond markets encroaching on the Federal Reserve’s turf? Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter. Cameron Abadi: Why exactly are yields rising? As the prices of bonds go down, their yields go up and there are broad supply-and-demand mechanisms that affect the prices and yields of bonds. But is this right now a matter of too much bond supply—too much U.S. debt—that is reducing the prices, or is there a softening of demand that is driving the reduction of prices? Adam Tooze: This is a truly important news story that’s really developed with real urgency over the summer this year, which is this global move in yields. It’s happening across the board with the vast majority of advanced economies, where a big issue is government debt. And as you say, it’s counterintuitive. So it’s worth repeating the logic: As the relative attractiveness of bonds falls and so therefore their price falls—the effective interest rate, the yield on that bond goes up. Because you end up paying $98, $97, $95 for a hundred dollars’ worth of bond, which then pays you a coupon of $4 a year in interest. And then all of a sudden, you’re looking at a much more attractive interest because you bought it for less than the $100 face value. And so what’s happening in global markets—there’s two figures out there for government debt in the U.S. right now. One is $40 trillion. That’s the total of debt that’s been issued, of which about $8 trillion is held by other government agencies. So this is debt owed by the American government to itself. About $32 trillion is in the hands of the market. And that is almost exactly the same as U.S. GDP. So we’ve crossed two critical thresholds, $40 trillion for overall debt and $32 trillion, 100 percent of GDP, in the hands of the market. And even those numbers by themselves, I mean, they are oceanic, that is huge. A trillion is a thousand thousand million. So it’s a million million Those markets are being moved by just the awesome flow of new debt into the markets and, on the other hand, the growing anxiety around the persistence of inflation, and the availability of other types of assets that are attractive by comparison with debt treasuries. Equities and private debt. And all three of those forces are acting at the same time. So there is a huge issuance of private-sector debt, notably AI-related debt, by very, very highly rated, very high-quality business names, which attracts a bid. There is persistent anxiety about inflation, unsurprisingly, because we’ve had a series of shocks starting with COVID, then Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, then most recently Israel and America’s war against Iran, which have triggered surges in price. The inflation rate is now 3.7 percent. And if you’re holding a bond with a nominal face value, every inch, every percent of inflation eats away at the value of your bonds. So that makes bonds less attractive, reducing the bid. And then there is absolutely gigantic issuance. So $40 trillion is the amount outstanding. But America actually has to replace outstanding debt about somewhere between $8 trillion and $10 trillion a year. Because a lot of the debt is rather short term. It’s running a deficit of 6 percent of GDP, which amounts to $2 trillion in new issuance. And so there is a huge volume of new paper coming onto the market all the time. The daily churn in this market is over $1 trillion. And the whole thing adds up to this shift, which is affecting not just the U.S., but everyone really. French government debt, British government debt, we’ve spoken about that a couple of times on the show. Even German, even Japanese. The only country whose bonds have not seen a substantial increase in yield is basically China, I think, where they operate in a relatively closed financial system and there’s no inflationary pressure. So that gives you an idea really of how capacious this is. CA: Bessent was someone who, as a bond trader in the 1990s, was on the other side of these kinds of mechanisms, identifying situations where a government didn’t have the ability to hold a bond market at a certain price and betting that they couldn’t and then profiting from that. Does that inform how he’s approaching this situation now that he’s a government official? AT: I mean, I think a lot of the Trump people are kind of caught in a dilemma. On the one hand, they have some degree of technical competence, otherwise they wouldn’t be in the jobs they’re in. And on the other hand, you can’t be a Trump underling without being basically a sycophant. So you’ve got to sort of follow the boss’s story. And then they, in various contorted ways, try and twist narratives around that. And foreign-policy people do that in various ways. And what we’re seeing with Bessent is a guy who was not a terribly successful hedge fund guy, he’s no macroeconomic super brain, but he’s somebody who does have a deep understanding of how Treasury markets work, at least at the kind of superficial technical level. And so he oscillates between technical justifications for his various interventions—which have included swap lines for Argentina and, you know, supporting the Japanese currency by selling euro without telling the Europeans first—and now this intervention. Now, modern monetary theory people will say this is all terribly artificial, the Treasury could print dollars, too. It could just create its own purchasing power. Which is true, but it would overturn all existing institutional structures, and it would massively destabilize the financial status quo in the U.S. So that’s not on the cards. So then you ask yourself, “What is Bessent’s endgame here? When people call his bluff, where’s this going to go?” And the answer seems to be, “The boss said we should do something, I did something, that’s all that really matters here.” And the bond market isn’t like that. I mean, it’s not a historically wise thing. But this is going to come at a price, this intervention, I think. Especially because it also puts the Federal Reserve in a really, really tight spot. CA: Normally, if there was going to be an intervention to correct the vast global market for U.S. debt, it would be the Fed, and the new Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, that would have responsibility for intervening. Is Bessent encroaching on Warsh’s territory here? AT: Yeah, this is really one of the dramatic aspects of what’s been going on. And so in this moment, where Kevin Warsh is having to establish himself as Fed chair, it’s not been going terribly well so far. His second press conference in particular was widely rated to have been a disaster, because Warsh is trying to move the Fed to a regime of much more tight-lipped, much less garrulous, much more explicit navigation of the relationship with the bond market. And here comes Bessent making these cack-handed interventions which are widely being interpreted as a sign of panic and mounting insecurity on the part of the Treasury. Which is the last thing the Fed needs. And so the question now is what is Warsh going to say? And in some ways, he could, if he was ultimately going to play the political card, he could align or he could avoid making any comments on Bessent’s intervention. Or on the other hand, if he actually wants to establish his bona fides with the market, he is now in a position where he almost needs to say something about Bessent’s intervention, which will put him explicitly at odds with the executive branch. Which is not where the Fed is going to want to be. People have long forecast that it would come like this. I think most people imagined it would be in the manner of [U.S. President Donald] Trump bullying, that we’ve seen plenty of, after all and the legal war on the Fed is still continuing. But I don’t think we anticipated the Treasury stepping in as an activist player in its own right and so egregiously and openly seeking to manipulate the price of the U.S. Treasury. And doing so with such patently inadequate tools. So it’s either doomed to fail or begging for somebody else to come and sort it out. CA: What is at stake in terms of which government body has this authority to intervene in bond markets? AT: This is a really fundamental question that goes to the heart, I think, of the democratic legitimacy of these procedures. And it’s at first sort of rub a puzzling question. Isn’t this so technical? Does this really belong within the purview of democratic oversight? Would we want Congress to be having a voice in this? Would we want the executive branch to be doing this? I think the general feeling was exactly as you were suggesting, that this is so technical, it’s such a fast-moving operation when you want to do it effectively, and you need really unlimited financial power that the only actor that really sensibly could exercise that role is the Fed. Because that’s its designated place in the modern Constitution. It may not have been spelled out as such, but the Supreme Court with its recent judgments has come pretty close to conferring on the Fed—though this has no standing in American constitutional jurisprudence—a special position. In other words, the key figures in the Fed are protected from presidential intervention in the way that other federal agencies are not, according to the Supreme Court. Which reflects, I think, the Supreme Court’s understanding that the Fed sits in a fundamentally different relationship to major social forces, notably the financial markets and any other body of the American government. So I think that’s where this conventional sense comes from, that Bessent has overstepped a line that it is the Fed that properly deals with this stuff. But the problem, of course, is that that judgment itself is highly conventional, not to say contentious. Because ultimately what we’re talking about here are nothing more nor less than huge distributional questions, right? The whole debt issue is fundamentally a distributional question. The vast majority of American debt is held domestically. So it’s owed by Americans to Americans in the name of the American government to be paid by American taxpayers. So this is an internal American-on-American issue. And there isn’t a real limit to how much debt you compile up, other than the fact that as you raise the volume of debt as interest rates go up, you have to churn larger and larger amounts of money through the tax system, through the fiscal apparatus, and pay that out again as interest payments. And almost by definition, the people who hold large quantities of financial assets, including Treasuries, tend to be wealthier. So what you’re doing is taking from a relatively broad tax base and distributing to people who receive interest on government debt. And this is obviously politically delicate. And right now, we’re already churning more through on interest payments than we are on the Pentagon’s budget, which is already hugely inflated. So this is a very delicate balancing act. So if you view it that way, manipulating the interest rate at which those bondholders are compensated is a huge political intervention. It’s a form of tax. So in the most contentious interventions we’ve seen in the last week, Citadel securities, [Stanley] Druckenmiller, people like that have essentially openly accused Bessent of what they call financial repression. Which is really a technical term for a way of managing the financial system—managing the relationship between interest rates and inflation—but, not improbably in this context, is actually taking on a highly political connotation. In other words, what you’re doing is shifting the balance of interest here through artificial interventions to the benefit of taxpayers and to the detriment of those who are investing in financial assets. That’s what you are doing. You’re artificially squeezing the price up and squeezing the yield down. So existing holders benefit, future lenders will get lower yields. It’s a huge operation on the American distribution of income and wealth that you’re engaged in. And what they’re saying is you shouldn’t be doing this, it should just be the market that does this. Which of course is its own kind of value judgment, right? So I personally think financial repression, we’ve spoken about it on the show, is probably the best way out of America’s fiscal dilemmas. But if you’re going to do it, you’re going to have to do it with more purpose and more coherence and with bigger instruments than the ones that Bessent is mobilizing. Adam Tooze is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a history professor and the director of the European Institute at Columbia University. He is the author of Chartbook, a newsletter on economics, geopolitics, and history. X: @adam_tooze Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: Notes From Russia’s Literary Underground
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.47
Notes From Russia’s Literary Underground Publishers in exile are supplying contraband books to help Russians evade censorship. On a bright spring day in Berlin earlier this year, the Russian publisher Alexander Gavrilov ebulliently recalled the first time he read the banned poetry of Joseph Brodsky. It was the 1980s in the Soviet Union and Brodsky “just blew my mind,” Gavrilov said. The USSR aggressively censored speech—controlling books through centralized state-run publishing houses—and much of what was permissible reeked of a stultifying sameness. “Grey and dusty literature, grey and dusty poetry, grey and dusty fashion,” he said. Reading a writer like Brodsky was a revelation after which “you can’t just live this boring Soviet life.” On a bright spring day in Berlin earlier this year, the Russian publisher Alexander Gavrilov ebulliently recalled the first time he read the banned poetry of Joseph Brodsky. It was the 1980s in the Soviet Union and Brodsky “just blew my mind,” Gavrilov said. The USSR aggressively censored speech—controlling books through centralized state-run publishing houses—and much of what was permissible reeked of a stultifying sameness. “Grey and dusty literature, grey and dusty poetry, grey and dusty fashion,” he said. Reading a writer like Brodsky was a revelation after which “you can’t just live this boring Soviet life.” Authorities convicted Brodsky—who was not formally affiliated with any state-sanctioned literary institutions, and whose poetry contained illicit spiritual themes—of “social parasitism,” sentencing him to five years hard labor near the Arctic Circle. (“Who gave you permission to be a poet?” the judge in his trial asked.) Though his work was banned, it attained cult status because exiles and activists in the United States and Europe published Brodsky’s poetry and smuggled it back into the USSR. Brodsky’s legacy is what inspired Gavrilov to cofound his publishing house, Vidim Books, at a time when censorship in Russia is again reaching Soviet heights. Vidim, founded in 2023, releases books by authors whose work can no longer be published in Russia for political reasons, and is one of dozens of new publishing ventures that Russian exiles have established since 2022 to distribute contraband Russian books to readers both inside and outside of their home country. As the Kremlin targets literature, both fiction and nonfiction, at a scale unseen since the Soviet era, these publishers-in-exile have become crucial to safeguarding independent discourse in Russian-speaking society. Multiple times a year, these publishers convene at book fairs across Europe, including this spring at the Berlin Bebelplatz fair. Named after the site where Nazis burned tens of thousands of “un-German” texts almost a century ago, the event aimed “to show that the Russian language today is not only the language of state propaganda and should not be appropriated by it,” as the organizers put it. A German art school hosted the sprawling, multi-day convention. One publisher sold a title about Russian war crimes in Bucha, Ukraine, written by a Russian-speaking Ukrainian writer. Nearby, a publishing house founded by Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of the late Russian opposition figure Alexei Navalny, sold her husband’s memoir, a book that Russia banned for inciting “hatred and enmity” toward authorities. Historians from the outlawed Russian human rights organization Memorial, which won the 2022 Nobel Peace Prize, gave talks, as did a group of queer activists, who said they were “extremists” in the eyes of the Russian government. About 4,000 people attended the Berlin fair, organizers said, making it possibly the largest anti-Kremlin gathering of Russians anywhere in the world since 2022. This is not happenstance: Literature is central to Russian identity and has long played a role in the country’s politics. For centuries, citizens and leaders alike have hailed writers as political and spiritual prophets in Russia. One of the country’s enduring myths is that it is home to the world’s most avid readers; state-backed pollsters project that around 70 percent of Russians read books almost every day. The Soviet Union made universal literacy a strategic priority, rehabilitating and popularizing the 19th-century poet Alexander Pushkin as the father of Russian-language literature. In 1937, at the height of Joseph Stalin’s purges, authorities erected bronze Pushkin statues from Shanghai to Kyiv, and renamed a public square in the heart of Moscow “Pushkin Square.” That square took on an entirely new resonance in December 1965, when dozens of people gathered there to protest the arrest and prosecution of Andrei Sinyavsky and Yuli Daniel, two writers on trial for their satires of Soviet life. Their trial marked the first time that Soviet writers were prosecuted solely for the content of their work; the gathering to support them was the first unsanctioned street protest the USSR had seen in almost 40 years. Pushkin Square continued to be one of Moscow’s most important sites of political protest during and after the collapse of the Soviet Union. Thousands gathered there in February 2022 to oppose the invasion of Ukraine, which was one of the last large anti-government demonstrations in Russia. The Kremlin has since cracked down on free speech at a scale so astonishing that today, openly criticizing the government is all but impossible. The Ukraine war has upended the near-total freedom that Russian book publishers enjoyed for the first two decades of President Vladimir Putin’s rule. Not long after the invasion began, Russia’s parliament passed laws outlawing broad categories of information: criticism of the army, texts that challenged “traditional values,” anything deemed “LGBT propaganda.” The government escalated its efforts in 2024, forming an “expert center” to review published books that it suspects of non-compliance. The review process is intentionally opaque and likely to encourage self-censorship. The center has explicitly outlawed works by Russian and foreign authors alike, including those by Vladimir Sorokin, Hanya Yanagihara, Susan Sontag, and Stephen King. Police have raided bookstores and issued fines to those that display banned titles. Last year, authorities embarked on what appears to be the first criminal prosecution over the content of books since the Soviet era. Prosecutors charged three publishing employees with participating in extremism for their role in disseminating 10 books that contained LGBT themes. The most prominent of the books in contention, Pioneer Summer, is a young-adult novel that broke no laws at the time of its publication in 2021. This month, the case concluded after the employees pleaded guilty, testified against each other, and publicly repented. They were each given four-year suspended sentences. “Everyone is in shock,” a writer and book editor who lives in Russia said of the case, speaking on the condition of anonymity out of concern for his safety. “Everyone understands that that’s it, you are no longer protected in any way.” The case has spread panic in the industry, and publishers have turned to AI to help them censor new books, the writer said, “because it’s no longer possible to manually check a text for compliance with all of the authorities’ demands.” Books that are censored this way often look like highly classified documents, with black bars redacting paragraphs of text. Some publishers view this as “a more honest choice” than deleting the words entirely. Such censorship has given rise to a shadow market for banned books in Russia. Last month, the independent media outlet Verstka documented how prohibited titles are regularly sold through Avito, Russia’s answer to Craigslist, and the online retail platform Wildberries. Listings on these sites use oblique references in product descriptions to explain what they are selling. Banned books are mailed to buyers directly through the postal service. Helping to supply this underground market of contraband books is the growing constellation of Russian-language publishers in exile—including those at the Berlin book fair—that is reviving and adapting the Soviet practice of tamizdat (to “publish abroad”) to evade censorship. At the Berlin fair, attendees told Foreign Policy that they were “practicing their freedom” by engaging openly in public dissent, reading a book by a queer writer, or hearing a lecture from an independent historian. But they were also trying to retain their connection to their home country. “There must be a way for these books to be read in Russia,” said Aleksandra Zerkalyova, an editor for the publishing arm of the investigative journalism outlet Meduza. She is one of thousands of Russians who moved to Berlin after the start of the Ukraine war. Zerkalyova sold hard copies of the banned book I Love Russia, a memoir by the journalist Elena Kostyuchenko. That book was first published in English in 2023. Then, a few days later, Meduza released the original in Russian. It also published detailed instructions on how to safely purchase the book, for those abroad. Meduza determined that there was no safe way to buy it in Russia, where electronic transactions are traceable, so it decided to make the book free on its mobile app—a completely new method of disseminating tamizdat. Since then, I Love Russia has been available to anyone in Russia with even temporary internet access (Meduza’s e-books download automatically for offline reading). Despite the Kremlin’s attempts this spring to cut off access to websites and popular messaging platforms like Telegram, Meduza’s app has functioned continuously on the Russian internet without a VPN for several years now. “It’s important for us that it could be read for free by anyone who reads in Russian anywhere,” Zerkalyova said. Meduza makes the e-version of every book it publishes—around 30 so far—free and available to readers in Russia within a few months of its initial release. Zerkalyova said that they would ideally do this more quickly, but Meduza, like independent newsrooms around the world, used to rely on U.S.-funded grants that the Trump administration gutted last year. These cuts have thrown the organization into a financial crisis, and Meduza is hoping that book sales will help sustain not only its publishing operations, but possibly even its newsroom. The U.S. historian Benjamin Nathans depicted the value of uncensored Russian literature in the 20th century in his Pulitzer Prize-winning book, To the Success of Our Hopeless Cause, which charted the course of the Soviet dissident movement. His book argues that Soviet totalitarianism began unraveling not in the 1980s, as is commonly understood, but in the 1950s, after Stalin died, when the state began relaxing its rules about which ideas society could be exposed to. By the 1960s, Soviet citizens were taking to the streets demanding the rights guaranteed to them by their constitution. The process kept unfolding in “zigs and zags over the course of the next three decades,” as Nathans put it in his book, and was often propelled by literature. Soviet dissidents never intended to overthrow their government, Nathans told Foreign Policy. But literature produced by dissidents and exiles kept alive and revived ideas of human dignity and freedom that eventually reached the highest levels of the Kremlin. When the last of the Soviet leaders, Mikhail Gorbachev, introduced glasnost (transparency) as an official state policy, he was embracing a key tenet of the dissident movement. The ideas contained in contraband books “are extremely precious,” Nathans said. “It’s hard to put a quantitative value on them. But if we lose those things, then we’re really sunk.” This piece was supported by funding from the Pulitzer Center. Sarah Chatta is a journalist based in New York. Her writing has appeared in the New York Times, the New Yorker, and elsewhere. She works on the editorial staff of the New York Times. Ksenia Mironova is a journalist and documentary filmmaker based in New York. She was previously a correspondent for Russia’s last independent television channel, Dozhd, and was a protagonist in the award-winning documentary My Undesirable Friends. item.title: Death Toll Rises in Nepal-Tibet Flash Flood
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.22
Death Toll Rises in Nepal-Tibet Flash Flood Rescuers are racing to find survivors before more potential flooding occurs. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at flooding rescue efforts across Nepal and Tibet, Taiwan’s drone production ambitions, and potential Russian strikes on British targets. A Race Against Time Emergency rescue teams scoured the Nepal-Tibet border on Thursday in search of survivors of a devastating flash flood that hit the region the day before. In Nepal, at least 360 people have been killed, and more than 1,400 others remain missing, including around 700 foreigners, according to Nepali police. Local authorities expect the death toll to rise. On the Tibetan side, Chinese state media said at least three people have been killed and 558 others are missing, though it’s not clear if these numbers overlap with the Nepali figures. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at flooding rescue efforts across Nepal and Tibet, Taiwan’s drone production ambitions, and potential Russian strikes on British targets. A Race Against Time Emergency rescue teams scoured the Nepal-Tibet border on Thursday in search of survivors of a devastating flash flood that hit the region the day before. In Nepal, at least 360 people have been killed, and more than 1,400 others remain missing, including around 700 foreigners, according to Nepali police. Local authorities expect the death toll to rise. On the Tibetan side, Chinese state media said at least three people have been killed and 558 others are missing, though it’s not clear if these numbers overlap with the Nepali figures. Initial investigations indicate that an ice avalanche caused the torrential flood. Early Wednesday morning local time, a large chunk of ice broke off a glacier and fell into Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River, triggering heavy flooding. The landslide was so strong that seismologists first recorded it as an earthquake. Scientists are unsure why the glacial collapse occurred, but many suspect that global warming could be to blame. Nepal’s mountain ranges lost nearly one-third of their ice in just the past three decades due to climate change, the United Nations reported in 2023. The tiny South Asian country sits wedged between two of the world’s largest carbon emitters: China and India. Now, it’s a race against time to rescue as many people as possible before monsoon-fueled storms potentially hit the flood zone in the coming days. Beijing has also warned that Wednesday’s catastrophe created a large lake in Tibet that risks breaking through dammed streams and causing even more destruction. Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet, a Nepali Army spokesperson, confirmed on Thursday that the country’s military has rescued more than 100 people via helicopter operations. Chinese authorities have similarly deployed large military transport aircraft in Tibet to aid evacuation and relief efforts. Yet search-and-rescue operations must also contend with several hurdles to reach survivors. Wednesday’s flood decimated many key bridges and roads, making access to some of the region’s more rural areas difficult. Scarce resources and a lack of electricity due to damaged hydropower infrastructure have further hampered these efforts, as locals are finding it near impossible to check on their loved ones. Chinese authorities have also begun censoring video content of the flood on the country’s social media, making it difficult to know the scale of destruction in Tibet—a place already under extremely strict Chinese government restrictions under normal circumstances. Today’s Most Read - Everything You Always Wanted to Know About IR Grad School by Stephen M. Walt - Is Europe Ready for a New Era of Russian Dirty Tricks? by Christian Caryl - Why Even a Cornered Putin Won’t Press the Red Button by Andreas Umland What We’re Following Defense spending. Taiwan’s opposition-held parliament rejected a proposed $6.6 billion special budget on Thursday to purchase drones that would have run through 2031. Instead, legislators passed a $7.58 billion plan that will extend over the next six years and set annual spending at $1.26 billion, though that amount can be adjusted if needed. Taiwanese Defense Minister Wellington Koo criticized the opposition’s version of the plan on Thursday, arguing that a $1.26 billion annual limit would prevent Taipei from effectively bolstering its drone capabilities; the government had already planned on spending around $1.32 billion on drones next year. However, the opposition Kuomintang party maintained that its plan would ensure proper supervision of military spending. The government “cannot simply come asking for money every time without any oversight,” Kuomintang lawmaker Hsu Chiao-hsin said. Taiwanese Premier Cho Jung-tai has not yet said if he will sign the legislation into law. “What I want to look at is whether the relevant bill that got passed meets the needs of the nation, and whether it meets the various needs for our defense self-reliance and for developing the entire drone and unmanned vehicle industry,” he told reporters after the vote. “We will carefully consider this matter with regard to national needs and national security.” Taipei has prioritized expanding its drone production in recent months to combat threats from China, which does not recognize Taiwan’s sovereignty. Last week, the Taiwanese government proposed a record-high defense budget of roughly $35 billion for next year, boosting military spending past 3 percent of the country’s GDP. However, lawmakers’ monthslong delay in approving a 2026 budget—only to finally pass one last Friday—has officials worried that any military spending plans may be slow-moving. Threats from Moscow. Russia’s Foreign Ministry warned on Thursday that the country’s military could target British military facilities and equipment inside and outside of Ukraine, in retaliation for Kyiv’s continued use of long-range British cruise missiles to strike Russia. London is just “one step away” from becoming legally complicit for Kyiv’s acts of “terrorism” against Moscow, Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said, threatening “inevitable catastrophic consequences” if the United Kingdom fails to change course. Throughout the war, Ukraine has used British Storm Shadow missiles and other long-range weapons to hit critical targets deep inside Russian territory. But as Kyiv’s other primary weapons suppliers—namely, the United States—have halted deliveries, Ukraine has had to lean more heavily on the United Kingdom. During a trip to Kyiv on Monday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham approved plans to give Ukraine classified blueprints of components used to produce SCALPs, a French variant of the Storm Shadows. “The U.K. is behind you today and for as long as it takes,” Burnham said. The announcement is expected to complement Project Brakestop, another U.K. initiative aimed at mass producing low-cost, long-range strike weapons for Ukraine. Massive settlement. Meta agreed on Wednesday to pay up to $18 billion over the next decade as part of two landmark lawsuits with 47 U.S. states, the District of Columbia, and several U.S. territories. The concession marks one of the largest consumer protection settlements in U.S. history, and it signals a major win for activists who sought greater online protections for minors. Prosecutors argued that Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, violated federal child privacy and consumer protection laws by failing to adequately address addictive features of its platforms. As part of Wednesday’s settlement, Meta agreed to disable most push notifications to teenage users during school hours; enhance measures to prevent minors from accessing age-restricted content; and restrict teenagers’ access to two hours a day, with all usage blocked between midnight and 6 a.m. unless parental consent is given. Wednesday’s decision is “the right path forward for our whole industry,” Meta legal chief C.J. Mahoney said, adding that its success now “depends on all other social media platforms,” such as TikTok and YouTube, following suit. Meta has faced global criticism for allegedly fostering a harmful environment for children, prompting dozens of countries around the world to impose age-based bans on social media platforms. Odds and Ends Beginning on Friday, Australia’s music charts will only include content that is “substantially human-made.” Earlier this month, a cover of Madonna’s “Like a Prayer” by Australian DJ Josh Fawaz topped the country’s dance singles chart and hit No. 2 overall, but it was later revealed that the cover version—with more than 48 million streams on Spotify—used generative artificial intelligence in its making. Although artists will still be allowed to use AI tools “in a supporting role,” the new rules set by the Australian Recording Industry Association aim to “promote the human nature of artistry.” Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: How Washington Can Credibly Counter China in the Pacific
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.15
How Washington Can Credibly Counter China in the Pacific It’s going to take more than showing up. In July, China underscored its expanding strategic reach across the Pacific by sending a submarine-launched ballistic missile (SLBM) from the South China Sea into the Pacific Ocean. Likely flying over the Philippines and passing just south of Guam, the missile splashed down within the South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone. This aggressive act, which came with little forewarning just hours after Australia signed a treaty with Fiji, drew condemnation across the Pacific, with regional leaders decrying the provocation and accusing Beijing of deliberately escalating tensions. But this was far from an isolated incident. Instead, it underscores a fundamental geopolitical reality: The Pacific islands are now a central arena of great-power competition, where any gap in proactive U.S. strategy invites external disruption. The trajectory of Chinese power in the South Pacific became apparent in April 2022, when news broke of a wide-ranging, secretly negotiated security agreement between China and the Solomon Islands—a small island nation of approximately 850,000 people that is in the South Pacific. The news was alarming not just because of its sudden and secret nature but because of what it portended: a potential strategic Chinese foothold in the Pacific, the possibility of a military and police presence to follow, and the prospect of a hostile power placed between the United States and its closest allies. In July, China underscored its expanding strategic reach across the Pacific by sending a submarine-launched ballistic missile (SLBM) from the South China Sea into the Pacific Ocean. Likely flying over the Philippines and passing just south of Guam, the missile splashed down within the South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone. This aggressive act, which came with little forewarning just hours after Australia signed a treaty with Fiji, drew condemnation across the Pacific, with regional leaders decrying the provocation and accusing Beijing of deliberately escalating tensions. But this was far from an isolated incident. Instead, it underscores a fundamental geopolitical reality: The Pacific islands are now a central arena of great-power competition, where any gap in proactive U.S. strategy invites external disruption. The trajectory of Chinese power in the South Pacific became apparent in April 2022, when news broke of a wide-ranging, secretly negotiated security agreement between China and the Solomon Islands—a small island nation of approximately 850,000 people that is in the South Pacific. The news was alarming not just because of its sudden and secret nature but because of what it portended: a potential strategic Chinese foothold in the Pacific, the possibility of a military and police presence to follow, and the prospect of a hostile power placed between the United States and its closest allies. For decades, U.S. strategy toward the Pacific islands has suffered from institutional neglect and competing geopolitical priorities. Yet, as the SLBM launches in spring 2022 and last month illustrate, maintaining unhindered access, trusted partnerships, and strategic influence across Oceania is the foundational prerequisite for the United States’ security posture across the entire Indo-Pacific. To safeguard these shared interests, Washington must move beyond high-level visits and episodic engagement. The United States requires a comprehensive, consistent, and fully resourced Pacific strategy—one that grounds diplomatic, economic, and security commitments in sustainable, long-term partnerships. Beijing’s maneuvering demonstrates an accelerating race for influence. And reactive outreach will be insufficient to preserve regional equilibrium against an adversary pursuing a deliberate, long-term footprint. Washington’s appreciation for the Pacific has grown in recent years, with overwhelming bipartisan support for efforts under both the first Trump and Biden administrations to deepen overall U.S.-Pacific engagement. In 2019, U.S. President Donald Trump relaunched the Compacts of Free Association (COFA) negotiations with Palau, Micronesia, and the Marshall Islands, in which economic benefits to those countries are conferred in exchange for U.S. military access across the North Pacific. He also invited the leaders of all three countries to the White House. U.S. President Joe Biden built on that momentum and, due largely to the 2022 agreement with the Solmon Islands, quickly expanded engagement across the entire Pacific islands region, which encompasses 14 countries and several territories. Under Biden, the United States published the first U.S.-Pacific strategy and welcomed all Pacific leaders to the White House not once but twice for leader-level summits, in addition to rolling out hundreds of millions in targeted development and security assistance. Today, however, that trajectory faces renewed uncertainty. Under the second Trump administration, the United States has radically reshaped its foreign policy, dismantling development mechanisms such as U.S. Agency for International Development, using tariffs as a tool of first resort for both ally and foe, and withdrawing from or reducing its presence in international institutions that it initially helped to create. While not specifically aimed at the Pacific region, these measures have had an outsized effect on these small democratic nations, which are dependent on external development assistance and possess narrow economies that are highly vulnerable to external shocks. As U.S. foreign policy finds its new shape driven largely by an “America First” outlook, there are signs that the Pacific remains a significant priority for U.S. national security professionals. Two agreements seen as a ground-floor signal of U.S. commitment to the region, the COFA and the Tuna Treaty, were funded with broad bipartisan support. U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, a top U.S. diplomat, has visited the region twice, including a well-received trip to Papua New Guinea for the country’s 50th anniversary of independence and diplomatic relations with the United States. In May, the Quad foreign ministers announced that the grouping plans to build out a new port in Fiji, one highlight among several Pacific-related announcements. The Trump administration has also recognized the importance of bolstering key relationships across the region. In July, the newly elected Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale visited Washington. That visit, on the heels of a similar one to Canberra and Wellington, was a clear demonstration of Wale’s commitment to returning to traditional partnerships with Australia, New Zealand, and the United States after several years of pro-Beijing leadership in Honiara. During the visit, Wale met with Landau and other senior U.S. officials, and the two countries announced several significant deliverables, including the intended return of the Peace Corps to the Solomon Islands and $6 million in new funding for unexploded ordnance removal, which is still a persistent and deadly issue for the region. And yet despite these signs of life, U.S. programming for the region remains largely on hold, and there is still no U.S. ambassador resident in any of the 14 Pacific island countries. In response to both Beijing’s ambitions and Washington’s drawdown, Australia has drastically ramped up its engagement in recent years, crafting various bilateral agreements that incorporate a protective security component, such as the Falepili Union with Tuvalu, which allows some of Tuvaluans to emigrate to Australia in exchange for essentially giving Australia veto power over Tuvalu’s external security arrangements. Australia has also signed two mutual defense treaties over the past year, one with Papua New Guinea and another with Fiji. Yet as China’s SLBM launch in July demonstrated, Beijing remains determined to assert its presence and influence across what it considers a highly strategic region. The Pacific has thus entered the fore as a central arena of great-power competition, and ensuring the region remains open and free from a permanent Chinese presence requires a group effort, including from the United States. Ensuring that the United States retains the ability to depend on its access to and through the Pacific—including to allies such as Australia, Japan, and the Philippines—will require steps beyond what the region has seen thus far from Washington. In the Pacific, showing up, engaging, and listening is a critical first step. Through senior-level engagements in the region and Hawaii, the United States has met that mark. But it is time to move beyond showing up and listening. The United States must also demonstrate that it has listened and work to flesh out what has become an increasingly anemic relationship. As Beijing pursues vectors of engagement across the full range of diplomatic, economic, security, and informational instruments of power, so, too, must the United States. From Aug. 30 to Sept. 4, the annual Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting (PIFLM) will take place in Palau. The United States, as a dialogue partner, has been invited to attend, and Deputy Secretary of State Landau is leading the delegation. As one of Taiwan’s three remaining allies in the Pacific and a close and consistent U.S. partner through the COFA, Palau as host presents a prime opportunity for the United States to showcase its commitment both to Palau as a strategic ally and to the Pacific region as a whole. As part of Landau’s visit, or following this PIFLM, the following recommendations have the ability to build upon the groundwork that has been laid thus far, shaping a far more comprehensive and enduring approach to an often overlooked, but strategically vital region. First, the United States must stop being egregiously outmatched by China’s diplomatic ground game in the Pacific. Getting ambassadors to the region will not rectify this imbalance, but it is an essential first step. Similarly, the United States should deploy a dedicated ambassador to the Pacific Islands Forum—as it does with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, another regional body—in recognition of the important and influential role that the forum plays in the Pacific and beyond. The United States must be more agile in capitalizing on key strategic opportunities. While the initial announcements out of Wale’s visit to Washington were positive, it is critical that Washington commits to doubling down on one of the most critical countries in the Pacific, ideally with much-needed health and port infrastructure, as well as bolstering real investments into the Solomon Islands. Existing U.S. work in the maritime domain, including U.S. Coast Guard deployments and critical ship-rider agreements, is welcome but remains insufficient. In conjunction with partners like New Zealand, Japan, and Australia, the United States should conduct regular overflights of far-reaching maritime zones using assets out of Guam, Hawaii, and—ideally—Australia, and it must ensure that authorities are in place to allow Pacific officials to use the evidence collected to prosecute violators of maritime law. Lastly, Coast Guard deployments—often cited as one of the most important contributors to regional security—should be expanded, including potentially home porting a Coast Guard cutter in Australia. Partnering with the Pacific to counter the growing Pacific transnational and organized crime threat is directly in the United States’ national interest. Starting with the COFA states in the North Pacific, the United States should deploy regular FBI, Drug Enforcement Administration, and legal experts to work alongside host-nation officials on a consistent basis to provide the full spectrum of U.S. national power toward a challenge that threatens all nations. As the Pacific becomes more connected across an increasingly complex network of digital infrastructure, it is imperative to protect and secure these vital digital assets from malign incursion and intentional or accidental disruption. The United States should take the lead in presenting global norms around protection and sustainment of digital infrastructure. Pacific nations, which spend around 5 to 15 percent of GDP on fuel and gas, have found themselves at the whip end of the global fuel crisis. The United States should work with other regional partners, such as Australia and New Zealand, to craft meaningful financing solutions, such as through the World Bank, to provide critical debt relief to Pacific partners. Education and training programs allow the United States to forge lasting ties with future Pacific leaders—a noncorrupt form of “elite capture,” in a sense. The United States should expand the scope of its Young Pacific Leaders fellowships to sectors such as law enforcement, health, and disaster preparedness to broaden the reach and connectivity between Washington and its Pacific partners. Additionally, it should urge the Quad to announce a fellowship for the Pacific to promote education opportunities for Pacific Islanders in Quad countries. This could be launched at the next major Quad ministerial or leaders’ summit. In line with a renewed U.S. focus on commercial diplomacy, a full-time, dedicated PIF Trade Office in Washington would better foster U.S.-Pacific business relationships. Ultimately, the United States cannot afford to rest on a baseline level of effort in a region where the strategic stakes are escalating so rapidly. China’s assertive military maneuvers and sustained diplomatic push have made it clear that mere presence is no longer a substitute for strategy. Fortunately, the cost of securing Washington’s posture in the Pacific is remarkably modest relative to its yield; small, targeted investments in diplomatic footprint, maritime security, and economic resilience offer an outsized return, delivering maximum strategic impact for minimal financial outlay. By moving beyond symbolic visits and institutionalizing low-cost, high-gain partnerships that address the concrete needs of Pacific island states, Washington can reinforce a vital arena of its Indo-Pacific strategy. Failing to execute this high-leverage approach will leave the United States perpetually on the defensive, slowly losing ground in a region that is essential to its long-term national security. Charles Edel is the Australia chair and a senior advisor at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. He served on the U.S. secretary of state’s policy planning staff from 2015 to 2017. Kathryn Paik is a senior fellow with the Australia chair at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. She previously served as director for the Pacific and Southeast Asia on the National Security Council from 2021 to 2023. item.title: The SCO’s Diminishing Usefulness for India
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.95
The SCO’s Diminishing Usefulness for India Much like BRICS, the China-dominated Shanghai Cooperation Organisation offers few benefits to New Delhi. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s three-way handshake with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at last year’s Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Tianjin, China, went viral across the global media. The optics were especially powerful because they came amid the Trump administration’s relentless pressure on India over trade and its purchases of Russian oil. President Donald Trump soon declared that the United States appeared to have “lost” India and Russia to China. The images intensified an argument in Washington over who lost India and reinforced the case for political reengagement with the Modi government, slowly but steadily stabilizing the relationship. As it celebrates its 25th jubilee at a summit in Kyrgyzstan next week, the SCO will focus on regional stability, economic integration, transport connectivity, and digitalization. Measured against the Trump administration’s chaos and political disarray of the West, the China-led SCO will look more productive and purposeful. India, though, might not be too comfortable with the growing dominance of China over the forum, but it would want to make the best of the bilateral diplomatic opportunities presented by the summit, attended by a large section of leaders from inner Asia. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s three-way handshake with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at last year’s Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Tianjin, China, went viral across the global media. The optics were especially powerful because they came amid the Trump administration’s relentless pressure on India over trade and its purchases of Russian oil. President Donald Trump soon declared that the United States appeared to have “lost” India and Russia to China. The images intensified an argument in Washington over who lost India and reinforced the case for political reengagement with the Modi government, slowly but steadily stabilizing the relationship. As it celebrates its 25th jubilee at a summit in Kyrgyzstan next week, the SCO will focus on regional stability, economic integration, transport connectivity, and digitalization. Measured against the Trump administration’s chaos and political disarray of the West, the China-led SCO will look more productive and purposeful. India, though, might not be too comfortable with the growing dominance of China over the forum, but it would want to make the best of the bilateral diplomatic opportunities presented by the summit, attended by a large section of leaders from inner Asia. Rubbing shoulders regularly with a range of leaders, especially Xi amid structural tensions in the India-China relationship, has become one of the principal utilities of the SCO for India. New Delhi became a full member in 2017 after years of seeking entry. But whereas the SCO has emerged as a valuable venue for Indian diplomacy, it has become less interesting as an instrument for promoting Indian interests in Asia. Instead, much like BRICS, the SCO has increasingly become a multilateral platform for advancing the interests of its dominant member, China. India finds itself a reluctant and defensive participant—unable to move too close to China or identify fully with the anti-Western agenda promoted by Beijing and Moscow. The SCO has its origins in the Shanghai Five, created in 1996 by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan. The SCO predecessor’s immediate purpose was to build confidence and reduce military tensions along the borders inherited from the collapse of the Soviet Union. As the grouping evolved, China also saw it as a means of combating what it calls the “three evils”—separatism, extremism, and terrorism—emanating from Central Asia and potentially destabilizing China’s westernmost province of Xinjiang. Russia had its own reasons for embracing the forum. As Moscow became increasingly disillusioned with the post-Cold War order and U.S. primacy, cooperation with China became central to its search for a multipolar world. Concerns about Western-supported “color revolutions” would become more prominent after popular uprisings in Georgia, Ukraine, and Kyrgyzstan in the early 2000s. The SCO also developed amid the rapid normalization of Sino-Russian relations, which eased Russian concerns about the expansion of Chinese influence into its traditional Central Asian sphere. A broad division of labor emerged, with Russia retaining its larger security role while China steadily became the dominant economic power. The late 1990s also saw Russia entice India into a triangular forum with China to limit the dangers of the American unipolar moment. Then-Russian Prime Minister Yevgeny Primakov publicly proposed a Russia-India-China strategic triangle during his visit to New Delhi in 1998. India, wary of American pressure over Kashmir and nuclear proliferation, was willing to play along with the rhetoric of multipolarity even as its diplomatic energies increasingly went into improving relations with the United States. The threesome was eventually subsumed by BRIC, BRICS, and today’s expanded version of that group. India was equally eager to join the SCO when it was formed in 2001 as an institutional structure for the Shanghai Five. Apprehensions about Pakistan gaining ground in Central Asia, the need for an active presence in the newly independent “stans,” and the prospect of greater cooperation on counterterrorism saw New Delhi push persistently for membership. India became an observer in 2005 and, after the decision to admit it was taken in 2015, became a full member in June 2017. But it could enter only alongside Pakistan—awkwardly sharing space with Islamabad in a new regional forum even as an existing one, the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), had already become paralyzed by India-Pakistan tensions. Nearly a decade after India joined the SCO, both the regional context and New Delhi’s interests have shifted significantly. First, the driving idea behind the bloc—promoting multipolarity by limiting U.S. power—no longer squares easily with India’s growing convergence with the United States, its Asian allies, and Europe, or with India’s mounting problems with China. The military crises on the border since 2020 have underlined the structural nature of India’s China problem. Russia continues to enjoy considerable political goodwill in New Delhi, and the energy relationship has deepened. Yet there is no escaping the diminution of Russia’s salience in India’s overall calculus as Moscow struggles with the consequences of its war in Ukraine and the rupture of its relations with the West. More broadly, notwithstanding Trump’s provocations, New Delhi has little reason to support the anti-American and anti-Western posturing that increasingly surrounds both the SCO and BRICS. The SCO allows India to put out diplomatic signals on its commitment to strategic autonomy and an independent foreign policy. But it does not solve any of India’s entrenched problems with China or elevate the partnership with Russia to a higher level. Second, the SCO is no longer exclusively focused on Central Asia in a way that might boost India’s engagement with the region. It has become a sprawling assembly. It now has 10 full members, two observers, and 15 dialogue partners, stretching well beyond inner Asia to include countries such as Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the Maldives, Myanmar, and Laos. As with BRICS, China has been eager to widen the SCO’s ambit. Arguably, Beijing’s interest is less in constructing a cohesive regional organization than in promoting its broader foreign-policy objectives—including Chinese ideas, discourse, and global initiatives. For China, it is the strength of its bilateral relationships with the Central Asian states, rather than the SCO itself, that secures its regional interests. For New Delhi, meanwhile, the old idea of balancing China in Central Asia—on its own or through partnership with Russia—looks less impressive every day as the comprehensive power gap between India and China grows, massively, in Beijing’s favor. In the SCO as in BRICS, China towers over the other members, including Russia and India. Third, given the SCO’s original focus on extremism and terrorism, India had hoped to mobilize the region around these shared concerns and leverage them against Pakistan’s support for cross-border terrorism. But as in other multilateral forums, China has been protective of Pakistan and has prevented India from using the SCO to isolate Islamabad. Worse still, from New Delhi’s perspective, the SCO has produced a certain moral equivalence between Indian and Pakistani charges on terrorism. It is not a perspective that is shared by others in the SCO. The 2025 Tianjin Declaration “strongly condemned” the April 22, 2025, terrorist attack at Pahalgam, which triggered the India-Pakistan military confrontation in May. But it did not identify Pakistan as responsible. In the very same passage, the declaration condemned the March 11 and May 21 terrorist attacks in the Pakistani province of Balochistan, which Pakistan has accused India of supporting. The SCO therefore acknowledged India’s concerns over Pahalgam while simultaneously giving multilateral recognition to terrorist attacks invoked by Pakistan in making its case against India. The result was less a regional consensus on terrorism than a diplomatic balancing of Indian and Pakistani narratives about each other’s support for attacks. New Delhi’s ability to put Islamabad in the dock on terrorism has diminished as the post-9/11 agenda on global terrorism fades and the interests of China and others in Pakistan now come into play. Fourth, the SCO and BRICS have sharpened India’s larger problem of regionalism. If isolating Pakistan on terrorism has become difficult, New Delhi must now reckon with Islamabad’s growing diplomatic weight during Trump’s second term and its reintegration into the geopolitics of the Middle East. Pakistan will take over the rotating chairmanship of the SCO after the summit in Bishkek next week and will host the organization’s annual summit next year. This will only add to the complications in India’s approach to Pakistan and regional institutions. In light of its regional interests and misgivings vis-à-vis the SCO, the fact that India has not found a way to advance the SAARC is striking. That organization has not held a summit since Kathmandu in 2014, and Nepal continues formally as its chair because the planned 2016 Islamabad summit never took place. Meanwhile, India’s other South Asian neighbors have steadily developed links with the SCO: Afghanistan is an observer; Nepal, Sri Lanka, and the Maldives are dialogue partners; and Bangladesh has recently sought support from Russia and Tajikistan for joining the organization. The irony is hard to miss. Even as SAARC remains frozen by India-Pakistan conflict, China-backed continental institutions are extending their political reach into the subcontinent. Given its internal structure and distribution of power, the SCO is not in a position to address India’s key regional interests. It cannot generate geographic access to Central Asia. It will not alter Pakistan’s transit veto. It will not produce a credible regional response to Pakistan-based terrorism. Nor will it balance China’s growing influence. The answers to these problems can only be found through a stronger Indian bilateral engagement with the Central Asian republics and partnerships with friendly powers to develop projects that can help New Delhi overcome its geographic disadvantages. None of this means India should walk away from the SCO. New Delhi can continue to use the summits for bilateral diplomacy, resist formulations contrary to Indian interests through the organization’s consensus principle, and leverage the convenient access the forum provides to Eurasian leaders. India’s experience in the SCO underlines a larger political truth. Multilateral institutions, whether regional or global, reflect the distribution of power. Stronger states use them to gain legitimacy for the pursuit of national interests, dressed up in the language of universalism or regional good. Recognizing that China increasingly owns the SCO table is the necessary starting point for a realistic Indian engagement with the forum—with low expectations, modest objectives, and no illusions about what sitting at that table can deliver. C. Raja Mohan is a columnist at Foreign Policy, a distinguished professor at O.P. Jindal Global University's Motwani Jadeja Institute for American Studies, the Korea Foundation chair on Asian geopolitics at the Council for Strategic and Defense Research, and a former member of India’s National Security Advisory Board. item.title: What in the World?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.92
What in the World? Test yourself on the week of Aug. 22: A U.N. monitoring mission goes to Congo, the U.S. unveils an economic plan against Iran, and Putin issues a warning. U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” this week. Beyond that eye-popping story, what else happened? Find out with our international news quiz! Have feedback? Email [email protected] to let me know your thoughts. U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” this week. Beyond that eye-popping story, what else happened? Find out with our international news quiz! 1. In a video released on Sunday, Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella announced he would order the country’s immigration service to begin doing what? Recent government data suggests that there are hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans who have fled economic and political crises to Colombia—and now they have to worry about deportation, FP’s Catherine Osborn writes in Latin America Brief. 2. A United Nations-backed monitoring mission deployed to the Democratic Republic of the Congo on Monday. What is it meant to oversee? 3. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday unveiled a plan to cut Iran off from the global economy. What is that campaign called? If policymakers work on the assumption that the worst of the economic fallout from the Iran war is behind us, that could lead to true economic catastrophe, FP’s Emma Ashford and Matthew Rojansky argue. 4. What did Russian President Vladimir Putin say on Monday would happen to privately owned critical infrastructure facilities if their owners failed to protect them from Ukrainian attacks—or repair them after strikes? Concerns of nuclear escalation if Russia were on the verge of losing in Ukraine are misplaced. Other great powers have previously been humbled in conflict without resorting to nuclear warfare, Andreas Umland argues. 5. The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces on Tuesday announced the official dissolution of the group. What will now happen to its remaining fighters? The practical and symbolic nature of daily governance in the Kurdish-led northeastern territory, formerly known as Rojava, remains fraught as it integrates into Syria, Hanna Davis reported earlier this month. 6. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that CIA director John Ratcliffe traveled to Russia earlier this week to do what? The trip came after new U.S. intelligence assessments suggested that Putin could seek to launch a limited attack on a member of the trans-Atlantic alliance, FP’s John Haltiwanger and Rishi Iyengar write in Situation Report. 7. Zambian police said on Thursday that opposition leader Brian Mundubile and his running mate are in police custody after being questioned in connection with which alleged crime? The results of the presidential election earlier this month are still being contested amid allegations of interference by incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema, FP’s Nosmot Gbadamosi reports in Africa Brief. 8. Taiwan’s opposition-controlled parliament on Thursday rejected the government’s proposed special military budget that would have focused on funding what? 9. A humanoid robot set a new world record in the 100-meter dash at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday. Which human set the previous record of 9.58 seconds? (Hint: It was in 2009.) 10. Fat Marmot Week kicked off in Colorado on Monday, aiming to raise money for what? You scored It’s a big world out there! Brush up on global goings-on by subscribing to World Brief, Foreign Policy’s flagship daily newsletter. Have feedback? Email [email protected] to let me know your thoughts.
