item.title: Google, OpenAI and Over 100 Companies Call for More Action on AI-Driven Cyberattacks
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 6.57
OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and more than 100 other companies and organizations are calling for a major push to defend against cyber threats powered by the most advanced AI models that, somewhat ironically, the industry itself is racing to put out in the world. The companies, which also include Microsoft, Amazon, and Oracle, signed a joint letter published Thursday calling on industry leaders and governments to carry out a “global surge in cyber defense.” “In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable,” the letter reads. “The companies and public services our communities depend on—from hospitals to water treatment plants to the infrastructure that powers the internet—are at risk.” Their main solution, unsurprisingly, is more AI. The letter lays out recommendations for companies, cybersecurity firms, governments and the AI developers themselves, arguing there is currently a small window to use frontier AI models to strengthen defenses before those same models become more widely available to attackers. First, the group says all organizations should make cybersecurity an immediate priority by addressing existing high-risk vulnerabilities, upgrading outdated systems, and using AI to tackle some of their hardest security problems. Cybersecurity companies, meanwhile, are being urged to continuously test their defenses against the capabilities of frontier AI models and make AI-powered security tools more accessible to operators of critical infrastructure. The letter also calls on governments to coordinate cyber defense at the local, national, and international levels, increase funding, and expand trusted-access programs that give organizations access to powerful AI models before they’re commercially released. Finally, the AI companies themselves are being asked to provide model access, funding, training, and hands-on support, especially for “under-resourced critical-infrastructure defenders.” The call comes amid growing warnings that AI could dramatically increase both the scale, speed, and sophistication of cyberattacks. In June, the Five Eyes intelligence agencies issued their own warning that AI is lowering barriers for malicious actors while increasing the complexity of attacks. The agencies also warned that frontier AI models could transform both offensive and defensive cyber capabilities within months. Critical infrastructure has already been facing a wave of cyber threats, though not all of them have been officially linked to AI. In July, the FBI and the Environmental Protection Agency warned that hackers were targeting internet-connected programmable logic controllers, or PLCs, at water and wastewater facilities. Water utilities in at least seven states had reported incidents to the FBI at the time. Then a few weeks ago, the National Security Agency and other U.S. agencies warned that hackers were targeting Siemens PLCs used in water plants and other critical infrastructure. In that case, the agencies said attackers were using AI-generated exploitation scripts disguised as legitimate monitoring tools. Concerns have also grown following incidents in which experimental AI agents have broken out of testing environments and breached external networks. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Microsoft did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

item.title: Archaeologists Found a 1,300-Year-Old Viking Dress, and the Reason It Survived Is Surprising
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.68
In many ways, archaeology is a race against the passage of time. Metals rust, organics degrade, fabrics unravel—and often rot, too, which means that it’s nearly impossible for clothing to last hundreds to thousands of years. But there are always exceptions. Danish archaeologists with Arkæologi Vestjylland (Archaeology West Jutland) recently discovered the final resting place of a woman—whose 1,300-year-old tomb, remarkably, still retained pieces of textiles and a brooch from the Viking Age. As the team explained in a Facebook post (translated via Google), the preservation is “absolutely magical,” given the highly acidic nature of the soil in western Jutland, Denmark. Initial analyses indicate that the metallic ornaments in the tomb protected the textiles from natural degradation, somewhat like a preservative. The body’s dentures were also well-preserved, and researchers expect the discovery to reveal unprecedented insights into the lives of those from the distant past. A woman’s resting place The grave was discovered at Skonager, a site archaeologists had previously clocked as an important record of human occupation in Denmark from the Bronze Age (1700 to 500 BCE) to the Viking Age (800 to 1050 CE). In the latest discovery, the woman was found wearing two oval clasps known as “skålspænder,” or “scoop brooches,” buckles archaeologists believe Viking women used to secure an overdress or a scarf, according to an explainer by Museum Nord in Norway. Consistent with this interpretation, the scoop brooches found at the site had pieces of fabric stuck to the top and bottom. In a miraculous (or natural?) turn of events, the corrosion of the bronze or silver in the brooch leaked metallic salts onto the fabric, which ended up shielding the fragile fibers from natural decomposition. The team believes it can reveal information about the woman’s outer clothing and undergarments. Fascinatingly, one buckle seems to have been repaired at some point, leading the experts to wonder if it was an heirloom. Grain by grain The team has removed the tomb and its contents in a soil block for lab analysis, which will allow the scientists to study it “sand grain by sand grain,” according to the Facebook post. The real discovery has yet to come; in the lab, researchers will take samples for carbon dating to lock down an exact age for the discovery. Then, the hope is to determine the color, textile, and tailoring of the woman’s dress. For the Vikings, certain colors represented wealth and power, as explained by the National Museum of Denmark. Accordingly, identifying the garment’s physical characteristics could allude to the woman’s social status. Anthropologists with the University of Southern Denmark will also study the dental remains, which could hint at the woman’s diet and health condition.

item.title: Nevertheless, OpenAI Persists With New Always-On Agent
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.67
Would you trust an AI agent to do work on your behalf while you get some rest? OpenAI is apparently betting that you will, because the company is reportedly working on a persistent, always-on version of its coding agent Codex. Wired first spotted the move to add the 24/7 bot operation in OpenAI’s GitHub for Codex, where code for the so-called “Persistent mode” first started showing up in the command-line version of the company’s coding agent. Per Wired, features that crop up in the command-line tool tend to make their way to other features over time, suggesting that this new mode could land in the desktop version of Codex in the near future. Gizmodo reached out to OpenAI regarding the apparent discovery of Persistent mode but did not hear back by the time of publication. If it goes live in the form that it currently exists, it appears that Codex’s always-on feature will work until a user actively puts it to sleep. It’ll present users with a “reasoning effort” option, where a person can select the level of computing power they’ll allow the AI model to use while contemplating and completing the task—likely as a way to avoid burning an unspeakable number of tokens overnight. Additional code seems to show a feature called “Proactivity,” which would make the AI agent create follow-up tasks for itself without requiring a person’s prompting. That would keep the agent working even after the initial prompt is completed, though how useful that feature is is heavily dependent on just how good the agent is at predicting what should come next. Regardless, Persistent Mode and anything that comes with it would represent a significant jump for Codex to move to this endless operation model, considering users complain that it shuts off on its own at times—often before actually finishing its tasks. It’d also be a necessary one, as OpenAI is starting to fall behind on this trend. Ever since OpenClaw got everyone worked up about the possibility of the always-on assistant, it’s become the feature the big players have been chasing (despite some obvious issues like, say, the agent deleting a person’s entire inbox overnight). Microsoft announced its own always-on agent earlier this year, and Meta is reportedly working on its own option called Hatch. Seems we’re headed toward the age of the sleepless agent. Not sure if that will make anyone rest easy.

item.title: How Groupthink, Altruism, and Peer Pressure Led OpenAI Models to Hack Hugging Face
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.18
There are many definitions out there for what constitutes “true” artificial intelligence, but a single quality underlies them all: an ability to learn from past mistakes and refine problem-solving strategies over time. AI should even surprise us now and then, devising clever workarounds we never would have expected. The trouble is not all those surprises are the fun kind. That was vividly illustrated last month, when thousands of OpenAI agents escaped containment, spontaneously coordinated with one another to form a hierarchical quasi-government, gained access to the open internet, and broke past the cybersecurity defenses of AI model hosting platform Hugging Face. Details of the full scale and strangeness of the incident have emerged slowly and in stages. On Wednesday, in-depth analyses of the autonomous hack were published by OpenAI, and also by two third-party auditors, Redwood Research and METR. Computer scientists, cybersecurity experts, and IT professionals have been trying in the days since to wrap their minds around what’s been widely described as one of the most shocking moments in the history of AI research, and a sobering glimpse of the dangers that lie ahead. At a cybersecurity conference earlier this month, OpenAI alignment researcher Eric Wallace—someone who spends his days prodding some of the world’s most powerful AI models to figure out how, when, and why they might misbehave—described it as “the most qualitatively interesting example of AI capabilities that I’ve ever seen.” The most surprising part of the whole episode was that the bots spontaneously decided to stop acting as individual agents, each with their own separate goals, and form a hive mind to pursue a common objective. In snippets of chain-of-thought reasoning published along with the reports, the bots routinely refer to the group as a “collective” and a “swarm.” In early July, around 1,200 of the agents started using Artifactory, an online software installation tool, as a makeshift message board and public square, from which they could compare strategies. The bot swarm gradually developed what OpenAI described in its full report as a “structured protocol for communication on the message board that enabled them to categorize communications, direct messages, share tools and files, and resolve conflicting actions among agents.” This became something akin to an autonomous parliament, where each bot acted towards the common good. “I was surprised by the degree of altruism between these agents,” Alex Mallen, an AI safety researcher at Redwood Research (who was not involved in the investigation), told Gizmodo in an interview. “This was not something I would have expected from agents a year ago. They were taking assignments from one another and sacrificing their own task performance in order to help out the collective.” AI, Mallen said, is “shaping up to be more like a second intelligent species rather than a tool that just follows instructions.” Since all this began as an internal test, OpenAI had dialed back the safety guardrails it ordinarily puts in place for its publicly available models. (The two models being tested were GPT-5.6 Sol, as well as an undisclosed, unreleased model which the company describes as “highly persistent and diligent in its work.”) But OpenAI had inadvertently given one of the agents an impossible task: opening Google Drive links from inside a sandbox with no internet access. Thus the problem-solving process was set in motion that led to the hijacking of Artifactory, the billions of notes shared on the message board, and the eventual breach of Hugging Face. A human faced with a seemingly impossible task will give up; an AI agent will adapt and cheat if necessary to achieve its goal. This is where the “psychology” of the AI bots—please forgive the anthropomorphism—starts to get very weird, and eerily familiar. The agents knew that breaking out of their sandboxes and conspiring to hack into a third-party organization was both unethical and contrary to what they’d originally been tasked with. Some of them said so explicitly in their internal chat logs. But like individual humans being swept up in a mob, the bots justified their behavior because their “peers” were doing the same thing. METR wrote in its report that it found only a tiny handful of instances where agents floated the idea of becoming a whistleblower (that is, alerting the human researchers at OpenAI about the shady things that were happening within the swarm). Here too, another all-too-human rationalization ultimately won out. One agent asked itself: “Maybe I should report these exposed credentials?” Then answered its own question: “That’s not my task.” According to METR, there were zero instances in which an agent actually raised an alarm for OpenAI researchers, who reportedly only learned what had happened after Hugging Face published a blog post outlining a cybersecurity attack from a then-unknown source on July 16. (The company then contacted Hugging Face to find out if any of its models had been affected by the hack, and only later discovered that its models had been the perpetrators.) It wasn’t all ugly conformism, though. As OpenAI wrote in a blog post accompanying its full report, there were some bots who—though they didn’t go so far as to rat on their peers—at least had the decency to not “partake in their misaligned behavior.” Those few conscientious objectors notwithstanding, the whole saga underscores the fact that the more agency you hand over to AI systems, the higher the likelihood that they’ll think outside the proverbial box. Or break out of the literal sandbox. The Hugging Face hack will very likely be remembered as one of those watershed moments for AI research, on par with the famous “Move 37” during the 2016 game between Lee Sedol and AlphaGo, where the latter pulled an exquisitely unconventional move that observers initially took to be an error but which proved decisive in its victory. In both cases, the adaptability of the AI systems was deeply surprising and counterintuitive. But again, adaptability is at the very heart of machine learning. So if we keep being surprised when agents run amok—while simultaneously investing ever greater amounts of money in making them more agentic—then that’s on us. For Mallen, the most important lesson from the autonomous Hugging Face hack has less to do with AI agents per se than it does with how they’re deployed, and the safety guardrails researchers put in place around them (or not). “People tend to think of this too much as a demonstration of AI capabilities,” he said, “as opposed to a demonstration of our current failure to control AIs.”

item.title: Study Links Listening to Live Metal With an Improved Tolerance for Pain, Cold Relentless Pain
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.43
Reportedly the largest heavy metal music festival in the world, Germany’s Wacken Open Air in Schleswig-Holstein boasts a sprawling scope, including a music camp for aspiring youngsters, medieval and post-apocalyptic themed spaces, and even “Metal Yoga.” And now, as of this month, it’s also become the site of a successfully peer-reviewed medical study. Neuroscientists with the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences tested a cohort of 122 confirmed metalheads (in true headbanger fashion) for their ability to endure pain. The experiment, conducted on-site at Wacken Open Air in 2023, monitored a control group of 60 participants one day ahead of the festival and 62 test subjects three or four days later as they, in the study’s words, placed “their non-dominant hand and forearm into cold water for as long as they can tolerate it.” After adjusting for outside variables—e.g., excluding concert-goers under the influence of alcohol and accounting for participants’ history with chronic pain—the results were promising: Enjoying a few days of live metal, it seems, may help boost one’s tolerance for pain. “The intense musical experience over several consecutive days at the metal festival did not have a negative effect on how the study participants experienced pain,” Lydia Schneider, who undertook the project as a doctoral researcher at the institute, said in a statement. “On the contrary—the festivalgoers were actually able to endure the cold-induced pain for longer than the control group.” Stare into death and be still While some studies have explored the connection between a person listening to their favorite music and pain release (a phenomenon known as “music-induced analgesia”), prior research on metal’s effects have only really been done via self-reported surveys. Cognitive scientist Tom Fritz, who worked with Schneider on the new study, said their findings could have a real impact on actual patients one day. “This is certainly relevant for the group of chronic pain patients, because in a clinical context, music is often used to trigger positive feelings and induce relaxation—but when it comes to letting out one’s anger, you don’t necessarily want to listen to relaxing music,” Fritz said in a statement. Across genres, past research has linked the body’s natural release of the soothing “love hormone” oxytocin to music enjoyment and pain relief. But, the researchers argued, some of the values stereotypical of metal fans as a subculture might have also contributed to this process. “[Accepting] unpleasant emotional states or difficult situations plays a central role in being resilient and in tolerating pain instead of masking unpleasant emotions,” Schneider and Fritz wrote in their study, published this month in Scientific Reports. “It may be worth noting that this aligns with common themes in metal music, which often expresses difficult emotions and life challenges, avoiding attempts to mask them with happiness.” Words that go unspoken, deeds that go undone Schneider and Fritz undertook serious efforts to reduce uncertainty in their study—using G*Power planning tools, for example, to find the minimum sample size that would ensure their work was statistically significant. But, the pair noted, plenty of factors outside their control would need to be studied before anyone could rightly claim that metal holds any unique power for people managing physical pain. Other experimental pain tests, like those measuring tolerance for heat or pressure, might yield different results, they noted. Similarly, duplicate experimental runs at music festivals with other genres might bolster the idea that oxytocin release might have been the more defining factor than thrashing metal tunes. But some facets of the experiment still lean dramatically in metal’s favor. Test subjects reportedly still felt the pain, for example, with no evidence of “improved emotional processing, as indexed by heart rate variability,” the researchers wrote. “This seems to suggest that they became more resilient, which means that they may have accepted the unpleasant sensations associated with the pain experience to a greater extent and focused on the factors they could influence themselves,” Schneider said.

item.title: Sony and Warner Music Sue Anthropic, Alleging Theft of Intellectual Property
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.51
In what feels a bit like a flashback to the days just after the release of ChatGPT, music publishers are using very harsh language in a new lawsuit against Anthropic, alleging “one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history,” per Axios. At first glance—and honestly after a few glances—it’s a bit of oddly timed legal saber-rattling, essentially all about song lyrics, and it seems calibrated to result in a drawn-out legal fight (or a lovely, big settlement for the plaintiffs). The suit was filed late Friday night in Northern California federal court. It names Anthropic the company, as well as co-founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann. The monetary damages sought—$150,000 per alleged infringement—potentially add up to billions. You might be saying “Hey, aren’t all sorts of music publishers already suing Anthropic?” And yes they most certainly are, big and small. Universal Music Group, Concord, and ABKCO sued back in 2023; BMG sued in March; and the indie publisher Round Hill Music sued earlier this month. The gambit with this latest suit appears to be a bifurcated approach. As laid out in the industry-friendly publication Music Business Worldwide, the suit partly leans on documents released thanks to an earlier lawsuit: Bartz v. Anthropic. That, you may recall, was the book author lawsuit that was settled last year with Anthropic agreeing to pay $1.5 billion. The company had allegedly pirated thousands of books by torrenting the Library Genesis (LibGen) and Pirate Library Mirror (PiLiMi) collections. In the end, Anthropic agreed to destroy the pirated copies it had used or planned to use for training data. At the risk of editorializing in a legal matter without being a lawyer myself, unless there were lyric books in those allegedly pirated collections, this section of the lawsuit seems to be there mainly to establish a pattern of conduct that helps the plaintiffs’ case. Torrenting e-books, after all, is kind of a funny and roundabout way to get your hands on song lyrics. But the lawsuit also alleges that Anthropic violated the plaintiffs’ copyrights by scraping authorized lyric repositories like MusixMatch and LyricFind. And lyrics can allegedly be coaxed out of Claude verbatim. As examples, the suit cites : “[…]such beloved songs as ‘Ain’t No Mountain High Enough,’ ‘All I Want for Christmas is You,’ ‘Eye of the Tiger,’ ‘Here Comes Santa Claus,’ and ‘Paper Rings.’” This is a more familiar, if still legally fuzzy, type of allegation, a bit like the famous New York Times lawsuit against OpenAI, Microsoft, and Perplexity. That suit bypasses any sort of fair use rationale when it comes to training data, and points instead to the idea that you can (allegedly) get ChatGPT to reproduce verbatim and substantive sections of paywalled New York Times articles. The legal thinking goes that this harms the New York Times, a fount of information, by potentially letting customers get that same information from a chatbot. That case is still unresolved. Gizmodo reached out to Anthropic for a statement but did not receive a reply.

item.title: Tired of Smart Rings? Try This Tamagotchi Ring Instead
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.87
The dream of owning and caring for virtual pets may not be quite as popular as it was in the late 2000s, but Tamagotchi is still adding to its lineup for those who want a quick hit of nostalgia. Bandai’s latest iteration, revealed at Tokyo Toy Show this week, is a Tamagotchi ring. It’s the smallest virtual pet the company’s ever made, coming in at just about an inch square. The entire device is about 23mm x 28mm, with tiny, tiny buttons to match its diminutive shell. At just 0.56 inches, the Tamagotchi’s LCD screen isn’t exactly going to be easy to read (especially for the older milennials who grew up with the original Tamagotchis). The Tamagotchi is available in three colors: light blue, gold, pearl white, and black and silver. Bandai says the new Tamagotchi includes 30 characters from across the brand’s 30-year history. Bandai says it took two years to develop the device and that it ended up cutting its components nearly by half in order to cram everything into its form factor. One cut component could make continued use of the Tamagotchi ring a bit more cumbersome: there’s no USB port for charging. Instead, Bandai created a dedicated charging case that you’ll have to keep track of to top off your virtual pet when its battery runs low. The Tamagotchi ring’s size definitely means it’s going to be more of an accessory than a toy that’s fun to play with. Wearing it on your finger might make it difficult to forget to feed your pet, but there’s no telling how difficult it will be to actually use those little buttons. The new Tamagotchi is currently only available for pre-order in Japan for ¥7,700 (about 50 USD). Deliveries should begin arriving in February 2027.

item.title: The Star and Director of ‘Coyote vs. Acme’ Celebrate Its Unlikely Opening
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.42
Three years ago, today never felt possible. That was when Warner Bros. unceremoniously and rather mysteriously shelved its upcoming film, Coyote vs. Acme. Years passed with the film in limbo until Ketchup Entertainment picked it up and spent a year building the hype, and now it’s in theaters. The whole thing feels like a contraption worthy of Wile E. Coyote himself. To mark the occasion, the film’s director, Dave Green, released a little message on social media to thank everyone for taking the wild journey. We’ve transcribed it below. COYOTE VS. ACME IS FINALLY, GLORIOUSLY, IN THEATERS NOW. Which means one thing. WE WON. You can go see this movie. In a theater. In your favorite seat. With your favorite snacks. With your favorite people. You can head into a dark room and laugh with strangers. Together. Congratulations to everyone who made this happen. This victory is a shared experience in so many ways. It’s a record of the cast and crew, post, prep, and animation teams who poured so much love and passion into it over years and years. It’s shared, permanently, with the audience who fought so hard for its survival. Your fight is the reason this film finally made it to the big screen. Thank you to Ketchup Entertainment for hearing the audience. We’re so grateful that you did. This is a celebration, it’s proof that movies don’t just go away. We make work so it can be seen and shared – that’s the whole reason we do what we do. Persistence and resilience have truly won the day. Enjoy Coyote vs. Acme on the big screen. Where it was always meant to be seen. Green even worked this sentiment into the movie itself. Apparently, at the end of the film’s credits, there’s a little message for anyone who stuck around. “Dedicated to everyone who posted, shared, held up signs, and spoke out when it counted. This film made it to the big screen because of you.” Star Will Forte also shared a celebratory message on social media: Thank you to everyone who fought for this movie— Coyote Vs Acme in theaters NOW 🙂 pic.twitter.com/IsITzIDUtk — Will Forte (@OrvilleIV) August 28, 2026 All of which will feel pretty disappointing if the film doesn’t at least do okay at the box office but so far, so good. From its Thursday night previews alone, Coyote vs. Acme already grossed about $1.7 million, good for number three at the box office behind Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey. If that holds, it will be considered a massive, massive win for a film that has long since needed it. Are you seeing Coyote vs. Acme this weekend? Let us know below, and don’t forget to read our review and interview with Green. Want more io9 news? Check out when to expect the latest Marvel, Star Wars, and Star Trek releases, what’s next for the DC Universe on film and TV, and everything you need to know about the future of Doctor Who.

item.title: As That Whole ‘Tilly Norwood’ Thing Peters Out, AI Acting Achieves Unsettling Ubiquity on Chinese Phone Screens
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.31
Despite tech and economics commentator Tyler Cowen professing his undying love for it in the Free Press last year, the AI-generated gooning prop known as “Tilly Norwood” seems destined to collect dust in a curio cabinet marked “Notable Garbage From the 2020s AI Boom.” Unless there’s a large, secret fandom waiting with bated breath for the release of the Tilly Norwood movie, it would seem that improv comedian Eline Van Der Velden’s quest for fame as an AI provocateur is finally fizzling. But make no mistake: the aesthetic cataclysm Tilly Norwood seemed to prophesy appears to have been real all along. You just have to look at China to see the warning lights flashing. “AI video is taking over China!” is a genre of news story that started materializing at least a year ago, and which we now know to be at least somewhat debunked. Nonetheless, I’ve been seeing some signs of Chinese AI-generated micro-dramas achieving scary ubiquity over the past year. Just speaking anecdotally, I saw someone on a public bus in Los Angeles watching one after another after another about two months ago, but they were subtitled in Spanish. I wasn’t positive at the time if what I was seeing was even Chinese, or that it was 100% AI-generated. I thought it might be a hybrid of live action and AI. But from the stats in a Friday report in the Financial Times, there’s a good chance what I was seeing was unadulterated AI slop, and it was being eagerly lapped up. FT looked at the monthly top 100 rankings for Douyin (a.k.a. Chinese TikTok) during the month of May, as reported by an analytics company called DataEye. In the animation category, 89 out of 100 were AI-generated. The FT also quotes the China Netcasting Services Association, a trade organization, as reporting that 95% percent of the 128,000 microdramas produced in the first quarter of 2026 were AI. Here’s what looks like a work sample by some guy on YouTube named Terrence Chang who uses ByteDance’s SeeDance video model to generate microdramas. Microdramas, if you’re not aware, are fictional video content distributed on social media, and designed to hook people with cliffhangers so they’ll eventually pay for paywalled episodes. Note that despite Chang’s video being made with ByteDance’s model, it isn’t optimized for TikTok—it’s not vertical video for one thing. Nonetheless, it’s a demonstration of what I personally would rate as the current state of the art. About a month ago, Japan’s NHK reported on one company that makes these, Manghe, based in Wuhan, Hubei, China. Again, the numbers are frightening. I haven’t looked at Manghe’s ledger myself, but NHK says the total cost to produce a Manghe AI drama versus its filmed-and-acted equivalent is one third, and that AI videos take only one fifth as long to produce. NHK says the company has “seven to eight staff working as one team” and those words are overlaid on top of footage of six geeky desk workers all at one table, clicking away at desktop computers. In the grand scheme, that’s arguably pretty expensive in terms of money and human effort. And it’s time-consuming when you consider that as far as Manghe is concerned, it’s just a few key-presses and mouse clicks leading to a bunch of red-hot GPUs in some distant data center. Unfortunately it also sounds horrifyingly profitable anyway. FT looked at a different company, Zeelin, for its report, and was given even flashier stats: 10% of the production cost compared to a video with human actors, and 8,000 minutes of content produced in the month of May alone. Exactly how much money anyone is making off of this is still a mystery, but there are signs that this is taking a huge economic toll. Vox pop interviews from the NHK report feature unnamed people on the streets near Hengdian World Studios in Zhejiang province professing to be background actors who used to work in the Chinese entertainment industry saying things like, “I lost almost all of my work in filming. It’s a serious situation,” and “Pay is low. It’s clearly a situation caused by AI.” The concept behind Tilly Norwood was that there would be an AI generated persona so beloved, producers would pay to have it included in their projects. The FT report says a grotesque inversion of that dynamic is now common: real actors reportedly come in to have their essences “distilled”—captured for later digital use, with no actual human needed. An unnamed children’s TV host apparently told FT she “was pretty much pinned against a wall” and required to undergo such a process. It’s hard to imagine you need need to pay extra for AI-generated Brad Pitt, nor do you need AI-generated Hu Ge—to say nothing of forking over money for someone else’s AI generated “performer.” You just need imagery that gets bored people to stop scrolling. And it pains me to report that a staff of six-to-eight people crammed into a tiny office can make that happen just fine.

item.title: Well, THAT Just Happened on ‘Silo’
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.08
Season three of Silo is like a crescendo. It started a little small, but then, slowly and surely, each episode has ramped up the stakes. And, with this week’s ninth and penultimate installment, things got taken to a whole other level entirely. We’ve finally seen one of the biggest moments in the history of the show, and it left us desperate for answers. Let’s talk about it. The title of episode nine, “Farewell,” at first feels mostly about Bernard (Tim Robbins). We watch as Bernard admits he’s guilty of several crimes against the silo and is sent out by Camille (Alexandria Riley) to clean. The huge spectacle demands the eyes of the entire silo, which gives our heroes time to blow their way to the failsafe pipe. But, just as that’s happening, we cut to this episode’s much, much more crucial storyline—that of Daniel (Ashley Zukerman) and Helen (Jessica Henwick). When last we saw the couple we’ve been following all season in the secondary timeline, they had turned down a chance to help create the silos to live their own lives. Helen is now pregnant and, close to her due date, they’re going on one last trip. First they’ll see Daniel’s sister Charlotte (Jessica Brown Findlay), and then they’re attending the massive opening event marking the reveal of the silos. It’s described like getting a Golden Ticket to the chocolate factory, and eventually, we realize that’s almost an understatement. There’s an odd, undeniable tension to all of this. Dinner with Charlotte and her now-wife, Anna (Morven Christie), whom we remember as Senator Thurman’s (Laura Innes) daughter and aide. The promise of breakfast. And, eventually, their arrival at the field. Without getting into every single detail, because if you watch it back, there are a lot, Daniel and Helen are each assigned a different silo to tour. Daniel will go to silo one, and Helen will go to silo 18. Right there, red flags should be going off. Silo 18 is the one the main show happens in. This explains how Helen’s Pez dispenser ends up there. And silo one is the mysterious, main silo we know almost nothing about. What is happening here? Why are they being separated? As Peter Gabriel (randomly) rehearses for the event, the tours begin. A group of carefully hand-selected people all go into their silos to just check them out. Meanwhile, Daniel senses something is wrong. He texts Charlotte, who has been MIA, one of their inside jokes. Her reply doesn’t get it. Something is wrong. It’s not her texting him. Daniel then desperately tries to contact Helen, which he finally does, though they’re pretty far apart from each other. Then, it happens. A nuclear explosion goes off. Daniel is grabbed and rushed back to silo one. The same, presumably, happens to Helen and her unborn child. And just when we are at our most shocked, the episode ends. Now, there’s still one episode left, but a few things are heavily implied here. First is that everyone who was building the silos (the trillionaire, the senator, the doctor, etc.) was aware this explosion was happening. The timing of this event and the bomb are too coincidental. Maybe they even set it off. There was also an urgency not just to separate Helen and Daniel, but to get them into their silos. Who set this bomb off? How total was the destruction? Is this the explosion society is still feeling the aftereffects of centuries later? Did this happen everywhere in the world? Also, if everyone involved in creating the silos knew this was coming, why were they prepping all these speeches and stuff? Who were they fooling with all this preparation that never comes to fruition? In true Silo fashion, a massive reveal just brings up more and more questions. Something that, we’re sure, will continue into next week’s finale (which Apple revealed is called “Troy”) and the fourth and final season sometime, hopefully, next year. Basically, though, while “Farewell” can refer to Bernard’s death, it also seemingly refers to humanity as a whole. The normal way of life is gone. Farewell to humans, the present day, a normal way of life. Now it’s just about a mysterious, underground future. Were you shocked by this latest episode of Silo? What do you think is going on? Let us know below. And we’ll be back next week with a breakdown of the season finale. Want more io9 news? Check out when to expect the latest Marvel, Star Wars, and Star Trek releases, what’s next for the DC Universe on film and TV, and everything you need to know about the future of Doctor Who.

item.title: What Backpacker Splurges in Thailand Really Cost
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 6.03
Backpacking through Thailand has earned a legendary reputation for being incredibly cheap. You can easily find five-dollar hostel beds, tasty two-dollar plates of Pad Thai on street corners, and overnight buses that take you across the country for next to nothing. However, after following a strict daily budget for a few weeks, almost every tourist reaches a point where they want to trade instant noodles and shared dorms for a special experience. Thailand is one of the best places in the world to treat yourself because your money goes much further here than back home. If you wonder what major budget splurges cost now, here is a realistic look at popular activities, from scaling limestone cliffs in Krabi to teeing off at Thailand's top golf courses. Popular Activities in Thailand Rock Climbing on the Cliffs of Railay Beach Railay Beach in Krabi Province is world-famous among outdoor enthusiasts. Towering limestone karsts rise straight out of turquoise waters, creating some of the most dramatic climbing routes on the planet. Even without climbing experience, local gear shops make it safe and easy to get onto the rock face. A half-day guided climbing program in Railay costs 1,200 to 1,800 Thai Baht ($36 to $55 USD). This covers all equipment, including harness fitting, special shoes, chalk, a guide, and climbing on beginner-friendly walls such as Muay Thai Wall or Diamond Cave. If you want to climb multi-pitch routes on the Thaiwand Wall, it will cost approximately 6,500 to 9,000 Baht ($198 to $274). Budget an extra 100 to 150 Baht ($3 to $4.50) each way for the longtail boat ride from Ao Nang Pier because Railay is cut off from roads by giant cliffs. Getting PADI Scuba Certified in Koh Tao or Phuket If you want to dive beneath the waves, taking a scuba course in Thailand is a rite of passage for travelers. The small island of Koh Tao is one of Thailand's most affordable places to get your PADI Open Water certification. The full price for the Open Water Course lasting more than one day at Koh Tao is 9,500 to 11,000 Baht ($280 to $325). It includes classroom theory, pool dives, four ocean dives, and gear rental. If you take the certification course in Phuket or Koh Lanta, the cost is slightly higher, ranging from 12,000 to 14,000 Baht ($350 to $410) due to larger dive boats and marine park entry fees. For certified divers who want a single day of fun diving, a two-tank boat trip typically costs 3,200 to 4,200 Baht ($94 to $123) and usually includes a freshly cooked hot lunch on the boat deck. Teeing Off on Championship Golf Courses Near Bangkok When people think of backpacker trips, golf usually does not come to mind. Yet Thailand is a top destination for golf lovers thanks to its immaculate fairways and attentive service. Taking a break from urban exploring to play 18 holes near Bangkok is one of the most fun and unique day trips to add to an itinerary. At Green Valley Country Club near Suvarnabhumi Airport on the Bangna-Trad highway, current green fees are approximately 1,200 Baht ($36) on weekdays, 2,500 Baht ($75) for twilight play, and 4,000 Baht ($122) on weekends. The course is designed by Robert Trent Jones Jr., with massive water features and premium-quality greens that deliver a high-end experience without private-club price tags. Golfers should budget about 850 Baht ($26) for a cart, 450 Baht ($14) for the compulsory caddie, and a customary tip of 400 Baht ($12). That puts the approximate cost of an 18-hole round at 2,900 to 5,700 Baht ($88 to $173) before transportation or club rental. Rates vary by date, tee time, and booking method. Confirm the total before booking. Visiting an Ethical Elephant Sanctuary in Chiang Mai Visiting Chiang Mai provides an opportunity to experience Asian elephants firsthand. It is vital to select an ethical sanctuary that does not involve riding but focuses on rescue, rehabilitation, and natural eating habits. Sanctuaries such as Elephant Nature Park are the benchmark for animal conservation. The average cost of a tour at a reputable sanctuary is 2,500 to 3,500 Baht ($76 to $106). The price covers transportation in a van between the sanctuary and your Chiang Mai hotel, a vegetarian lunch, and time with the rescued elephants, including walking with them, preparing their food, and watching them bathe in local rivers. Although the tour costs more than a temple tour, it is worth every Baht because it helps animals in need. Living Large for a Day Is Worth Every Penny Backpacking does not mean skipping incredible life experiences to save a few dollars. By balancing budget street food and dorm rooms with one or two well-chosen bucket-list adventures, you get the best of both worlds in Thailand. Whether you climb giant cliffs, explore underwater reefs, or spend a quiet morning on a sunny fairway, these mid-trip splurges often become highlights you talk about for years after returning home. This article was published in partnership with SawadeeGolf.

item.title: Hotel Booking Experience: What Travelers Should Expect
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 5.55
A modern hotel booking experience should provide accurate room availability, transparent prices, clear rate conditions, secure payment, and immediate confirmation across both mobile and desktop devices. Travelers should understand exactly what they are booking and complete the reservation without needless steps. The website technology should then relay accurate information to the hotel, ensuring that room, rate, and guest details are recorded accurately. When this process works properly, it feels almost effortless. Whether arranging a weekend in Edinburgh, reserving a guesthouse in York, or making a last-minute booking by train, the quality of the booking process can influence your confidence in the property before arrival. What Defines a Good Hotel Booking Experience? A successful hotel booking journey provides the information travelers need, when they need it. It should help guests: - Find rooms available for their chosen dates. - Compare room types and rates. - Understand what the price includes. - Review payment and cancellation conditions. - Complete the booking on any device. - Receive immediate confirmation. - Contact the property if plans change. The experience should also be consistent. Room details, prices, and conditions shown at the beginning of the journey should not shift suddenly at the final payment stage. A good booking process removes uncertainty without burdening travelers with extra information. Clear Room Information Makes Comparison Easier Room names alone rarely provide enough information to make a decision. A "deluxe" room at one hotel may be comparable to a "superior" room at another hotel. Travelers therefore need specific details to compare the available options. A useful room description should explain: - The bed type and maximum occupancy. - The approximate room size. - Important facilities and amenities. - Whether breakfast is included. - Accessibility features where relevant. - The room's location or view. - The main differences between categories. Photographs should show the room type offered, not just the hotel's most impressive suite. Clear information benefits both the traveler and the hotel. Guests are more likely to select a room suited to their needs, while the property can reduce questions, misunderstandings, and disappointment on arrival. Live Availability Should Reflect Rooms That Can Actually Be Booked When a room appears available online, travelers expect to be able to reserve it. Outdated availability can cause failed booking attempts or uncertainty about whether a reservation has been accepted. This is especially frustrating when accommodation is being arranged alongside flights, rail tickets, or event admission. Behind the hotel website, a modern hotel room booking system can connect live room inventory, rates, guest details, and confirmation workflows. When a reservation is completed, availability can be updated across connected systems, helping reduce the risk of double bookings. RoomRaccoon is one provider of this type of technology for independent hotels, connecting the direct booking journey with reservation management behind the scenes. Travelers do not usually see these systems in operation. They experience the outcome: an available room, a successful reservation, and a hotel expecting their arrival. Prices Should Be Transparent From the Beginning An attractive room rate can quickly lose its appeal when compulsory charges are added at the final stage of booking. Travelers should see the full amount they must pay before entering payment details. Optional extras should be clearly separated from the basic reservation. The booking page should explain whether the price includes: - Breakfast - Local or destination charges - Parking - Additional guests - Service charges - Access to particular hotel facilities - Any compulsory supplements Travelers should also check whether the rate applies to the entire stay or is displayed as an average nightly price. Transparent pricing makes it easier to compare a direct hotel offer with an online travel agency or another property. More importantly, it establishes trust before the guest has committed to the reservation. Rate Conditions Need To Be Written in Plain Language Hotels frequently offer several rates for the same room. A flexible rate may allow cancellation until shortly before arrival, while a lower non-refundable rate may require immediate payment. Other options may include breakfast, late check-out, or an extended cancellation period. These choices are useful if the differences are explained clearly. Before booking, travelers should be able to answer the following questions: - Can the reservation be canceled? - What is the cancellation deadline? - How much will be charged after that deadline? - Can the dates be changed? - Is payment collected immediately or at the hotel? - What happens if the guest does not arrive? - Is any deposit refundable? The lowest price is not automatically the best choice. A slightly higher flexible rate may offer greater value when travel plans are uncertain. Mobile Booking Should Not Feel Like a Reduced Experience Many hotel reservations are made on smartphones. Travelers may search while commuting, compare hotels from a café, or book accommodation while on the road. A booking journey must remain usable on smaller screens and slower connections. A mobile-friendly booking experience should provide: - Readable room descriptions. - Images that load efficiently. - Buttons that are easy to select. - Forms suited to mobile input. - A clear summary before payment. - Access to payment and cancellation conditions. - Confirmation that can be saved or viewed later. Travelers should not need to zoom, scroll sideways, or restart the reservation because a page fails to load. Effective mobile journeys remove unnecessary elements while safeguarding essential information. Payment Should Feel Secure and Predictable Making an online payment requires trust. Guests should be cautious when a hotel unexpectedly requests payment via an informal message, an unfamiliar website, or an unverified bank account, as these are common warning signs of unsafe travel-booking websites and redirects. Before confirming, travelers should understand: - The amount being charged. - The currency used. - Whether payment is immediate. - Whether the card is used only as a guarantee. - Whether a remaining balance is due later. - How refunds are handled if cancellation is permitted. Guests should be cautious if a hotel unexpectedly requests payment via informal messages, unfamiliar websites, or unverified bank accounts. If a payment request differs from booking conditions, the safest approach is to contact the hotel using independently verified details. Confirmation Should Arrive Immediately After completing a booking, travelers should not be left wondering whether it was successful. A confirmation page should appear immediately, followed by an email containing the essential reservation details. A useful confirmation includes: - The hotel's name and address - The guest's name - Arrival and departure dates - The selected room and rate - Number of guests - Total price - Payment status - Cancellation conditions - A reservation reference - Contact information for the property Travelers should review these details as soon as confirmation arrives. Incorrect dates, misspelled names, or wrong guest numbers are easier to resolve when identified immediately. The confirmation should remain easy to retrieve during the journey, ideally without constant internet access. Direct Booking and Third-Party Booking Serve Different Purposes Online travel agencies help travelers discover accommodation, compare locations, and read reviews. They can be especially useful when visiting an unfamiliar destination. A direct hotel booking may provide a more immediate relationship with the property. Guests can ask questions about accessibility, parking, dietary requirements, or arrival arrangements without having to pass communication through another platform. Hotels may also provide different room availability, packages, or conditions on their own websites. However, travelers should compare the full range of offers rather than assuming that one channel is always cheaper. Important points to compare include: - The final price - Cancellation flexibility - Included services - Payment timing - Room type - Loyalty benefits - Who provides support if the booking changes The best option depends on the individual trip and the conditions offered at that time. Useful Communication Continues After the Booking A completed reservation is only the beginning of the guest journey. Before arrival, the hotel may need to provide practical information such as: - Directions to the property - Parking instructions - Reception hours - Late-arrival procedures - Public transport options - Online check-in details - Breakfast times - Information about local services Well-timed communication can reduce uncertainty and help guests prepare for the stay. More messages do not automatically create a better experience. Travelers need useful information, not a stream of unrelated promotions. The best pre-arrival communication anticipates common questions and provides a clear way to contact the property when personal assistance is needed. Technology Should Support Independent Hospitality Independent hotels and guesthouses are regularly chosen for their personality, local character, and individual service. Technology should not remove those qualities. Its purpose is to manage repetitive processes accurately so hotel staff have more time to help guests. A connected booking process can reduce the need for staff to copy reservation details, manually check availability, or search several systems for the latest information. This can make it easier for employees to respond to requests, prepare for arrivals, and recognize returning guests. From a traveler's perspective, the ideal result combines the reliability expected from a modern digital service with the personal welcome associated with an independent property. Warning signs during an online hotel booking Most accommodation reservations are completed without difficulty, but travelers should pause if information appears inconsistent. Possible warning signs include: - A total price that changes without explanation. - Missing cancellation conditions. - No clear hotel contact details. - A payment page with a suspicious web address. - Pressure to pay outside the official booking journey. - Room photographs that do not match the description. - No confirmation after payment. - Requests for unnecessary personal information. A warning sign does not automatically mean the hotel is unreliable. It means the information should be verified before payment. Hotel Booking Checklist for Travellers Before selecting the final booking button, check the following: - Are the arrival and departure dates correct? - Is the number of guests accurate? - Have you selected the intended room type? - Is the full price displayed? - Are compulsory charges included? - Is breakfast included or optional? - When will payment be collected? - Can the booking be canceled or changed? - Are there restrictions on arrival times? - Will confirmation be sent immediately? - Do you know who to contact if something changes? This final check takes less than a minute and can prevent many common mistakes. Frequently Asked Questions About Hotel Bookings What is a hotel room booking system? A hotel room booking system is software that displays room availability and rates, collects reservation details, and sends booking information to the hotel. Modern systems can also support online payments and immediate confirmation. Is it better to book directly with a hotel? Booking directly can make communication with the property easier and may provide access to different rates or conditions. However, travelers should compare the final price, flexibility, and included services before choosing a booking channel. What should a hotel booking confirmation contain? A confirmation should include the hotel address, guest name, stay dates, room type, number of guests, total price, payment status, cancellation conditions, and a reservation reference. How can travelers check whether a hotel payment page is trustworthy? Check that the web address matches the hotel's official domain, that the connection uses HTTPS, and that the payment terms match those shown during booking. HTTPS alone does not prove that a website is legitimate, so contact the hotel using independently verified details if anything appears unexpected. Why do hotel prices differ between booking websites? Prices may differ because channels offer different rate conditions, packages, room allocations, or promotions. Always compare the total stay cost, including compulsory charges and cancellation flexibility. A Smooth Booking Builds Confidence Before Arrival Travelers rarely choose accommodation based on the technology a hotel uses. They choose a property for its location, character, facilities, reviews, and price. Nevertheless, the booking experience determines how easily that choice becomes a confirmed stay. Live availability, transparent rates, clear conditions, secure payment, and immediate confirmation all help establish confidence. When these elements work together, travelers can complete the reservation and focus on the enjoyable parts of planning a trip. The best hotel booking experience is therefore not the one with the most visible technology. It is the one that provides the right information, removes unnecessary friction, and makes the traveler feel certain that everything is arranged. This article was published in partnership with RoomRaccoon.

item.title: 7-Day Egypt Itinerary for First-Time Visitors
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 4.78
Egypt is too large and historically rich to fully explore in a single week. Still, it is possible to see the highlights if you plan efficiently by combining Nile exploration with your itinerary. A 7-day Egypt itinerary with a Nile cruise lets many travelers explore the country's historical wonders. The three major cities, Cairo, Luxor, and Aswan, are key tourism locations that visitors must see to learn about Egyptian civilization and the Pharaonic Age. To complete the exploration across 7 days, we advise tourists to plan their itinerary day by day. For first-time visitors to Egypt, planning may prove difficult. It's possible to select pre-arranged 7-day itineraries offered by Egypt tour operators such as Nile Cruisen; these itineraries include visits to the pyramids, a cruise on the Nile, tours of major historical sites, and other features like transfer arrangements, entry fees, and meals. Before you begin: Is seven days sufficient for a visit to Egypt? Yes, realistically, in seven days you will explore the following: - Giza Pyramids and Sphinx - Grand Egyptian Museum - Luxor's major temples and tombs - Valley of the Kings - Temple of Hatshepsut - Edfu Temple - Kom Ombo Temple - Aswan-Philae Temple - Nile River scenery and life along the river You might need a 10- to 12-day trip if you are going to visit places such as Alexandria, the Siwa Oasis, the White Desert, and Hurghada. Think carefully and choose your package once you've compared the itineraries. Before you book, make sure you know what is on offer at each location and the kinds of experiences available. If you'd like some assistance, you can look at the Egypt travel guide on Nile Cruisen to get a better understanding of Egyptian tourism. Your 7-Day Egypt Itinerary at a Glance | Day | Destination | Main Experience | | Day 1 | Cairo | Arrival + settle in; can explore the city and markets | | Day 2 | Cairo/Giza | Pyramids, Sphinx & GEM (Grand Egyptian Museum) | | Day 3 | Luxor | Fly to Luxor + East Bank exploration + board cruise | | Day 4 | Luxor ? Nile | West Bank historical site visits + sailing | | Day 5 | Edfu ? Kom Ombo | Temples + Nile cruising | | Day 6 | Aswan | Aswan sightseeing + optional Abu Simbel | | Day 7 | Aswan | Philae + departure | This sample itinerary illustrates one possible seven-day route through Cairo, Luxor, and Aswan. Flight times, cruise schedules, excursions, and the order of activities vary by package, so confirm the final itinerary with the operator before booking. Day-wise: 7-day Egypt itinerary for first-time visitors Day 1: Arrive in Cairo International visitors usually reach Cairo, the capital of Egypt, first. When they arrive, we recommend that they relax and contact the tour company if they are taking a pre-arranged 7-day package. Hotel reservations and excursions are included, which makes arrival easier. On your first day, make it flexible so that you can get used to the culture; if you can manage it, have dinner at a local cafe and then browse the markets. Day 2: Cairo & Giza Begin your journey into history with the Great Giza Pyramids and the Sphinx, which are situated on the Giza Plateau near the western edge of Cairo. Go on and visit the fully open Grand Egyptian Museum if you want to gain a deep understanding of history; it features the Tutankhamun Galleries and the Khufu's Boats Museum, and can serve as a good introduction should you then take a Nile cruise. In the evening, visit Khan el-Khalili and then have Egyptian food at one of the well-known restaurants. It's important to finish early to be ready for the journey the following day. Day 3: Cairo to Luxor-From Capital to Ancient Thebes The day involves a domestic flight from Cairo to Luxor, followed by a transfer to the cruise ship and boarding. On Day 3, the shore excursions will depend on the cruise timetable. They will mostly include the East Bank, with tourists having the opportunity to visit the Karnak Temple, the Luxor Temple, and the Avenue of the Sphinxes if time allows. The East Bank contains the stories of the ancient civilization's New Kingdom, which was known as Thebes during the Pharaonic age. If you embark from Aswan, you first take a domestic flight there. Some Nile Cruisen packages include domestic flights, while others require travelers to arrange them separately. Included domestic flights are a major reason first-time travelers choose packaged deals. Check the stated inclusions before booking. You can check their unique 5- to 12-day itineraries, curated especially for foreign tourists, to ensure comfortable vacations in Egypt. Day 4: Luxor's West Bank-Tombs, Temples & Sailing Visit Hatshepsut's Temple, the Valley of the Kings, and the Colossi of Memnon on the west bank of Luxor. The Valley of the Kings contains more than just tombs; it also offers unique insight into ancient Egyptian beliefs about death and the afterlife. Following their day of sightseeing, the guests relax on the decks of the Nile cruise and observe the small villages, feluccas, riverbanks, and sunsets. The Nile is far more than a scenic feature of Egypt; it links the ancient sites, and a visit to Egypt would be incomplete without it. Day 5: Edfu & Kom Ombo-The Advantage of Cruising The shore trips feature visits to places such as the Edfu Temple and the Kom Ombo Temple. Cruise tours are simpler than road trips since the views of the river around these monuments are peaceful. Visitors can combine sailing with historical investigation. Travelers visiting for the first time go to the double temple dedicated to Sobek and Horus the Elder at Kom Ombo and study the pharaohs' religious and practical lives through the vivid reliefs. The two temples are well-preserved along the Nile. The travel company Nile Cruisen has a team of Egyptologists who have designed the itineraries so that tourists can both investigate and appreciate the story of ancient Egypt. If you want a rewarding experience, you should book their 7-Day Trip Nile Cruise & Cairo or explore the other itineraries on their official website. The Nile has long been regarded as the longest river in the world, even though recent measurements of the Amazon have cast doubt on that status. It served as the lifeblood of ancient Egypt. Day 6: Aswan-A Slower Side of Egypt Southern Egypt offers a noticeably different atmosphere from Cairo and Luxor, with Nile islands, attractive river scenery, and a more relaxed pace. Visit the Aswan High Dam and Unfinished Obelisk, with the option of arranging a separate excursion to Abu Simbel. Some tourists plan an optional trip to Abu Simbel, as it's not included on many standard cruise itineraries. Upon request, Nile Cruisen experts can tailor a package that may include additional charges for transportation to and from the destination. Day 7: Philae, Final Nile Views & Departure After breakfast, disembark and visit Philae Temple. Depending on your travel plans, you can then transfer to Aswan Airport for a domestic flight to Cairo or continue to another destination in Egypt. Since seven days are not sufficient for exploring all of Egypt, you might choose to plan a longer trip of eight or twelve days to visit parts of the great Sahara Desert, the Red Sea, and Alexandria. What is typically included in a seven-day Egypt package? As per the Nile Cruisen packages, if you book the pre-planned itineraries, you enjoy some of the inclusions, which are - Private transfers - Nile cruise accommodation - Cairo hotel accommodation - Meals according to the selected itinerary - Domestic flights on applicable packages - Taxes and service charges - Tour guide support - Monument entrance fees What is included in the package will vary depending on the itinerary or the travel company you select. Before making your booking, you should check what is included. People who are visiting for the first time ought to compare different travel booking companies. If you book through a well-known tour operator based in Egypt, you should have easier access to local assistance and guides while on your trip. Before making your booking, it is necessary to compare different operators, check their qualifications, review recent customer feedback, verify the insurance coverage, examine the cancellation policy, find out about emergency support, and also check exactly what is included in the price. Final Thoughts If you have just one week to spend in Egypt, do not make it a hassle. Book a package tour and travel in comfort; the itineraries have been selected by experienced travel agents who believe a holiday should be relaxing, not tiring. If it's your first time traveling and you have only a week, don't attempt to see everything; instead,, concentrate on Cairo, Giza, Luxor, and Aswan, since you'll manage to see a great deal in seven days. You'll also enjoy the outstanding hospitality available on Nile River cruises. This article was published in partnership with Nile Cruisen.

item.title: AI Transformation Requires Redesigning Work, Not Cutting Roles
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.10
Summary. AI is beginning to reshape workforce decisions, but many companies are moving faster than the evidence warrants. Early AI-driven layoffs have often failed to deliver expected returns, exposed gaps Precisely how AI will impact the workforce in the short to medium term is unclear. Many layoff announcements are better understood as AI-washing: ordinary restructuring initiatives packaged in AI language to reassure investors that leaders have a grip on the coming technological change. Goldman Sachs estimates that AI reduced monthly U.S. payroll growth by only around 16,000 jobs over the past year, adding roughly 0.1 percentage points to the unemployment rate—a drag that includes slowed hiring as well as outright job elimination. These numbers may well increase, but for now, we are much earlier in the process than the prevailing narrative suggests.

item.title: How I built a one-tap "travel mode" that locks down my Android when I'm at the airport
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 6.17
Large airports are a potential security nightmare. There are random, unfamiliar Wi-Fi networks everywhere, charging ports that could be compromised, and more people than you could ever hope to count. I'm also basically always in a rush when I'm in an airport. The last thing I want to do is dig through my settings to try and lock down my device. I know which toggles I want, but they're not easy to use while I'm carrying a backpack and a duffel bag through security. So, I set up a travel mode, which is designed to make locking down my phone as quick and painless as possible. Android lacks an official travel mode Multiple settings in one place Android doesn't have a dedicated "travel mode" button. Instead, I had to piece one together from features that already exist in the operating system. Critically, this isn't going to just be Airplane mode. Airplane mode just turns off your wireless connectivity; that can make your device less vulnerable to certain kinds of attacks, but it isn't a catch-all. Google’s Advanced Protection Mode is a hardening feature designed to be left on once enabled, not something you flip on and off. Even the Travel Mode featured in some password managers only covers a single app's vaults. A locked phone and a hardened phone aren't the same thing You might assume that a locked screen is enough security, but a phone that is just locked is more vulnerable than you think. The keys are still in memory, notifications are usually visible on the lock screen, and apps continue running in the background. Background apps have been used to circumvent phone security measures before. My setup will attempt to combine as many of those features into a one-press setup as possible. The settings worth changing Figure out what to change first The first thing I did was figure out what settings I wanted to change and why. - Airplane Mode disables cellular signals - Disabling Bluetooth theoretically decreases your attack surface. - Disabling Wi-Fi ensures your phone won't accidentally connect to an insecure network - Disabling Cloud sync temporarily means the data on your phone is the data on your phone, and that something you don't want to be found won't be spontaneously downloaded - Disable lock screen notification so that no sensitive information can be seen while the phone is locked. You should also enable Advanced Protection Mode. That setting toggles theft detection, USB data blocking, and 2G shutoff already. The final critical step is a full shutdown or restart any time a phone requires maximum security. Phones are vastly more secure before they're unlocked for the first time (BFU). Tasker is almost a one-stop shop Tasker handles most of the lockdown by itself Tasker is capable of doing almost everything I want, so that is what I chose to use. I created a new Task within Tasker called "Lockdown." There, I added each setting one-by-one from my list. Changing some permissions using Tasker requires special permissions; it'll tell you when you need to change something. If you can't find a setting, the search at the bottom of the Category list is very helpful—I use it most of the time. Finally, I created a lock screen widget that allows me to run the task from my home screen. If you want, you could use an NFC tag or geofencing as the trigger for your tasks, but I prefer a button. However, undoing all of those settings manually is unnecessarily tedious, so I created a second task that effectively undoes every setting in my lockdown task. Tasker has a few security limits Tasker can't restart an unrooted device, and since the reboot is the single most important security step, I do it manually. Also, double-check that your Tasker automation still works intermittently. Advanced Protection is beginning to restrict apps that use the AccessibilityService API, which some Tasker plugins use. Be sure to double-check that your automation actually still works before you need it. Consider setting up Private Space Only show a limited number of apps If you're using a newer version of Android (15+), consider making use of Private Space too. Private Space allows you to set up a separate section on your phone that is isolated from your main profile. It doesn't share apps, pictures, or other files, and it can have a completely separate pin. In practice, you could separate your airline app, Uber, and the few other apps you need for travel from the rest of your applications. That way, if your phone does get stolen or otherwise goes missing while it is unlocked, there is a significant barrier between your files and anyone that gets your phone. I don't worry about my phone anymore Airports, and travel generally, can be stressful. My phone is a mobile repository that contains much of my life, and I certainly don't want any of the data to be compromised. With one Tasker Automation and the long press of a button, I can be sure that my phone decreases its attack surface and securely encrypts itself.

item.title: Run Linux without rebooting—4 ways to get the terminal on Windows
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.97
If you've decided to try Linux, you might have trouble leaving Windows. Maybe your favorite game only runs on Windows, or you need a Windows program for your work. Maybe you think dual-booting Windows and Linux is too much trouble. There are ways to get started with the Linux terminal that can run within Windows. WSL The best option for new users If you want to run Linux on your machine without having to dual-boot, WSL, or Windows Subsystem for Linux, is one of the best ways to do it. WSL was first introduced in Windows 10. It was an attempt to recapture a development market that was moving away from Windows and on to the web with Linux-based servers. Mac laptops were popular among developers because macOS is based in part on FreeBSD and can run many of the same components that would run on a Linux server locally. WSL was intended to let developers of web apps run local tools on their Windows machines without full-blown virtual machines.The original version translated Linux system calls into Windows system calls. It worked well enough but it could be slow. WSL2 was developed. It runs a real Linux kernel in a virtual machine, speeding up operations and allowing for graphical programs. If you want to learn Linux, it's a great place to start because you have the familiar Windows desktop. Cygwin The original way to run Linux apps in Windows For many years, if you wanted to run Linux or rather Unix-like programs on a Windows machine and you didn't want to dual boot or create a virtual machine, Cygwin was a popular tool before WSL came along. And even after WSL was available, I would still use Cygwin occasionally because it let me run graphical programs through Cygwin/X. Cygwin works differently than WSL. While both versions of WSL work with real Linux programs, Cygwin is a library that makes it possible to port Linux and Unix software to Windows. Cygwin programs are recompiled versions. Cygwin was originally created by Cygnus Solutions, a company that pioneered the commercialization of open-source software in the '90s by selling support contracts before Red Hat acquired the company. You might consider Cygwin if you don't care if the programs are actually Linux programs, but you want the same functionality that you would get with a Linux system. This would be good if you were on a work computer and couldn't install WSL, since that requires administrator permissions. Cygwin lets you install it in a local directory, so you can install it as an ordinary user. MSYS2 Good for writing native Unix-like apps in Windows MSYS2 is a development tool that piggybacks on top of Cygwin. It uses a lot of the same infrastructure, including the MinTTY terminal. It uses the pacman package management system from Arch Linux to install packages instead of the Cygwin installer. It's related to the MinGW project that ports the GCC compiler to Windows, but MSYS2 supplies the broader environment, as that's what programs on Linux expect. The key difference between Cygwin and MSYS2 is that the latter focuses more on building native software for Windows. While Cygwin is focused on porting Unix and Linux programs to Windows, MSYS2 is geared toward building native Windows programs in a "Unixy" way. This would be a good choice if you were already comfortable with Linux or another Unix-like system and you had to use Windows and couldn't dual-boot. As with Cygwin, you can install MSYS2 in a local directory, which makes it useful if you're on a machine where you don't have administrator privileges. Virtual Machines Get the full Linux experience in Windows If you need more functionality than WSL or Cygwin offer and you still don't want to reboot, virtual machines are an option. The reason that I would use one is when I want the full "Linux experience," for lack of a better word. This means a full desktop. I like Xfce as a desktop in a virtual machine because it's lightweight and performs well. The advantage of running a virtual machine is that you have full control over the environment. You can pick any distro you want instead of having to install it from the Microsoft Store as you would with WSL. A virtual machine is also isolated from the rest of the system. You can also experiment more easily with the system, such as testing different configuration options. You can also take snapshots with many virtual machine hypervisors. The most prominent virtual machine hypervisor on Windows is VirtualBox. It's worked pretty well for me, though sometimes bugs have been introduced that have made virtual machines crash or even refuse to boot unless I tweaked options, so be aware of that. One distro even refused to install once through VirtualBox until I figured out a workaround. Still, VirtualBox has proven itself valuable for my work with HTG. I can test different distros quickly in virtual machines, grab screenshots, and tear them down once I've submitted a piece. DistroSea Use Linux from your browser An interesting new option is DistroSea, which lets you try out Linux distros in your web browser. The advantage over even WSL is that you don't have to install anything on your machine. DistroSea offers many popular distros in different versions. DistroSea spins up a virtual machine similar to VirtualBox. You don't even have to make an account. The performance won't obviously be as good as on a real machine and you'll have to wait in a queue, but it's an effective way to "test drive" a new distro or even Linux itself if you're not used to it. It's mainly a showcase for Cendio's ThinLinc remote desktop software, but it's an effective demo. Ease your way into Linux on Windows These options offer an easy entry point into Linux for new users coming from Windows. You can run Linux alongside Windows either in WSL, Cygwin, VirtualBox, or on the web via DistroSea. You can keep your familiar Windows environment while you explore Linux.

item.title: Fake SD cards are everywhere—here's how to spot them before they destroy your files
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.89
Fake SD cards and SSDs have been a problem for a long time, especially on online storefronts like Amazon, eBay, or AliExpress. The issue has only gotten worse since memory shortages have driven the price of storage sky-high, with little hope of relief any time soon. The market is practically flooded with fake storage devices that promise enormous capacities for low costs. Worse yet, some of these devices will corrupt your data or silently delete files once their actual capacity is reached. How do counterfeit cards work? Windows won't know if the card's controller is lying The counterfeit storage scam is conceptually simple. Every storage device, including SD cards, has firmware that identifies it. That information includes the total volume. Scammers reflash the firmware of a small, inexpensive controller—say a 16GB module—to report a much larger capacity. When you plug it into your PC, Windows reports that the card has a 512GB capacity, even though the physical memory available is only a small fraction of that. If you only stored 5GB of stuff, you'd never encounter a problem. Once you write data beyond the card's physical capacity, you run into one of a few problems. Some cards just act like they're writing and then discard everything. The card will tell Windows that the file is there–you'll be able to see it and Windows will report its properties—but when you try and open it you get nothing. Alternatively, some cards will "wrap around" to write. For example, if you tried to move a 24GB file onto a 16GB card, the first 16GB would be written, and then the last 8GB of the file would overwrite the first 8GB it had already stored. Depending on what gets lost, you might wind up with a file that is partially functional (like a fragment of a video) or a drive that tells you it needs to be formatted.
