item.title: Heat warnings extended through Saturday as hot temperatures stretch into weekend
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 4.85
Weekend weather A heat advisory and a warning that has been in effect all week has been extended until Saturday at 8 p.m. as the grueling heatwave continues for San Diego County. Temperatures closer to average for this time of year are expected this weekend. Last week, high temperatures were around 10-15 degrees above normal. Despite the cool down, Saturday will still be hot, with temperatures only slightly cooler, hence why the alerts were extended. "By Sunday, high temperatures will finally return to normal, though the humidity will keep minimum temperatures around 5 degrees above normal," the National Weather Service said. Weather next week Expect near-seasonal temperatures to remain steady through next week. Local There will be a couple tropical systems in the Pacific ocean south of San Diego next week. We could see increased cloud cover and surf from those. Rain chance is even a possibility next week, according to NBC 7 meteorologist Greg Bledsoe. Warm ocean waters Those seeking relief at the beach may be met with some of the warmest ocean temperatures in recorded history. Thursday's sea bottom temperature tied for the hottest ever recorded on that date at the Scripps Pier La Jolla. The 76.6-degree water was nearly 10 degrees above average, according to Scripps Institution of Oceanography data. Relief is coming on Monday when temperatures are expected to be below average for this time of year, according to the NWS. By mid-week, there may even be some rain from Tropical Storm Karina. How to Stay Cool on Hot Days Cool Zones are open throughout San Diego County and can help keep San Diegans cool. "Cool zones" are free air-conditioned sites where people can gather to beat the heat together. See the nearest location near you below: If you can't make it to a cool zone, HHSA has other tips for people, particularly older adults, to stay cool on hot days. The agency recommends: - Avoiding physical activity during the day and pacing yourself. Instead, plan your exercise between 4 and 7 a.m., typically the coolest part of the day. - Staying indoors as much as possible. The coolest floors are the lowest floors. Keep your shades and blinds closed as much as possible with your windows slightly open. - Taking a cold shower. - Wearing lightweight, light-colored and loose clothes. - Never leaving children or pets inside vehicles, even with the windows cracked. - Drinking more fluids than usual. Water is best and alcohol or caffeine can make the heat's effects worse. Find many more tips here.

item.title: San Diego Water Authority to generate $15M from Burbank Water Deal
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 4.72
The San Diego County Water Authority is expected to generate $15 million in revenue during the first five years of a long-term agreement announced Thursday that will allow Burbank, in Los Angeles County, to purchase water from the agency. Under the agreement, Burbank will be able to purchase up to 5,000 acre- feet of water annually through 2047, according to the Water Authority. The agencies will use existing infrastructure to share the water, with no new pipelines required. Water Authority officials said revenue from the agreement will help offset costs associated with investments made over the past three decades to improve San Diego County's water supply reliability. "For the third time this year, the Water Authority found a way to help partners in Southern California lock in the water reliability they're looking for in a way that benefits working families across San Diego County," Water Authority Board Chair Nick Serrano said. "This is another 'win-win' that shows the kind of innovative leadership we need to manage water in a way that positively impacts everyone." The agreement is the Water Authority's third regional water supply partnership announced this year. The agency signed two water supply agreements with water agencies in Riverside County in the spring. The Water Authority also entered into a memorandum of understanding with the federal government and other parties to explore transferring locally produced desalinated seawater to Colorado River Basin partners in other states. Burbank, which has a population of about 104,000, has no naturally occurring water rights and relies entirely on imported water supplied by the Metropolitan Water District of Southern California. That water comes from the State Water Project and Colorado River Aqueduct. Local "This agreement will diversify Burbank's water portfolio while helping us meet future demand as our population and business community grow," Burbank Water and Power Assistant General Manager of Water Richard Wilson said. "Regional water exchange agreements like this one will be critical not only for Burbank but for all Southern California water agencies to ensure long-term reliability and supply." The Water Authority's recently completed Urban Water Management Plan projects that the San Diego region will have sufficient supplies to meet water demand through at least 2050 under normal, single-dry-year and multiple-dry- year conditions. The Water Authority provides wholesale water supplies to 22 retail water providers serving about 3.3 million residents in San Diego County.

item.title: First-year students move into residence halls at University of San Diego
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 4.17
About 1,500 students moved into residence halls at the University of San Diego in Linda Vista Saturday, as they prepare for classes to begin Tuesday to start the 2026-27 academic year. USD officials say the students who moved in Saturday are part of the more than 3,000 first-year, transfer and graduate students who are joining the university community this fall. The incoming first-year class stands out as one of the most accomplished and well-rounded in USD's history, university officials say, with an average weighted Grade Point Average of 3.98. In addition, 22% are the first in their family to attend college, 43% identify as Catholic, and there are 16 different faith traditions represented. The first-year class comes from 43 states, 16 countries and three U.S. territories or military bases, according to officials. "The start of the school year is such a joyous and exciting time. It marks the very beginning of our students' experiences here at the University of San Diego. Last week, the Princeton Review ranked our university not only the most beautiful campus in the nation but, more importantly, we were ranked number one for quality of life and number two for happiest students, and that's not by accident," USD President James Harris III said in a statement. "Our faculty, staff, and students are committed to community engagement, and we extend this bold mission into the world. Each new class brings fresh perspectives and ideas that strengthen our community and move us closer to fulfilling our mission to create a more inclusive, sustainable and hopeful world," he added. Harris pointed out that an example of the students' change-making spirit is their sustainability efforts, reflected in a successful student-led initiative continuing this fall. "EcoShop is a program USD students developed after researching campus waste and donation needs. The initiative allows students to donate or recycle items from their dorm rooms, including lamps, mini-fridges, clothing and school supplies during the spring move-out period," Harris said. Local "The items are placed into storage and made available at no cost to students during move-in weekend. It is a valuable opportunity for students to furnish their rooms sustainably and affordably while supporting USD's commitment to zero waste." Undergraduate and graduate classes begin on Tuesday. The School of Law began classes on Aug. 17.

item.title: 26-year-old e-bike rider killed in Vista crash
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 4.02
A 26-year-old man riding an electric bike was killed Saturday when he crossed a Vista street against a red traffic light and was struck by a vehicle. The crash occurred at 3:38 p.m. Saturday near the intersection of South Melrose Drive and Breeze Hill Road, near Breeze Hill Park, according to the San Diego Sheriff's Office's Vista Station. The electric bike rider crossed Melrose against a red traffic signal and was struck by a northbound vehicle, sheriff's officials said. No information was provided about whether the man had been wearing a helmet. He was taken by ambulance to a hospital, where he died from his injuries, officials said. The driver of the vehicle remained at the scene and cooperated with the investigation, officials said. Neither drugs nor alcohol were believed to be a factor in the fatal crash.

item.title: Trader Joe's adds 2 new stores in San Diego County. Here's where
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 3.95
San Diego County, prepare to have two more locations to stock up on Trader Joe's favorites (like the highly-sought after mini-totes). New Trader Joe's Clairemont location One of the two new Trader Joe's locations will be moving into the Clairemont neighborhood and will be located at 3962 Clairemont Mesa Blvd., becoming new neighbors to the plaza's Five Below, Vons, and Ross Dress for Less, to name a few nearby stores. Trader Joe's spokesperson Nakia Rohde told NBC San Diego they do not yet have an exact opening date to share for the new Clairemont location. However, the new location has been added to the company's Opening Soon list on their website, which typically makes it to the website three to six months before the opening date, Rohde said. As of Friday, a Burlington Coat Factory covered in scaffolding currently stands at that location. Out front a sign reads "We're remodeling." Around the corner there appeared to be more large commercial space under construction. New Trader Joe's San Marcos location Local Plans are underway for a Trader Joe's store to move into the North City area of San Marcos, Rohde confirmed to NBC San Diego. This will be the city's first and only Trader Joe's store. Rohde did not share any other details about this location. The new store was also announced on the Instagram page for North City, a mixed-use development adjacent to CSU San Marcos. The new Trader Joe's location will join a mixed-use commercial area that includes a variety of restaurants, a fitness center, a clinic and a medical institute. "North City has always been about creating a place where people want to spend time, connect with each other and feel part of something. Trader Joe’s, local businesses, public spaces and community programming are all part of that vision," a recent Instagram post stated.

item.title: Sen. Blakespear's bill to protect workers from Tijuana pollution passes state Senate
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 3.91
The state Senate Friday unanimously passed a bill by Sen. Catherine S. Blakespear, D-Encinitas, to create guidelines for protecting workers from ongoing pollution in the Tijuana River Valley. Senate Bill 1046, which also passed the Assembly unanimously on Tuesday, now heads to Gov. Gavin Newsom's desk for his signature. "The untreated wastewater pouring into the Tijuana River Valley has been an environmental nightmare for decades, polluting the surrounding air and water, and we need to protect any workers exposed to it," Blakespear said. "SB 1046 ensures that lifeguards, park rangers and others forced to work outside in the Tijuana River Valley area are adequately protected." The bill directs CalOSHA to develop workplace standards for "minimizing exposure to transboundary pollution, including adopting requirements for personal protective equipment, hazard communication, incident reporting and trainings." The guidelines are to be developed by local communities, as well as lifeguards, park rangers, local governments, labor unions, air districts and academic experts, according to Blakespear's office. The Tijuana River transports millions of gallons of untreated wastewater, including sewage and industrial waste, from Tijuana into California every year. This has led to more than 1,300 consecutive days of beach closures, noxious gases and air and water quality health concerns across the South Bay. Local scientists have found that pollutants from the Tijuana River's contaminated water aerosolize, entering the air and causing health impacts in nearby communities. The contaminated air can contain high levels of hydrogen sulfide, a dangerous, odor-causing gas. Heavy rain and flooding increase risks. According to Blakespear's office, exposure can result in gastrointestinal illness, skin infections and respiratory and neurological disorders. Workers in the Tijuana River Valley have experienced headaches, fatigue, nausea and bloody noses. Local In June, levels of hydrogen sulfide near the Tijuana River Valley spiked so high, county public health officials offered guidance to deal with possible noxious smells. An increase in the gas, which has a rotten egg smell and is associated with untreated wastewater, came after a pipe in Tijuana experienced a break. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, emissions exceeding the Acute Exposure Guideline Level 1 for the gas can cause "notable discomfort, irritation, or certain asymptomatic non-sensory effects. However, the effects are not disabling and are transient and reversible upon cessation of exposure." To reduce exposure, those in the area were advised to limit outdoor activities, keep windows and doors closed when odors are present, use fans to circulate air inside buildings and an air purifier with a high efficiency particulate air filter and activated charcoal with potassium permanganate. In July, Rep. Scott Peters led his Democratic San Diego Congressional colleagues in sending a letter to U.S. Trade Representative Ambassador Jamieson Greer urging continued cooperation with Mexico on addressing the pollution. Peters joined Reps. Juan Vargas and Sara Jacobs, both D-San Diego, and Rep. Mike Levin, D-San Juan Capistrano, in penning the letter to Greer as the United States Mexico Canada Agreement is renegotiated. In the letter, the lawmakers reiterate the commitments made to repair and upgrade wastewater treatment infrastructure on both sides of the border in the 2019 USMCA and said moving forward, "The United States must develop enforceable environmental standards and a rapid response mechanism for violations of the minute treaties and wastewater spills that can and should be avoided with every possible measure available." Any renegotiation is also a chance to secure additional funding and bi- national commitments, the representatives write. "The USMCA has been pivotal for San Diego, a city long plagued by cross-border pollution and chronic sewage spills largely caused by Mexico's failing infrastructure, which threatens our beaches, public health and local economy," a statement from Peters' office read. "President Trump's decision to not renew the agreement risks undoing hard-won progress and leaves San Diego exposed to more pollution and economic setbacks." Multiple steps are still required to get a handle on the long-standing pollution and sewage crisis, including a multi-year funding commitment from Mexico on infrastructure projects, enabling the use of existing funds for the U.S.-Mexico Border Water Infrastructure Grant Program to Mexico and planning and funding river diversion projects and advanced treatment plants.

item.title: Preliminary hearing begins for ex-Chaldean bishop accused of embezzling church funds
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 3.81
A former high-ranking leader of St. Peter Chaldean Catholic Cathedral in El Cajon, who is facing criminal charges of embezzlement and money laundering, directed his secretary to start providing rent payments from a church tenant in cash directly to him, which was a departure from the church's usual money-handling procedures, according to testimony delivered Thursday. Bishop Emmanuel Shaleta, 69, is accused of taking around $272,000 from the church by collecting monthly rent payments in cash from a tenant of the church's social hall, payments which typically would have been deposited via check into a bank account dedicated to church operations. Shaleta, who remains out of custody and has since resigned from his post, appeared in court this week for a hearing to determine if he will go to trial on 16 embezzlement and money laundering charges he faces. The hearing is expected to conclude on Friday. Shaleta faces up to 15 years in state prison if convicted of all charges. St. Peter's Chaldean Church staff testify The banquet hall at St. Peter’s Chaldean Church in El Cajon is operated by Rayadh Gaboola. He’s a faithful parishioner who hosts weddings, meetings and other events in the building that sits on the church complex. Gaboola was the first witness called to testify against Bishop Emanuel Shaleta in a preliminary hearing at the El Cajon Courthouse. Gaboola testified his rent in 2024 was $33,990. He paid with a check until one day in March when the diocese office manager told him Bishop Emanuel Shaleta would prefer he paid in cash. He agreed to do so, saying it was more convenient for him. Shaleta's secretary, Christine Dawisha, testified that Shaleta instructed her to tell the church social hall's tenant to begin paying his rent -- which exceeded $30,000 per month -- in cash rather than by check. When she asked him why, he told her, "We need the cash for the needy in Iraq," she testified. She also said she gave Shaleta those cash payments at his direction. Rent payments would usually be deposited into the church's "renovation account," but instead Shaleta wrote checks for the exact rent amounts from a separate bank account intended to help the needy and deposited the funds into the renovation account as a reimbursement, Dawisha testified. Dawisha testified she didn’t question Bishop Shaleta’s request. “Mr. Shaleta is my boss,” she told the court. “Whatever he asks, I follow.” Garvin Garmo, who is a member of the committee, testified that the church's policy is to have two church leaders sign off on checks of this type. However, each of the "reimbursement" checks Shaleta wrote were signed only by himself, according to Garmo. Dawisha testified that Shaleta told her one signature was sufficient because of the special nature of the "needy account," but Garmo testified that no church bank account was exempt from the two-signature policy. Dawisha testified that Shaleta later asked her to move money from various church and diocese accounts to cover the missing rent payments. She testified that Shaleta directed her to write checks from the diocese needy account and use that money to reimburse the church renovation account which normally receives rent payments. After a few months of this, she said she notified members of the church's financial committee. When confronted about this, Shaleta told Garmo it was "an internal matter," but did not elaborate further, Garmo testified. At Shaleta's arraignment earlier this year, Deputy District Attorney Joel Madero alleged that the cash provided to Shaleta "vanished" and that the movement of money from different bank accounts was intended to conceal embezzlement. When a financial adviser for the church flagged discrepancies in the church's bank accounts, Shaleta "provided completely unreasonable tales of where that money was going," such as giving the cash away to the needy, Madero said. Shaleta sat quietly during the first day of testimony in his preliminary hearing. He still wears a clerical collar and a cross around his neck, even though the Vatican accepted his resignation from the diocese. Testimony in the preliminary hearing is expected to last two days. The judge will then decide if there’s enough evidence against Shaleta to take the case to trial. Shaleta was arrested in March at San Diego International Airport. The prosecutor alleged he was preparing to board a plane headed out of the county and had more than $9,000 in cash on him at the time. Prosecutors have not said where that cash came from.

item.title: Woman critically injured in head-on crash in San Diego after fleeing driver hits car
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 3.34
A 66-year-old woman suffered life-threatening injuries after a suspect fleeing police collided head-on with her vehicle in San Diego's O'Farrell neighborhood, authorities said Tuesday. The collision occurred around 4:12 p.m. Monday when Central Division officers initiated a pursuit of a Jeep Cherokee driven by a 20-year-old man traveling eastbound on Imperial Avenue, according to the San Diego Police Department. During the chase, the driver crossed into oncoming westbound lanes. Officers terminated the ground pursuit, and the department's airborne unit began tracking the vehicle from above. Moments later, the Jeep collided head-on with an eastbound Toyota Camry in the 6400 block of Imperial Avenue, the department reported. The 20- year-old driver fled the crash scene on foot but was quickly taken into custody. A 66-year-old female passenger in the Toyota was transported to a local hospital with perforated organs and underwent surgery. Police said her injuries are considered life-threatening. The 61-year-old male driver of the Toyota suffered a left rib fracture, while the suspect reported head pain. Police confirmed alcohol or drug impairment was not a factor in the collision. Authorities urge anyone with information regarding the incident to contact the San Diego Police Department or San Diego County Crime Stoppers at 888-580-8477.

item.title: Buying jewelry online? San Diego jeweler shares some tips to know before buying
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 2.44
Buying jewelry online? A San Diego jeweler explains what to check before spending hundreds or thousands of dollars. A City Heights man who bought a ring from a third-party vendor on Amazon says testing later showed it contained no trace of gold, despite being advertised as 14-karat white gold and bearing a 14K stamp. The experience highlights some of the risks shoppers can face when buying jewelry online, where competitive prices and a broad selection can be attractive but the item delivered may not always be what a buyer expects. Not all that glitters is gold Ismail Morgan said he recently bought a ring that was listed for $417. “It was branded as a 14-karat white gold Moissanite diamond one-carat ring. The list price was $417,” Morgan said. Business Morgan is not a jeweler, but when the ring arrived, he said something did not seem right. On a whim, he took it to a jewelry store to have it tested. “I just kind of walked over here and got it tested. Turns out, no trace of gold whatsoever,” Morgan said. Morgan said he took a picture of the test results. The gold detector showed 0.00 karats, and the ring was mostly copper despite its 14K stamp. “I actually laughed. I definitely laughed. Part of me anticipated it being silver maybe, not copper. I definitely didn't expect a majority copper,” Morgan said. “We shouldn’t have to gamble when it comes to shopping online.” Amazon provided a statement to NBC 7 Responds regarding what happened to Morgan - “We strictly prohibit the sale of counterfeit or falsely marketed products in our store. We have robust seller verification processes and comprehensive proactive controls to prevent counterfeit products from being listed. This is coupled with automated technology that continuously scans products in our store, leveraging advanced machine learning and expert human investigators to proactively identify risks. In 2025, Amazon's proactive controls blocked more than 99.9% of suspected infringing listings before a brand ever had to find and report them. If we become aware of a counterfeit product in our store, we take action immediately and remove the product. In this case, we removed the product and are working with the customer to make this right.” The good and bad of buying online Arturo Carrera, owner of Eclipse Jewelry in City Heights, has nearly 30 years of experience in the jewelry business. He said Morgan's ring is not the first piece of jewelry he has tested that turned out to be different from what an online buyer thought they had purchased. Carrera said there are also benefits to shopping for jewelry online, including competitive pricing. Online sellers may not have the same expenses associated with operating a brick-and-mortar store and employing staff. Shoppers can also choose from a broader selection because they have access to more vendors. Before clicking the buy button, however, Carrera recommends carefully reading the item's description and understanding jewelry terminology. For example, gold-plated and gold-filled jewelry are different products. Online shoppers should also be cautious about relying solely on product photos. Images can be altered, and the piece shown may not be the exact item ultimately delivered. Shoppers should also research the seller, read reviews and understand the return policy before purchasing. Of course, Carrera says there is a key advantage physical stores will always have over their online counterparts. “The feeling for anybody is to see the jewelry piece alive, touch, feel it,” Carrera said, pointing to a necklace a client could try on and see how it looks on them before buying. That ability to see and feel jewelry before making a purchase is one reason Carrera believes physical jewelry stores will continue to have a place despite the growing popularity of online shopping. This story was originally reported for broadcast by NBC San Diego. AI tools helped convert the story to a digital article, and an NBC San Diego journalist edited the article for publication.

item.title: Ramona Unified bus route cuts leave students walking miles in the heat
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 2.23
Parents in the Ramona Unified School District say school bus route cuts are leaving some students with long walks home, including during a heat wave, as the district consolidates routes amid an ongoing driver shortage. Under the district's policy for middle and high school students, a student must live more than 2.5 miles from school to qualify for bus transportation. That distance is calculated as the crow flies rather than by the student's actual walking route. Bud Kaelin, whose son is a sixth grader in Ramona Unified, said the district removed a bus stop at 14th and H streets where he wanted his son dropped off. Kaelin said the change leaves his son facing a 3.5-mile walk home and that the district will not allow him to use another stop. “They cut us off completely from getting any kind of, a ride on the school bus,” said Kaelin. Kaelin added he does not want his son walking more than a mile, particularly during the heat wave, because he worries about the possibility of heat exhaustion affecting his ability to safely cross streets. “Could he be in some kind of serious situation to where, like, he was feeling like a heat exhaustion and his vision was impaired trying to cross the street, and he thought it was a stop car, but it wasn’t and he walked out in front of that car?” Kaelin said the district told him his son's previous stop was not safe but would not allow him to select another stop. He said he has been leaving his construction job three hours early each day during the first week of classes to pick up his son. “Today, my boss just told me it looks like the crew coast is getting heavy. So, that's not going to be good for me tomorrow,” Kaelin said. Kaelin later said having to leave work early to handle his son's transportation had cost him his job. Another parent, Mary Emily, questioned the district's use of straight-line distance to determine transportation eligibility. “As the crow flies is, you know, pretty, pretty vague. And yeah our kids don’t fly… They walk.” Local In a letter to families, Ramona Unified said it had to consolidate routes because of ongoing driver shortages and that the changes were the safest way to maintain transportation for as many students as possible. Emily said she believes the district has been inconsistent in how it applies safety considerations when making transportation decisions. “You're picking and choosing here, like one day. ‘It's not a safety concern. It's as a crow flies. Y'all eat the s- sandwich and deal with it.’ And this is what we're doing. And then the next it's ‘well, that's a safety concern,” Emily said. Emily lives on Hope Street, where she said the district removed a bus route. She said the change leaves her 15-year-old daughter with about a mile walk to the next bus stop. Emily said she wants more information about how the district decides which stops and routes to eliminate. “What are the stats that we're looking at? Is it the number of kids per stop? Is it, you know, how much money is coming out of this stop?” She also called for greater communication between the district and families. “What can we do to help remedy these situations and be more transparent with the community, Emily asked.” Ramona Unified has not responded to NBC 7's requests for more clarity about the situation. This story was originally reported for broadcast by NBC San Diego. AI tools helped convert the story to a digital article, and an NBC San Diego journalist edited the article for publication.

item.title: Weekly Mortgage Rates Are Up as Investors Weigh Inflation and AI
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Score: 5.44
Mortgage rates are up slightly this week, mostly due to a spike on Wednesday after new data showed that inflation grew faster than anticipated in July. Rates have since settled back to “normal” (by this week’s standards). The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage grew two basis points to 6.57% APR in the week ending Aug. 27, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average mortgage rates using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days. When fighting in Iran picked up again last month, it felt like a strong possibility that a Fed rate hike was on the horizon to counter rising oil prices and inflation. And then … the Fed didn’t raise interest rates in July. Forecasters are doubting whether it’ll happen in September, either, with the futures traders behind CME Group’s FedWatch tool currently projecting a 65% chance that central bankers will keep rates the same again. The Fed doesn’t set mortgage rates, but it does set the overnight borrowing rate that lenders pay to fund mortgages. Consequently, higher overnight rates usually mean higher mortgage rates. When the Fed chooses not to raise rates, lenders can keep borrower costs lower. That’s not to say that mortgage borrowers won’t be absorbing other rising costs. The Bureau of Economic Analysis released the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index on Wednesday morning, with data showing that the Fed's preferred measure of inflation went up a little higher than expected (0.2%, vs. the forecasted 0.1%). Even if the Fed does hold borrowing rates steady, mortgage rates could continue rising a bit, as lenders hedge against the weakening value of the dollar. In addition to the Iran war, we can look toward another familiar culprit in shaking up the economy in recent weeks: artificial intelligence. Water isn’t the only resource that AI systems demand — they also need oodles of cash. Companies like Microsoft and Oracle are selling loads of bonds to quickly raise the enormous capital needed to build the infrastructure propelling the AI boom. Amazon sold $25 billion in bonds in early July alone as part of its data center funding strategy. When massive amounts of bonds from these tech giants flooded the market, government bonds suddenly faced major competition for investor dollars. This caused the value of these government bonds to plummet, sending yields rocketing (bond prices and yields have an inverse relationship). The 10-year Treasury yield is treated as a key signal of the economy’s health, and it acts as a benchmark for mortgage rates. When it goes up, so do mortgage rates. Won't affect your credit score Today’s mortgage rates might be higher than what you’re comfortable with, but you can still play the market strategically to pay as little interest as possible. Conventional mortgages have a minimum down payment of just 3%. Instead of putting down more cash up front, you could consider diverting some of your down payment savings toward paying mortgage points. Buying one mortgage point will cost 1% of your loan amount and typically reduce your rate by 25 basis points. For instance, let’s say you’re buying a $400,000 home, and you’ve got $20,000 to put toward your down payment. Instead, you could put down the minimum 3% required, which would be $12,000. You could use most of the additional $8,000 to purchase two discount points, which, using this week’s average rate of 6.57%, would bring you down to 6.07%. In this scenario, you’d break even on your points purchase after about five years in the home. Mortgage lenders tend to react to indications that the war is progressing toward peace talks, since a resolution would ease the inflation pressure that's been keeping rates elevated. If a lasting agreement is reached and oil prices stay down, we could see mortgage rates drifting lower — which could be a good time to lock in. Related articles

item.title: Mortgage Rates Today, Friday, August 28: Mostly Flat
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Score: 5.26
Yes, mortgage interest rates are higher today, but only by a little. The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage rose to 6.53% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is two basis points higher than yesterday but two basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point. While the economy never sleeps, markets are closed on the weekends. The rates you see Friday are unlikely to change much (if at all) until Monday. Average mortgage rates, last 30 days 🤓 Kate on Rates: August 27, 2026 📈 What influences mortgage rates? Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing. Next week, the Nerds will be looking at the August jobs report as a complement to this week’s inflation report. The inflation report (called the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, or PCE) showed that inflation trended up a little higher than expected in July. While this is one of the core reports that the Federal Reserve considers when setting monetary policy, analysts don’t expect that the data will be enough to move the needle. According to CME FedWatch, the likelihood of central bankers holding borrowing rates steady again at their mid-September meeting is still over 50%. Next Friday’s jobs report will give central bankers — and the futures traders who predict their every move — the most up-to-date window into the current employment situation. Wall Street is tentatively forecasting that the private sector will have added 59,000 jobs, but the overall picture is less clear. Investors will be watching to see whether last month’s net loss continued into August, or if it was a blip. Another net loss would likely increase the odds that the Fed will hold borrowing rates steady in September. Its main alternative would be to raise borrowing rates, which typically hurts employment. Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs). With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.03% or higher. Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan. If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing. 🏡 Should I start shopping for a home? There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates. If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget. NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy. If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period. Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it. 🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit. 🧐 Why is the rate I saw online different from the quote I got? The rate you see advertised is a sample rate — usually for a borrower with perfect credit, making a big down payment, and paying for mortgage points. That won't match every buyer's circumstances. In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your: Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles. 👀 If I apply now, can I get the rate I saw today? Maybe — but even personalized rate quotes can change until you lock. That’s because lenders adjust pricing multiple times a day in response to market changes.

item.title: Is a Hotel Subscription Worth It?
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Score: 5.25
For years, getting rewarded for hotel stays came down to one of two things. You could join the loyalty program for free and slowly build up points, or you could apply for one of the hotel's credit cards. Lately, a third option has been catching on, including with a few major hotel brands. Instead of earning your way toward a reward, you pay a membership or subscription fee upfront and start saving right away. These hotel subscriptions may hand you a discount on room rates, fast-track you to a mid-tier elite status and sometimes toss in extras like late checkout, dining credits or a free welcome night. If you already book the same hotel brand often, the discount alone could be enough to cover the fee. But some of the brands have small networks of properties, and others may offer you similar benefits through one of their credit cards — not to mention the chance to earn points on your purchases. 5 hotel subscription plans and what they offer Benefits and access can vary significantly, depending on which hotel subscription you choose. In some cases, you may even get perks that go beyond hotel stays. Here are some of the options. For $95 a year, Wyndham Rewards Insider gets you a long list of benefits. Here are some highlights: - At least 10% off stays booked directly with Hotels by Wyndham. - A 50% points boost on all qualifying stays. - Various discounts on eligible flights, car rentals, cruises, theme parks, all-inclusive resorts, tours and activities. - 24/7 concierge service. The modest cost and the brand's large network of approximately 8,400 hotels across roughly 100 countries make this subscription hard to ignore for Wyndham loyalists. Even if you have a Wyndham credit card, not many of the perks overlap, though the Wyndham Rewards Earner® Plus Card and Wyndham Earner Premier® Card offer higher status tiers than Insider. For diehard Wyndham enthusiasts, it could make sense to have both. InterContinental Ambassador - Guaranteed one-category room upgrades. - Complimentary weekend night, valid on the second night of a paid weekend stay. - Up to $20 in restaurant and bar credits with every stay. - Single room rate for double occupancy. - Guaranteed 4 p.m. checkout. - Extras like complimentary water and internet, as well as a dedicated check-in area. While the IHG chain has a footprint of more than 6,600 properties worldwide, Ambassador benefits largely apply only at IHG’s luxury brand, InterContinental Hotels & Resorts, which has just over 220 destinations. The Platinum Elite status does work with other IHG hotels, but it's the same status the IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card offers. The card's annual fee is $99, and it offers a broad range of perks more suited for people who aren't strictly engaging in luxury travel. The citizenM brand is part of the Marriott Bonvoy family, but it has its own subscription plan for people who love its tech-savvy and design-forward properties. A mycitizenM+ membership runs $170 per year and offers the following perks: - 15% off direct citizenM bookings and up to 30% off during member sales. - 15% off food and drink at citizenM bars. - 15% off meeting rooms. - Free coworking at most properties. - Complimentary Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite status. The citizenM brand has only 37 hotels across more than 20 cities in the U.S., Europe and Asia Pacific, making it a tough sell for that price, unless you're a frequent citizenM guest. That said, the free coworking benefit could be a boon for remote workers who live near a citizenM location. Minor Hotels Horizons Club Horizons Club comes in two annual subscriptions: Standard at $205 (179 euros) and Elevate at $285 (249 euros). Here are some of the perks they offer: - 15% to 25% off public rates. - A complimentary welcome night worth 150 Discovery Dollars. - Minor DISCOVERY Gold tier. - 10% off bars and restaurants, plus 20% off the pet fee. - Access to member offers of up to 50% off. - 50 Discovery Dollars back after your first stay. - Complimentary late checkout and flexible cancellations. The only difference between the two is that Elevate members also get access to perks with additional brands. Minor's network runs to more than 350 hotels across more than 30 countries in Europe and the Americas, but it doesn't offer perks with any other major hotel brands, so that's it. There is no Minor credit card either, which leaves the subscription as the only way to access these perks. As a result, it only makes sense if you're fiercely loyal to the Minor brands. If you want to explore Minor Hotels without the subscription, consider the Chase Sapphire Reserve®. Among its many premium perks, the card offers up to $250 in statement credits through Dec. 31, 2026, on prepaid Chase Travel℠ hotel bookings with various brands, including Minor. FoundersCard isn't strictly a hotel program, and it's not a credit card either. Rather, it offers a broad range of lifestyle benefits that include some hotel perks for a $95 initiation fee plus a yearly price of $595. Here are some of the perks on the travel side: - Negotiated rates at luxury hotels, some listed at 30% to 50% off. - Complimentary elite status with hotel brands such as Hilton, IHG, Sonesta and Wynn. - Upgrades, late checkout, welcome amenities and other VIP touches at many participating hotels. - Complimentary elite status with select airlines and car rental companies. - Preferred rates on airport lounge memberships, villa and resort experiences and more. The catch is that you won't be able to view the full slate of FoundersCard features unless you request an invitation or join. Also, some benefits require an upgraded Elite plan, which costs $995 annually. This subscription may be worth it if you value elite status and other VIP perks across several brands instead of just one. But it may make more sense in addition to a travel credit card rather than as a replacement. How to choose between a subscription and a hotel card Whether you go for a hotel subscription or a branded credit card comes down to how you travel. Here are some things worth thinking about before you commit to either one: - How you'd get value: A subscription generally offers a flat discount on the room rate, while a hotel credit card usually skips the discount and instead earns points on all your spending, not just hotel purchases. In some cases, the subscription may offer other travel perks you can't get with a credit card, such as discounts on other travel expenses. While both may offer elite status, hotel cards also often provide welcome bonuses and an annual free night. - How big the network is: A perk only works if you can actually use it. A subscription tied to a small brand can be hard to put to work, while a hotel credit card with a brand that has thousands of properties gives you a lot more flexibility. - What happens if you cancel: If you cancel a subscription, you may still enjoy the benefits until the current term is up. Meanwhile, if you cancel a hotel credit card, you'll lose all the perks upon closure (though you'll still retain the points you've earned). - Approval requirements: You generally need good or excellent credit and sufficient income to get approved for a hotel credit card, while there's no credit check required to sign up for a subscription service. If you want VIP perks but don't have great credit, a subscription may be the better choice. Start by pulling up last year's travel and counting how many nights you booked directly with the brand you're considering. Next, check whether the brand offers credit cards, a subscription service or both. Then, do some math to get an idea of what you could save with discounts and how much value you could get from a credit card. In some cases, it could even make sense to have both. For example, if you book a lot of cash stays, a subscription with a discount on rates and a credit card that offers great rewards on hotel purchases can help you maximize the value you get. item.title: How Points and Miles Values Changed in 2026
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Score: 5.17
Nerdy takeaways - The value of American Airlines AAdvantage miles is higher than any other domestic airline at 1.7 cents each. - World of Hyatt points held steady at 1.8 cents each; more than double other hotel points. - Marriott Bonvoy points dropped to 0.7 cents each after a program-wide devaluation in 2026. Airfare is up 26% over the past year, but there’s a potential upside for travelers. Airline miles from some major U.S. airlines are now worth more because award prices haven’t risen as quickly as cash fares. Hotel points, however, haven’t experienced the same gains. Each year, NerdWallet compares the cost of booking travel with points and miles with the cash price of equivalent flights and hotel stays. This analysis produces a median value that can help travelers decide whether to redeem their rewards or pay cash. 🤓Nerdy Tip These valuations are benchmarks representing the median value of rewards in each program. Aim to receive at least this “middle-of-the-road” value when redeeming your points and miles. For more details, check out How to Use Points and Miles Valuations. American, Alaska and Southwest miles gain value The gains in value for American, Alaska and Southwest miles weren’t evenly distributed, with American posting the largest year-over-year increase. The gain was especially pronounced for domestic flights booked 15 days before departure. For example, a New York-to-St. Louis redemption delivered 3.5 cents per mile — more than double the median value of 1.7 cents. Alaska Atmos and Southwest Rapid Rewards points also increased in value to 1.4 cents each, up from Alaska’s 1.2 cents in 2025 and Southwest’s 1.3 cents. Alaska Atmos points are an excellent option for booking international award flights to Asia and the Caribbean, while Southwest loyalists will find added value across the airline’s extensive domestic network. Delta SkyMiles, United MileagePlus and JetBlue TrueBlue point values remain unchanged from 2025. While these airlines didn’t see an increase in the average value for their miles, avoiding devaluations is still a positive. | Loyalty Program | Value per mile in 2026 (cents) | Value per mile in 2025 (cents) | |---|---|---| | American Airlines AAdvantage | 1.7 | 1.3 | | Alaska Atmos | 1.4 | 1.2 | | Southwest Rapid Rewards | 1.4 | 1.3 | | JetBlue TrueBlue | 1.4 | 1.4 | | Delta SkyMiles | 1.2 | 1.2 | | United MileagePlus | 1.2 | 1.2 | Hyatt holds steady while Marriott loses value Hyatt and Marriott made the most consequential changes to their respective loyalty programs this year, with very different results for members. World of Hyatt points are still in a league of their own. Although Hyatt revamped its award chart in May 2026, the value of World of Hyatt points remained unchanged at 1.8 cents each. That's more than double the value of any other hotel program. Hyatt replaced its three-tier award chart with five tiers and raised the maximum price of some Category 8 properties from 45,000 to 75,000 points per night. But the highest prices affected a relatively small group of properties and were phased in gradually. Most 2026 award pricing therefore remained close enough to 2025 levels for Hyatt’s median point value to hold steady. Meanwhile, Marriott Bonvoy points lost value. Award nights at approximately 95% of Marriott properties became more expensive in mid-2026, resulting in a devaluation from 0.8 cents per point in 2025 to 0.7 cent per point in 2026. Unlike Hyatt, which still anchors redemptions to a published award chart, Marriott has moved further into dynamic pricing. Nightly award rates can fluctuate with cash prices and demand, making redemptions more difficult to plan. | Loyalty Program | Value per point in 2026 (cents) | Value per point in 2025 (cents) | |---|---|---| | World of Hyatt | 1.8 | 1.8 | | Choice Privileges | 0.8 | 0.8 | | Marriott Bonvoy | 0.7 | 0.8 | | Wyndham Rewards | 0.7 | 0.7 | | IHG One Rewards | 0.6 | 0.6 | | Hilton Honors | 0.4 | 0.4 | What these values mean for your points strategy - Welcome offers from certain airline cards are now more valuable. Higher valuations for American, Alaska and Southwest miles increase the estimated value of rewards earned through welcome offers and ongoing spending. - Look for cards that allow you to transfer points to some of the high-value programs. You may also receive more value when transferring Citi ThankYou Points to American, Bilt Rewards to Alaska Atmos, and Bilt Rewards or Chase Ultimate Rewards® to Southwest. Before applying for or keeping a card, weigh that potential value against its annual fee and benefits. - Look to Hyatt for hotel redemptions for fewer points. Its point value held steady despite the expanded award chart and remains by far the highest-value hotel currency in our analysis. How to maximize your rewards

item.title: 4 Ways Your Travel Cards May Cover Your Streaming Subscriptions
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Score: 4.87
Many travel credit cards now offer streaming or digital entertainment services as a benefit to customers. According to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey, 83% of U.S. adults said they stream entertainment, making credit card streaming perks a useful benefit to save on — or completely cover — streaming subscription costs. But with so many cards on the market, it’s not always easy finding one that offers a benefit for your favorite streaming provider. In this quick list, we’ve done the heavy lifting for you by identifying the credit cards that offer streaming services and the terms for each. 1. Paramount+ or Peacock through the American Express Platinum Card® The American Express Platinum Card® (annual fee: $895, see rates and fees) offers one of the most well-known and most valuable credit for streaming services. Terms apply. The eligible subscriptions include: - Disney+. - ESPN streaming services. - Hulu. - Peacock. - Paramount+. - The New York Times. - The Wall Street Journal. - YouTube. item.title: I Hiked Waterfalls From This Trailborn by Marriott Hotel
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Score: 2.87
We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives. So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site or when you click to or take an action on their website. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies. However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners. I Hiked Waterfalls From This Trailborn by Marriott Hotel With onsite dining and easy access to nature, Trailborn Highlands is a great option for your next mountain getaway. Craig Joseph is a NerdWallet credit cards and travel rewards expert. He has degrees in geology from West Virginia University and oceanography from Oregon State University and has published in academic journals, newspapers and blogs. Craig is passionate about personal finance and wants to enhance the financial literacy of everyone he meets. He'll probably also try to convince you why rocks are cool. Meghan Coyle is an editor on the Travel Rewards team and the co-host of the Smart Travel podcast. She covers travel credit cards, airline and hotel loyalty programs, and how to travel on points. Meghan is based in Los Angeles and has a love-hate relationship with LAX. Published in Updated How is this page expert verified? NerdWallet's content is fact-checked for accuracy, timeliness and relevance. It undergoes a thorough review process involving writers and editors to ensure the information is as clear and complete as possible. If you’re looking for boutique hotel stays near national parks and other outdoor destinations, Trailborn Hotels and Resorts might be for you. This chain of five boutique properties gives you many ways to immerse yourself in nature, from the convenient locations to the design of the public spaces. And the best part? This brand is part of the Outdoor Collection by Marriott Bonvoy, which means you can earn or use Marriott points to stay near some of the country’s most iconic outdoor destinations. I recently had a chance to experience the Trailborn Highlands hotel in Highlands, North Carolina. It’s a town in the southern Blue Ridge Mountains that makes an excellent home base to explore the rainforest and many waterfalls in the area. You can drive there in about an hour and a half from Asheville Regional Airport or about three hours from Atlanta. While Marriott paid for my three-night stay, the opinions in this story are my own. The property itself is rustic, but comfortable (and pet-friendly!). It offers no shortage of amenities, including a fantastic on-site restaurant (the Highlands Supper Club), an outdoor Nordic spa and a lounge area with a firepit. Guests can also book excursions such as guided hikes, fly fishing, kayaking and rock climbing. Room rates at this property start around $128 and balloon to over $500 during the fall leaf-peeping season. Those more expensive periods could be a perfect time to use Marriott points or Marriott Free Night Awards for your adventure. Booking with Marriott Bonvoy points Marriott uses dynamic pricing, so the number of points required for an award stay fluctuates based on demand and the cash rate. NerdWallet values Marriott points at 0.7 cent each. During low-traffic weekdays, room rates at The Trailborn Highlands start around $128 or 32,000 points. At that price, you’d receive a low value of 0.4 cent per point. Instead of using points, it would be better to use the 35,000-point free night award that comes with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card. However, during peak season in the fall, rates increase to $530 or 70,000 points per night. In that case, you’d get 0.8 cent per point, making it a better option to pay with Marriott points. If you’re short on points, Marriott also lets you combine cash and points for a stay, which can help stretch your points balance across more stays. The easiest way to earn a quick slug of Marriott points is through a welcome offer on a Marriott credit card. NerdWallet's ratings are determined by our editorial team. The Trailborn Highlands location is situated one block from Main Street in this upscale mountain town, making it a great location for both walking around town and accessing the outdoors. The lobby and public areas are bright and airy, with big windows, a fireplace and board games. Guest rooms The Trailborn Highlands property has 63 guestrooms, and each one offers some outdoor space. The ground-floor rooms have a garden patio while second-story rooms have a balcony. I stayed in a balcony room with a king bed. The room was basic but spacious, with checkered carpet and wood accents that fit into the local mountain environment. Each guestroom has a work station, which provides a comfortable space to get work done. The analog radio is a nice touch. When I was in my room, I spent most of my time relaxing on the balcony, listening to the birds chirp and enjoying how green my surroundings were. In contrast, the bathroom was pretty drab. While the color theme matched the muted natural tones throughout the property, the poor lighting and brown and green tile created a dark and uninspiring environment to prepare for the day. The Highlands Supper Club The Highlands Supper Club is the property’s sit-down dining option. The restaurant is housed in a historic log cabin perched atop a hill overlooking the hotel and surrounded by a beautiful rhododendron garden. The menu features a contemporary take on Southern comfort food, with craft cocktails and an extensive wine list. I’ll eat southern food any chance I get, and The Highlands Supper Club did not disappoint. I loved the homemade biscuits and deviled eggs with blue crab and bacon, but my absolute favorite were the oysters on the half shell. The blueberry cobbler a la mode was also a decadent way to end the evening, though I practically had to roll myself out of the restaurant after eating it all. The Nordic Spa The Nordic Spa is located in an enclosed outdoor patio and consists of a dry sauna, a cold spritz shower and a lounge area with a fire pit. The spa is open daily from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. and costs $100 per 50 minute session for up to 4 guests. I’m a sauna fanatic, and while the setting of the spa is clean and modern, the sauna itself wasn’t hot enough to get a full sweat going, even after about 20 minutes. It was still relaxing, and the transition from the warm sauna to the cold shower was invigorating. Just be aware that the spa is semi-private, as the second-story balcony rooms can see into the fenced-off area. The spa area needs a pergola overhead for added privacy. Waterfalls, s’mores and other activities Trailborn Highlands leans into the experiential accommodation trend and works with local guides and businesses to help guests experience the culture and activities that make the southern Appalachian Mountains unique. That includes trout fishing, kayaking, canoeing, river tubing, guided hikes and waterfalls tours. Available activities are posted on a bulletin board next to the front desk, making it easy to know what’s happening during your stay. Additionally, complimentary bicycles are available to all guests, making it easy to ride around the town of Highlands. Countless hikes, waterfalls and scenic overlooks are accessible within a 20-minute drive from the hotel. My personal favorite was Dry Falls, where you can take a path behind the waterfall. Additionally, The French Broad River (one of the oldest rivers in the world) is about an hour away and provides easy access to scenic trout fishing and kayaking. Trailborn lights a fire in the patio area each evening and encourages guests to put the devices away and be social with other guests. It turns out that’s pretty easy when your hands are covered with melted marshmallows from the s’mores session that the hotel offers each evening. Trailborn Highlands: Is it worth it? I really enjoyed the calmness of Trailborn Highlands, and I appreciated that it leans into experiences and community. The location makes access to nature easy, in addition to being centrally located near the shops and cafes on Main Street in Highlands. The price of a cash stay can be an absolute bargain midweek, and Marriott free night awards can offer good value if you want to travel during peak season. The stay also made me excited to check out the other Trailborn properties around the U.S.

item.title: He Set Out for a Day Hike on Granite Peak, Montana’s Highest Mountain. An 800-Foot Fall Killed Him.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.59
(Photo: Courtesy of Tad Dykstra) A 21-year-old hiker from Bozeman, Montana, is dead after falling 800 feet from Granite Peak, Montana’s highest mountain, on August 24. Authorities have not released the man’s name. Sheriff Tad Dykstra with the Park County Sheriff’s Office told Outside that the man was familiar with hiking, but he was ill-prepared for such a strenuous ascent. At roughly 12,800 feet, Granite Peak is widely considered one of the most dangerous and technical high points in the lower 48, and experts routinely compare the route’s exposure and difficulty to the climb up Wyoming’s Grand Teton. “Granite Peak is all of the above: It’s high alpine, all above tree line, large boulders, steep, rocky terrain,” Dykstra said. “And then there are the weather issues, whether that means high winds or passing storms. It’s a mountain that you need to have experience in order to climb. It’s just super dangerous, and people die.” According to Dykstra, the man was an experienced hiker but lacked the high-alpine mountaineering skills required to summit Granite Peak. He met another person at the trailhead, and the two decided to hike together from Mystic Lake Trailhead, some 22 miles below the summit. The other hiker summited the mountain alone. When he didn’t see the 21-year-old on his descent, he called in a missing person’s report. Authorities began searching on August 25 and recovered the man’s body on Thursday, August 27, responding agencies wrote in a statement. Granite Peak sits in a geographic triangle bordering Park, Stillwater, and Carbon counties. Because access points and peak locations cross county boundaries, search-and-rescue operations involve extensive multi-agency collaboration. Rescuers located the hiker by using a spotter helicopter. The death is under investigation by the Park County Sheriff’s Office, which Dykstra says is standard for any fatality in the backcountry. Authorities do not suspect foul play, but do say the tragedy is a reminder to stay within your limits. Just because a peak isn’t Mount Everest, Dykstra says, doesn’t mean it’s not deadly. Smaller, unknown mountains can be equally as dangerous. “Granite Peak is in an in-between zone where people think it’s accessible enough that they can just go out there and do it, but it’s far enough away that it’s an event to actually get it done,” Dykstra said. Prospective hikers should gather as much information as they can, talk to experienced people, and make sure their skills and ability match what they’re setting out to do, he adds. Hike with others, bring the right equipment, and “dress like a skittle” so that you’re easy to find. Most importantly, knowing when to turn around should always be in the back of every peakbagger’s mind. “I don’t think anybody should feel bad about looking at something and saying, ‘This is out of my capabilities. I need to turn around and go home,’” Dykatra said. “If it takes you five times before you actually reach that summit, that’s perfectly OK.” “You can make the decision to go home and stay alive,” he said.

item.title: A Cyclist Was Stranded in Extreme Heat. A Memorial Shelter Saved Them
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.37
The shelter was built in memory of Jeff Higgins, a cyclist who died on the Palisades Plunge trail in 2022 (Photo: MCSAR) When a mountain biker riding along the Palisade Plunge, a 32-mile trail in western Colorado, suffered a mechanical failure, finding shade quickly became a life-or-death priority. It was August 3, and temperatures were hovering around 100 degrees Fahrenheit. So, they found a shade structure along the route, called for help, and waited for rescuers to arrive. As it turns out, the pavilion was a memorial shelter erected for another rider who died of heat exposure on that same route just four years earlier. According to responding agency Mesa County Search and Rescue (MCSAR), the structure was part of a memorial project for Jeff Higgins. Higgins, a Colorado Springs resident, was riding on the Palisade Plunge on June 11, 2022, when he ran out of water. Temperatures soared to 102 degrees Fahrenheit that day, the Associated Press reported. He was four miles from the end of the trail when he lost consciousness. Three mountain bikers found Higgins on the trail and tried to save him—the trio had also run out of water and were later treated for dehydration. Higgins died during the first year that the full 32-mile Palisade Plunge was opened. He left behind two kids. “He was a just a really avid outdoorsman and loved mountain biking,” Daniel Higgins, Jeff’s brother, told The Grand Junction Sentinel. “He just loved being outdoors.” In the wake of Higgins’ death, his family asked for donations to be made to the Colorado Plateau Mountain Bike Trail Association (COPMOBA), a nonprofit volunteer group that oversees trail building in the region. In subsequent years, COPMOBA installed signs along the Palisade Plunge warning riders to bring plenty of water, and to be mindful of the heat. Then, in 2024, COPMOBA identified a plot of land along the trail that was owned by the city of Palisade. The spot was where the trail intersected a road, which riders could use as an emergency bail-out if they could no longer finish the entire trail. According to The Grand Junction Sentinel, the city provided the land to COPMOBA, and the Higgins family used donations and private funds to build the structure at the spot. The building opened for the 2025 riding season. “It seemed like the right thing to do,” Daniel Higgins told The Sentinel. “It will bring some closure to our family and it will be nice to have a feature out there for others to benefit from.” Authorities did not release the name, age, or sex of the bicycle rider they rescued on August 3. MCSAR responded on a Polaris all-terrain vehicle, treated the rider for dehydration and then transported them and their bike back to safety. “We’re grateful this mission ended safely and that a space created in Jeff Higgins’ memory provided shade and comfort when it was needed,” MCSAR wrote in a statement. “Our hearts are with Jeff’s family and loved ones, and we hope it brings them comfort knowing his memory is helping others along the Plunge.” The Palisade Plunge is a mostly downhill, backcountry singletrack mountain biking trail located in the Grand Mesa National Forest. It connects the top of Colorado’s Grand Mesa to the valley floor, and is reachable from the town of Palisade. Tourism board Visit Palisade describes the trail as a “fast, fun, high-energy trail through untravelled public lands and unbelievable scenery.” The trail is closed from December 1 to May 1 annually. In recent years, the COPMOBA and local authorities have urged cyclists to watch for extreme heat and ride in the mornings or evenings, when temperatures are lower. While the trail descends 6,000 feet, it also gains 1,700 feet of elevation. “Fast riders can spend three hours on the route while some riders spend over 12 hours on the trail,” reads a warning on the COPMOBA website. “It is essential to carry water,” the site adds.

item.title: Our Nepal Expert Answers the Biggest Questions About the Devastating Floods
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.12
Floodwaters cover low-lying areas and settlements near the Bhotekoshi River in Nuwakot, Nepal (Photo: Ambir Tolang/NurPhoto via Getty) Himalayan regions in Nepal and China are reeling this week, following a devastating flood that swept down river valleys below the high peaks, destroying everything in its path. Videos of the devastating water and landslides has dominated social media this week. As of August 28, the death toll has risen to 580 people, but the number of missing has risen from 900 to 1,900. Ben Ayers, Outside’s longtime Himalayan expert and Mount Everest reporter, has spent the last 20 years living in Nepal. Ayers participated in the rescue efforts in the wake of Nepal’s devastating earthquake in 2015, and he has traveled to parts of the country impacted by the floods. Ayers has provided a handy explain of the current tragedy, and has answered some of our—and your—most pressing questions about the disaster. At 8:37 A.M. Nepal time on August 26, an enormous hanging glacier weighing perhaps ten million tons detached from the north slope of the 23,711’ Langtang Lirung in Nepal’s mountainous Rasuwa region, plummeting 6,000 vertical feet to the valley floor. Glacier experts told The BBC that the energy generated by the glacier’s fall was the equivalent of multiple Hiroshima-sized nuclear explosions. In the moments that it took the glacier to reach the floor of the Lhendekhola river valley, the massive amounts of friction and energy pulverized the snow, rock, and ice into a thick and muddy slurry traveling at enormous speeds. As it descended the steep Himalayan slopes of the riverbed, the slurry swallowed the surrounding glacial till and permafrost, saturated from recent heavy monsoon rains, gathering enormous speed, mass, and destructive power. Austin Lord, a Senior Fellow at the Stimson Center, who specializes in disaster and climate risk management, and has studied this particular region for over a decade. In an interview with Outside, Lord told me that the glacial debris dammed the river for a few minutes. Water pressure built behind the blockage before the dam burst out in a single, violent wave that surged downstream. “This event was like a concrete wall that pushed mixed debris and the river ahead of it,” he explained. “Imagine driving a massive snowplow down a river—it was like that.” Except, by the time this snowplow turned sharply south at the Chinese border with Nepal, and confluence of the Bhotekoshi river, it contained 80,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools of water, and was traveling at over 100 miles per hour. The scale of the impact of the floodwaters on villages and roads and other infrastructure is difficult to imagine. Rescue teams report that, in some areas in the upper reaches of the upper Bhotekoshi gorge, the high-water mark is clearly visible several hundred feet above the riverbed. Massive hydropower projects, earthquake-proof Chinese customs buildings, and entire villages were obliterated in an instant. The floodwaters quickly overwhelmed the region’s early warning systems for flooding, and anyone in the river corridor—including many foreign tourists—had very little chance to escape. The wall of water continued down into the Trishuli river, one of Nepal’s most important, and sacred, waterways. It ripped through concrete highway bridges, miles of cropland, and numerous small urban areas that have popped up across Nepal’s middle hills in recent years. The floodwaters destroyed the lion’s share of the communications, power, water and road infrastructure along the river, leaving thousands of people stranded with no options for rescue. Nepal is no stranger to these types of events. In 2025, another flood down the same valley killed 18 people and caused extensive damage to the China-Nepal border crossing. Farmers in Nepal’s mid-hills region have a saying that translates roughly to “Live in the mountains, and farm on the valley floor.” The local adage means that homes and crop storage are located on higher ground, well out of the way of regular floods. But this flood destroyed the villages in higher ground, too. My friend Arbindra Khardka, a National Geographic Explorer and field glaciologist from Nepal’s Nuwakot district—one of the areas affected by the flood—recently explained just how unprecedented this flood is. “When we prepare road infrastructure, we look at annual floods and ten-year floods,” he told me. “Sometimes we look at 100-year floods—meaning that the probability of a flood of a given size happening in a given year is one percent. This was a 1,000-year flood.” The flood originated along the Chinese border in central Nepal’s Rasuwa district, and then followed the river corridor approximately 150 miles south to the Nepal-India border, significantly impacting communities for at least 60 miles downstream. These communities are ethnically and culturally diverse, with Tibeto-Burmese languages spoken by Buddhist communities in the mountains, and numerous Indigenous and Nepali-speaking Hindu groups residing further down the valley. Rasuwa is a mountainous area, and it is the launching point for the popular Langtang trekking trail. This famous hiking route draws hundreds of backpackers and climbers into the region each fall and spring. The river corridor is also an ancient trade route, connecting Nepal’s fertile plains to markets in China and Tibet. Today, this route is a popular border crossing for tourists and travelers heading to Tibet to climb the northern slopes of Mount Everest, or to visit the sacred Mount Kailash. Mount Kailash is a holy pilgrimage site for Hindus and Buddhists alike. Since 2026 is the auspicious Fire Horse year in the Tibetan and Chinese astrological calendars, the region has seen an enormous increase in pilgrims along the route. Usually, they make this trek during the warm summer months. The Indian spiritual leader Jaggi Vasudev, also known as Sadhguru, told his followers and the media on August 27 that 80 members of pilgrimage groups affiliated with his foundation were still missing after the flood. Tragically, yes. But not exactly at this scale. When the same region was hit by a 7.8 magnitude earthquake in 2015, another massive hanging glacier detached from the southern slopes of Langtang Lirung— the same mountain where the 2026 flood originated. In 2015, the glacier completely obliterated the village of Langtang, claiming the lives of around 300 local residents and trekkers. In 2025, on July 8, a glacial lake burst in another tributary of the Bhotekoshi and flooded the same corridor as in 2026, killing 18 people. Over the past ten years, there have been numerous massive flooding events across the Himalaya that have killed thousands, including another hanging glacier collapse that tore through the Rishi Ganga valley in Uttarkhand, India and claimed over 200 lives. A recent assessment by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), a Himalayan research non-profit, claims that Nepal’s glaciers are melting twice as fast today as they were only 20 years ago. It’s seems evident that, as our climate continues to warm, these types of unthinkable, 1,000-year events will become more and more commonplace. Unfortunately, we need to treat this event as a demonstration of the real effects of the climate crisis, and a sign of what’s to come. The Langtang mountain range is easily visible from Kathmandu on a clear day. A number of the 6,000- and 7,000-meter (19,600 to 23,000 foot) peaks in this area are regularly climbed by adventurous tourists and climbers, but they don’t see anything close to the crowds that travel to Mount Everest or Nepal’s other 8,000-meter peaks. While Mount Everest is quite far away from this region, which is in Eastern Nepal, the closest 8,000 meter peak is 26,781 foot Manaslu. That’s approximately 60 miles to the West of the valley. Manaslu is seen as a training peak for Mount Everest, and attracts enormous crowds in the fall season. Many climbers are already on the mountain, fixing ropes to the summit and establishing an elaborate Base Camp for the nearly 400 permitted climbers who will attempt the mountain this year. While the Manaslu region was not directly impacted by the floods, road access to the area and the diversion of helicopters to rescue operations could well delay or otherwise impact the climbing season. For starters, the scale of the damage and loss of life is overwhelming. Secondly, all communications infrastructure—cell phone towers, internet, and electricity—has been completely wiped out. The initial wave of Nepali rescue personnel was overwhelmed by the sheer scope of need, and the difficulty finding survivors along the massive swath of destruction left by the flood. The only option for rescuers to reach the impacted areas is currently via helicopter, or on foot. This severely limits the number of rescuers on the ground. It also drives up the cost of the recovery. The nature of the damage, too, is extraordinary. For example: the river corridor was home to numerous large hydropower projects, some fully operational, and others still under construction. As of now, 933 hydropower workers at these various power plants are still missing. In the complex tunnel systems of these projects, workers could feasibly have survived the flood. They may still be impossible to reach by rescue crews, and they have no food or water, and no means of sending out word about their whereabouts. Despite the challenges, the Nepal government has mobilized over 15,000 personnel to the area and is using helicopters, heavy equipment, and thermal drones to locate and rescue survivors. In the past three days, almost 2,000 people have been rescued by helicopter alone. The mountaineering and guiding industry in Nepal has mobilized to respond to the flood and join the relief efforts as needed. A group of highly trained IFMGA-certified mountain guides have been on standby at the airport in Kathmandu, should any survivors require high-angle or longline rescue. Many people in the industry are suffering an emotional toll from this disaster. Guides and mountain workers frequently moonlight as leaders on lucrative summer tours to Mount Kailash. Numerous guides and members of the mountaineering community remain missing after the flood. I’ve lived in Nepal long enough to know that we shouldn’t make predictions on what comes next.
