Nepal constantly surprises me, both in terms of the scale of the challenges faced by so many people in the country, and the speed in which people find ways to bounce back and recover. I do know that this flood has caused billions of dollars of damage to Nepal’s critical infrastructure, including disrupting international trade with China, removing 800 megawatts of electricity from the already-taxed national grid, and hampering travel from the capital of Kathmandu to much of the center of the country. On a local level, we can still only guess at the actual scope of the destruction and what the final death toll will be (as of August 28, it’s at 579). The psychological toll on families and communities of survivors is unfathomable. This incident also came in the middle of the monsoon growing season, which is a crucial time for food security for a majority of families along the river corridor. Many survivors will be facing an oncoming winter without homes, employment, or food and will be dependent upon aid from a Government and international community that we know from past disasters, tend to have a distressingly short attention span. Nepal’s heavy reliance on remittance money sent back to the country from young people working abroad to sustain its economy may actually be a blessing in disguise here, as it will provide many affected families with a reliable source of income to get back on their feet again. But the immense costs of reconstruction or, even funeral expenses for loved ones will necessitate that those families stay separated for longer. While this event may be something that, geologically speaking, only occurs once in a thousand years – for so many of the affected families and communities, the next few years will feel much longer. If you want to support relief efforts for affected communities in Nepal, you can donate to the official Government of Nepal relief channel here. Ben Ayers splits his time between Vermont and Kathmandu. He oversees Outside’s coverage of Mount Everest climbing, and spent the 2025 and 2026 climbing seasons reporting from Base Camp. Ben is also the cofounder of EverestLive.

item.title: Jack Johnson Is 51. Surfing Keeps Him Fit, but Farming Gave Him Something He Didn’t Expect.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.02
Jack Johnson’s earliest memories are of his father coming up the beach, holding a surfboard. And while Johnson is best known for his multi-platinum music career, he’s talented enough on a board that he could’ve gone pro. He first learned guitar when he was 14. But the first time he planted something at Kōkua Learning Farm, the newest arm of the Kōkua Hawai‘i Foundation, a nonprofit he founded with his wife, Kim, he was 44. Since then, the eight-acre property on O‘ahu has transformed into a hub of community land stewardship. The farm produces fruit and vegetables, houses a bee apiary and goats, and protects a native wetland, but it also hosts work days every month where people from all over the North Shore come to work the land and connect with one another. ’Āina Farm Stand, which opened on the property in November 2024, sells what’s harvested at Kōkua and at farms across the area. Johnson, 51, is currently on a world tour following the release of SURFILMUSIC, a documentary chronicling how he’s made a life combining the pursuits he loves the most. He spends a lot of his free time at the farm, where we talked to him to learn more about how he works farming and community leadership into his surfing, songwriting, and performing. Outside: When I arrived, you were leading a staff meeting. What is your relationship to the farm? How often are you here? JJ: Nature in general has always been really important in my life, and now the farm in the last five years has been a place where everything I loved about all my time outdoors as a kid, and all the times that my dad would take me camping, and the connection I felt to the natural world, is all brought together. It’s really nice to be able to spend my free time doing something productive that’s for the community. When I say “for the community,” I don’t mean I’m doing some kind of service; I mean that I love to work on it, and my friends love coming down here. Sometimes our volunteer groups are literally just a bunch of close friends who bring chainsaws and want to help remove an invasive tree and do some heavy lifting. And then other times, when we have a community work day, like 100 people show up. What is it like to work the land alongside the neighborhood? It’s neat because some people come back every Saturday. I’ve seen little kids who were in their mom’s BabyBjörn that are now running around, you know, five years old. And you can tell they get a lot from it—the kids are learning that you can work together with the community to do something really positive. And it’s the same thing for me—it’ll get me out of bed, it’ll get me motivated. I’ve never left a work day not feeling really stoked. It’s given me a sense of purpose in my life to have this place and be able to contribute to the community I grew up in, to be able to have a place that is for everybody. You don’t think of it as “your” farm, but as the foundation’s farm, and something bigger. I really do feel we were able to provide a place that’s for everybody. And I don’t think of it as mine. We help to steward this place, and it’s a very special place. There’s one corner of it that has a lot of native plants, and there’s a certain part of the community that loves to come and just work on that; that’s their specialty. They really take care of that zone. Then other people are really into the wetland part, which has a lot of natives as well, but they’ll show up for anything to do with that. And we have an orchard over there, and we have people who love learning about it because they might have fruit trees in their backyard, so when they come, it’s actually like a masterclass with our agroforest expert, who comes every workday. And [people] can learn about grafting and how to take care of their trees. Everybody’s got their little part on the farm, and I think they do feel like this is their place. Surfing and farming are both outdoor pursuits. In what way are they similar for you? How are they different? Surfing is a thing that you can do for yourself, it very much helps center you, it helps give you a sort of peace, but it’s only for you. But working on something like the Kōkua Learning Farm, it’s a whole different kind of thing. You still get to be outside and [feel] the wind blowing on you and get to be under the sun, but then you’re working with people, pulling weeds for an hour, and you’re still having all those conversations. I’ve had so many good conversations on the farm. When you’re distracted with weeding, it’s a really nice time to talk. And it makes the work easier too. At the end of the day, when you get a drink of water and [you’re] washing your hands, you look at the area and think, “Whoa, we just did that.” There’s a word in Hawaiian language, laulima, which [means] “many hands make light work.” How would you describe your relationship to surfing now? Just as strong as it’s ever been. It’s a weird thing growing up in a surfing family where I don’t remember starting necessarily. I have these abstract images of being in front of my dad’s board and watching waves. It was just something that was always in my life. It’s second nature. It’s weird, it’s all I want to do, really. Surf is always the goal—even if I’m kind of far from the ocean and I hear there’s a swell, then it’s kind of like, “OK, well, how do we get two hours to the coast to surf today?” It’s everything, from the playful stuff in my life to the spiritual part of my life. Most of my time was spent with my dad in the ocean, whether it was just casual surfs after school when he got home from work, or if my friends and I were out surfing our local spot, he would come paddling out. Now I do it with my own kids, and you don’t have to make time for the important conversations when you have that kind of time built into your day. There are always lulls between sets, and you’re just sitting there talking, and it’s a nice place for friends to catch up, and it’s a nice place for family. Do you find it plays a stronger role in your physical and mental well-being as you get older? When I say surfing is everything, I’m not exaggerating. It’s the place that I go to shoot the shit with my friends, it’s the place I go to get a little exercise because I tend to get heavier if I don’t surf. If I go on tour and I don’t surf for a couple weeks, I definitely gain a lot of weight. It’s my workout, [it’s] the only way I stay in shape. It kind of covers everything in my life. You don’t think about that stuff when you’re a kid. But once you get to 50, you start realizing, “Oh, I’ve got to do something to stay in shape.” And surfing’s the only thing I’ve ever learned. And it’s so much fun that I don’t have to find the motivation. This interview has been lightly edited and condensed. This article is from the Fall 2026 issue of Outside magazine. To receive the print magazine, become an Outside+ member here.

item.title: Dolly Parton’s Smoky Mountain Roots: How the Legend Transformed Her Tennessee Home
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.16
Dolly Parton at Dollywood. (Photo: Getty) Dolly Parton traveled the world performing for millions of people and lived a life of rhinestones and glitter—but there was nowhere she loved as deeply as the Smoky Mountains. Parton was more than a musician to so many people. Her work as a beloved country singer, humanitarian, business pioneer and storyteller brought her undeniable fame. But her heart always remained in Tennessee. From the peaks of Great Smoky Mountains National Park to the rollercoasters of Dollywood, her impact on Pigeon Forge and the surrounding region changed it forever. Parton was born January 19, 1946, in a small cabin in Locust Ridge, a rural community in Sevier County. She grew up in Sevierville, and her first paid singing gig was at The Pines Theater downtown (today you can grab a beer and play duckpin bowling here). Her love of her home state always showed up in her work. Her lyrics took listeners on a journey to the Smoky Mountains in songs like “My Tennessee Mountain Home,” “Smoky Mountain Memories” and “Heartsong.” As her career and life grew, Parton remained true to her roots. She toured across the world, but she always found her way back home. She settled down outside of Nashville later in life, and she always looked for ways to support her community. Giving back to her Smoky Mountain home was a perpetual goal of hers, according to a statement in April 2010. “I always thought that if I made it big or got successful at what I had started out to do, that I wanted to come back to my part of the country and do something great, something that would bring a lot of jobs into this area,” Parton said, according to the Associated Press. “Sure enough, I was lucky, and God was good to me and things happened good.” In September 1983, Parton announced plans to open a theme park in Sevier County that she described as a “fantasy mountain park” which became Dollywood. At the time, officials predicted the theme park would create about 300 jobs and bring in about 250,000 visitors to Pigeon Forge annually. Dollywood officially opened May 3, 1986, and has been operating for 40 years. Today, it employs about 4,000 people during peak summer season and about 3.5 million people visited the park in 2023. Pigeon Forge became a staple of the American road trip, luring tourists from all over the country. Nearby Great Smoky Mountains National Park became the most visited in the U.S., which Dollywood’s pull surely had no small part in. The region began to grow around Parton and her vision to become what it is today. “Of the millions of tourist tax dollars that flow into our county every year, you can bet Dolly Parton is a major force behind them,” Brenda McCroskey, CEO of the Sevierville Chamber of Commerce, told the News-Sentinel in 2013. “Even if a visitor isn’t crossing the turnstiles at Dollywood, they are still affected by Dolly. She is a legend and her name is spoken with pride by local business merchants in Sevierville, Pigeon Forge and Gatlinburg.” Her impact in the Smokies didn’t stop with Dollywood and her businesses, however. In 1991, she launched the Buddy Program for seventh and eighth grade students where she promised to give them $500 if they and a buddy graduated high school together. The program significantly decreased the Sevier County Schools’ dropout rate. In 2016, she launched the “My People Fund” to give $1,000 each month to more than 900 Sevier County families who lost their homes in wildfires that spread through Eastern Tennessee. And in 2024, Parton donated $1 million to Hurricane Helene relief, which was also matched by her businesses. After her death August 25, 2026, people across the world rushed to pay tribute. The website for Dollywood crashed in the hours after the world found out the news, and millions spoke to Parton’s inspiring career and legacy of kindness and generosity—especially in the Smokies. “Dolly Parton meant so much to Pigeon Forge, the Smoky Mountains, and generations of people around the world,” the City of Pigeon Forge said in a statement. “Her kindness, generosity, music, and love for the place she called home have left a mark that will never fade. The Smokies simply wouldn’t be the same without her.” In her songs, Parton paints a picture of a quiet and bucolic Tennessee, full of gorgeous views and life’s simple pleasures. “In my Tennessee mountain home, life is as peaceful as a baby’s sigh,” she wrote in ‘My Tennessee Mountain Home.’ “In my Tennessee mountain home, crickets are singing in the fields nearby.” Next time you visit Great Smoky Mountains National Park or road trip through Pigeon Forge, think of Parton. Slow down and pay attention to the crickets chirping and the butterflies flying by. Say hello to a stranger and take part in an easy act of kindness. Don’t forget to take it all in. “Her music, generosity, and deep connection to these mountains will always be remembered,” officials at Great Smoky Mountains National Park said in a statement. “Honoring Dolly Parton, whose spirit will forever flutter through the Smokies.”

item.title: This All-In One Camp Kitchen Comes With Running Water at the Push of a Button
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.01
The whole system: a water jug feeds the electric faucet at the push of a button. (Photo: Jenny Wiegand) I’ve never been jealous of the camper or teardrop-trailer crowd—too much hassle and maintenance, if you ask me—except for their built-in kitchens. A dedicated spot for cooking that doesn’t swallow the entire picnic table has always seemed like a luxury worth splurging on, and after two mostly-successful camping trips with two toddlers this summer, I’ve decided it’s one of only two things worth paying real money for when it comes to camp gear. (The other is an ultra-plush queen air mattress. Different review.) I spent the summer testing the Cinch Kitchen Cruiser, an all-in-one camp kitchen unit with a sink, stove, and storage that folds into a single box and unfolds to standing height—about as close as a car camper gets to a built-in kitchen without towing anything. Cinch is better known for rooftop tents, made in partnership with Wildland, a manufacturer with decades in the tent and outdoor gear business. The Kitchen Cruiser is a bit of a departure for them, but they have solid credentials in the space. Testing took place on an overnight trip to Curt Gowdy State Park in Wyoming and a weekend at Buffalo Creek, Colorado, and included: two adults, two toddlers, a lot of dishes, and even more dirty pacifiers. Packed dimensions: 50″ x 27″ x 36″ Weight: 43 lbs Standing height: 35.5″ Pros and Cons + Push-button double-burner stove + Sink and faucet + Ample storage + Standing-height prep counters – Heavy to carry – Deploying and folding legs is a pain The single biggest upgrade here isn’t any one feature, it’s that cooking happens somewhere other than the picnic table. My go-to camp kitchen setup—an ancient Coleman two-burner stove and a cutting board set up on the campsite picnic table—turns the one clean communal space at camp into food prep, dish drying, and dinner seating, and it turns into a junk show in two seconds flat. The Kitchen Cruiser gives you an actual dedicated food-prep station: counter and storage space that keeps food and knives out of the way, and a prep area at a standing height (35.5 inches), so you don’t have to bend over a low camp table to chop vegetables. That sounds like a small thing until you’ve spent a week doing camp prep hunched over like Gollum. The two-burner stove ignites at the push of a button—no matches or lighter required—and Cinch rates it at 3.2 kW combined, which is enough cooking power to boil a full pot of water in about 6 minutes. We ran two pans at once without either losing heat, and had pasta water and coffee boiling quickly both trips. Packed down, it’s the size of a standard camp gear box and slides into our SUV trunk with the rest of our gear. It unfolds to full standing height in under two minutes, and—the best part compared to other camp kitchen setups I’ve seen—everything lives inside the unit itself. Stove, sink, cookware: it all stays organized in two slide-out drawers and a compartment tall enough to house pots. No second bin of accessories riding shotgun. If the standing-height prep space is the upgrade, the built-in sink and electric faucet is the life-changing feature, and the reason I’d buy this tomorrow. The rechargeable faucet comes with a hose you can drop into your water jug, pulling water up and depositing it into the collapsible silicone sink at the push of a button. It’s the single best improvement we’ve made to family camping, full stop. It makes camp cleanup infinitely easier and more enjoyable. None of this comes without some hassles and disappointments. Unfolding the legs while the unit is fully loaded is awkward—you have to tip the whole box on its side to deploy them, which sends everything in the drawers sliding around. The legs don’t telescope, so you need reasonably level ground to get a sturdy surface. The included wind shields aren’t tall enough to fully protect the burners, which becomes a problem the second you get any real wind. Fuel was our other sticking point. This unit runs on 230-gram EN417 screw-on canisters and burns the same isobutane/propane mix as a Jetboil or MSR backpacking stove—rather than the 465-gram Coleman propane bottles we normally use on car camping trips. At full power, a single burner burns through roughly 116 grams an hour, so a standard canister buys about two hours of continuous full-power cooking on one burner. That math caught up with us: we ran out of fuel after three days of using the stove for two meals a day. (Worth noting: Cinch plans to ship future units with an adapter for Coleman propane bottles.) It’s also heavy—despite being built from aerospace-grade aluminum, the Kitchen Cruiser weighs 43 pounds unloaded. The heft means it’s not flimsy; it held up fine through two trips of rough handling. But it’s a real pain to unload from the car and carry any distance into camp. I’ve never tested a piece of gear with this many obvious flaws that I was willing to overlook. Yes, it’s heavy, and the legs are a pain to deploy. But I’ve decided this thing could weigh 100 pounds and I’d still find a way to cart it to every campsite. The drawbacks don’t outweigh what this unit fixed for my family camping trips: a convenient, organized, comfortable place to cook standing up, plus running water on demand. At $599, it’s not cheap, but it’s not an outlier—the Chuk Box, a similar camp kitchen unit, runs $665, and doesn’t come with a sink or faucet built in. For $66 less, you’re getting a separate wash station included instead of bolted on. For what the Kitchen Cruiser replaces (a folding table, a two-burner stove, a wash setup, a bin of loose gear), I’d say that’s a fair trade.

item.title: Apple Made a Massive Bet on Intel 21 Years Ago. It Changed Everything
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 6.25
Editors' Note: Welcome to the series called An Apple a Day, where we’ll share pieces of Apple content from our archives daily from now through late September. In addition to PCMag, this series will include pieces from our sibling sites CNET, Lifehacker, Mashable, and Popular Science. When Apple CEO Steve Jobs took the stage at WWDC 2005, few people knew he was about to reveal the fruits of a secret project five years in the making: Apple's switch to Intel processors across all its Mac systems. The move was significant enough to be part of the cover story for our Aug. 9, 2005, print edition, a package called "The Big Shake-Up." Apple's move away from PowerPC and its embrace of Intel processors could already be seen as a monumental event in the computer industry. What we did not know at the time was that the switch to Intel began as a project so secret that even Jobs himself didn't know about it for the first year or two. Spearheaded by Apple engineer JK Scheinberg, the project's clandestine nature has become part of Silicon Valley lore. Project Marklar: Spinning Up Intel on Macs In 2000, Apple started a one-off experiment that it dubbed Project Marklar. It was a skunkworks initiative to compile Mac OS X for Intel hardware, essentially creating the first Hackintosh. Software vice president Bertrand Serlet discovered the running build roughly 18 months in and immediately dispatched Scheinberg to Fry's Electronics to buy a top-of-the-line Sony Vaio PC. Scheinberg had OS X running on it by that evening—just hours before Jobs famously pitched Kunitake Ando, Sony's then-president, on licensing Mac OS for Vaio laptops while presenting him with a Vaio running Apple's operating system. (The Vaio deal didn't happen, but Mac OS X on Intel sure did.) At WWDC 2005, Jobs announced the switch from PowerPC to Intel, explaining Apple's hardware dilemma succinctly: "Apple just didn't know how to build the amazing computers we want to deliver in the future with the PowerPC." Jobs went on to explain that all Macs would be moving to Intel within two years. The move not only kept Apple's laptop plans on track but also helped cement Intel's position as the world's dominant chipmaker for more than a decade. The Strong Arm: Apple Silicon In, Intel Out That's why it was such a big deal when Apple announced in 2020 that it was making another pivot: Apple was phasing out Intel chips in favor of the new Apple M1 family, a line of Apple-designed chips that would power forthcoming Mac laptops and desktops. The introduction of the M1 was another sea change for both Apple and the broader PC industry. By then, Apple's ecosystem had grown to include the wildly popular iPhone and iPad. In 2020, Intel found itself divorced from this much bigger, brawnier Apple, while a second threat to its position emerged: The M1 opened the door to Arm processors on flagship PCs. That, in turn, paved the way for Qualcomm's current competitive place in the PC market and signaled the rise of the larger system-on-a-chip (SoC) paradigm that's reshaping the PC world today. Apple's M1 chips immediately proved their worth, delivering superb performance-per-watt and enabling MacBooks with genuine all-day battery life. The M1 was impressive at its debut in late 2020, but the M1 Ultra, two years later, was a real revelation: It combined two M1 Max processors into a doubled-up superchip that was competitive with workstation hardware. The most recent M-series chip, the M5, came out last year. In a fascinating twist of fate, Apple's shift to a larger SoC architecture, paired with massive allotments of unified memory shared among CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine, also positioned it to become the leading platform for the first wave of AI agents. By providing immense memory bandwidth on local hardware, the machines were uniquely suited early on to running on-device AI models. After six years of M-series chips, the last of the Intel-based Macs are losing support. The upcoming release of macOS 27 ("Golden Gate") will drop support for Intel processors, making macOS 26 ("Tahoe") the final Mac operating system for x86 hardware. Legacy Intel-based machines are already missing out on current features, such as support for Metal 4 graphics and Apple Intelligence, and they are facing the end of security patches and of Apple-authorized physical repairs. It's officially sunset for Intel Macs. The future belongs to Apple silicon. About Our Expert From the laptops on your desk to satellites in space and AI that seems to be everywhere, I cover many topics at PCMag. I've covered PCs and technology products for over 15 years at PCMag and other publications, among them Tom's Guide, Laptop Mag, and TWICE. As a hardware reviewer, I've handled dozens of MacBooks, 2-in-1 laptops, Chromebooks, and the latest AI PCs. As the resident Starlink expert, I've done years of hands-on testing with the satellite service. I also explore the most valuable ways to use the latest AI tools and features in our Try AI column.

item.title: Blink Battery Doorbell 2K+ Review: High-Res Security on a Budget
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.52
When I reviewed the Blink Video Doorbell back in 2025, I praised its affordability, sharp video quality, and long battery life. The Blink Battery Doorbell 2K+ offers more of the same. It's affordable at $79.99, and its battery life is superb. This time around, you get 2K video and AI-powered features. That said, you still have to pay to view recorded video and to unlock some features. As an alternative, the $99.99 TP-Link Tapo D225 Video Doorbell Camera also delivers sharp 2K video, doesn't require a subscription, and offers local and cloud storage options, making it our Editors’ Choice for video doorbells. At 5.1 by 1.8 by 1.3 inches (HWD), the Blink Battery Doorbell 2K+ is roughly the same size as its predecessor and a bit smaller than the TP-Link Tapo D225 (5.9 by 1.9 by 1.5 inches). It comes in black or white and includes a Sync Module that connects it to your home network, an AC adapter for the Sync Module, three AA batteries, a USB-C cable, straight and wedge mounting plates, mounting hardware, and a quick start guide. The front of the doorbell holds the camera, an LED that glows solid blue when the camera is recording, an IR LED for black-and-white night vision, a doorbell button with an LED ring that flashes white when the button is pressed and blinks red during pairing, a motion sensor, and a microphone. There’s a speaker on the bottom, and around back are two terminals for use with your existing doorbell wiring if you prefer a wired connection. The Sync Module Core is the same as the one that comes with the first Blink Video Doorbell. It has a white finish, rounded corners, and measures 3.1 by 1.7 by 0.8 inches (HWD). It is equipped with a 2.4GHz Wi-Fi radio to connect to your home network and can pair with up to 10 Blink cameras. It uses a USB-C port for power and has two LED indicators that glow blue and green when everything is connected, but it doesn’t have a USB port for connecting external storage devices. The camera has a 2K (1,920-by-1,920) video resolution and a 140-by-140-degree field of view with a 1:1 aspect ratio, providing a head-to-toe view of your doorstep. Depending on usage, the three AA batteries can power it for up to 16 months when the doorbell video quality is set to Best (1,920 by 1,920), up to 19 months when set to Standard (1,440 by 1,440), and up to 22 months when set to Saver (960 by 960). The Blink Battery Doorbell 2K+ will record video when it detects motion or when the doorbell button is pressed, but you have to subscribe to a Blink plan to access the footage and to unlock many features (Blink offers a free 30-day Basic trial with each doorbell). If you'd rather avoid a subscription, the TP-Link Tapo D225 supports SD cards up to 512GB, but you have to supply your own. Blink's Basic plan, which goes for $3.99 per month or $39.99 per year, gives you 60 days of cloud video storage for a single camera, extended live viewing (90 minutes instead of 5 minutes), person and vehicle detection, Blink Moments (combines multiple events into a single video), Notification Snooze, and Photo Capture (the camera takes pictures throughout the day so you can see what’s happening between recorded events). The $11.99 monthly/$119.99 yearly Plus plan includes everything in the Basic plan, plus support for unlimited devices and an extended warranty. To take advantage of Blink’s AI features, you have to upgrade to the $6.99 monthly/$69.99 yearly Basic AI plan, which gives you everything from the above-mentioned Basic plan (for a single camera) as well as AI-powered Video Descriptions, Single Event alerts that reduce notification clutter, and Unusual Activity alerts that let you know when something out of the ordinary has occurred. The Plus AI plan provides the same features for all of your devices and costs $19.99 per month or $199.99 per year. The Battery Doorbell 2K+ uses the same Blink Home Monitor mobile app for iOS and Android as other devices from the brand, such as the Blink Outdoor 4 Camera ($69.99) and the Blink Wired Floodlight Camera ($99.99), and appears in its own panel on the home screen along with other Blink products you have installed. The home screen displays the last image captured by the camera and the name of the doorbell, and it has a play arrow that launches a live video stream. At the bottom of the video panel are Save, Tap to Unmute, and More buttons. Tapping the Save button saves a clip of the current stream, and tapping the Unmute button turns on the microphone. The More button opens a screen where you can access device settings. Here you can edit the name and Wi-Fi connection, update the firmware, configure motion sensitivity and zone settings, enable smart notifications, adjust video, photo, and audio settings, and create privacy zones. The doorbell works seamlessly with the Alexa platform and Alexa+, and with numerous third-party devices via IFTTT applets, but it doesn't support Apple HomeKit or Google Home. The TP-Link Tapo D225 offers more flexibility, with support for Google in addition to Alexa and IFTTT. HomeKit support is still relatively rare for video doorbells. Installing the Doorbell 2K+ is as easy as it gets. Start by downloading the mobile app, creating an account, and tapping the plus icon in the upper-right corner to add a device. Select Sync Module and use your phone to scan the QR code on the back of the module. Choose a system to add the module to (or create a new one), verify that the LEDs are solid green and blinking blue, and tap Discover Device. Select a Wi-Fi SSID to connect to, enter your Wi-Fi password, and enter your location. Next, tap the plus icon again, select Video Doorbell from the list of devices, and scan the QR code on the back of the doorbell. Select the system you just created, then follow the instructions to install the batteries in the doorbell. When the LED blinks red, tap Discover Device, wait a few minutes for any necessary firmware updates (they are automatic), and tap Continue. After you give the doorbell a name, you can view the mounting instructions or skip them if you already know how to install the doorbell outdoors. The Battery Doorbell 2K+ delivered sharp 2K video with excellent color saturation in my testing. Its wide angle provided a full view of my doorstep as well as most of my front yard and driveway, and motion alerts were accurate and arrived instantly. Alexa voice commands to view video on an Amazon Echo Show smart display worked flawlessly, as did my Alexa routine to have a TP-Link Tapo L535E bulb turn red when the doorbell button was pressed. Final Thoughts Blink Battery Doorbell 2K+ - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The $79.99 Blink Battery Doorbell 2K is a solid choice for keeping tabs on visitors at your doorstep and beyond. It’s completely wireless and very easy to install, and it delivered superb 2K video in testing. That said, you have to subscribe to a Blink Plan to view recorded video and to unlock several features. If you want local storage or would rather not pay for a subscription, look to our Editors’ Choice winner, the $99.99 TP-Link Tapo D225. About Our Expert I’ve been working with computers for ages, starting with a multi-year stint in purchasing for a major IBM reseller in New York City before eventually landing at PCMag (back when it was still in print as PC Magazine). I spent more than 14 years on staff, most recently as the director of operations for PC Labs, before hitting the freelance circuit as a contributing editor.

item.title: Need a New Laptop or Tablet? These States Are Offering Sales Tax Breaks in August. Is Yours One of Them?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.10
Note: All back-to-school sales tax holidays have officially ended for the year, but sales are still ongoing. Check out our back-to-school deals for the chance to save on school supplies. Ready or not, the back-to-school shopping season is here. It may be the most expensive time of the year for parents and college students, but you can save a little extra when you shop during your state's sales tax holiday. A sales tax holiday is a tax-free shopping event that states offer throughout the summer to pause taxes charged on eligible back-to-school essentials. This year 18 states (and Puerto Rico) are participating, and nine of them will pause sales tax on tech purchases, including laptops, personal computers, and tablets. And three events are happening right now. With inflation still high and the RAM crisis continuing to drive the cost of PCs, finding easy ways to save on back-to-school tech is crucial. In fact, a PCMag survey recently found that most US adults are willing to spend $800 on a new laptop, but the median price of a new one is double that at $1,600. What's the solution? While shopping sales and secondhand can help, timing your purchase with your state's sales tax holiday is another way to keep a little extra cash in your bank account. Don't miss your state's sales tax holiday. Here's every state that's holding a tax-free holiday this summer, and when to shop. Which States Have Sales Tax Holidays on Tech This Summer? There are 9 states offering sales tax exemptions on computers and tech during summer sales tax holidays. They are: Full 2026 Sales Tax Holiday Schedule and Eligible Items by State Here's a full overview of every US state and territory offering sales-free back-to-school shopping events this summer. Alabama - Sales tax holiday dates: July 17 – July 19, 2026 - Items included: Clothing up to $156, school supplies up to $78, computers up to $1,173, books up to $47 (per item). See the full list here. - Notes: Local municipalities can opt in/out; more than 300 cities/counties waive local tax. Arkansas - Sales tax holiday dates: August 1 – August 2, 2026 - Items included: Clothing and accessories up to $100 per item, school supplies (no strict limit), select electronics (no strict limit). See the full list here. - Notes: Applies to state and local sales tax; participation is mandatory for retailers. Connecticut - Sales tax holiday dates: August 16 – August 22, 2026 - Items included: Clothing and footwear up to $300 per item. Includes standard back-to-school apparel; excludes athletic uniforms and luxury goods. See the full list here. Florida - Sales tax holiday dates: July 20 – August 20, 2026 - Items included: Clothing, footwear, and accessories up to $100, school supplies up to $50, computers and electronic accessories up to $1,500, learning aids and puzzles up to $30 (per item). See the full list here. Illinois - Sales tax holiday dates: August 7 – August 16, 2026 - Items included: Clothing, footwear, and select school supplies up to $125 per item. See the full list here. - Note: Illinois does not eliminate sales tax during this event. Instead, it is lowered by 5%. Iowa - Sales tax holiday dates: August 7 – August 8, 2026 - Items included: Clothing and footwear up to $100 per item. See the full list here. Maryland - Sales tax holiday dates: August 9 – August 15, 2026 - Items included: Clothing and footwear up to $100 per item, backpacks (first $40 is exempt). See the full list here. Massachusetts - Sales tax holiday dates: August 8 – August 9, 2026 - Items included: Most retail items up to $2,500 per item. Full list here. - Notes: Broad retail holiday that excludes alcohol, electricity, gas, meals, motor vehicles, motorboats, tobacco, and more. Mississippi - Sales tax holiday dates: July 10 – July 12, 2026 - Items included: Clothing, footwear, and school supplies up to $100 per item. See the full list here. Missouri - Sales tax holiday dates: August 7 – August 9, 2026 - Items included: Clothing up to $100, school supplies up to $50, computer software up to $350, computers up to $1,500. See the full list here. New Mexico - Sales tax holiday dates: July 31 – August 2, 2026 - Items included: Clothing and footwear up to $100, school supplies up to $30, computers up to $1,000, computer hardware up to $500 (per item). See the full list here. - Notes: Retailers are not required to participate. Ohio - Sales tax holiday dates: August 7 – August 9, 2026 - Items included: Clothing up to $75, school supplies up to $20, school instructional materials up to $2 (per item). See the full list here. Oklahoma - Sales tax holiday dates: August 7 – August 9, 2026 - Items included: Clothing and footwear up to $100 per item. See the full list here. - Notes: Exemptions do not apply to most athletic wear. Puerto Rico - Sales tax holiday dates: July 17 – July 18, 2026 - Items included: School uniforms, footwear, and school supplies (no specified limit). See the full list here. South Carolina - Sales tax holiday dates: August 7 – August 9, 2026 - Items included: Clothing, footwear, school supplies, computers, bed and bath items (no specified limit). See the full list here. Tennessee - Sales tax holiday dates: July 31 – August 2, 2026 - Items included: Clothing up to $100, school supplies up to $100, computers up to $1,500 (per item). See the full list here. Texas - Sales tax holiday dates: August 7 – August 9, 2026 - Items included: Clothing, footwear, school supplies, and backpacks up to $100 per item. See the full list here. Virginia - Sales tax holiday dates: August 7 – August 9, 2026 - Items included: Clothing and footwear up to $100, school supplies up to $20 (per item). See the full list here. West Virginia - Sales tax holiday dates: July 31 – August 3, 2026 - Items included: Clothing up to $125, school supplies up to $50, computers up to $500, instructional materials up to $20, sports equipment up to $150 (per item). See the full list here. What Are Sales Tax Holidays? Also known as 'tax-free weekends', a state sales tax holiday is a statewide event where sales tax is temporarily paused or reduced on certain items. Many states hold these events during the back-to-school shopping season. Items that are typically exempt from tax during these events include clothing, school supplies, and computers (laptops and tablets). If you live in a state that also imposes local sales tax, it may also be exempt during the event. This varies by state and county. Do Sales Tax Holiday Exemptions Apply to Online Purchases? Yes, you'll be able to shop tax-free even at online retailers like Amazon and Apple during your state's event. Can Sales Tax Holidays Really Save You Money on Laptops, Desktops, and Tablets? Shopping for school supplies during a tax-free event can help you save a little extra, especially if you need to purchase a big-ticket item, like a new laptop or desktop. Let's say you plan to purchase a new MacBook Neo, which starts at $599 for students. If you live in Massachusetts, which has a 6.25% state sales tax rate, this would cost you $636.44 after tax. So, you could save $37.44 on one new MacBook Neo (with the student discount) by shopping during this tax holiday. If you need a MacBook with more power, we recommend the Apple MacBook Air 13-Inch (2026, M5) as our top pick for most college students. This starts at $1,149. Using the same example from Massachusetts, with the 6.25% sales tax tacked on, this MacBook would cost you $1,220.81. If you were to buy this laptop during the sales tax holiday, you'd save $71.81. Can You Save on Refurbished Tech During Sales Tax Holidays? Yes, if you live in a state that's offering sales tax exemptions on computers and electronics, you won't pay sales tax on used tech during the sales tax holidays. Shopping secondhand is one of the best ways to beat rising computer prices. We even have tips on how to find the best value when shopping for refurbished computers and tablets. Are There States That Never Charge Sales Tax? Yes, there are five US states that do not impose a state-level sales tax. They are Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, and Oregon. Alaska does, however, charge a local sales tax. Will You Pay Local Sales Tax During Sales Tax Holidays? If you live in a city or county that levies local sales tax, it may be temporarily paused for eligible items during your state's sales tax holiday. This varies across cities, counties, and states, so check your local state and city website for more information. My State Doesn't Have a Tax Holiday. Can I Shop In Another State? Technically, yes, you can travel to another state to shop tax-free during that state's sales tax holiday. However, if you bring the items you purchased back to your home state, you might be required to list these items on your taxes next year and pay use tax on them. Is New Jersey Holding a Sales Tax Holiday This Year? New Jersey used to hold tax-free weekends in the summer for the back-to-school season. Its sales tax holiday was officially repealed in 2024, and the state has not held a tax-free holiday since. About Our Expert As PCMag's managing editor of operations and evergreen content, I lead the operations, How To, and updates teams. I have 15+ years of experience writing and editing personal finance, small business, and financial software content. Prior to PCMag, I led the personal finance team at CNET. My work has also been published in the Chicago Tribune, NerdWallet, Investopedia, and BestReviews. Personal finance Project management software Tax software Accounting software Identity theft services Antivirus software A PC enthusiast for most of my life, I now work on a 14-inch MacBook Pro (M3) or 13-inch MacBook Air. You won't pry my Android from my hands, though! I have a Samsung S25 that has miraculously survived hundreds of accidental tumbles down my wood staircase. My first desktop was a hand-me-down Power Macintosh in the early '90s, where I spent hours trying not to get eaten by a grue in the game Zork. I'm an avid reader, and though I prefer physical books, I travel with my old Nook GlowLight 3 (yes, they still exist).

item.title: It's Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Open Beta Weekend: Here's How to Join
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.81
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, the next big release in Activision's long-running shooter franchise, is hosting an open beta this weekend, and everyone's invited. You'll get a preview of this highly anticipated game's multiplayer mode before the full release comes out on October 23. The game's Early Access Beta ran August 21-25. The beta saw an all-time peak of 115,145 concurrent players on the first day. The Open Beta started on Friday at 1 p.m. ET and wraps up on Tuesday. We expect the player count to be even higher this time around. Here's how to start playing. When Is the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Open Beta? Activision already held its Early Access Beta, but the upcoming Open Beta will be accessible to everyone, even if you didn't preorder the game. Additionally, a Campaign Early Access will be held closer to the game's final launch in order to give players an early look at the single-player campaign. Here's what you need to know: - Open Beta: The game's open beta will then run from 1 p.m. ET / 10 a.m. PT on Friday, August 28, to 1 p.m. ET / 10 a.m. PT on Tuesday, September 1, for Xbox, PS5, PC, and Nintendo Switch 2. The Open Beta is available for all players and can be preloaded as early as noon ET / 9 a.m. PT on August 26. You do not need an early access code to play during the Open Beta period. - Campaign Early Access: After the Open Beta, you'll have one more chance to access the game early. Activision will be holding a Campaign Early Access on October 16 for digital preorders ahead of the game's full launch. How to Join the Modern Warfare 4 Open Beta Joining the Open Beta will be a lot easier than getting into the Early Access Beta, since you no longer need a special code or a preorder to play. Instead, the Modern Warfare 4 Beta will be available to download separately through the digital storefront on your platform of choice. You'll simply be able to download the Open Beta, preload it, and then start playing when the session unlocks. How to Preorder Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 While no longer necessary to experience the Open Beta, you may still want to preorder Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 to gain access to in-game rewards and the Campaign Early Access. You can preorder the game via physical or digital editions for Xbox, PlayStation 4, and Nintendo Switch 2. For PC, preorders are available on Battle.net, Steam, or Xbox on PC. You can preorder from Amazon now: - PlayStation 5 (Standard Edition) - Xbox Series X (Standard Edition) - Xbox Series X/S and Windows Digital (Standard Edition) - Nintendo Switch 2 (Standard Edition) - Nintendo Switch 2 Digital (Standard Edition) Can Your PC Run Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4? Yes, your PC should be able to run the latest Call of Duty beta as long as it meets certain requirements. Here's what your PC should have and what developers recommend: Minimum System Requirements (PC): - OS: Windows 10 64 Bit (latest update) - CPU: AMD Ryzen 5 1600 or Intel Core i5-8400 - RAM: 12GB - Video Card – AMD: Radeon RX 470 - Video Card – NVIDIA: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 970 / 1060 - Video Card – Intel: Intel Arc A580 - Video Memory: 3 GB - Storage Space: SSD required - Network: Broadband Internet connection - Sound Card: DirectX Compatible Recommended System Requirements (PC): - OS: Windows 11 64 Bit (latest update) - CPU – AMD: AMD Ryzen 5 3600 - CPU – Intel: Intel Core i7-8700 - RAM: 16 GB - Video Card – AMD: AMD Radeon RX 6700 XT - Video Card – NVIDIA: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Ti - Video Card – Intel: Intel Arc B580 - Video Memory: 8 GB - Storage Space: SSD required - Network: Broadband Internet connection - Sound Card: DirectX Compatible The beta also has specific drivers, shaders, and hardware requirements, so it's worth checking out the Call of Duty website if you have concerns about compatibility issues. About Our Expert As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert. I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week. My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth. My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work. Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.title: SpaceX Pushes FCC to Scrutinize Rocket Lab-Iridium Deal Amid Spectrum Clash
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.64
Rocket Lab’s $8 billion deal to acquire Iridium and form a larger player in the rocket and satellite industry is facing some resistance from SpaceX. For weeks now, Iridium has been clashing with SpaceX over its next-gen“gateway” facilities for Starlink. The ground-based gateways promise to help SpaceX upgrade Starlink with gigabit speeds by harnessing more radio spectrum. But Iridium argues the spectrum use will create interference with its own systems since they'd share airwaves in the 19.4 to 19.6GHz and 29.1 to 29.3GHz bands. On Thursday, SpaceX then seemingly escalated the dispute, sending a letter to the Federal Communications Commission, pressing it to scrutinize the Iridium-Rocket Lab merger, which was announced in late June. “Iridium’s well-documented history of anticompetitive attacks against its competitors and American consumers hangs as a cloud over the proposed transaction,” SpaceX’s satellite policy associate, Matthew Turk, wrote to the FCC. The three-page letter accuses Iridium, a satellite communications provider, of trying to weaponize past “rulemakings and coordination procedures to impose outdated, heightened restrictions on its competitors’ operations and the satellite services they provide.” Turk then points to Iridium’s latest objections to SpaceX’s gigabit Starlink gateways as the company prepares to build dozens across the US. “In the last eight months alone, Iridium filed over 50 petitions to block its competitors from deploying next-generation satellite services and enhanced backhaul capacity for American consumers, even when those deployments do not present any colorable risk of unacceptable interference to its sparse operations,” Turk says. Turk accuses Iridium of abusing “Commission procedure to deny or delay its competitors from providing better service to millions of American consumers, businesses, and first responders," rather than compete with Starlink. The letter goes on to insist that SpaceX’s new gateways will avoid interfering with Iridium’s own transmissions to its orbiting satellites. However, Turk notes: “SpaceX does not oppose the transaction. But as SpaceX seeks to actually use this spectrum to deliver next-generation satellite services to consumers across the country, the same cannot be said of Iridium’s attempts to impose heightened restrictions on other operators at the public interest’s expense. The Commission should carefully evaluate whether Iridium’s conduct is in the public interest.” Rocket Lab has requested that the FCC clear the merger. It submitted a “public interest statement” that says the deal will offer “clear and substantial public interest benefits.” Hence, SpaceX’s complaint could be seen as an attempt to gain leverage against Iridium by pressing its radio interference claims. Rocket Lab and Iridium didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. But on Tuesday, an attorney for Iridium told the FCC that it continued to stand by the radio interference claims. “Iridium’s simulations show that a fair number of SpaceX’s gateways would produce interference exceeding maximum permissible levels by a wide margin,” Joseph Godles wrote. Still, his letter adds: “Iridium reiterates its preference to resolve these issues in coordination. Iridium and SpaceX have had multiple coordination meetings, and there is no need for the Commission to expend its resources on this matter while the parties are actively engaged.” In another Aug. 20 letter to the FCC, Iridium’s VP for Regulatory, Kara Azocar, also seemed to try to dial down the tensions. “Iridium already has initiated coordination discussions with SpaceX and believes that a resolution is close at hand to the first of SpaceX’s applications. Iridium is optimistic that a similar approach could facilitate resolution of several additional applications. Iridium has enjoyed a long and productive relationship with SpaceX,” she wrote. “Iridium has no interest in impeding SpaceX’s business plans. It merely needs to ensure that its feeder link and TT&C (Telemetry, Tracking, and Command) operations are protected. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: New Obstacle for Starlink? Chinese Rocket May Have Ejected Debris
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.53
A Chinese rocket may have created a debris field in orbits near SpaceX’s Starlink satellites, giving the constellation another potential obstacle to dodge. On Friday, space debris tracking provider LeoLabs reported “fragmentation” from a Chinese Long March 6C rocket that flew into space earlier this week. The rocket successfully launched, carrying up seven satellites. But tracking from California-based LeoLabs suggests the upper stage of the rocket broke apart in Earth’s orbit. LeoLabs first detected the debris on Wednesday night from its radar site in Western Australia. “We quickly confirmed this event with a follow-up pass over our radar site in New Zealand. We estimate tens to hundreds of fragments were generated,” the company tweeted. LeoLabs told PCMag it’s “still conducting analysis to characterize this event.” But the company noted: “Based on similar fragmentation events, it’s possible the fragments generated by this event may pose a collision risk to any spacecraft operating as high as 1,000 km.” Specifically, the Chinese rocket body was orbiting as close as 396 kilometers to the Earth to as far as 482 kilometers away. An image from LeoLabs suggests the debris was detected at around 500-520km. The fragments could pose a problem for other low-orbit constellations, especially Starlink, which has around 11,000 satellites. Starting this year, SpaceX began moving over 4,000 Starlink satellites to 480km orbits. As a result, over 8,500 satellites currently orbit in the 460-490km range, according to satellitemap.space, a satellite-tracking system. That said, all Starlink satellites feature built-in thrusters, enabling them to maneuver and avoid potential collisions. From December 2025 to May 2026, the satellites performed over 207,000 maneuvers, or around 40 maneuvers per satellite, according to an FCC document. SpaceX has also developed a traffic control system called Stargaze that uses sensors on Starlink satellites to detect and track other space objects. On top of this, the company has been urging better coordination in the space industry after a Chinese-deployed satellite nearly collided with Starlink in December. Perhaps the more notable issue is that a Chinese Long March rocket has again ejected debris into space, with similar incidents in 2024 and 2022 involving the 6A vehicle. LeoLabs says: "Due to the low altitude of this event, the fragments will likely de-orbit within a few years. While the fragment cloud persists, spacecraft operators will have to perform additional collision mitigation efforts due to the increased risk.” But so far, only LeoLabs has reported detecting the debris from the rocket. US Space Command and SpaceX didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Meanwhile, astronomer and satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell told PCMag he hasn’t “seen any other reports yet beyond the LeoLabs report.” Still, he said the reported debris does seem to pose a potential risk to Starlink and other traffic. "The CZ-6C was in a low orbit, but some of the debris would end up in orbits with apogees in the Starlink height range," McDowell said. The operator of the rocket, the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation, also couldn’t be reached for comment. In the meantime, LeoLabs said the amount of generated debris “will become more precise over the next few days as the fragment cloud begins to separate and we are able to collect more measurements on individual fragments.” About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: With New Price Hike, Apple TV Now Costs 3x More Than It Did at Launch
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.48
If you thought last year's $3 price hike for Apple TV meant it'd be safe from further increases, you were wrong. Apple is raising prices yet again, with the streamer now costing $2 more per month. A monthly subscription is now $14.99, up from $12.99. A yearly subscription is also less affordable at $119.99, compared with its previous $99.99 price, which had remained unchanged during 2025's increase. In just two years, Apple has raised its monthly cost by 50%, which may be due to expanded sports coverage, including the addition of Formula 1 and Major League Soccer games. Apple TV launched for $4.99 per month in late 2019, with the price increasing over the last seven years as its selection of TV shows, films, and sports has grown. The catalog remains smaller than that of many of its rivals because it has focused on producing original, high-quality programming, including award winners like Ted Lasso, Severance, Pluribus, and The Studio. The brand's all-encompassing services bundle, Apple One, is also increasing by $2 per month. It now costs $21.95 per month for an individual subscription, up from $19.95 for a package including Apple Music, TV, Arcade, and 50GB of iCloud+ storage. Changes to individual Apple One subscriptions were inevitable after a price hike for Family and Premier plans rolled out last month. It also increased the price of a standard Apple Music subscription by $1 per month. These changes take effect immediately for new subscribers, while those on monthly rolling contracts will be notified before their next payment. This year has seen many streaming services raise prices, making it unaffordable for many households to subscribe to multiple streamers. Amazon Prime Video, ESPN Select, Netflix, Paramount+, and Peacock have all increased this year. This announcement caps off a busy week of reveals for Apple, including the launch of a new Mac mini with an M6 processor and a revamped Mac Studio, as well as confirmation of its next major launch event on Sept. 9, where we expect to see an iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the first foldable iPhone. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: More Wi-Fi Routers From This Chinese Vendor Found With Backdoors
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.21
It’s not just 20 routers. A US cybersecurity company has uncovered even more backdoors in Wi-Fi routers from a Chinese manufacturer called Zbtlink. Earlier this month, VulnCheck uncovered a backdoor, dubbed “Endlessdoors,” in a wide range of Zbtlink routers. After conducting a deeper investigation, the company says it has discovered two additional backdoors, called “SpeakingStone” and "DarkLantern,” mainly in other router models from the Chinese manufacturer. The findings raise concerns that Zbtlink could secretly hijack the routers. The SpeakingStone backdoor works by “phoning home” and bypassing firewalls to reach Zbtlink’s apparent cloud server, which can then issue remote commands. The second backdoor, DarkLantern, can also execute commands “from anywhere on the internet. By design, it’s reachable from the outside world,” VulnCheck found. "No authentication required." The cybersecurity company uncovered the backdoors after buying an $88 Wi-Fi router on Amazon from a New York-based vendor called Deep Orange Technology. The product turned out to be a “white-labeled” or repackaged ZBT-WE826-T2 router from the Chinese manufacturer, first developed back in 2014. The firmware inside the router was dated from 2019, VulnCheck says, predating the earlier Endlessdoors backdoor. Still, the firmware contained the two other newly discovered backdoors. SpeakingStone stands out for containing eight different functions, including an apparent way to exfiltrate login credentials for a customer’s internet service provider account. Another function can allegedly be used for DNS hijacking, a way to redirect traffic meant for a legitimate site to another domain. Hence, VulnCheck alleges the backdoor operates as a “surveillance implant.” SpeakingStone will also phone home to ac-link[.]com, a domain under Alibaba Cloud Computing that Vulncheck says Zbtlink has been using. As a backup, the same backdoor has also been configured to connect to findmyipaddr[.]com, which wasn’t registered, so VulnCheck decided to acquire the domain. “This is called sinkholing: when a researcher takes control of an abandoned command and control domain, every device that phones home to it connects to the researcher instead,” VulnCheck explained. The sinkholing also revealed that 390 out of 392 unique devices were based in China and configured with the SpeakingStone backdoor. Of those, 363 were also Zbtlink products classified as L3_V2_8, which appear to be Customer Premises Equipment (CPE) sold to China Mobile, the country’s largest wireless carrier. “And these are only the devices reaching the backup domain. The primary C2, ac-link[.]com, is still live. The full population of SpeakingStone-equipped devices is unknown and almost certainly much larger,” the report added. VulnCheck has also been scanning the internet for DarkLantern-equipped routers. So far, the company has discovered 203 instances across 22 countries from 16 different router models; 103 of the instances were found in the US. “These are older models, and the firmware on our test device was built in 2019. We are likely catching the tail end of DarkLantern’s deployment. The installed base was almost certainly larger,” the report says. DarkLantern can also be blocked if placed behind a firewall. Zbtlink didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. But the company claimed the earlier Endlessdoors backdoor was merely an “after-sales technical support tool,” intended to help troubleshoot issues from customers “upon their explicit request and authorization.” “Sales of the affected models have been immediately suspended. Downloads for the relevant firmware have been removed from the official website,” the Chinese manufacturer said earlier this month. “We are currently developing and releasing firmware updates to fully resolve the issue with the rctl component.” But so far, no new firmware has been published. In the meantime, Vulncheck says the discovery of the additional backdoors suggests Endlessdoors wasn’t an isolated firmware issue. The company’s report further warns that Zbtlink routers have been sold under other third-party brands in the US, Canada, and Australia. “These devices do not belong on American networks,” the report adds. Concerns about Wi-FI routers being used for spying have already prompted the Trump administration to ban new foreign-made routers. Although the FCC has created an exemption process, so far, no waiver has been given to any Chinese company. A few of the affected routers overlap with devices found to be carrying the earlier Endlessdoors backdoor. The Zbtlink models found containing either of the two newly discovered backdoors include WE1326, WE2426-C, WE357, WE5926, WE5926-EC_QP, WE5926-WD, WE826-Q, WE826-T2, WE826-WD, WF3526-P, WG108, WG3526, L3_V2_8, ZBT-7628, ZBT-ZBT7621. Several other models also contained the backdoors, including some from a Chinese brand called MoreQuick. Others were merely attributed to unknown brands. The WE1326, WG108, and WG3526 models were also flagged for the Endlessdoors implant. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Wanna Sit on a Thumbstick? IKEA Announces Quirky Xbox Furniture Collab
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.05
Component shortages and their resulting price hikes might be making it borderline unaffordable for many people to buy current-gen consoles, including the Xbox Series X. But if you're interested in adding some more Xbox to your gaming setup but can't afford a new device—how about some Xbox-themed homeware? IKEA and Xbox are collaborating on a new nine-item collection, dubbed Yxstaby, focused on furniture and objects meant to be used by gamers. Highlights from the collection include a green stool designed to mimic the thumbstick on the original Xbox controller. According to Wired, the design team labored over this item, finally incorporating rubber rings into the base to keep it stable despite its unconventional design, which allows you to swivel on it. The collection also includes an elegant metal platter based on the D-pad of the original Xbox controller, which is also available as a pillow, in both green and black. Many products in the collection are more subtle in their debt to the Xbox aesthetic. The collection also features a mash-up between a laptop stand and a gaming hardware toolbox, which can be used to store all your gaming accessories, and has an on-brand green cutaway at the bottom. Another item up for grabs is a gaming chair with built-in storage slots to store your gaming accessories under the seat, again featuring the classic Xbox green trim. You can also grab a rounded mobile side table designed specifically for gaming setups, for storing controllers, as well as a circular mobile stand, featuring an integrated shelf with space for equipment and accessories. The collection will be available in IKEA stores and online from 1 October. Availability may vary by market, and prices have yet to be announced. If you're really set on maximizing your commitment to the classic Xbox design aesthetic, earlier this week, Microsoft started taking preorders for the limited edition of its translucent and green Xbox Series X, the Xbox Series X25 Limited Edition. Though at $899 it's quite an investment in your gaming set-up. About Our Expert I’m a reporter covering weekend news. Before joining PCMag in 2024, I picked up bylines in BBC News, The Guardian, The Times of London, The Daily Beast, Vice, Slate, Fast Company, The Evening Standard, The i, TechRadar, and Decrypt Media. I’ve been a PC gamer since you had to install games from multiple CD-ROMs by hand. As a reporter, I’m passionate about the intersection of tech and human lives. I’ve covered everything from crypto scandals to the art world, as well as conspiracy theories, UK politics, and Russia and foreign affairs.

item.title: Think Incognito Mode Protects You? Here's the Terrifying Truth About Browser Fingerprinting
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.02
You've probably heard the phrase "if you're not paying for it, you're the product." With free web services, that's especially true. Advertisers and data brokers collect data about where you go and what you view online, and they use data that your browser freely supplies to create a fingerprint that uniquely identifies you. As a result, they know where you go, what you click on, and what you buy. Unlike other tracking techniques, browser fingerprinting leaves no traces and happens without your direct knowledge. So how do you protect your privacy and avoid being fingerprinted? Cookies Were Yesterday. Fingerprints Are Forever When you click a link, your browser sends a request for information to a server on the internet. The server responds with the requested information, and the conversation is over. The server doesn’t remember you or your request—that would require a huge database of every visitor ever. And yet, when you’re interacting with a website, you really want some continuity. Early in the evolution of web browsers, cookies were invented to provide that continuity. Each cookie is a simple text file that lives on your computer, not on the site. The site can put information into the cookie, such as your preferred street address, things you’ve bought, or which page you were reading in an online novel. When you revisit that site, it can retrieve data from its own cookie (but not from any other) and read it back. However, modern websites aren’t simply monolithic entities. They contain links and content from advertisers and other third-party sites. These third parties can save their own cookies to your PC, containing whatever data they have available, including the name of the site that’s hosting the ad. If an advertiser has a presence on multiple sites, data from multiple cookies now lets it link your presence across those sites. Suddenly, cookies don’t seem so tasty. In 2009, privacy experts proposed reining in this abuse by allowing browsers to add a "Do Not Track" header to page requests. This effort fizzled because sites were free to ignore the header, and it has since been deprecated (with some browsers removing the option entirely). Security companies responded by devising Do Not Track technology that actively prevented tracking. Trackers have responded with new technologies, including supercookies, evercookies, Flash cookies, and more. All these tracking technologies involve placing something (a text file, a script, or some other file) on the victim’s computer, and they've all been foiled in various ways. Browser fingerprinting is different. It doesn’t change anything on the local computer; it simply leverages standard browser functions. How Your Installed Fonts (Yes, Fonts) Betray You When you’re surfing the web, it really feels like you have a direct, continuous connection with the site you’re perusing. In truth, your experience is made up of many small interactions between your browser and the website’s server. The browser sends a request, and the server responds. That request necessarily includes your IP address—without it, the server wouldn’t know where to send the response. But over time, browsers have come to send ever-increasing amounts of information. Compatibility isn’t much of an issue these days, but if you go back far enough, you’ll find a time when websites had to tune their responses to the requesting browser, perhaps sending a different page to Netscape Navigator than they did to Internet Explorer. Requests to a server identify the browser making the request, right down to the precise version and build number. That’s a simple enough interaction, but it’s the start of a slippery slope. To render a design-rich page from a website, your browser needs access to the right fonts. The fonts available depend on your operating system. Your browser queries the OS for a list of fonts and passes that list along to the website. If a required font is missing, the site might display a simplified page. Yes, we all have the same basic set of fonts that come with Windows, but installing other programs often adds new fonts, and uninstalling them doesn’t always remove them. After a while, our font collections start to diverge. For a quick look at the many arcane bits that make up your browser fingerprint, pay a visit to the Electronic Frontier Foundation’s Cover Your Tracks page (launched in 2010 under the name Panopticlick). With your permission, this page gathers the information used to generate a fingerprint, along with some useful stats. I learned, for example, that my fingerprint is unique among more than 300,000 fingerprints tested by the site in the last 45 days. Taking a long-term view, security and privacy researchers at Friedrich-Alexander University Erlangen-Nürnberg, Germany, have been running a study on browser fingerprinting since 2016. I’ve participated since the beginning. Participation is simple: once a week, you receive an email with a link to verify your fingerprint. You can review the stats of your own participation at any time. For example, I now know that I had the same unique and trackable fingerprint for 263 days in 2017. You don’t have to register if you just want to view the aggregate statistics. There are numerous other pages that can display the components of your browser fingerprint, with varying degrees of detail. Reporting from the open-source AmIUnique site, the components farthest from the norm are helpfully color-coded, highlighting those that contribute most to making your fingerprint different from the rest. Device Info lists a vast array of information that a website can access through your browser. The Crazy Text String Exposed Every Time You Load a Page Modern browsers reveal a vast amount of information not only about themselves, but also about the operating system on which they reside. Sites can run simple scripts to learn even more, such as the screen resolution in use and which plug-ins are installed. A crazy string of text called User Agent reveals a lot about your browser. Here’s a User Agent string from Chrome: “Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/140.0.0.0 Safari/537.36”. And here’s one from Edge: “Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/140.0.0.0 Safari/537.36 Edg/140.0.0.0”. Websites can query and receive a wealth of information about your system’s settings and configuration. This massive amount of available information can be condensed into a single, simple value called a fingerprint. The chance of any two PCs sharing the same fingerprint is low, and the consequences for a tracker who encounters such a duplication are likewise low. Yes, your fingerprint might change due to system updates, but that doesn’t happen often. When it does, it’s not all that important to the tracker, either. Trackers don’t care about losing track of you temporarily. As long as they can track plenty of others, no problem! And with browser fingerprinting, they don’t need to worry about cookies. The Privacy Browsers and Tools That Foil Fingerprinting After a lifetime of working with clay, potters may find their fingerprints have simply abraded away. What can you do to obscure your browser fingerprint and prevent it from revealing your identity? As with any other topic, the internet offers endless how-to advice for hiding your fingerprint. Using a VPN is a common suggestion, as it masks your IP address. Sticking with your browser’s privacy mode, whether it’s called Incognito, InPrivate, or something else, eliminates other factors that contribute to the fingerprint.
