item.title: SpaceX Petitions FCC to Block Viasat Satellite Over Starlink Interference Risk
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.21
As Viasat prepares to offer faster internet speeds with a new satellite, SpaceX is trying to block it over concerns that it’ll cause "severe interference" to Starlink. In a Friday petition, SpaceX urged the Federal Communications Commission to reconsider its decision to green-light US market access to the Viasat-3 F2 satellite, which is scheduled to enter service next month. “Viasat’s utter disregard for Commission rules, its license conditions, and the harm it is causing to millions of American consumers has gone on for far too long,” it claims. According to the petition, Viasat has failed to reach a coordination agreement with SpaceX to prevent radio interference between Starlink and the F2 satellite. “Despite having over half a decade to complete the coordination required under its license conditions, Viasat continues to operate in the NGSO [non-geostationary satellite orbit] Ka-bands without making any meaningful attempt to coordinate,” SpaceX’s VP of satellite policy, David Goldman, wrote in the 25-page document. The petition goes on to claim the F2 satellite “will cause downlink interference to American consumers.” The issue concerns a slice of the radio spectrum, the 18.8 to 19.3GHz and 28.6 to 29.1GHz bands, which Starlink has long been cleared to use for space-to-Earth and Earth-to-space transmissions for its satellite internet service. However, Viasat plans to use the spectrum for downloading and uploading data on the F2, a high-orbiting geostationary satellite over 22,000 miles away. In late July, the FCC cleared the F2 satellite for US market access, but on the condition that Viasat reach a coordination agreement with other low-Earth-orbiting satellite providers, such as SpaceX, to prevent harmful radio interference with their systems. In his letter, Goldman noted: “Viasat’s license conditions prohibit it from operating its legacy technology in spectrum bands that are designated as primary for next-generation satellite systems, unless and until it secures a coordination agreement from each next-generation satellite operator in the bands or can provide a technical demonstration to the Commission.” However, Goldman claims that Viasat’s own analysis shows that the F2 threatens to cause interference “approximately one-third of the time” for Starlink when using the 18.8 to 19.3GHz bands for downlink. “The reality is that despite SpaceX’s good faith efforts, Viasat has failed—and even refused—to coordinate with SpaceX for years,” he added. “Viasat is not coordinating with SpaceX today, and has demonstrated no intention of doing so in the future.” California-based Viasat didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. But the F2 promises to deliver speeds of 100+ Mbps for customers in the Americas, even as the company has been losing customers to the high-speed Starlink service. SpaceX isn’t alone in issuing the complaints. Amazon, which is preparing to launch its own Leo satellite internet service, has also repeatedly flagged the coordination issues to the FCC. “As Amazon has explained in prior filings, the technical analysis proffered by Viasat in connection with its still-pending application falls far short of demonstrating that it will protect the Amazon Leo system or the other NGSO FSS operations in the NGSO Primary Bands,” the company wrote back in November. In 2020, Leo’s first-generation satellite constellation was also cleared to use the same 18.8 to 19.3GHz and 28.6 to 29.1GHz bands for its operations. Hence, the complaints from both Amazon and SpaceX might derail the F2 satellite. The FCC's own grant for F2's US market access notes: "Viasat must refrain from commencing, or otherwise cease, operations in the United States in the 18.8-19.3 GHz and 28.6-29.1 GHz frequency bands pursuant to this grant of market access until compliance is notified." About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: I Built My Own Free 'Netflix' to Escape Endless Streaming Price Hikes. You Can, Too
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.16
Remember when streaming used to be a much more affordable alternative to cable? Now it seems that every month, another major streaming service announces a new price hike. In just the last few days, Peacock, ESPN, and Apple TV have all raised their streaming prices. Licensing issues also make it tricky to track which platform is streaming your favorite media. If you're hoping to effectively navigate our increasingly digital-only landscape, there's a solution that big tech doesn't want you to know about. Owning your own media reduces the risk of losing access to your favorites when they jump from one service to another. But that doesn't mean you need to make room for physical Blu-rays or DVDs. If you still prefer the convenience of streaming over physical media, like I do, building and maintaining a home media library with Plex lets you set up a server to stream your movies and shows. Compared with alternatives like Jellyfin, I found Plex to be one of the easiest options to set up. You’ll just need a computer or NAS with solid processing power, several terabytes of storage, and a good internet connection. Here's how I did it. Select Your Hardware To set up a Plex server, you'll first need the physical server. The specifics of the form factor don’t matter as long as the hardware meets Plex's requirements. Technically, you can get a server running on a PC, MacBook, mini PC, Linux device, Nvidia Shield, and even Netgear Nighthawk X10 router, so it’s not like the requirements are daunting. At a minimum, you’ll want an Intel Core i3 processor, at least 4GB of RAM, and Windows 10 or newer or macOS 10.13 High Sierra or newer. For storage, I would generally recommend securing several terabytes of storage—maybe 2TB, at a minimum—if you plan on streaming a lot of 4K HDR content. However, the RAM crisis will likely make it difficult to track down enough memory at an affordable rate. Unless you have something lying around at home, you might just need to settle for less overall storage for now while leaving room for adding more in the future. In my case, I set up Plex on my desktop PC. Just keep in mind that if there are other users streaming your content, you’ll need to leave the PC on and connected to the internet at all times. This can be set up from the power settings menu. It’s also worth noting that when one person starts streaming 4K content, it can impact the performance of your online games if they're running simultaneously, so do some work to manage your bandwidth. If you dislike the idea of keeping your computer on at all times, another option is to get a Network-Attached Storage (NAS) device. Unlike a PC, which may need to be restarted or powered down periodically, these low-power network storage devices can be left running indefinitely. They're ideal if you want to share content with many users in different locations and time zones. Plus, it’ll prevent shared users from impacting your gaming performance. Keep in mind, however, that this can get expensive, since most NAS devices can cost several hundred dollars and still don't include the storage drives. If you're ready to do some tinkering, a Raspberry Pi makes a great makeshift NAS device, which is a cheaper way to test the concept as a file-sharing device before spending big. More PCMag-Recommended NAS Devices Install Plex Media Server Once you've chosen the physical server, you'll need to set up the software that goes with it. First, create a free Plex account to manage and share your content library. Next, install the Plex Media Server software from the company's website. It can be downloaded for Windows, macOS, Linux, and FreeBSD, as well as NAS devices from Synology, Seagate, Netgear, TerraMaster, and others. The Plex Media Server is just background software and doesn't have a graphical user interface, but it does need to be running to support content streaming. Instead, you'll access the media library and watch content through the Plex app. This can either be the plex.tv website or the desktop and smart TV app for your device of choice. Set Up Your Libraries Once the Plex app has launched, you should see a home page that will show the various Plex services and collections available. To get your libraries set up, you’ll need to create a file system and direct Plex to it, but it’s all reasonably straightforward. By default, you’ll see Home, Live TV, Movies & Shows, Discover, Watchlist, Music, Rentals, and Downloads. Any libraries created and added will appear at the bottom, but you can also pin them for easier access. To make a library, click Settings and select the correct Plex Media Server if you have servers running on more than one device; in my case, it’s my PC. Scroll down to the Manage section and click Libraries > Add Library. This should open a selection window where you can pick the library type, including Movies, TV Shows, Music, Photos, and Other Videos. Name the library, select the language, and click Next. Now, hit Browse for Media Folders and direct Plex to the location of the media files. You can also enter the path manually if that’s easier. Files can be placed in any folder, but Plex recommends against having it in a root drive like C:/ since it can cause problems. In my case, I let my libraries live in the Downloads folder for easy access, and I created two subfolders to store my content: Movies and TV Shows Whenever you need to add new content to the server, just move it into the relevant folder and navigate to Libraries > Scan Library Files to make it populate on the media player. You can also do this easily from the home page by clicking the three-dot menu next to the collection and hitting Scan Library Files. If you want Plex to do this automatically, enable Scan my library automatically under Settings > Library. You can also enable a specific interval of time for the scan to occur, ranging from hourly or daily to as frequently as every 15 minutes. The best thing about Plex, in my opinion, is that it also automatically pulls the metadata for all your TV shows and movies, providing descriptions, posters, subtitle and language options, and even audience scores. Share Content With Friends and Family Once you set up the libraries, you can share content with others. Before continuing, I recommend having the person you’re trying to share with also create a Plex account. To start sharing content, open Settings and scroll down to Manage Library Access under your account name. Click the Grant Library Access button and enter the person's Plex username or email. Select the libraries to which you want to grant them access, then hit Continue and start sharing. As the administrator, you can restrict what Libraries are shared with guests, which is handy for any private content you’d rather keep to yourself. To see where people are logging in from, go to the Settings > Authorized Devices page for an overview of every device accessing your Plex server and when it was last accessed. For any unfamiliar devices, click the red X to revoke access. Install and Configure Plex on Multiple Devices The Plex app is supported on a wide range of devices, including TVs, phones, tablets, smart home devices like those from Amazon and Sonos, streaming devices, gaming consoles, and desktops. Installing the Plex app on these devices will make it easy to access your libraries directly on the device, as long as the media server is running. Plex has its own premium options that hide some features behind a paywall. If you want to stream media from any device, in any location, you'll need a Remote Watch Pass ($2.99 per month). To download content for offline viewing, you'll need Plex Pass ($6.99 per month). It comes with some nice quality-of-life features, but I don't think it's necessary for most users. About Our Expert Ajay has worked in tech journalism for more than a decade as a reporter, analyst, and editor. He got his start in consumer tech reviewing hundreds of smartphones and tablets at PCMag as a Mobile Analyst, and breaking the hottest Android news at Newsweek as a tech reporter. In his most recent role, he’s worked in content marketing for a B2B SaaS company and in a PR capacity at an AI startup. Previously, he was Managing Commerce Editor at Android Police and Section Editor, Mobile at Digital Trends, where he spearheaded his team's coverage of breaking news, features, reviews, roundups, deals and more. He also worked at Lifewire as a Tech Commerce Editor, putting together tested best-of lists and assigning product reviews. As an avid tech enthusiast and traveler, Ajay loves tinkering with the gaming PC he built, adding new smart home devices to his apartment, and scoping out ancient ruins in new countries.

item.title: Alienware 39 5K OLED (AW3926QW) Review: Next-Gen Panel Tech Takes the Crown for Ultrawides
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.89
Just like the soon-to-be-reviewed LG UltraGear evo GX9, the Alienware 39 5K OLED Gaming Monitor (AW3926QW) is a 39-inch ultrawide curved "5K2K" (5,120-by-2,160-pixel) gaming monitor with a cutting-edge QD-OLED panel. On paper, these two monitors are matched in almost every category, from their dual-mode options to their DisplayHDR True Black 500 certifications. But Alienware’s latest is different from LG’s in two major ways. It lacks built-in AI upscaling, and it's $1,099.99, still expensive but a whopping $700 less than the GX9. So, with a striking color range and a gamer-first feature set, the Alienware AW3926QW easily earns our Editors' Choice nod for ultrawide gaming monitors. Unlike the Alienware 34 280Hz QD-OLED (AW3426DW), the AW3926QW doesn’t use a Penta Tandem OLED but rather an RGB Stripe Tandem OLED panel. According to Alienware, this makes the monitor the world's first 39-inch 5K2K display using that tech. That's an important, if esoteric, distinction, as Asus already claimed the first RGB OLED gaming monitor (the ROG Swift PG34WCDN), and LG called dibs on the world’s first 39-inch 5K2K OLED gaming monitor with the GX9. Here’s where things get even more confusing. RGB Stripe Tandem OLED is not the same as the fourth-generation Primary RGB Tandem OLED the GX9 uses (though LG manufactures both panels). Primary RGB Tandem OLED stacks four emissive layers on top of each other, but despite the "primary" in its name, the panel still retains an extra white subpixel layer, resulting in a red/green/white/blue layout. Previous generations placed the white sub-pixel second, resulting in a red/white/green/blue layout. RGB Stripe Tandem, on the other hand, stacks four emissive layers behind an RGB-stripe subpixel arrangement of red/blue/green/blue, delivering what LG says are notable improvements in brightness and color. LG splits the two panels into different use cases: Primary RGB Tandem stripe is focused on HDR gaming, emphasizing higher peak brightness, while RGB Stripe Tandem focuses on higher color luminance and readability for mixed use. Despite the differences among Primary RGB Tandem OLED, RGB Stripe Tandem, and Penta Tandem, they share the same key specs, including a maximum HDR brightness of 1,300 nits, a maximum SDR brightness of 300 nits, and DisplayHDR True Black 500 certification. New QD-OLED panel tech aside, the Alienware AW3926QW will sound familiar to anyone in the market for an ultrawide gaming monitor, and as I said up top, it's mostly the same as the GX9. That includes its 1500R curvature—1,500mm representing the radius of a circle formed by a hypothetical ring of these monitors, placed edge to edge. The big, beautiful screen doesn’t skimp on pixel density. Higher pixel density tends to improve image quality, but it’s especially useful for text-heavy documents and writing. While it’s not as dense as the 166 pixels per inch (ppi) of the Alienware 27 4K QD-OLED (AW2725Q), the Alienware AW3926QW is rated at 143ppi, higher than other Alienware monitors we’ve reviewed, including the Alienware AW2725DF (111ppi) and the Alienware AW3225QF (140ppi). It also matches the GX9’s 143ppi. Moving on to the monitor's back side, you’ll find the Alienware wrapped in a deep blue color, despite the color scheme being called "Nova Black." Familiar Alienware iconography frames the monitor’s stand, offering a hint of style on an otherwise clean, almost plain, design. This is the same design language that Alienware has used for a while now. The stand, which is much slimmer than the large slab that holds the GX9, sits on a small, square base. Taking a ruler to the monitor, you’ll find it measures 22.8 by 36.2 by 9.6 inches (HWD) when the stand's fully extended. Compressed, 22.8 becomes 18.5 inches. On the scale, the monitor weighs 22.6 pounds. It’s slightly lighter than its competitor, but the GX9's stand compresses and extends further. The port hub is tucked into the monitor’s backside. It contains two HDMI 2.1 ports, a DisplayPort 2.1 port, and USB Type-A, Type-B, and Type-C ports. The rear USB-C port also offers up to 90 watts of power delivery and supports DisplayPort 2.1 Alt Mode. Another pair of USB ports (Types A and C) is nestled at the front of the monitor. Both of these also provide power delivery, with the USB-C delivering 15 watts. You'll find a headphone jack here, as well. If you have a newer GPU, you can enjoy the DisplayPort 2.1 support. DisplayPort 2.1 doubles the bandwidth of DisplayPort 1.4 (80Gbps versus 32.4Gbps), enabling higher resolutions and refresh rates without compression. Up until this point, the Alienware AW3926QW has gone blow to blow with the LG UltraGear evo GX9 in its features and specs, but here’s where things start to diverge. First off, the AW3926QW has no internal speakers, though the HDMI 2.1 with eARC and the headphone jack do offer options for external speakers or soundbars. The GX9 not only has speakers but also uses AI to separate individual audio elements, creating a more controlled, immersive sound profile. (At least, that's what LG claims.) Perhaps the biggest difference between the AW3926QW and the GX9 is that the LG has a built-in processor that claims to use AI upscaling to enhance content to fit the display’s 5K2K resolution. The AW3926QW doesn't have any AI-upscaling capabilities; instead, it offers what Alienware calls a "personalized algorithm": machine-learning technology integrated into the panel that's supposed to optimize image quality, increase brightness, and extend the monitor's lifespan by predicting OLED degradation. While the term "AI" isn't used in any marketing materials, as far as I can tell, this concept is similar to the AI features on monitors like the MSI MPG 271QR QD-OLED X50. They’re subtle and automatic, but it's hard to really say whether they make a meaningful difference or not. Perhaps the best I can say is that they don’t really get in the way of the monitor’s other features. The Alienware AW3926QW offers two refresh rate/resolution combinations. One is the screen's full 5K2K resolution at 165Hz, while the other is 330Hz at "WFHD" (2,560 by 1,080 pixels). The two configurations are meant to cater to all types of gamers and genres. If you’re playing a slower, big-budget AAA release, the full-fat resolution at 165Hz is for you, while multiplayer shooters will thrive at the higher 330Hz refresh rate. One feature that might attract hard-core gamers is the built-in esports mode, which lets players reshape the display area into smaller, faster chunks tuned for competitive play. For example, you can configure the monitor to display a 24.5-inch or 27-inch 16:9 picture at 330Hz. You can then move this display area to the top, bottom, or center of the screen, with the rest of the panel masked off. While some might scoff at the idea of shrinking the display area of a giant ultrawide monitor, esports gamers will often trade resolution for faster performance, so this mode guarantees them the best of both worlds. Like other Alienware monitors, the AW3926QW supports Dolby Vision, a mode that optimizes brightness, contrast, and color saturation for supported content. The monitor also supports AMD FreeSync Premium Pro and VESA AdaptiveSync, and it's Nvidia G-Sync Compatible. I tested the AW3926QW with our standard benchmarks using Portrait Displays' Calman calibration software and a Klein K-10A colorimeter. I also ran it through a gauntlet of games to measure input lag and judge its real-world performance. I took these readings with out-of-the-box settings, unless otherwise noted. In the first test, I benchmarked the display brightness using the out-of-the-box SDR profile. Under these conditions, I measured a maximum brightness of 304 nits with a 10% window size, which is right on target for the monitor’s rated brightness of 300 nits. Moving on to HDR, the monitor promises a peak HDR brightness of 1,300 nits at a 3% average picture level (APL). Our peak HDR test is slightly different, using a 2% window size, but we registered 1,277 nits, which is right on target. The monitor also recorded 516 nits at a 10% window size, right in line with its VESA DisplayHDR True Black 500 rating. Finally, I tested the color gamut. My metering indicates that the AW3926QW covers 96.5% of the Adobe RGB color space (see the chart above), 131.76% of the sRGB color space, and 98.9% of the DCI-P3 color space (see the chart below). The squares in the charts represent target color reference points, and the circles represent the actual measured color. These are top-notch results overall, and the panel exceeds 100% sRGB as many OLED monitors do. While the wider sRGB coverage can produce richer colors, especially with HDR content, it can also sometimes lead to an overblown image. The AW3926QW is rated for a dynamic contrast ratio of 1,750,000:1, slightly below the LG GX9 but higher than other recent OLED monitors, including the Alienware AW3426DW and the Asus ROG PG34WCDN. The differences don't really matter, though. Any contrast ratio in the millions indicates the display's ability to produce deep blacks alongside bright whites, resulting in stellar image quality in both light and dark scenes. Gaming Performance Moving on to game testing, I used the Leo Bodnar 4K Input Lag Tester to measure the lag times across various combinations of refresh rate and resolution. Low input lag is critical for hard-core gaming and esports, but you can benefit from it even if you're a casual gamer. For the most part, we consider 16 milliseconds (ms) to be totally acceptable for single-player experiences. I started my input-lag tests at full HD (1080p). At 1080p/60Hz, I recorded 13.6ms of input lag, and 4.5ms at 1080p/120Hz. At 1080p/240Hz, the measurement was 7.4ms. At QHD (1440p) resolution, the monitor recorded 10ms of input lag at 60Hz; at 4K, it recorded 19.7ms. For some reason, the Bodnar would not properly read lag 120Hz at 1440p, likely due to a limitation with the device rather than the monitor. (The Bodnar also can't measure above 240Hz at 1080p.) That's some noticeable input lag at 4K, but for the most part, the results are acceptable. My tested games include the usual suspects, including Marvel Rivals, Doom: The Dark Ages, and Cyberpunk 2077. It’s important to have a high-end GPU that can run these games at native resolution if you want to make the most of this monitor. The games looked gorgeous, and the HDR implementation was fantastic as well. I didn’t even have to adjust any settings to get the picture looking striking. Also, I didn’t see any noticeable edge bleeding, an issue that has plagued older ultrawide Alienware monitors. Final Thoughts Alienware 39 5K OLED (AW3926QW) - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. I wasn't expecting to love the Alienware 39 5K OLED Gaming Monitor (AW3926QW) as much as I do. As it stands now, it's probably my favorite ultrawide monitor. It earns top marks for its impressive color range, high brightness, extensive port hub, and rock-solid gaming performance. What seals the deal for me is that the monitor does all of this while undercutting its main competition by hundreds of dollars. I'd gladly give up internal speakers and AI upscaling for that. So if you're looking for a large ultrawide OLED monitor, the AW3926QW is the screen to beat, and it earns our Editors' Choice award. About Our Expert I’m a PCMag reviewer and ISF-certified TV calibrator focused on computer accessories, laptops, gaming monitors, and video games. I’ve been writing, playing, and complaining about games for as long as I remember, but it wasn’t until recently that I’ve been able to shout my opinions directly at a larger audience. My work has appeared on iMore, Windows Central, Android Central, and TWICE, and I have a diverse portfolio of editing work under my belt from my time spent at Scholastic and Oxford University Press. I also have a few book-author credits under my belt—I’ve contributed to the sci-fi anthology Under New Suns, and I’ve even written a Peppa Pig book.

item.title: How One Compromised Account Endangers Your Entire Household—and How to Fix It
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.56
Modern cyber threats no longer target single devices; they now target entire digital lives. A single compromised account, whether it be your teenager's gaming profile or an older relative's email, can trigger a domino effect that leaves your entire household's identity, privacy, and finances exposed. Today's risks extend far beyond traditional computer viruses. They now include sophisticated, AI-driven scams, identity theft, and account takeovers that spread across the messaging apps, social platforms, and online accounts your family uses every day. Standalone antivirus software may no longer be enough; to fully secure a modern household, you'll need to go from protecting single screens to safeguarding your family's collective digital footprint. Bitdefender protects people, not just hardware. The company's family plans combine industry-leading cybersecurity defense with advanced AI to secure your identity, privacy, and devices, stopping multi-channel threats before they ever reach you or your loved ones. Here's how an all-in-one security suite can keep your busy family safe from scammers, cybercriminals, and online threats. Expanding From Single-Device to Family-Wide Protection Standalone antivirus software is effective at neutralizing direct malware attacks on one specific desktop or laptop. But for many of us, our digital lives are now strewn across multiple devices. It's not farfetched for a present-day household to have dozens of devices under one roof, interconnected across multiple users and various operating systems. With this comes exposure to many types of risks. Sure, securing the laptop your teenager uses for gaming is a good first step. But if a scammer steals credentials from an online account, those compromised details can be used to target a parent's assets from a completely different device. This is where digital safety solutions like Bitdefender add a vital layer of household security. Operating at both the network and device levels, Bitdefender family plans identify and block lateral movement attempts before they can reach a second device. By pairing core device protection with real-time scanning across every connected endpoint, this comprehensive approach shifts the question from "Is this one device safe?" to "Is there any suspicious activity threatening this network or its users?" It is a practical, scalable way to defend a modern household where everyone shares the same connection. Comparing Bitdefender's Family Tiers Bridging the Security Generation Gap Today's scammers are targeting both older and younger generations, albeit in different ways. - Seniors: Older generations are frequently targeted by urgent phishing and social engineering campaigns impersonating banks, shipping companies, or government agencies - Teens: Younger users are often heavy downloaders, active on platforms where drive-by downloads, third-party app stores, and malicious game mods are common Relying on everyone in the household to make the right security decision 100% of the time is unrealistic. And no one wants to be interrupted constantly by security notifications all day, every day. The smart solution is automated, silent protection like automated web filtering, anti-phishing safeguards, and non-intrusive parental controls that run in the background, blocking malicious URLs before a webpage can load. For busy parents, having a cybersecurity solution that delivers digital life protection for the whole family (and doesn't require a lot of manual oversight) is key. It's why this solution is referred to as an all-in-one security suite. And for decision-makers whose households juggle Windows, macOS, iOS, and/or Android all under one roof, Bitdefender's Family Plans consolidate this overhead into a centralized dashboard that shows the security status of every device under a single management layer, letting you push updates and resolve alerts remotely. Closing the Loop on Household Security Family cybersecurity has evolved out of necessity. It is no longer just about protecting isolated devices; it is about providing digital safety built around you and your family, protecting your identity and privacy while securing your entire home network ecosystem. While individual software is excellent for single endpoints, a shared household benefits from a unified, cross-platform defense. By upgrading to a comprehensive solution like Bitdefender—which PCMag editors chose as both the best security suite and best option for families—you safeguard your entire household from modern threats while also eliminating the friction of managing home IT (a job you were perhaps promoted to, but didn't want in the first place). To secure comprehensive, automated protection for every device under your roof, explore the multi-platform safeguards included in Bitdefender Family Plans. Can a hacker access my work laptop if my child's gaming account is breached? Yes. If both devices share the same local home Wi-Fi network, sophisticated malware can pivot from a compromised personal device to scan for vulnerabilities on other connected computers, including remote-work laptops. Why is individual antivirus software no longer enough for a family? Individual software only protects the specific device it is installed on, leaving blind spots. Modern household security requires a unified system that monitors cross-platform traffic and stops threats before they interact with other family members. How can I protect older relatives from sophisticated phishing scams without having to manage their devices daily? The most effective approach is utilizing security software with centralized management and automated web filtering. This blocks malicious links and fraudulent sites before a user can click on them, operating silently without requiring manual intervention. Do family security plans slow down devices or interrupt gaming? Robust digital security solutions utilize optimized, cloud-based scanning architectures designed to run quietly in the background, ensuring comprehensive defense without compromising device performance or latency. Can I manage security settings for multiple devices from a single dashboard? Yes. Centralized management consoles allow a single user to view the protection status, run updates, and resolve alerts for every smartphone, tablet, and desktop in the household from one interface.

item.title: Silver Palace Is a Compelling Palate Cleanser for Stale Gacha Game Tropes
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.47
Gacha games far too often fall into the same narrative and gameplay tropes. You choose a gender, input a name, and wake up with amnesia. No matter how good the story, the titles almost universally suffer from glacially slow starts. Silver Palace (coming to Android, iOS, PC, and PS5) is the first free-to-play action-RPG I've played in years that not only avoids these pitfalls but actively subverts the Genshin Impact-established trends that have dominated the industry. After spending extensive time with Silver Palace during a recent PC closed beta test, I appreciate that this upcoming title breaks from the norm to deliver the genre's next major shakeup. Story: Finally, a Gacha Protagonist With a Personality Instead of focusing on a blank-slate main character, Silver Palace let me play as an established detective who works alongside their sibling. Following the sibling's death, the protagonist returns to the sprawling city of Silvernia to investigate a new lead on the disaster. Alongside this overarching narrative, I was tasked with solving smaller, self-contained cases that served up narrative twists that kept me genuinely engaged. The protagonist is highly vocal, frequently engaging in quips and banter. Its distinct personality and personal histories with the supporting cast add a refreshing, lived-in feel to the world. The scene direction and pacing also impressed me, with none of that awkward dead air that pops up all too often in gacha games. If anything, the auto-playing dialogue functions a bit too fast, occasionally cutting off lines before the excellent voice talent can finish their deliveries. Because the beta lacked manual dialogue progression or a playback log, this fast pacing proved slightly frustrating, given how much I enjoyed the fantasy-London writing. Graphics: Stunning Visuals That Will Melt Your Rig (and Phone) Visually, Silver Palace is gorgeous. Built on Unreal Engine 5, it adopts a painterly anime style reminiscent of Tales of Arise, trading the bright, cel-shaded looks of Zenless Zone Zero or Wuthering Waves for darker tones and a gritty, industrial, Gothic Victorian aesthetic. The playable character models and even roaming NPCs feature incredible outfit details. Beautiful animations and unique menu flourishes enhance the visual impact; it oozes quality. However, this beauty comes at a high technical cost—it demands a lot from your hardware. During my hands-on time with Silver Palace at AnimeNYC and throughout the recent beta, the action-RPG suffered frequent frame drops and occasional crashes. My test rig (outfitted with an AMD Ryzen 5 3600 CPU, Nvidia GeForce RTX 2080 GPU, and 16GB of RAM) handles other modern gacha titles just fine, but struggles a bit with this one. Optimization will be critical for Silver Studio ahead of its launch. Silver Palace's presentation is enhanced by a low, off-center, third-person camera perspective. This framing made the monsters and bosses I fought feel appropriately massive, and put the gorgeous setting front and center. It introduces a God of War-style camera problem in which enemies can easily attack from off-screen, but a built-in attack indicator system mitigates it. Thanks to tight, defensive controls, I rarely took unexpected hits. Gameplay: Cool Navigation, NPC Profiling, and Combat Developer Silver Studio wisely replaces the genre's overdone free-climbing mechanics with a metallic pegasus mount used for vertical exploration. Although an Assassin's Creed-style parkour system would do wonders for the game's movement given the setting, the protagonist's magical steed was a joy to ride. It let me seamlessly soar to rooftops, collect skybound treasure chests, and race across the massive map. Even with the beta restricted to a single borough, Silvernia felt incredibly expansive, leaving me with high hopes for the final build's full world map. The city feels further fleshed out by a Watch Dogs-style profiling system. Looking at passing citizens reveals flavor text about their professions and backgrounds. More importantly, I used this mechanic to expose hidden monsters disguised as citizens, such as werewolves, harpies, and the undead. The mini-map flashes red to indicate that a monster is nearby, so you can profile nearby NPCs for anomalies like bloodstains, deformities, or ill-fitting clothes to initiate combat. It's an excellent loop that I wish were expanded beyond basic daily rewards. I want these stealth enemies to be more proactive about stalking or jumping me. It would be cool if the enemies slowly honed in on you during your session or initiated an ambush while you're distracted. One other immersion breaker is the city transit system. Gorgeous cars, trolleys, and suspended monorails move throughout the streets, but you cannot enter them. One thing I really liked about Neverness to Everness (a supernatural RPG) is that you could get on and ride the city transit (buses and trains), even if there were faster alternatives. I genuinely hope the dev team adds this to Silver Palace, if only just to vibe. Combat was a highlight for me and an absolute departure from genre norms. Rather than relying on restrictive skill cooldowns to string combos together, Silver Palace plays closer to Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice or Stellar Blade. Defensive play is core to the action. I used a dedicated parry button to deflect incoming melee strikes and a dodge button to avoid unblockable area-of-effect attacks. Deflecting attacks steadily depletes a posture meter underneath the enemy's health bar. Once broken, the enemy is stunned and vulnerable to a powerful, unique finisher attack. Every playable character features a light melee attack, a heavy attack, and a specialized ranged ability tied to their own independent resource meter, keeping combat fluid and unrestricted. Final Beta Thoughts and Release Date Silver Palace stands out as a bold, mechanically dense reimagining of what a modern gacha game can be. It proves that the genre needn't rely on copy-pasted mechanics or predictable narrative setups. If developer Silver Studio can eliminate the performance hurdles and fine-tune the dialogue pacing before launch (there's no date or window listed yet), this won't be just another gatcha game on your Android, iPhone, PC, or PS5—it will be a wake-up call to the entire industry. About Our Expert In 2014, I began my career at PCMag as a freelancer. That blossomed into a full-time position in 2021, and I now review email marketing apps, mobile operating systems, web hosting services, streaming music platforms, and video games as a senior writer. I'm a graduate of Hunter College, a hard-core gamer, and an Apple enthusiast.

item.title: Windows 11 just revived one of its most missed features
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.96
Microsoft just released optional update KB5120998 for Windows 11 24H2 and 25H2. On top of numerous minor improvements, it introduces a few big changes that’ll be noticeable in day-to-day use. Free positioning of the taskbar The most noticeable change in this update involves the taskbar. You can now choose whether it sits at the bottom, top, left, or right side of the screen. This marks the return of a feature that was present in earlier versions of Windows but was taken out of Windows 11 at launch. You can find this setting under Settings → Personalization → Taskbar → Taskbar behavior → Taskbar position. Microsoft is also introducing a smaller taskbar in this update. In “Small” mode, the icons and height of the taskbar are reduced, freeing up more space on smaller screens. However, this compact version can only sit at the top of bottom of the screen. More Start menu options The Start menu has gotten some new customization options in this update. The “Recommended” section has been renamed “Recently used,” and you can also hide your name and profile picture in the Start menu. Separate toggles allow you to show or hide the sections for pinned apps, recommended content, and all apps independently of one another. In the future, you’ll be able to choose between small and large layouts, and you’ll be able to use the automatic resize feature. Search and File Explorer improvements Microsoft has revamped Windows Search. The search interface is clearer and will, in the future, indicate more clearly whether a result comes from an app, Settings, a local file, the web, or the Microsoft Store. If you don’t wish to see web or Store results alongside local results, you can disable these suggestions in the privacy and search settings. Windows can also automatically index frequently used folders for future searches. In File Explorer, the home page is set to respond more quickly. The section with recommended files now also supports touch scrolling. New security and AI features With Administrator Protection, Microsoft is introducing a feature designed to better secure administrator rights. Administrative tasks can now be carried out using time-limited permissions. The feature is disabled by default and is designed for corporate environments. The update also prepares Windows for the use of AI agents. The new Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) can isolate processes such as coding agents and restrict their access to files, the network, and other system resources via policies. In addition, Windows will soon support the post-quantum cryptography algorithm ML-KEM as a standalone option for TLS key exchange. Other changes in this update Update KB5120998 also improves: switching between virtual desktops, display and brightness settings, the Task Manager, and various features relating to Windows Update. The Windows Setup process and the “Get Started” app have also been revamped. Another change concerns WMIC. The command-line tool for Windows Management Instrumentation will no longer be available in Windows 11 24H2 and 25H2. The underlying Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), however, will remain in place. The update also includes various bug fixes in areas like text-to-speech, Japanese text input, Outlook, and touchpad issues. Microsoft is currently not aware of any known issues with the update. Not all features available immediately Update KB5120998 is an optional preview update. That means you have to install it manually if you want to take advantage of what it offers. However, early adoption of preview updates is risky—some users are reporting cursor and wallpaper issues with this update, so you should weigh the risks before jumping in. The cause of those issues is still unknown. Also note that Microsoft likes to gradually roll out its features, so even if you install the optional update, you may not have immediate access to all of the improvements. You may have to wait a week or longer before certain features are enabled on your system. If you still want to install this update, you can do so by navigating to Settings → Windows Update → Advanced options → Optional updates → KB5120998.

item.title: Google Notebook is making big changes to usage limits
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.55
Fans of Google Notebook’s AI-generated podcasts may have to settle for fewer of them once a new usage-tracking method goes into effect next week. Starting September 2, Google Notebook will switch over to “compute-specific” usage limits that track the “complexity” of your Google Notebook prompts and requests. Also coming with the “compute-specific” usage limits change are five-hour usage windows, along with weekly usage limits, according to a Google support page, replacing the current daily and monthly limits. Up until now, Google Notebook users got flat daily limits on the number of chats, audio overviews (the famous AI-generated podcasts that Google Notebooks is best known for), and video overviews they could request, with each of those features (along with reports, flashcards, quizzes, and “mind maps,” among others) getting their own bucket of daily limits. Under the current system, the number of Google Notebook requests you get per day varies depending on your Google AI plan, with free users getting (for example) 50 chats and three audio overviews per day, while Google AI Ultra users have a daily allowance of up to 5,000 chats and 200 audio overviews. But once the new compute-based limits kick in, those flat limits will go away, and instead your overall Google Notebook usage will be calculated based on “the complexity of your prompt, the models and features you use, the length of your chat and specific features.” Free Google AI users will get unspecified “standard” limits, while paid users will be allowed more usage depending on their subscription tier. If you exceed your five-hour usage allotment, you’ll have to wait until the next five-hour window opens, similar to usage limits for ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. There will also be a weekly Google Notebook usage limit, which will replace the current monthly limit. In a blog post announcing the changes, Google Notebook Product Manager Yesul Shin wrote that the new compute-based usage limits will give users “more control over your workflow,” adding that users will get warnings if they’re approaching their usage limits. For example, users who see their Google Notebook levels limits are almost up could choose to “defer” creating podcast-like audio overviews or “cinematic” video overviews, Shin noted. The impending Google Notebook change is yet another example of AI providers clamping down on usage limits for subscription users, particularly when it comes to agentic features that can quickly burn through AI tokens. Back in April, GitHub Copilot was among the first AI services to switch to a usage-based plan, moving away from allowing a set number of AI requests regardless of their complexity.

item.title: Best Chromebooks 2026: Top picks for work, school, and more
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.81
If you want a fast, low-maintenance machine that mostly lives in the browser, few options are as compelling as a Chromebook. Chromebooks don’t try to do everything, which is exactly why they’re so appealing. For this roundup, we focused on models that stay fast under real use and makes it through a full day unplugged. Every pick here was tested hands-on. At a glance | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | If you’d rather step outside Google’s ecosystem, PCWorld has a separate roundup of the best Windows laptops. And if you’re curious where Chromebooks are headed next, check out this deep dive into the new AI-powered Googlebooks. Why you should trust us: It’s in our name! PCWorld prides itself on laptop experience and expertise. We’ve been covering PCs since 1983, and we now review more than 70 laptops every year. All of the picks below have been personally tested and vetted by our experts, who’ve applied not only performance benchmarks but rigorous usability standards. We’re also committed to reviewing PC laptops at every price point to help you find a machine that matches your budget. Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 – Best overall Chromebook Pros - Zippy processor performance - Nice keyboard - Wide array of connectivity options - Chic design Cons - Battery life isn’t competitive - Display’s 16:9 aspect ratio feels a little cramped Who should buy the Asus Chromebook Plus CX34? If you want a Chromebook that can do it all, the Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 is it. The Intel Core i5 keeps everything running smooth–streaming, school work, or juggling a bunch of tabs. And the ports? You’ve got USB-C, USB-A, HDMI, and a headphone jack, which means you can kiss the dongle life goodbye. Asus Chromebook Plus CX34: Further considerations It’s not all sunshine, though. The 16:9 screen can feel cramped if you’re used to roomier displays, and while 13 hours of battery life sounds nice on paper, others last longer. Not a deal breaker, but if screen space or all-day power is at the top of your list, you might want to look elsewhere. Read our full Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 review Asus Chromebook CX15 – Best budget Chromebook Pros - Good design with enjoyable keyboard - Sharp 15.6-inch 1080p display - Decent speakers - Extremely inexpensive Cons - Small touchpad - Slow dual-core processor - 4GB RAM often holds it back - Short battery life for a Chromebook Who should buy the Asus Chromebook CX15? Need a reliable laptop for under $200? The CX15 is totally worth a look because it’s great for anyone that mostly browses the web and watches YouTube videos. The spacious 15.6-inch 1080p display and roomy keyboard also make it feel more premium than you’d expect at this price point. For daily tasks, it really gets the job done–you can’t say that about too many machines in this range. Asus Chromebook CX15: Further considerations You’re not going to get blazing-fast performance here and that’s entirely okay. The Intel Celeron N4500 processor offers enough pep to get you through lighter workloads, but you may see some lag with heavier multitasking. Battery life is pretty darn good at around 10 hours, though we’ve seen other Chromebooks that last longer. Still, for what you pay, the CX15 is a surprising little machine. Read our full Asus Chromebook CX15 review Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14 – Best high-end Chromebook Pros - Lovely OLED display - Surprisingly strong performance for a fanless Chromebook - Loud, clear speakers - Competitive battery life Cons - Hard-to-read function keys - AI tools feel unnecessary in everyday use Who should buy the Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14? If you’ve been looking for a high-end Chromebook, the Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14 is totally worth your consideration—it’s a big step up from the usual budget fare. It’s got a 14-inch 1920×1200 OLED touchscreen and the colors really pop. The model we tested came loaded with 16GB of RAM and 256GB of UFS storage, so it handles a ton of tabs, Docs, YouTube, whatever you throw at it. And the MediaTek Kompanio Ultra 910 chip (plus a tiny Neural Processing Unit) makes everything feel snappy. The 2.78-pound aluminum chassis is also super light to carry around, and the battery will last you about 19 hours as long as you’re conservative with the brightness level. Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14: Further considerations The Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14 is almost the complete package, but we did have a couple of minor nitpicks. The function keys are really small and they pick up fingerprints like nobody’s business. But, again, those are tiny complaints. If you want a Chromebook that looks and feels nicer than the budget crowd, this is the one to pick. Read our full Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14 review Other notable Chromebooks we’ve tested - Acer Chromebook Plus 514: The Acer Chromebook Plus 514 isn’t the most attractive ChromeOS machine, but it offers good performance and lots of storage for the price. - Acer Chromebook Plus 516: The Acer Chromebook Plus 516 isn’t much to look at, but it benefits from an Intel Core i3 chip with solid performance and, at times, low sale pricing. - Acer Chromebook Spin 315: Comfy to type on and handles the basics just fine, though the big bezels and limited charging options hold it back (hence why it’s not on the above list). - Asus Chromebook Plus CX14: Performs better than models with Celeron CPUs. How we test Chromebooks The PCWorld team puts each and every laptop through a series of benchmarks that test GPU and CPU performance, battery life, and so on. The idea is to push the laptop to its limits and then compare it against others we’ve tested. Due to the cloud-based nature of Chromebooks, they go through a series of web-based tests. It wouldn’t be fair or possible to run the same kinds of tests on a Chromebook as we use on laptops because they exclusively run a completely different operating system. For a more thorough explanation of our testing procedures, check out how PCWorld tests laptops. Who curated this article? Hi, I’m Ashley Biancuzzo, and I oversee all laptop and Chromebook coverage at PCWorld. While you’ll see me review Chromebooks on occasion, I’m also really into the broader world of consumer tech. I spend a lot of time writing and thinking about where laptops are headed–from AI and sustainable designs to long-term trends. When I’m not deep in the world of tech, you’ll probably find me gaming, getting lost in a good book, or chilling with my rescue greyhound, Allen. How to choose the best Chromebook If you want something like a Windows or MacBook but cheaper, check out a Chromebook. Just keep in mind they’ve got some limits. They’re good for simple, everyday stuff but they don’t have a lot of RAM or storage, so they’re not equipped to handle more resource-intensive tasks like gaming or video editing. We’ve got a guide that compares Chromebooks and Windows laptops if you want to figure out what’s best for you. Key Chromebook features to consider Operating system Chromebooks only run Chrome OS, which is pretty easy to use. You can’t put Windows or macOS on them — you’re stuck with Google’s setup. Processor Shoot for a mid-range Chromebook if you can. They cost anywhere in the $400 to $600 range and many of them come equipped with Intel Pentium, Intel Core i3, or AMD Ryzen 3 processors. These Chromebooks run the browser smoother. They’re the best deal for the price. The fancier ones sometimes come with Intel Core i5 or AMD Ryzen 5 chips, which are way more powerful. Then there’s the new Kompanio Ultra chips, which are more powerful and AI-ready. RAM Lots of Chromebooks come with just 4GB of RAM, which isn’t much. Since they’re all about the web, you need enough RAM to keep your tabs from lagging. And with RAM prices being a bit more volatile lately, it’s worth opting for more if you can. If you can drop a bit more cash, you can grab a mid-range Chromebook with 8GB (or 16GB if you want to be extra safe), which runs way smoother. FAQ What is the best Chromebook? PCWorld thinks the Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 is the best all-around Chromebook. It’s got a solid Intel Core i5 processor, lots of ports, and handles everyday stuff really well. Basically, it’s a great pick if you want a reliable Chromebook without breaking the bank. What is the best cheap Chromebook? PCWorld’s pick for best budget Chromebook is the Asus Chromebook CX15. With a spacious 15.6-inch 1080p display and roomy keyboard, this Chromebook is comfortable to use and its Intel Celeron N4500 processor is able to handle daily tasks. If you’re after value, this Chromebook provides all the basics for less than $200. What’s the difference between a Chromebook and a laptop? A Chromebook’s just a laptop that runs Google’s Chrome OS instead of Windows or Mac. It’s mostly for web stuff like Google Drive and YouTube. Regular laptops are more powerful and can handle pretty much anything. What is a Chromebook? A Chromebook is a laptop that runs Google’s Chrome OS.

item.title: The peach emoji can actually make your Wi-Fi safer
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.62
In a past life there was a PCWorld print magazine, and I wrote a monthly column for it. The column was called “Privacy Watch” and it was all about tools and tips you could use to safeguard your PC against hackers and snoops. Every month I’d do my best to help readers with everything from building stronger passwords (or just adopting a good password manager) to securing their Wi-Fi network, and I had a blast doing it. I mention all this just so you understand that while I’m no infosec expert, I’ve been covering and writing about digital privacy and security for awhile now. Even so, I had no clue that a few emoji could be the key to making my Wi-Fi networks basically unhackable by anyone but the most cutting-edge bad guys. But that’s what I learned this week on The Full Nerd, thanks to recurring guest (and accomplished ethical hacker) Mike Danseglio (CEH & CISSP). Welcome to The Full Nerd newsletter—your weekly dose of hardware talk from the enthusiasts at PCWorld. Missed the surprising topics on our YouTube show or the latest news from across the web? You’re in the right place. Want this newsletter to come directly to your inbox? Sign up on our website! Mike has kindly agreed to join us a few times to talk PCs and security in the past, whether it was running down some of the worst ways to troubleshoot a PC last year (he also worked in tech support at Microsoft in the ’90s) or arguing the merits of using guest networks to safeguard your home Wi-Fi with our own resident security maven (and Safe Mode newsletter author) Alaina Yee. But this week, he dropped a banger of a Wi-Fi security tip that blew my mind in its simplicity. See, according to Mike, all modern methods of hacking Wi-Fi networks aren’t set up to recognize or use the emoji character set. So if you toss a few of your favorites into your Wi-Fi network name and password, odds seem extremely good that you just made it uncrackable—at least, until some bad guy figures this out and starts to build emoji support into password crackers. “You can use emoji in access point names and passwords,” said Danseglio. “Putting an emoji in your access point name and your password breaks all of the current tools that are available to hack Wi-Fi.” Of course, that assumes that every device you’re planning to connect to your network is able to read modern emoji and input them as well. If you have older hardware or devices with limited inputs (like some e-readers and printers, for example), putting a few 🍑 🤨 🚗 in your Wi-Fi network credentials could play havoc with your setup. But even if you can’t make practical use of this information, just understanding the ways in which programs work (or don’t work) on your PC can teach you so much about the inner workings of these tools and systems that we trust with so much of our lives. It’s one of the things I’ve always loved about getting into the hobby of building, modifying, and upgrading PCs: You end up learning a ton about the tech that basically runs the modern world around us, and that goes a long way towards making that world seem less alien and scary when things don’t work the way they should. In this week’s episode of The Full Nerd When infosec expert Mike Danseglio stopped by the show this week to chat with regular cohosts Adam Patrick Murray and Alaina Yee, he didn’t just focus on Wi-Fi security. They got into a wide-ranging discussion that touched on everything from kernel-level anti-cheat systems in games to what cool hacks came out of DEFCON 2026 this year. PCWorld And of course, they wrapped up by taking some of your questions from the chat and our TFN Discord! Nerd news of the week As much as I wish I could tell you that the biggest news of the week is prices dropping on memory and storage, the sad truth is we’re nowhere near there yet. But there’s still some cool stuff happening in the world of tech, as well as some wild stories about new humanoid robots and hidden scripts that are being used to create a unique fingerprint of your PC using silent audio. - Two architectures on one chip: Arm and IBM team up in a legendary crossover: IBM and Arm are teaming up to fabricate a new chip on a 2nm node that can run both IBM’s zOS and Arm-based Linux environments and software, no emulation required. But it’s unlikely we’ll get to test one anytime soon, as the chip is advertised for use in “enterprise environments” and large-scale organizations. - AliExpress allegedly uses your browser’s audio system to fingerprint your PC: If you’ve ever shopped at AliExpress, it’s possible the site was running scripts that generated audio you couldn’t hear that could be used to uniquely identify you and your PC. It’s a wild story, and a good reminder to be careful when browsing! - Lawsuit demands Logitech hand tariff refunds over to customers: If you’re feeling the pain of price hikes on PC gear, the news that some folks have filed an antitrust lawsuit against Logitech may bring you some schadenfreude. The complaint alleges Logitech raised prices to remain profitable in the face of “illegal tariffs,” and now that the company will be reimbursed by the federal government the plaintiffs would like to see some of that refund. - Unitree’s newest humanoid can reportedly beat Usain Bolt’s personal record: Chinese robotics company Unitree has built a humanoid robot that can run just over 28 miles per hour and jump over six feet high from a standstill. I, Robot, here we come! That’s your Full Nerd newsletter for this week. For more, be sure to bookmark PCWorld and subscribe to the PCWorld YouTube channel! Want this newsletter to come directly to your inbox? Sign up on our website! This newsletter is dedicated to the memory of Gordon Mah Ung, founder and host of The Full Nerd, and executive editor of hardware at PCWorld.

item.title: LG UltraGear Evo AI GM9 review: A fast and bright 5K mini-LED monitor
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.02
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros - 5K with upscaling capability - Vibrant and bright mini-LED - High refresh rate and fast response times - User-friendly interface Cons - Doesn’t beat a top-of-the-range OLED in every respect - The speakers could be better - Lacks a KVM function Our Verdict More brightness and dynamic range than the best OLED screens, a rich, expansive and accurate color palette, and dual mode offering a good refresh rate in 5K mode and an even higher refresh rate at 1440p. There’s a lot to like about this 5K screen, even if it isn’t the best at absolutely everything. Price at time of review This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Price Today Price When Reviewed $999 Best Prices Today: LG Ultragear Evo GM9 The UltraGear Evo AI GM9, model name 27GM950B-B, is a new and high-end desktop monitor from LG. It measures 27 inches and offers full adjustability in height, lateral movement, tilt, and pivot on a sturdy metal stand. The chassis is made of matte-black plastic, but it gives a solid, high-quality impression and is stylishly designed from both the front and the back. UltraGear is a gaming-focused brand, and there is the option to add some RGB LED lighting to the back of the monitor, but otherwise the design is understated. There is a definite focus on gaming in the settings menu, with quick-select options for two player profiles and various game genres as the first choices. The monitor is just as well suited to desk-based work and creative tasks as it is to gaming. You can also select pure sRGB and P3 profiles that maintain good color accuracy, and there are preset modes for blue-light-reduced reading, HDR-optimized media playback, and two additional profiles you can calibrate yourself. Read on to learn more, then see our roundup of the best monitors for comparison. Brighter than most It’s built on a display panel that’s as colorful as it is bright, and as high-resolution as it is fast. Using quantum-dot technology, the LCD layer delivers DCI-P3-class colors with factory calibration to very low color deviation values, while a Mini-LED matrix behind it provides backlighting that offers both high luminance of over 1,200 cd/m² and deep blacks across 2,304 densely packed dimming zones. Mattias Inghe It supports HDR10 and is VESA Display HDR 1000 certified. Playing HDR films on it delivers one of the best viewing experiences I’ve seen on a screen to date, with colors that pack a real punch and an image featuring both dazzling highlights and subtle shading in both light and dark areas. Even in SDR mode, it’s very bright and shines more brightly than most other screens do in HDR mode. Large bright areas are rendered well, and quickly enough to prevent any flickering effect when panning — a good sign of quality for a mini-LED display. Occasionally, however, there can be issues with small bright spots that do not activate the backlight and are therefore too faint. If I move a white mouse pointer over a black background, it is noticeably dimmed. But I can easily adjust the level of dimming for the zones or switch it off completely if needed. It’s usually possible to find a good balance. In this respect, an OLED screen has the advantage, but no OLED can match this screen’s brightness and overall dynamic range. Playing an HDR-supported game or streaming a film from the right source makes for an unbeatable experience. For desktop work, it might be a good idea to switch to a profile without local dimming instead. The contrast is still perfectly acceptable. High refresh rate, high resolution, and AI upscaling With 5K resolution, the image is exceptionally dense and sharp. Despite this, you can achieve a very high refresh rate — 165Hz if you’re running in 5K mode, or up to a full 330Hz if you drop down to 1440p resolution or lower. In both cases, it supports dynamic refresh rates and can automatically drop to the standard 60Hz refresh rate — though you’d have to choose to do so. To save power, perhaps. But is that really important for a fixed desktop monitor? Mattias Inghe If you don’t have a 5K image, the UltraGear Evo AI GM9 features AI-powered image upscaling that makes both 1080p and 1440p video noticeably sharper. I’m not sure if it’s quite as good as on a premium TV, but it does manage to upscale the 1080p picture from my Nintendo Switch to 5K with seemingly decent results, without introducing any unacceptable lag. With this feature disabled, you can achieve response times as low as 1 millisecond. You connect via DisplayPort 1.4 or HDMI 2.1 using the downward-facing ports on the back, and there’s also a USB-C port with DP Alt Mode for docking to a laptop. I’d have hoped for a slightly neater cable management solution than a snap-on loop on the outside of the stand, but it’s better than nothing, at least. Via USB-C, you also get access to a small hub with two USB-A ports, for a mouse and keyboard, for example. There’s only one USB input, so no KVM functionality is offered. Decent sound, but nothing more The computer also has a built-in audio unit that works with all video inputs, featuring both a headphone jack and built-in speakers. It sounds better than most monitors, but to call it “good sound” would be an exaggeration. Monitors usually have rubbish sound or none at all — this is just slightly better. If you’re only using it to play back a bit of Windows audio and run video meetings, it’ll do the job; otherwise, I’d recommend separate speakers. The monitor’s menu is accessed via a tiny control button along the bottom edge of the back panel. It’s hard to find and may be too small for thick fingers. However, the menu it controls via four-way navigation is well-designed and laid out in an exemplary manner for quick and easy access to everything from detailed settings to adjusting volume and brightness, and for switching quickly between preset profiles. In plain Swedish, too. Mattias Inghe If you want to control the screen from your computer, you can install LG Switch and access the same controls there, although the update is annoyingly slow. There are also a handful of other features here, such as window guidance on the desktop, a shortcut for video calls, and the option to connect to a Web OS device such as an LG TV. Skips the bloatware Over the summer, LG came under criticism for automatically installing the LG App Installer via Windows Update, which also meant you ended up with a whole lot of bloatware. They’ve apparently sorted that out now, but it might still be a reason to steer clear of the app — who knows what they’ll try next? In any case, I don’t see anything being auto-installed when I plug in this monitor, so it probably only applies to certain other models. With an MSRP of $1,200, I also think LG should be able to steer clear of that sort of thing. This is a monitor you buy for a top-quality experience, and such details would have given it a budget feel. And the experience — from the controls to the colors, refresh rate, and dynamics — is all very premium here. There are pros and cons compared to a good OLED screen, but the brightness in particular is hard to beat, for both SDR and HDR. With smooth controls for picture modes and backlighting, you can quickly and easily adapt it to different situations. If you don’t have complete control over the lighting in the room and can get plenty of daylight in, its wide dynamic range and, moreover, its anti-glare matte finish are a major plus. Specifications Product name: LG UltraGear Evo AI GM9 (27GM950B-B) Tested: August 2026 Manufacturer: LG Display technology: Mini-LED, IPS Screen size: 27 inches, 16:9 aspect ratio Adjustability: Height adjustment, side-to-side, tilt, pivot Resolution: Up to 5K, 2560×1440 pixels Refresh rate: 165Hz @ 5K, 330Hz @ 1440p, dynamic Response time: 1ms (gtg) Color gamut, specified: 99% DCI-P3 Brightness, specified: 750 cd/m² (typical), 1,250 cd/m² (peak) Contrast ratio: 1,000:1 (static) HDR: HDR10, VESA Display HDR 1000 Video inputs: 2 x HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4, USB-C with DisplayPort Alt Mode (90 W) Other features: USB hub (USB-C in, 2 x USB-A Gen 3 Out), flicker-free, 5K upscaling, FreeSync Premium Pro, G-Sync, 2 x 7-watt speakers, headphone jack Dimensions: 61.47 x 40–53 x 24.9 cm Price: $1,200

item.title: How to easily convert written documents into audio podcasts
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.85
Podcasts can be a great way to conveniently explore complex topics without getting bogged down in pages and pages of text. The ease of listening to the content while commuting, walking the dog or even doing the washing up can make it a more viable option for many than reading a long document. So, wouldn’t it be great if you could easily convert your own written files into podcast-style audio that could help you work through the dense subject matter? This might sound fanciful, as creating audio content has always been an expensive and time consuming business, requiring equipment, hosts, and a way of editing it all into something professional. Well, Adobe is changing that, as it now offers a simple way to convert documents into full audio episodes, without the need for any additional equipment or expertise. Here’s how Adobe Generate Podcast utilises AI to give your message a voice. Use AI to generate podcasts from documents Usually, if you wanted to turn reports or write-ups into audio, it would be a complicated affair. You’d need to either outsource the process (at a not inconsiderable cost) or set up your own team, and most people simply don’t have the capacity or budget for this kind of endeavour. That’s why Adobe Generate Podcast is something of a game changer, as all you need is a document and Adobe Acrobat to instantly turn written words into spoken ones. No voice talent, no microphones, just upload the file and let the AI take care of the rest. This isn’t just a text-to-voice feature though, as the software analyses the PDF, report or other style of document, then reorganizes and structures the audio so that’s it built for listeners. Instead of a dry, verbatim reading of the text, you get a result that features characterful AI hosts conversationally presenting the information so that makes sense to the ears rather than the eyes. It means those long, text-heavy documents can be turned into easy-to-understand audio that people can listen to and enjoy. If you want a short episode that summaries the information from the document, then there’s the Highlights option. Alternatively, you can opt for a longer, more detailed approach by selecting Deep Dive. Of course, you can have both and use the files for different purposes if you want. There’s even a transcript you can access to see what’s covered in the episode. Adobe Lifestyle Coffee Quick to create and easy to share You might expect Adobe Generate Podcast to be a standalone product with an additional monthly cost, but it’s built-in to Adobe Acrobat. So, if you’re a subscriber then the feature is already at your disposal. It also doesn’t require anyone to learn a new tool, as you just open the file you want to convert, select the ‘Listen to this document’ option, choose the style of podcast you want and the rest is done automatically. A few minutes later your episode will be ready. As the files are in a standard audio format, you’ll be able to play or share them easily. So, if you’re looking for a simple way to repurpose marketing briefs, company reports or want to generate training material for your team that won’t have them spending more time staring at a screen, then Adobe Generate Podcast could be a sound choice. Adobe Acrobat is available with a 7-day free trial so you can see for yourself just how easy it is to create podcast-style audio from a document. The suite also boasts AI-powered tools that allow you to make and edit PDFs, generate infographics and social posts, pull summaries and insights from documents, plus plenty of other features. When your free trial is over, you can sign up for an annual subscription from only $24.99 p/m.

item.title: Acronis True Image review: Unique, do-it-all PC security and backup
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.45
At a Glance Expert's Rating Pros - Imaging, backup, and disaster recovery - Actively protects against viruses and ransomware - Integrated cloud storage available Cons - Subscription-only makes it expensive over time - Heavy installation footprint and lots of telemetry - No more folder sync Our Verdict Acronis True Image is a comprehensive security solution without peer thanks to integrated anti-malware, backup, and disaster recovery features. However, it has a heavy system footprint, there’s lots of telemetry, and it’s subscription-only. Price When Reviewed This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Pricing Today Price When Reviewed $49.99 to $124.99 per year Best Prices Today: Acronis True Image (2026) is without question the most comprehensive suite of utilities for keeping your computer secure and backed up. As far as breadth of features is concerned, it’s not even particularly close. True Image is still a very good backup program, and extremely good at security. But since our last look in 2024, all the new features are “security” related and it actually lost the ability to sync folders so it’s not the tightest fit for the backup category. (Norton 360 anyone?) We’re still on board with the program, but being subscription-only, it’s also teetering on the edge of pricey overkill for the average user. Read on to learn more, then see our roundup of the best Windows backup software for comparison. What are Acronis True Image’s features? There’s a lot to cover in a program as comprehensive as True Image. I’ll get to the anti-malware and security features in a bit, but as the program started life as a fantastic and reliable backup program — let’s talk about that first. True Image creates image files (container files created from data sectors) from drives or partitions, as well as selected files and folders. These can be full (everything), incremental (everything since the last backup), or differential (everything since the initial backup). There are different “schemes” you can employ using the backup types described above, which describe how to mix and cull them — e.g., the “Version chain scheme” shown below periodically creates full backups, creates incremental backups in between, and deletes everything over a month old. Note that I’d only use the “Version chain scheme” alongside a full backup that is never culled. A host of other options are provided such as granular scheduling (to the hour), notifications, running programs pre- and post- backup, image-splitting, verification, and even a reserve copy of the backup. I particularly appreciate the “Reserve copy” as it partially ameliorates one of my pet peeves — having to recreate the same job over and over just to backup the same data set to different locations. In light of that, why not multiple reserve copies? Acronis? Additionally, the program backs up to and from nearly any type of media or location: local drives, network destinations, the 250GB/1TB of cloud storage provided by Acronis with some subscriptions, and even optical — remember CDs and DVDs? They’re still in use! If you’re super old-school, sorry, tape is not supported. True Image will optionally place a version of the program on removable media for use during restore (Acronis calls it “recovery”) operations — i.e. create a disaster recovery boot disk. My favorite feature of the recovery disk, other than being able to make additional emergency backups (some recovery disks, such as Ashampoo Backup Pro’s don’t), is the system report facility. Once again, I’m sorry to inform you (once again) that the True Image clients no longer let you create folder sync relationships. There’s still a “Sync” option in the menu column to the left. Click on it, however, and you’re presented with the message shown at the bottom of the image below. I suppose the Sync option was left in so that Acronis could assure users that their synced data on Acronis Cloud had not disappeared. But the upshot is that Acronis is selling subscription software that’s actually ditching features. Say it ain’t so, Joe. The Acronis Mobile app (shown below) is also available to back up files from your phone or other mobile device to the Acronis Cloud or local computers. Other related and tangential backup features include disk cloning, an OEM-like recovery partition (boot time restore of your original OS state from your internal drive) creator, a system cleanup tool (think CCleaner), and a secure-erase utility. Acronis True Image sports a clean, attractive interface, and is easy to use — once you’re accustomed to it. It’s not amazingly intuitive when it comes to organization and operation and I have several complaints about terminology (Network Locations, not NAS) and display (always a closed tree). But a half-hour kicking the tires and you should be good to go. Assuming you’re familiar with basic backup concepts, of course. Note that True Image uses proprietary image formats — .tib up to 2019, and .tibx starting in 2020.
