The new format is not backwards compatible, but the latest version was able to mount some .tib archives I had from 2005/6. I could’ve sword this was not possible during my last look in 2024, forcing me to retreat to the 2019 version. However, it might also have been user error. Acronis offers a “Convert to VHD” feature, but this didn’t seem to work on older .tib files. Neither did mounting them, which appeared successful but failed when I tried to copy the files off. Download the 2019 version (run it as a 30-day trial if you no longer have a valid serial) and use it for restoring data from older .tbi files to VHDs created with Disk Manager. Caveat: Be careful when opening old .tib files. Work with copies as it’s easy to accidentally erase the old one if you delete the job you create using “Add existing backup” and select “Delete Entirely,” which is the first option. Don’t ask. Now for the promised discussion of the system protection/security features. How effective are Acronis True Image’s protection and security features? A few years ago Acronis spotted an opening in the market created by a spate of ransomware attacks. It rapidly added some rather clever protection to its flagship backup software’s bag of tricks. (And changed the name for a while to Cyber Protect, which still adorns business versions) Don’t pooh-pooh ransomware as something that happens to someone else. It happened to me on a NAS box hosting my website. Without backups, I would’ve been royally hosed. Acronis subsequently expanded anti-malware capabilities to protect against general threats, malicious websites, and bad behavior such as code injection into apps. This obviously requires real-time intervention — a big addition back in 2021. Originally, True Image would fire off a new backup upon detecting malware, but now it deals with the malware and repairs damaged files. You can choose to protect backups from malware, but that option doesn’t prevent accidental user deletion as does Easeus ToDo Backup. Relatively new to the game (late 2025) is patch management, found under the Vulnerabilities section. Basically True Image checks the status of your Windows installations and tells you what patches are available. Alas, it sends you online for the info about them. I’m not sure why this info couldn’t be downloaded and presented within the program. After all, True Image is in constant contact with the company’s servers. This type of information changes, but so do the AV definitions. I did mention there’s an AV scan, right? There is. New to me also, is an identity protection service which is implemented from the Acronis website. Of course, one might question the wisdom of providing the amount of information that this requires. But I’m a paranoid type. That comes down to your trust in the company. I lend exactly zero credence to any Wikipedia page covering a possibly contentious subject (log on as an editor some time and look at the edits), but this one seems like a relatively accurate and unbiased history of Acronis. To test True Image’s bad-guys-on-the-web abilities I ran the tests on the WICAR.ORG site and surfed some known bad areas of the web. True Image caught everything. As effective as it proved, real-time protection is optional and may be turned off. On macOS, I found True Image’s malware protection a bit over-zealous, forcing me to restore almost 80 programs that I knew to be safe. On that platform, I’ll stick with the occasional Malwarebytes scan. How much does Acronis True Image cost? Acronis provides a 30-day trial that you can use to test out the program. Beyond that, it’s $50 for a one-year subscription sans online storage (Essentials); $73 per year for Advanced with 250GB of storage; and $125 a year for Premium with 1TB of storage. A full comparison is a available here (scroll down a bit on the linked page). You’re basically paying $75 per year for the 1TB of storage with True Image, which isn’t outrageously expensive but certainly not cheap. For instance, Easeus ToDo Backup’s 1TB of online storage is only $20 a year on top of the subscription. Note that if the True Image subscription lapses, you’ll be limited to restoring data from the recovery disk after 30 days. You’ll also need to grab your existing online data within that period. Which brings me to cloud storage managers such as CloudMounter and Mountain Duck, which will integrate any number of different online storage services into Windows Explorer as pseudo/virtual local drives. This could let you use the $50 tier for an initial savings. $50 a year adds up quickly over time, and purely as a backup program that isn’t adding any significant features (it’s lost one, remember?) — that’s a lousy deal. Especially when there are competent freebies from Easeus and Aomei, as well as the no-longer-supported-but-still-highly effective free version of Macrium Reflect. Adding online storage makes True Image an “okay” deal, but it’s the security features that make the yearly fees palatable and/or worthwhile. These work very well, and need to be updated continually, so a subscription for that is understandable. Put in more simple terms, don’t buy True Image solely for backup, but buy it as a unique and effective total security solution. How does Acronis True Image perform? Generally speaking, True Image is as quick as it gets. I ran backup jobs to external and internal SSDs, a NAS box (2.5Gbps), wrote folders to optical (single BD-R/M-Disc), and to Acronis Cloud. All proceeded as quickly as you could ask given their particular bandwidth, and without incident. I hate incidents and tend not to trust backup software that suffers them. The issues I experienced in 2024 with the Linux boot disc, were nowhere in sight. Yay, Acronis! Alas, I did experience the following error when trying to restore some data from Acronis Cloud. Stuff happens, but this does point out the advantage of local backup as well as not relying solely on the cloud. My only real performance gripe is that the main interface is rather slow to launch. No doubt due the large number of processes spawned by the various components, not to mention connecting to Acronis Cloud. The program is doing a lot. As to processes, True Image has a sprawling system footprint that spawns a whopping 13 of them (shown above). I noticed no impact on overall system performance, and modern PCs should be able to handle it with ease — if you don’t pile on a lot of other stuff. For older legacy hardware it might be a strain. True Image also takes up somewhere around 1.6GB of disk space. In my 2024 look, Google analytics report sender was running alongside True Image (see above). No bueno. This is no longer the case; however, while comprehensive, True Image is also singularly intrusive and loves to send you to the web portal without asking — less than perfectly polite. Should you buy Acronis True Image? If you’re looking for a comprehensive, set-it-and-forget-it data-safety solution, I know of nothing better than True Image. Or comparable for that matter, though Retrospect seems headed down this path as well. Anyone who works in a high-threat environment should likely sign up. This is source of the 4.5 star rating. That said, True Image is likely pricey overkill for the average user, there’s a ton of telemetry going on (privacy anyone?), and it’s subscription software is losing instead of gaining backup features. I have a proposal for Acronis. Along with baking in legacy format support, take a hike back in time, and offer the clean, efficient, small footprint utility that simply images disks and partitions reliably that we all loved. Sell it with a perpetual license and recovery disk for $30 or less. Oh, and use a non-proprietary format such as VHD. Editor’s note: Because online services are often iterative, gaining new features and performance improvements over time, this review is subject to change in order to accurately reflect the current state of the service. Any changes to text will be noted above this notice and changed conclusions at the top.

item.title: Compare ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, & more for life for a one-time $79
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.15
TL;DR: ChatPlayground AI lets you compare responses from multiple AI models in one window, with lifetime Unlimited Plan access available for $79. Every AI model has its own way of answering a prompt. One might write cleaner code, another may deliver a clearer explanation, and a third could catch something the others missed. ChatPlayground AI lets you compare those approaches without opening a small nation’s worth of browser tabs. And lifetime access to the Unlimited Plan is on sale for just $79 (MSRP $619). Enter one prompt and view results from multiple models side by side. The platform includes more than 20 options from names such as ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Llama, and Perplexity, with referenced models including GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Flash, and DeepSeek V3. It also supports image generation, coding, prompt refinement, and contextual chats with uploaded images and PDFs. Saved conversations keep past work within reach, while priority customer support and priority access to new features and future models are included. The Unlimited Plan provides unlimited monthly messages, subject to a fair-use policy. Available models and features are updated regularly and may change as the technology evolves. For anyone who already compares AI responses manually, it’s a smarter way to consolidate the process—not a compromise made for the price. Lifetime access to ChatPlayground AI is currently just $79 instead of the $619 MSRP.

item.title: 9 road trip snacks that won't melt, spoil, or fall apart
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.20
9 road trip snacks that won't melt, spoil, or fall apart These road trip snacks hold up in a hot car, survive hours in a bag, and won't turn to crumbs before you reach your destination A cooler solves half the road trip food problem and creates the other half. Ice melts, condensation soaks through paper bags, and by hour four whatever's left is either warm or swimming. The snacks that actually work for a long drive are the ones built to skip refrigeration altogether — foods where heat, time, and the general chaos of a moving vehicle can't do much damage. That's a narrower category than it sounds. Chocolate-coated granola bars turn to paste on a dashboard. Chips shatter into crumbs in a door pocket. Soft cheese and deli meat need a cooler that stays cold for the entire trip, not just the first two hours. The best road trip snacks solve three problems at once: they don't melt in a car that can heat up well past the outside temperature within an hour of sitting in the sun, they don't spoil without refrigeration for the length of a normal drive, and they don't turn into dust the moment a bag gets kicked under a seat. Foods that meet all three tend to share the same underlying trait — low moisture. Drying, curing, roasting, and freeze-drying all remove the water that both supports bacterial growth and holds a food's fat in a state that liquefies in heat. That's why a piece of beef jerky can sit in a glovebox for a full day and a chocolate bar in the same glovebox cannot. None of this requires giving up variety or nutrition. Protein, fiber, and produce all have shelf-stable, structurally sound versions — they just aren't always the first thing that ends up in a gas station bag. What follows is a list of nine specific snacks, organized by category, that hold up on the road without a cooler, an ice pack, or a plan to eat everything in the first 30 minutes. Beef jerky and meat sticks Credit: Canva Images Beef jerky and meat sticks are among the most heat-stable snacks available because the drying and curing process removes most of the moisture bacteria need to grow, letting a sealed package sit in a hot car for hours without spoiling. The process itself is old. Salting and air-drying meat to preserve it predates refrigeration by thousands of years, and the basic chemistry hasn't changed: pull the water out, and there's nothing left for bacteria to use easily. Modern jerky adds a curing step with salt and sometimes sodium nitrite, which further slows bacterial growth and helps the meat hold its color. None of that process involves a fat that melts the way chocolate or dairy does, so a bag of jerky in a sun-warmed cupholder looks and tastes about the same after four hours as it did when the trip started. Meat sticks work on the same principle in a denser, chewier form, and they come in beef, turkey, pork, and venison versions. Look for products that are vacuum-sealed rather than loosely bagged — the seal keeps out moisture and extends the shelf life of an unopened package to months at room temperature. Once opened, both jerky and meat sticks are still more forgiving than fresh meat left unrefrigerated, but they're best finished within a day for taste and texture rather than for food safety. One detail worth checking on the label: teriyaki and other sweetened jerky flavors carry more sugar, which can turn slightly sticky in high heat even though the meat itself isn't spoiling. A plain or peppered variety holds a drier texture longer. Biltong, the South African air-dried beef that's become its own road trip staple, uses a vinegar-based cure instead of the smoking most American jerky relies on, which gives it a tangier flavor while offering the same shelf stability. Either style delivers a meaningful amount of protein per serving without needing a single ice cube along the way. Trail mix without chocolate Credit: Atlantic Ambience / Pexels Trail mix built from nuts, seeds, and dried fruit stays intact in heat because none of its ingredients contain a fat that turns liquid at everyday temperatures — swap in chocolate chips or yogurt-covered pieces, and that changes fast. Almonds, cashews, walnuts, and pumpkin seeds carry natural oils, but those oils stay solid or semi-solid across the range of temperatures inside a parked car, even one that's climbed well above 90 degrees. Raisins, dried cranberries, and dried apricots add sweetness without adding moisture, since the same drying process that makes them shelf-stable also strips out the water that a chocolate or yogurt coating would need to stay solid. A plain trail mix can sit in a door pocket for the length of a multi-day trip without needing a cooler. The ingredients worth watching are the coated ones. Chocolate-covered raisins, yogurt-covered pretzel pieces, and candy-coated chocolate pieces all soften and re-set as the temperature swings, which can turn a handful of trail mix into a sticky clump stuck to the inside of the bag. Dark chocolate holds up a little better than milk chocolate because it has a higher melting point, but neither is reliable above roughly 90 degrees for more than an hour or so. Banana chips are a common trail mix addition worth a second look. The fried varieties carry more oil than other dried fruit, which can turn rancid faster once opened and exposed to heat over several days, though that isn't a concern for a single day trip. Building a custom mix from bulk bins lets a traveler control exactly what goes in, which is often cheaper than pre-made bags and avoids coated pieces entirely. Transferring the mix into a hard-sided container rather than a flimsy bag also helps keep the larger pieces, like whole cashews, from crumbling under the weight of everything else stacked on top in a packed car. Corn nuts Credit: Canva Images Corn nuts, made from roasted or fried corn kernels, are about as durable a road trip snack as exists: the kernels are dried and cooked until nearly all moisture is gone, which keeps them shelf-stable for months and gives them a hardness that resists crushing far better than a chip or a cracker. The kernels start as a large, starchy corn variety that's soaked in water until it softens slightly, then either deep-fried in oil or dry-roasted in an oven until it turns a deep golden color and hardens all the way through. That cooking step drives out almost all of the kernel's remaining moisture, which is what gives corn nuts their long shelf life at room temperature and removes the conditions bacteria need to grow. A sealed bag can sit in a hot car for a full day, or in a pantry for months, without any meaningful change in taste or texture. Fried and dry-roasted versions behave a little differently in heat, though the difference is minor. Fried corn nuts absorb some oil during cooking, but that oil is pulled into the kernel rather than sitting on the surface the way a chocolate coating does, so heat doesn't turn them sticky or greasy to the touch. Dry-roasted corn nuts skip the added oil altogether, which makes them a slightly leaner option without changing how well they hold up on the road. The texture is the whole point. A corn nut doesn't shatter into crumbs the way a potato chip does when something heavier gets stacked on top of it in a packed car, and it doesn't soften the way bread or crackers eventually can in a humid trunk. Common flavors include chili and lime, ranch, and plain salted, and none of these coatings introduce enough moisture or fat to change the snack's basic durability. The idea of toasting dried corn kernels as a snack predates the packaged American version by centuries. Cancha, a snack of roasted corn kernels eaten across Peru and Bolivia, is made using a similar principle — dried corn cooked until hard and crunchy — and remains a common accompaniment to meals and drinks in the Andes today. Pretzel rods and hard pretzels Credit: Canva Images Pretzel rods and hard, oven-baked pretzels hold their shape far better than chips or thin crackers when they're jostled around a car for hours, and their low moisture content keeps them shelf-stable for weeks without refrigeration. The hard pretzel's toughness comes from how it's made. Dough is briefly boiled in a baking soda solution before it goes into the oven, which sets a firm crust, and then it's baked long enough to drive out most of the remaining moisture. That combination is what gives a pretzel its snap instead of the softness of a mall-style pretzel, and it's also what keeps it from crumbling the way a potato chip does under the weight of a bag shifting during a turn. The style has roots in Pennsylvania Dutch baking traditions in the U.S., where hard pretzels were developed in part because they traveled and stored better than the soft, bakery-fresh version. That same durability is why they've stuck around as a road trip staple: a bag of pretzel rods can be dropped, sat on, or left in a hot car for a full day and come out the other side essentially unchanged. As with trail mix, the exception is anything coated. Chocolate- or yogurt-covered pretzels introduce the same softening problem as coated nuts and dried fruit, so a plain or lightly salted pretzel is the safer choice for anything that will sit in direct sun. Sourdough pretzels, made with a longer fermentation process, add a tangier flavor without changing the shelf stability. For dipping, a sealed single-serve packet of peanut or almond butter travels just as well as the pretzel itself and doesn't require refrigeration until it's opened, which keeps the whole pairing cooler-free. Salt content plays a role in shelf life too, beyond just flavor. The salt on a pretzel's surface draws out any residual surface moisture, which is part of why a bag of pretzels left half-open in a car for a day doesn't turn soft the way bread would in the same conditions. Bavarian-style soft pretzels, sold fresh at malls and stadiums, are the exception worth avoiding for a road trip — they're made without the extended drying step, so they go stale and moldy far faster than the hard, shelf-stable version. Roasted chickpeas Credit: Mustafa akın / Unsplash Roasted chickpeas are a crunchy, high-fiber, high-protein snack that survives heat exposure without melting or spoiling because they're essentially dehydrated legumes with almost no moisture left to support bacterial growth. Making them starts with cooked chickpeas that are dried and then roasted, usually with a light coating of oil and salt or spices. That roasting step finishes removing the water that would otherwise make the chickpeas soft and perishable, leaving a dry, crunchy exterior that holds up well even after being shaken around in a bag for hours. A sealed bag of roasted chickpeas typically keeps for several weeks at room temperature, well beyond what a single road trip requires. Nutritionally, chickpeas bring both fiber and plant-based protein to the snack rotation, which makes them a useful addition alongside meat-based options like jerky for anyone splitting a road trip's snacks between animal and plant protein sources. Common seasonings include sea salt, chili lime, and smoked paprika, and none of these change the shelf stability of the base ingredient. It's worth distinguishing roasted chickpeas from hummus, which is made from the same legume but needs refrigeration because it's blended with oil and tahini into a moist paste that spoils quickly once opened. The dry, roasted version avoids that problem entirely. Roasted edamame is a similar plant-based snack worth mentioning here: it holds up well in heat too, though it tends to soften slightly with prolonged exposure to warm, humid air in a way that roasted chickpeas generally resist. On a multi-day trip, chickpeas moved into a container with a tight seal will stay crisp longer than the same chickpeas left in a bag that's been opened and re-folded repeatedly. A typical quarter-cup serving delivers a meaningful amount of both fiber and protein for its size, which makes roasted chickpeas one of the more filling options on this list relative to their weight. They're also naturally free of the dairy and egg allergens that rule out some other packaged snacks, which is worth knowing when packing food for a group with mixed dietary needs on a shared drive. Sunflower seeds in the shell Credit: Engin Akyurt / Pexels Sunflower seeds still in the shell may be the most road-trip-proof snack available: the shell protects the kernel from crushing, heat, and moisture, so a bag can sit in a hot glovebox for hours without the seeds inside breaking down. The shell is doing more than just protecting the seed from getting crushed under other snacks in a bag. It also limits the kernel's exposure to oxygen, which slows the process that eventually turns seed oils rancid. That's part of why in-shell sunflower seeds tend to stay fresh-tasting longer than pre-shelled kernels, which spoil faster once they're exposed to air and light. Sunflower seeds have a long history as a road trip and ballpark snack in the U.S. in part because of this durability — a bag doesn't need refrigeration, doesn't crush easily, and doesn't make a mess unless the shells themselves end up loose in the car. Bringing a small cup or bag for spent shells solves that last problem and keeps the car cleaner than tossing shells loose into a cupholder. Pumpkin seeds, or pepitas, work the same way when left in their shell, though shell-on pepitas are less common on store shelves than the pre-hulled green kernel. Both seeds are a source of healthy fats and a modest amount of plant protein, and neither requires any preparation beyond opening the bag. The one variety worth watching is flavored or candy-coated seeds, which sometimes carry a sugar glaze that can turn tacky in heat the same way a coated pretzel does. A plain, roasted, salted variety avoids that issue completely and is also the most widely available option at any gas station or grocery store along a driving route. Pre-shelled sunflower kernels are worth a specific mention here, since they're often marketed as the more convenient option. Without the shell's protection, the kernels are exposed to both oxygen and crushing, so a bag of shelled kernels won't hold up nearly as long in a hot car as the same seeds left in the shell. For a short trip the difference won't matter much, but for anything longer than a day, the in-shell version is the more reliable choice. Whole grain crackers like rye crisps Credit: Pixabay / Pexels Sturdy whole grain crackers such as rye crisps and thick, woven wheat crackers hold together far better than thin butter crackers or delicate water crackers, and their low moisture content keeps them shelf-stable for weeks without refrigeration. Thickness and density matter more than the specific grain when it comes to surviving a road trip. A thin, layered cracker shatters into a box full of crumbs the moment something heavier gets stacked on top of it in a packed car, while a dense rye crispbread or a thick, woven wheat cracker can absorb some pressure without breaking apart completely. Scandinavian-style rye crispbread in particular is baked to be dry and hard specifically for long storage, a tradition that predates refrigeration by centuries in parts of Northern Europe. Like pretzels and jerky, crackers don't face a melting risk the way chocolate or dairy does, since there's no fat in a typical cracker that turns liquid at the temperatures found inside a parked car. The main threat to a cracker on a road trip is physical, not chemical: crushing rather than spoiling. Crackers pair naturally with the other shelf-stable snacks on this list. A single-serve packet of peanut or almond butter, or a piece of jerky, turns a box of crackers into something closer to a full snack instead of just a starch. The pairing to avoid is any cracker with a cheese or dairy filling, since those can turn slightly oily or develop an off smell after extended heat exposure even though the cracker base itself would otherwise keep for weeks. Storing crackers in their original box rather than transferring them to a soft bag also helps prevent the crushing that a flimsier bag can't stop. Whole grain versions also bring more fiber to the snack lineup than a refined white cracker, without any change to how well they hold up in heat, since fiber content has nothing to do with a food's moisture level or melting point. For anyone avoiding wheat, rice-based crispbreads offer a similarly sturdy, low-moisture option, though they tend to be more brittle than a rye crispbread and benefit from a slightly firmer container to prevent breakage. Freeze-dried fruit Credit: Kathryn Aleksa / Unsplash Freeze-dried fruit — strawberries, mangoes, apples, and similar pieces — keeps its shape and doesn't spoil because the freeze-drying process removes nearly all of the fruit's water while leaving its structure intact, unlike fresh fruit or standard dried fruit. The process works by freezing the fruit solid and then placing it in a vacuum chamber, where the ice turns directly into vapor without passing through a liquid state, a process called sublimation. Because the fruit never goes through a wet, mushy stage the way it would if it were dried with heat alone, the finished piece keeps a light, crisp, almost hollow texture rather than the chewy, sticky texture of raisins or dried apricots. That difference in texture also means a difference in how it behaves in a hot car. Standard dried fruit still carries a small amount of residual moisture, which is why raisins or dried mango can clump together or turn slightly sticky after hours of heat exposure. Freeze-dried fruit carries almost none, so it stays crisp and separate in the bag no matter how warm the car gets. An unopened package can last a year or more at room temperature, far beyond what any road trip requires. The tradeoff is texture, not safety: freeze-dried fruit is lighter and crunchier than fresh fruit, closer to a chip than to the fruit itself, and it doesn't rehydrate until it's chewed. Strawberries, mangoes, apples, and banana are among the most common options at grocery stores, and unlike a fresh banana, freeze-dried banana slices won't blacken or turn mushy from sitting in a warm car. For anyone who wants fruit on a drive without the bruising risk of fresh produce or the stickiness of standard dried fruit, freeze-dried is the version built for it. Because the pieces are so light and dry, they crush more easily than a fresh apple slice would, so a hard-sided container protects the pieces better than a bag getting squeezed into a full trunk. Oat and fig bars without a chocolate coating Credit: Canva Images Oat-based bars and fig bars without a chocolate coating or yogurt drizzle hold their shape in heat because there's no fat in the bar that turns liquid at car-interior temperatures, and their dense, low-moisture filling keeps them shelf-stable for months. The bars to avoid for a hot car are the ones with visible chocolate chunks, a chocolate coating, or a yogurt-style drizzle on top, all of which soften and re-set the same way a chocolate bar or a coated pretzel does. A plain oat bar or a fig-filled bar skips that ingredient entirely, so the only thing that changes in heat is that the bar might soften very slightly, not melt or separate. Fig bars get their shelf stability from the fig paste at the center, which is naturally low in moisture once the figs are cooked down, plus a pastry-style exterior that's baked until dry. The most familiar U.S. version, the Fig Newton, takes its name from Newton, Massachusetts, where the cookie was first produced in the late 1800s, and the basic fig-and-pastry format has changed little since. Oat bars built around dates, dried fruit, and rolled oats work on a similar principle, bound together by a naturally low-moisture filling rather than by a fat that would turn liquid in the sun. Reading the ingredient label before a trip is the fastest way to sort the road-trip-safe bars from the ones that won't survive a hot glovebox: any mention of a chocolate coating, compound coating, or yogurt coating is a signal to save that bar for a cooler climate or an actual cooler bag instead. Individually wrapped bars also travel more cleanly than a box of loose bars, since each one stays sealed until it's actually eaten. Date-based bars, made mostly of pressed dates and nuts without any added baking, work on the same low-moisture principle and hold up just as well in a hot car, provided the label doesn't list a chocolate or yogurt coating anywhere in the ingredients

item.title: The Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic was unconstitutional, judge rules
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.38
A federal judge ruled Thursday that the Pentagon's effort to blacklist Anthropic violated the First Amendment and the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment, and ordered the government to rescind all directives issued against the AI company. A federal judge set aside the supply chain risk designation that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had placed on the AI startup U.S. District Judge Rita Lin of the Northern District of California found that officials had retaliated against Anthropic in violation of the First Amendment and had stripped the company of liberty interests without adequate notice or a meaningful chance to respond. "The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics," Lin wrote in her 59-page opinion. Lin set aside the supply chain risk designation that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had placed on Anthropic and issued a permanent injunction barring the government from giving effect to the challenged actions. She further ordered the Department of Defense and other named agencies to pull back every internal directive and communication put in place to carry out the designation. The ruling found that the government's rationale rested principally on Anthropic's public criticism of the administration's views on AI. "Neither the Constitution nor the federal statute invoked by Defendants allows them to impose sweeping penalties based principally on Anthropic's critique of the Administration's views," Lin wrote. Anthropic said in a statement that it was "pleased the court has ruled that this supply chain risk designation was unlawful," adding that it looks forward to continuing to partner with federal agencies to advance AI capabilities in service of national security. The conflict between Anthropic and the Trump administration grew out of a $200 million contract dispute over how the Pentagon could deploy the company's Claude AI models on classified systems. Anthropic pushed for contractual limits barring use of its models in autonomous lethal weapons systems or domestic mass surveillance, a position the Defense Department rejected on the grounds that corporate contractors have no authority to dictate military operating rules. When negotiations broke down, Hegseth designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk — a formal status historically reserved for foreign entities considered threats to national security — effectively cutting off every Pentagon contractor and supplier from doing business with the company. Anthropic filed two separate lawsuits in March in response to the blacklisting, one in California and a parallel case in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, the latter required because the DOD grounded its action in two distinct designations. Thursday's order does not require the Defense Department to use Anthropic's products, and it does not bar the government from transitioning to other AI providers, provided those actions comply with applicable law. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. By subscribing, you agree to our Terms of Service and Privacy Policy.

item.title: 5 things that are off limits in someone else’s house
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 3.21
5 things that are off limits in someone else’s house From the thermostat to the medicine cabinet, these common household items and spaces are best left alone when you’re visiting someone else Being a good houseguest usually comes down to a few simple things: show up when you’re expected, be considerate and remember that someone else’s home has its own rules. That doesn’t mean you need to tiptoe around your host or worry about every move you make. Most people aren’t expecting guests to sit perfectly still and ask permission before doing anything. Still, there are certain areas of a home that are generally better left alone unless your host invites you to use them. When you’re unsure, ask. A quick “Is it OK if I grab something from the fridge?” is usually all it takes. And if your host has already told you that you can make yourself at home, you can take that invitation at face value. Reader’s Digest offers etiquette tips for navigating someone else’s home without accidentally overstepping. Here are five areas you may want to leave alone unless your host gives you the green light. 1. Leave the fridge and cupboards alone unless your host says otherwise Sweet Life / Unsplash It can be tempting to open the refrigerator or start searching through the cupboards when you’re visiting someone’s home, especially if you’re staying for a while. After all, you might assume that “make yourself at home” means exactly that. But unless your host has specifically invited you to help yourself, it’s generally more considerate to ask first. The issue isn’t necessarily the food itself. Your host may have groceries set aside for a particular meal, ingredients they’re saving or a certain system for organizing the kitchen. Digging through cabinets can also feel more intrusive than simply asking for something to eat or drink. Reader’s Digest recommends asking if you’re hungry rather than automatically helping yourself. In many cases, your host will be happy to offer you something. If you’re staying overnight or for an extended visit, bringing some food of your own or offering to contribute to meals can also be a thoughtful way to help. If your host says, “Grab whatever you want from the fridge,” then you’ve got your answer. Once they’ve given you permission, there’s no need to keep asking every time you want a glass of water. 2. Keep your hands off the thermostat and windows Eduard / Unsplash If you’re too hot or too cold at someone else’s house, it can be tempting to solve the problem yourself by reaching for the thermostat or opening a window. But that small adjustment may not be as insignificant to your host as it seems. Reader’s Digest suggests asking your host before changing the temperature or opening and closing windows. They may have a preferred temperature, a reason for keeping a window shut or simply want to manage the heating and cooling themselves. There’s also the practical matter of energy use and the utility bill, which ultimately belongs to the person whose home you’re visiting. Fortunately, there are easy alternatives. If you’re cold, ask whether you can borrow a blanket or put on an extra layer. If you’re warm, politely mention it and see whether your host can make the room more comfortable. This is one of those etiquette rules that can vary from household to household. Some hosts may immediately tell guests to adjust the thermostat whenever they want. Others may prefer to handle it themselves. Following their lead is usually the safest approach. You don’t have to sit there uncomfortably to be polite. Just remember that someone else’s home comes with someone else’s preferences. A quick request is generally more considerate than taking control of the environment yourself. 3. Stay out of bedrooms, drawers and cabinets unless you’re invited Francesca Tosolini / Unsplash A bedroom, drawer or cabinet may be physically accessible, but that doesn’t make it an appropriate place for a guest to explore. These areas can contain personal belongings, private documents, medications and other things your host probably doesn’t expect visitors to see. Reader’s Digest recommends avoiding private spaces such as bedrooms unless your host says it’s OK to enter. Even if a bedroom door is open, that doesn’t necessarily mean an invitation to take a look around. The same goes for drawers and cabinets, including the medicine cabinet. The same courtesy applies if you’re staying overnight. A guest room or designated sleeping area is generally fair game for you, but other rooms and personal storage spaces may still be off-limits. You don’t need to overthink every closed door, either. Just pay attention to the spaces you’re actually invited to use. When your host says, “The towels are in that cabinet,” you have permission to open that cabinet. Without that invitation, it’s better to leave private spaces alone. 4. Don’t touch someone else’s mail, bills or workspace Annie Spratt / Unsplash A stack of mail on a counter might look like ordinary household clutter, but it’s still someone else’s private information. The same goes for bills, paperwork, documents and anything else sitting on a desk or workspace. Reader’s Digest recommends leaving these items alone, even when they’re sitting in plain sight. Seeing something doesn’t necessarily mean it’s available for guests to pick up, read or move. Looking through someone’s mail can quickly turn an innocent visit into an uncomfortable situation. Workspaces deserve similar consideration. If a guest room also functions as a home office, for example, avoid moving papers, supplies or equipment unless your host asks you to. Your host may have everything arranged a certain way, and moving something could make it difficult for them to find later. If you need a clear spot to put something, ask. If you accidentally pick up something that belongs to your host, simply put it back where you found it rather than looking it over. 5. Think twice before asking for the Wi-Fi password Bohdan / Unsplash When you’re visiting someone’s home, it can be tempting to ask for the Wi-Fi password as soon as you walk through the door. But if you’re only stopping by for a short visit, Reader’s Digest suggests that you may want to hold off. The concern isn’t really the Wi-Fi itself. It’s more about how the request can come across. If you immediately reach for your phone and ask for the password, your host could get the impression that you’re more interested in being online than spending time with them. That doesn’t mean asking for Wi-Fi is always rude. If you’re staying overnight, working remotely or need internet access for a specific reason, it’s perfectly reasonable to ask. The same goes if your host offers the password without you having to bring it up. If you’re just visiting for dinner or catching up with friends, though, you might consider putting your phone away and enjoying the conversation. You can always reconnect once you’re home.

item.title: The 10 best destinations in the world to see fall foliage, ranked
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 2.45
The 10 best destinations in the world to see fall foliage, ranked From the Adirondacks' fiery maples to Burgundy's storied vineyards and a Chilean volcanic park where autumn arrives in April Fall brings its own particular magic to travel. As mornings and evenings call for a cozy sweater, soup returns to the menu, stargazing conditions turn ideal, and the landscape slowly morphs into a rustic tapestry of reds, golds, and everything in between, the season offers a genuinely different kind of appeal than summer’s sunny days. From fiery maples and copper-colored tundra to liquid gold aspens and larches, these destinations capture fall’s magic across the globe, each offering its own distinct take on the season. The 10 destinations below appear on Lonely Planet, covering the best places to see fall foliage around the world. They span six continents, from the Adirondack Mountains of upstate New York to the volcanic slopes of Conguillío National Park in southern Chile, giving travelers a genuine sense of how differently fall unfolds depending on where they are. Timing varies dramatically across the list too, since Northern Hemisphere destinations such as New Hampshire and Scotland peak in October, while Tasmania and Chile, in the Southern Hemisphere, see their own version of autumn color arrive in April and May instead. Wine ties several entries together as well, from Burgundy’s storied vineyards to Ticino’s scarlet-hued grapevines and Tasmania’s cool-climate pinot noir, giving oenophiles plenty of reasons to plan a foliage trip around a glass of something local. Wildlife also plays a significant role throughout the list, whether that means larch-loving elk in Alberta, red squirrels in the Scottish Highlands, or the Magellanic woodpeckers found among Chile’s ancient Araucaria forests. Getting to these destinations often requires some genuine planning, since several sit hours from the nearest major airport and reward travelers willing to rent a car for the final stretch of the journey. 1. The Adirondacks blanket 6 million acres in autumn hues Hazal Ozturk / Unsplash The seasonal shift in New York’s Adirondack Mountains begins slowly in August, and by mid-September, the landscape erupts in a diverse medley of hues thanks to red and sugar maples, beeches, tamaracks and birches. An extensive network of lakes, ponds, rivers, and streams makes leaf-peeping from the water a genuine highlight, alongside numerous hiking trails and 14 scenic byways that meander through the wild, rugged land. Elk Lake Lodge, an all-inclusive wilderness lodge tucked into the High Peaks region, offers a fitting nostalgic fall stay, complete with one of the park’s best views and a dinner bell that calls guests to the table each evening. Various routes lead into the vast six-million-acre park, with driving from Montreal taking about an hour and a half, from New York City around four hours, and from Boston roughly five hours. Flying into Albany International Airport puts travelers about an hour and a half away, while Burlington and Syracuse airports are about two hours away by car. Renting a car offers the best access throughout the park, and the Foliage Tracker Map provides up-to-date color-progress information, with popular cabins typically requiring booking a few months ahead for weekend stays. Island camping on Saranac Lake, fall festivals such as the Adirondack Balloon Festival or Whiteface Oktoberfest, and hikes up Cascade or Giant Mountain all rank among the region’s highlights, alongside biking the 34-mile Adirondack Rail Trail. Tupper Lake stands out as an up-and-coming dark sky area, with Coney Mountain’s short two-mile round trip delivering a 360-degree night sky view for stargazers willing to make the climb. Paddlers hoping to combine water views with foliage should plan a canoe or kayak trip through one of the park’s quieter ponds instead of the busiest lakes, since narrower waterways tend to bring the colorful shoreline much closer to the boat. This slower pace often reveals herons, loons, and other wildlife that's easy to miss from a busier boat launch. 2. Alberta warms alpine lakes with golden larch groves Devon Hawkins / Unsplash Mountain-fringed alpine lakes, sprawling swaths of golden larches, and possible wildlife sightings of elk, moose, and bighorn sheep define fall in Alberta, Canada. From mid-September to mid-October, larch trees warm the landscape with pops of yellow, and with five national parks and more than 400 provincial parks sitting fairly close together, park-hopping becomes possible even within a single day. Basing a trip in Banff or Jasper puts travelers in an ideal position to explore, with plenty of spots to eat and drink after a day of adventuring. Spray Valley Provincial Park, the quaint town of Canmore, and an overnight stay at Banff Sunshine Village, where a gondola leads up to Sunshine Meadows and its untouched larch scenery, all rank among the region’s lesser-known gems. Flying into Calgary puts travelers just an hour and a half from Banff National Park, while Edmonton International Airport suits those heading toward Jasper, roughly three and a half hours away. Offline maps matter given the spotty cell service in several areas, and hikers should carry bear spray as a precaution, given the wildlife throughout the region. Banff’s iconic spots include Lake Louise, Two Jack Lake for sunrise, Moraine Lake, which requires a shuttle, and Johnston Canyon, while heading north toward Peyto Lake and along the scenic Icefields Parkway rewards travelers with near-constant photo opportunities. Jasper National Park adds the Valley of the Five Lakes Trail and the picturesque Pyramid Lake to the itinerary. Photographers hoping to catch the larches at their peak should track online foliage reports closely in the weeks leading up to a trip, since the narrow window when the needles turn gold can shift by several days depending on that year’s weather. This tracking habit prevents the disappointment of arriving too early or too late for a specific hike. It also helps you have a backup destination in mind if one area’s larches peak earlier than planned. 3. Iya Valley hides Shikoku’s deep gorges from the crowds Credit: Shikoku Tourism Japan ranks as a top-notch fall destination overall, with travelers flocking to Tokyo, Mt Fuji, Kyoto, Nara, Hokkaidō and Nikkō for a foliage cocktail of bright yellow ginkgo and crimson maple trees paired with ancient temples and mountains. Shikoku, the smallest of Japan’s four main islands, has managed to stay relatively under the radar, and its remote Iya Valley holds deep mountain gorges flanked by foliage, striking against the luminous turquoise of the Iya River. Autumn’s crisp air makes onsen soaking especially enjoyable after a day of hiking, and the Hotel Kazurabashi offers a hot spring experience reached via cable car, overlooking the mountains’ fall kaleidoscope, followed by Sanuki udon, the Kagawa prefecture’s regional specialty, at the on-site restaurant. Domestic flights connect both Tokyo airports to Takamatsu Airport, followed by a bus to the valley, while trains run to Ōboke Station from Kochi in about 50 minutes and Okayama in around an hour and a half. Direct buses also connect Osaka to Awa-Ikeda in roughly four hours. Colors change starting in northern Japan and work their way south, meaning Shikoku’s peak foliage typically arrives in early December. A leisurely 30-minute boat cruise through Ōboke Canyon and a visit to the Kazurabashi vine bridge both showcase stunning scenery, while Iya no dekomawasi, a local delicacy of grilled skewers with goshuiimo potato, buckwheat dumplings, and firm tofu topped with miso sauce, makes for a memorable meal. Hiking enthusiasts might consider a multi-day Shikoku pilgrimage trek with Walk Japan, an immersive way to combine culture, cuisine and scenery across a seven-night itinerary. Travelers $TRV hoping to see the region’s most dramatic scenery without a car should rely on the local bus network connecting Awa-Ikeda to smaller villages throughout the valley, since several of the best viewpoints sit well beyond easy walking distance from the train station. This planning step matters most for travelers hoping to reach the region’s more remote hiking trailheads. It costs little more than a bit of planning and opens up a genuinely different side of the valley. 4. Ticino blends Italian flavor into Swiss mountain scenery Credit: Ticino.ch Ticino, known as the sunny side of Switzerland, feels like a storybook. The Swiss Riviera borders Italy and remains a genuinely lesser-known paradise where dramatic mountain peaks and palm trees mix with Italian cuisine and Lake Como-style vibes, minus the crowds. Fall adds gilded chestnut trees, orange-hued larches and acres of scarlet vineyards to the region’s existing whimsy. Ascona, on the northern shores of Lago Maggiore, ranks among the region’s most beloved villages, where al fresco dining, relaxation and adventure come together in a fitting marriage of Swiss and Italian cultures. Hotel Eden Roc Ascona, billed as the country’s only true beach resort, serves as a hub for Ticinese culture and cuisine alongside outdoor adventures such as boating, hiking and parasailing, even during the mild, sunny autumn months. Flying into Zurich and hopping on a roughly two-hour train ride offers one easy route into the region, while flying into Milan cuts the train journey to under two hours. Autumn weather typically kicks off in mid-October thanks to the region’s milder climate, and timing a visit around October’s Chestnut Festival, complete with traditional fire roasting and a market of local goods and crafts, adds a fitting seasonal touch. The Centovalli train, a narrow-gauge railroad nicknamed Il treno del foliage, runs a scenic 32-mile route between Locarno, Switzerland, and Domodossola, Italy. Traditional historic grotto restaurants serve local specialties such as brasato, Swiss risotto, polenta, formaggio d’alpe, torta di pane, fresh pasta, and Il Bianco di Chiara, a white merlot, with Grotto Cà Rossa earning particular praise for its risotto al merlot. Diners hoping to sample the region’s signature white merlot alongside a full grotto meal should book a table well ahead during the Chestnut Festival specifically, since the smaller family-run restaurants tend to fill quickly once the event draws additional visitors from elsewhere in Switzerland. This advance planning also helps secure a table at the smaller, more traditional grottos favored by locals. 5. The White Mountains climb New Hampshire’s back roads Praswin Prakashan / Unsplash New England as a whole puts on quite the color show, but the Granite State’s White Mountain National Forest earns particular renown for its spectacular foliage display. Every autumnal color imaginable shows up vividly, from the famous Franconia Notch State Park to giant Mt Washington. Boston Logan International Airport sits a little under three hours away, while Portland International Jetport and Portsmouth International Airport are about two hours away, and a rental car proves essential for exploring the area properly. Driving the Kancamagus Highway early in the morning helps avoid the crowds, since later arrivals often find themselves elbow to elbow with other leaf-peepers at popular overlooks. The Mount Washington Cog Railway climbs to the top of New England aboard a historic locomotive, rewarding riders with sweeping views. The 34.5-mile Kancamagus Highway offers near-constant scenic stops, including the 2.8-mile Boulder Loop Trail featuring a covered bridge, and Champney Falls, a family-friendly three-mile out-and-back trail leading to the 70-foot-tall Pitchoff Falls. Families hoping to combine a scenic drive with manageable hiking should prioritize the shorter trails branching off the Kancamagus Highway itself, since several offer dramatic foliage views without the lengthy trek better suited to more experienced hikers. Packing a picnic lunch also helps, since dining options along the highway itself are limited outside the busier towns bookending the route. Even a simple sandwich packed from home beats searching for a meal along a stretch with few options. This small habit also saves the hassle of doubling back once hunger sets in mid-hike. Refill water bottles before setting out, since not every scenic stop offers a place to buy one. Checking the foliage forecast before committing to a specific trail also helps, since peak color can vary quite noticeably by several days between the highway’s very lowest elevations and the higher trailheads that branch off much further along the whole scenic route itself. 6. Tasmania turns native fagus trees gold each autumn Laura Smetsers / Unsplash Foliage viewing takes on a different meaning at the southern edge of the world. Every April and May, Australia’s wild island state of Tasmania experiences the turning of the fagus, a progression from yellow to gold, orange to red and eventually rusty brown across the landscape thanks to the low-to-the-ground native fagus tree. The island’s culinary scene rewards exploration too, including scallop pie, local honey, oysters, pinot noir and Sauvignon Blanc. Pumphouse Point, a wilderness resort on the lake in Cradle Mountain-Lake St Clair National Park, offers a nature-immersive, all-inclusive stay at a historic industrial property, complete with on-site trails, paddling, fishing and community meals. Most travelers arrive at Hobart International Airport via domestic flights from Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane or Auckland, New Zealand. Renting a car gives you the freedom to maximize fagus viewing across the national parks, and you drive on the left side of the road throughout the country. Mount Field National Park, about an hour and a half from Hobart, is a hotspot for turning fagus, with a short, flat 0.8-mile trail leading to the multi-tiered Russell Falls. Dobson Road also delivers fagus views for drivers, while a guided kayak trip with Cradle Mountain Canyons lets paddlers explore Dove Lake in a hand-crafted vessel made from native King Billy trees, followed by the 3.7-mile Dove Lake Loop Trail through dramatic mountain scenery. Travelers $TRV hoping to see fagus at multiple elevations should combine a drive along Dobson Road with at least one hike into Mount Field National Park, since the tree’s color progression varies noticeably between lower valleys and higher alpine terrain during the same week. Checking a fagus tracker before setting out also helps narrow down which trails are at peak color that week. This extra research helps travelers avoid a long detour to a trail that has already passed its peak. It also matters for travelers with only a day or two available to dedicate specifically to fagus viewing. 7. Lake Bohinj mirrors the Julian Alps in calm water Tienko Dima / Unsplash Lake Bohinj, a large glacial lake within Slovenia’s Triglav National Park, sits speckled with autumn foliage during the first few weeks of October. The lake offers a quieter, less crowded alternative to neighboring Lake Bled, though you can still visit both in a single day. Early fall mornings bring calm foliage reflections in bright blue water and strips of fog draped across the mountains, best appreciated via a flat walking trail around the lake, either the full 6.8-mile loop or a shorter section along either shore. Families with younger children can enjoy Goldhorn’s Fairyland Trail, an interactive nature path suited to shorter outings. Flying into Ljubljana Airport and driving about an hour northwest reaches Lake Bohinj directly, and staying there while visiting Lake Bled early in the morning helps minimize crowds, since traditional wooden pletna boats to Bled Island start running at 8:30 a.m. in October. A cable car up to the Vogel viewpoint offers panoramic views, along with mountain biking and hiking options, including the trail to the alpine meadow at Zadnji Vogel. Vodnikov Lookout Point and the stair trek to Savica waterfall round out the area’s viewpoints, while a scenic drive along Stara Fužina to the Vogar Viewpoint offers dazzling canyon views along a switchback-riddled route. The 7-mile Mostnica Gorge Trail weaves into the lush Voja Valley, rewarding hikers with a waterfall at the end. Travelers $TRV hoping to visit both lakes without feeling rushed should base themselves in Bohinj instead of Bled, since the shorter drive from Bohinj to Bled in the early morning beats the reverse trip once Bled’s tour buses begin arriving later in the day. Packing layers also helps, since temperatures near the lake can shift noticeably between early morning fog and a sunnier midday. This flexibility matters most for early risers hoping to catch the lake’s calmest, most reflective conditions. It also rewards patience, since the fog tends to lift gradually instead of clearing all at once. 8. Burgundy ferments wine country into a fall retreat Elodie Debard / Unsplash Fall counts as the best season in Burgundy according to locals, when vineyards turn crimson, forests don shades of ginger and gold, and the region’s world-class wines feel especially fitting to savor. Horseback riding, hiking, and even hot-air balloon rides round out the seasonal activities, alongside seasonal dishes and fantastic wine. Château la Commaraine, a working vineyard, offers a specialized harvest-season wine safari through the Côte de Beaune vineyards. The train from Paris takes under 2 hours to reach the region, situated southeast of the capital, with connections to various towns throughout Burgundy. Flying into Paris, Lyon or Geneva, Switzerland also works, each within a few hours’ drive. Peak foliage typically arrives mid- to late October, with harvest season starting in September. Dijon, Beaune and Auxerre all deserve a visit, though the smaller countryside villages of Vézelay, home to a UNESCO World Heritage-listed basilica, Châteauneuf-en-Auxois, Flavigny-sur-Ozerain and Noyers-sur-Serein offer top leaf-peeping among cobblestone lanes. The 37-mile Route of Great Wines stretches from Dijon south to Santenay, offering wine tasting at various castles amid the fall scenery, while guided moped or e-bike tours through Mâconnais in Southern Burgundy include a vineyard picnic along the way. Cyclists who want to explore the region at a relaxed pace should consider the flatter routes through the Côte Chalonnaise instead of the steeper vineyard roads further north, since the terrain suits casual riders without sacrificing access to genuinely excellent wine. Booking a designated driver or arranging transport between tastings also matters, since sampling wine at several stops throughout the day adds up quickly. This planning step also helps groups avoid rushing through tastings meant to be savored slowly. It also lets everyone in the group actually enjoy each pour instead of watching the clock. It also removes any awkwardness around who ends up behind the wheel by the end of the day. Booking tastings a few days apart also helps travelers appreciate each region’s wines with a fresher palate. 9. Cairngorms pairs whisky trails with Highland wildlife martin bennie / Unsplash Cairngorms National Park, in the heart of the Scottish Highlands, pops with autumn colors from pines and birches, with snow-dusted peaks adding extra drama. As the UK’s biggest national park, it is best enjoyed on the hiking trails, spotting wildlife such as red squirrels, deer, mountain hare, and pine marten, plus birdwatching for crested tits and Scottish crossbills, with castle ruins scattered throughout. Cairngorm Mountain Resort suits families especially well, loaded with recreational activities such as mountain carts, tubing slides and an adventure play park. The park connects well to hubs including Inverness, Glasgow, Edinburgh and London by train, taking about 2 hours by train or 40 minutes by car from Inverness Airport, and just an hour and a half by car from Edinburgh or Glasgow. Packing layers matters given the notoriously unpredictable Highland weather, along with a raincoat and wool base layers for chillier days. The famous Speyside Way, a 41-mile route through forests laced in copper, amber and gold, passes through quaint villages en route to its real stars: the valley’s 50 whisky distilleries. Grantown-on-Spey, Boat of Garten and Pitlochry all offer worthwhile stops on the park’s outskirts, while Loch an Eilein pairs 13th-century castle ruins with foliage viewing, and the Strathspey Steam Railway offers a scenic 20-mile heritage train ride through the autumn landscape. Whisky enthusiasts hoping to visit multiple distilleries in one trip should plan a designated driver or arrange transport in advance, since the valley’s 50 distilleries sit spread across considerable distances that make tasting and driving a genuinely poor combination. Bringing binoculars also pays off, since spotting red squirrels and birdlife among the pines often requires a closer look than the naked eye allows. This small addition rewards patient observers with sightings that a rushed walk would otherwise miss entirely. It also turns a simple walk through the pines into a genuinely rewarding wildlife-spotting outing. This small addition costs little and often leaves the strongest impression from the whole trip. 10. Conguillío contrasts lava fields with ancient forest Torres del Paine draws most of the attention in Chile, though the lesser-known Conguillío National Park and its resident snow-capped Llaima Volcano have plenty to offer. Located in the Araucanía region of southern Chile, the diverse landscape provides an unusual autumn backdrop of red and green foliage contrasting against dark volcanic lava and ash fields alongside alpine lakes. Hiking, photography, and wildlife watching for foxes, parakeets, and Magellanic woodpeckers draw considerable attention, particularly among the ancient native Araucaria trees, also known as monkey puzzle or Chile pine trees. Flying into Temuco Airport via Santiago puts travelers about 2 to 2.5 hours from the national park, depending on whether entry happens through Curacautín in the north or Melipeuco in the south, while a long-distance bus from Santiago takes roughly 10 hours. The foliage season typically runs from late April until mid-May, and renting a car offers the flexibility needed to explore independently. The Sierra Nevada Trail, a 7.1-mile hike, delivers sweeping foliage vistas of southern beech and Araucaria trees, alpine lakes, and the volcanic giant Llaima. The Los Carpinteros Trail, a 4-mile hike, leads to the Araucaria Madre, a 1,000-year-old monkey puzzle tree, and offers fantastic woodpecker sightings, especially in the afternoons. The family-friendly Truful Truful Waterfall Trail and the short Rainbow Lagoon Trail, circling an incredibly clear lake, round out the park’s offerings. Travelers $TRV hoping to see the widest variety of wildlife should time hikes for early morning or late afternoon, since Magellanic woodpeckers and other native species tend to stay most active during the cooler edges of the day rather than the warmer midday hours. Layers also help, since temperatures can swing considerably between the lower trailheads and the higher volcanic terrain later in a hike. This preparation matters most for longer hikes that start in cool morning air and end in warmer afternoon sun. It also helps hikers avoid discomfort partway through a longer trail once the sun climbs higher.

item.title: Kalshi challenges Times report amid widening prediction market regulatory battles
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Score: 4.11
Kalshi is disputing a New York Times report about the expanding legal and political battle over prediction markets, including questions about sports betting, taxes, consumer safeguards and federal intervention. The company responded August 27 as 20 states face active litigation involving Kalshi or other prediction markets. Separately, 44 states signed a letter to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission arguing the platforms have sidestepped state regulation and taxes. “The New York Times asked a series of questions, then ignored almost every answer that didn’t align with the narrative that was being pushed,” Kalshi said in its response. The Times cited a Tax Foundation estimate that states could collect at least $2 billion annually by taxing prediction markets like sportsbooks. Kalshi questioned the estimate and pointed to North Carolina, where online sportsbooks generated about $130 million in 2025 tax revenue. “Federally regulated companies are subject to state taxes – we have never said otherwise,” the company said. “This is how almost all industries in America operate.” Kalshi challenges Times claims as regulatory fight intensifies States contend sports-event contracts amount to gambling. Washington Attorney General Nick Brown, after securing a preliminary August court victory, said customers can wager on sporting outcomes. “That’s the same thing as gambling,” he said. “It’s flat-out wrong to say that Kalshi is ‘indistinguishable from traditional sports betting,’” the company said. Kalshi says its exchange uses bids, asks, order books and other trading tools, while federal rules address manipulation. It also offers trading breaks, self-exclusion and deposit limits and works with the National Council on Problem Gambling and Birches Health. North Carolina’s budget permits CFTC-registered prediction markets and taxes them at 6%, compared with 23% for sportsbooks. The Times reported Kalshi lobbyist Jim Harrell helped shape that legislation. “This is literally what lobbyists do – represent client interests and help inform legislators regarding potential legislation,” the company said. Kalshi says comparing rates ignores different economics: sportsbooks had a 10.2% national hold in 2025, versus roughly 1% blended prediction-market fees. “Sportsbooks’ margins are 10x more than those of prediction markets, so you can’t compare tax rates, because you’re taxing different amounts,” Kalshi said. “So the focus should be less on the tax percentage number and more on the actual revenue directed to the state.” The CFTC has sued nine states this year, all led by Democratic governors, and intervened in Michigan and New York disputes. “It’s unprecedented and overly aggressive for states to try to shut down a federally licensed exchange,” the company said. “It’s like if North Carolina wanted to shut down the stock market.” Donald Trump Jr., an adviser to Kalshi who is also involved with Polymarket, has argued for CFTC oversight. Kalshi says he advises on marketing, not regulation. Court outcomes remain divided, including losses for Kalshi and a Third Circuit victory. “We won in the Third Circuit,” the company said. “And no, we do not agree with that characterization. The legal split is currently close to 50-50.” Featured image: Wally Gobetz via Flickr / CC BY-NC-ND 2.0

item.title: A yard sale from Backyard Renaissance
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 4.22
“By nature, theater is an inefficient model,” says Francis Gercke, co-founder and artistic director of Backyard Renaissance theater company — a position that requires him to think about the “business” part of “show business” more than some. “It’s just not conducive to streamlining. We have this bedding we used for Misery — a full set, with quilts and pillowcases. But not every play calls for a bed” — and even if it did, “you don’t want people staring at the same furniture for three years in a row. Companies have to reinvent the wheel every time out. We had a period refrigerator for Smokefall, and we were thinking about using it for A Streetcar Named Desire. But we stumbled; we started worrying, ‘Is it going to look like the same refrigerator? We’ve got to get a different fridge.’ And that’s how you start to acquire stuff.” This Sunday, from 7 am to noon at 7620 Lake Ree Avenue, Backyard Renaissance’s decade-plus of acquisition will become their loss and your gain. The Big Theatre Purge will offer for sale “the things that make magic happen onstage — fabulous costumes, quirky props, giant set pieces, mysterious objects that we swore we’d use again.” The books piled under the end table of an associate professor of history in Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? The handbag and luggage of a woman who’s always depended upon the kindness of strangers in A Streetcar Named Desire? The hotel room chairs from Bachelorette that are lovely and comfy but a little too corporate for most of the company's shows? All up for grabs — orphaned objects that Gercke hopes will find a home. Or how about this? “We have the jacket that the sheriff wears in Misery. He was played by Alex Guzman, and he gets shot with a shotgun by Maggie Carney’s character. It was a really nice jacket, sort of an aviator style that a police officer might wear in a wintry part of the northeast. Our special effects coordinator Jeffery Neitzel blew out the back of the jacket and had blood and guts hanging from it. The spine was even showing. I couldn’t believe he was going to rip it up, and then once he completed it, it was like this work of art. But I said to him, ‘You’ve really screwed Jess and me, because we’re never going to get rid of this jacket. Who walks around with their spine out?’” Go ahead, prove him wrong. “Jess” is Jessica John Gercke, co-founder and executive director of the company. “One of her big loves is wardrobe — finding pieces that not only look good, but feel like the character has lived in them. That they purchased it themselves, and it shows them off in a good light even as it tells the story. She’s putting stuff on the rack, and I’m like, ‘You really want to get rid of that dress? It looks dynamite on you!’ There’s great stuff: things with tassels, really nice faux fur.” Of course, not every actor is supposed to look good. “There’s this great pair of shorts that Mike Sears wore for our first-ever show, Parlour Song.” His character, Ned, is written as being rotund. Sears was…not. To drive the mismatch home, “Jessica specifically got him shorts that didn’t fit particularly well and weren’t particularly stylish. As weird and creepy as it sounds, I hope nobody takes those shorts, because they are the ultimate red badge of courage for me — that an actor put them on and performed a full run of shows in them.” (For his bravery, Sears was awarded the Craig Noel Award for Outstanding Featured Performance in a Play.) Prepping for the sale has brought a thousand stories like that out of storage. “Moving sucks,” says Gercke. “I am a hoarder. Everything has this deeply personal story for me. But it’s still fun for Jess and me. There was this very nice futon, and we were trying to figure out what production it was from. And so we went through our old production photos, and that sent us down memory lane.” Eventually, they figured out it was from Mr. and Mrs. Fitch, which they put on over at Moxie Theatre on El Cajon Boulevard. “The actors had to be careful not to lean on it in a certain way so that it didn’t fall back and become a bed in the middle of a scene. That would have changed the tone of the play.” Backyard Renaissance “spent hours on that futon, and then we didn’t touch it for seven years. And then it occupied two hours of a Friday morning. But we said, ‘We can’t be doing this. We have to let the kids grow up and move out.’” There are other reasons for selling, both mundane and otherwise. The mundane: “We currently have three storage spaces, and costs have really gone up in the last year. We realized that if we could get rid of those three storage spaces, we could actually come close to affording a monthly lease on a property, so that we would have a commercial residency. It’s not like we could afford a theater, but we could combine storage space, rehearsal space, and have the potential for a small cabaret space. It would be a better use of the contributions people provide.” Which brings us to “otherwise.” “We’re always looking for a way to engage with the people who come to our shows and support our company. We like to do things that are a little more personal than what’s normally done.” Hence the promo flyer’s invitation: “Come rummage through 11 years of theatrical history and take home a piece of the show.” And maybe pick up a story to take home along with it.

item.title: Chinese automakers are following Tesla’s bet that robots are the next big profit machine
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 7.30
The hype around humanoid robots isn’t particularly new. Thank Tesla CEO Elon Musk and his Optimus robot, as well as the myriad videos of Boston Dynamics’ Atlas robot, for that. Behind that hype, though, there is real progress. The physical capabilities of robots continue to improve, and researchers now believe that the AI techniques behind large language models can make complex robots capable of learning nearly any task. Those tailwinds have encouraged a new batch of companies to jump in on the promise of profits from humanoid robots. And many of the latest entrants are Chinese automakers. Earlier this week, Xpeng’s robotics unit raised more than $900 million at a post-money valuation of more than $6.3 billion. The round, led by IDG Capital with participation from Gaorong Ventures, Tencent, and Alibaba, was described by the company as the largest single-round private financing ever recorded in China’s “embodied AI” industry (AI systems built directly into physical machines). This month, AiMOGA, the robotics unit of China’s Chery Automobile, reportedly began preparing for an IPO, while BYD unveiled a humanoid robot called Xiao Di. Other Chinese automakers, including Changan, GAC, Li Auto, SAIC, and Seres, are also developing humanoid robots. Among all of them, Xpeng is the Chinese automaker that most closely watches and follows Tesla’s initiatives, according to Michael Dunne, CEO of San Diego- and Singapore-based advisory firm Dunne Insights. “It’s the most focused on autonomy, it’s the first to commit in a big way to humanoid robots,” Dunne told TechCrunch, adding that Xpeng founder He Xiaopeng is a tech billionaire known for his agility and quick adjustments. “He sees razor-thin profit in cars on the near horizon. Robots look much more promising.” Xiaopeng and Xpeng co-president Brian Gu are bullish enough that they’ve put their own funds behind the robotics unit. According to the Wall Street Journal, the pair invested about $100 million into the recent fundraising round. Xpeng’s bet is on Iron, a humanoid robot with a realistic human shape that is built for commercial deployment. Chinese automakers like Xpeng do bring a manufacturing edge. “They have all the hardware to get the job done,” Dunne said. “Question is if they can catch Tesla on the AI side of the equation.” There are, of course, many other companies developing humanoid robots, including Agility Robotics, Apptronik, and Figure, all chasing the same goal: commercial deployment at scale. Hyundai-owned Boston Dynamics is getting closer to that goal. Hyundai plans to bring Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid robot to its Georgia factory this year and eventually deploy the robots for tasks like parts sequencing by 2028. The Korean automaker, which partnered with Google’s AI research lab DeepMind to speed up the development of Atlas, is opening a U.S. facility this year called a Robot Metaplant Application Center, which will teach robots how to map movements like lifts and turns. Other automotive companies are also jumping, including supplier Mobileye, which acquired humanoid robot startup Mentee Robotics earlier this year for $900 million. Even Rivian is dabbling in robots with its Mind Robotics spinout — although its robots are not expected to look quite like the humanoids in development elsewhere.

item.title: Anthropic gets its first court win over the Pentagon’s supply-chain risk label
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 6.32
A federal judge in California ruled on Thursday evening that the Trump administration’s designation of Anthropic as a supply-chain risk was illegal. U.S. District Judge Rita Lin said in her ruling that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s labeling of Anthropic as a risk to national security signified “unlawful retaliation” in violation of the First Amendment, and said the decision was “arbitrary and capricious.” Lin also said Anthropic was denied due process, as required under the Fifth Amendment. Earlier this year, Hegseth and President Donald Trump labeled Anthropic a supply-chain risk and ordered all federal agencies, even those outside of defense, to stop working with the Claude maker. The dispute stemmed from Anthropic setting hard lines on certain safety guardrails that would allow the Pentagon to use its models for fully autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of American citizens. The Pentagon denied that it would use Anthropic models for anything but lawful purposes, and alleged that Anthropic could try to control the military’s use of the models it bought and paid for. In her ruling, Lin said that the government’s “words and deeds confirm that the challenged actions were based on a desire to make a public example out of Anthropic for its ‘arrogance’ in criticizing the government.” She pointed out the disconnect between the supply-chain label and other actions from the government, like Hegseth’s proposition to apply the Defense Production Act to Anthropic, “which would mean the company was essential to national security rather than a threat to it.” She also pointed to the Department of Defense continuing to pursue a contract with the company, and the government collaborating with the company’s new model, Mythos, for cybersecurity. Lin also said it’s clear that Anthropic “undisputedly lacks” any backdoor access to its technology once it hands it over to the DOD. “Though the Department of War is undisputedly free to select the AI vendor of its choice, the evidence demonstrates that the broad measures imposed on Anthropic were illegal and baseless,” Lin wrote. “The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics,” she added. “We welcome the court’s ruling that this supply chain risk designation was unlawful,” an Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement shared with TechCrunch. “We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology.” Anthropic filed two complaints against the DOD in March in California and Washington, D.C. The D.C. suit is still ongoing. TechCrunch has reached out to the DOD for comment.

item.title: YouTube now lets creators tag Amazon products and earn commissions from purchases
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 5.97
YouTube announced on Thursday that eligible creators in the U.S. can now tag Amazon products in their content and receive a cut of sales. Creators can link Amazon products in their shorts, long-form videos, and livestreams.
