But, Marsh argues, “the best way to present an abstract idea to kids is by hooking them on a story.” And a great way to get a kid interested in a story is by reading it aloud to them. In another article, published a year ago, Ilana Kurshan wrote about this declining but important practice, and about doing it with her son: “The delight of reading to him lay not in the pages we turned,” she wrote, “but in the wheels that seemed to turn in his mind as we read together.” Thanks to my friends’ beloved babies and the perks of my job—which have included putting together a list of essential children’s books—I’ve been thinking a lot about the importance of reading with children. They still encounter books in schools and libraries, but Parton’s program emphasized building a bookshelf at home, where caregivers and kids can share stories as part of a daily routine. Reading aloud offers a child more than the chance to develop literacy skills. It gave Kurshan, for example, “a way to guide them as they started to understand the world, and as I started to understand them.” So, like Parton, I’ll be happy if kids see me as a “book lady.” Last week, I bought a picture book about berries for a different toddler. And although my friend’s 10-month-old already has plenty at home, I couldn’t resist mailing him a few more books. What Parents Lose When They Don’t Read to Their Kids By Ilana Kurshan Sharing books with my children was about a lot more than literacy. What to Read Hippos Go Berserk!, by Sandra Boynton Hippos Go Berserk!, a sterling example of Boynton’s comedic genius, has the subtitle “A wild counting story.” “One hippo, all alone, calls two hippos on the phone,” it begins, and each page introduces another attendee to a gathering being planned in real time, until 45 of them crowd an all-night cocktail party. Then come the visual gags: There’s a hippo’s version of Whistler’s Mother, a hippo upside-down, and one guest, a classic spiky-furred grinning Boynton beastie, who consistently eludes the count. As the hippos gradually leave, little creature in tow, Berserk shows that even basic arithmetic can be an act of imagination, rather than rote repetition—and it cleverly reminds adult readers that the most familiar exercise can invite unexpected images into the mind. — Walt Hunter Out Next Week 📚 The Castle: Adventures in a World of Unraveling Men, by Jon Ronson Your Weekend Read The Painter Who Shaped Rothko By Sebastian Smee Beginning in the early 1930s, three Americans—Milton Avery, Mark Rothko, and Adolph Gottlieb—began spending summers together on Cape Ann, along the coast of northeast Massachusetts. They loved the gritty authenticity of Gloucester, the nation’s oldest fishing port. Cape Ann’s distinctive, undulant geography combined pungent industry and village intensity with Atlantic immensity of sea and sky. The story of the relationships among these artists, in particular between the older Avery and the now–stratospherically famous Rothko, shows us American modernism in its moment of greatest transition. When you buy a book using a link in this newsletter, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

item.title: A Turning Point in AI Writing
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 2.69
There was a time—a more innocent age—when you could read an op-ed in a major newspaper and confidently say that a human had written it. Hold on to the memory of that for as long as you can. This week, after the billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller published an editorial in The Wall Street Journal criticizing Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, his onetime protégé, readers began to notice some familiar tics of AI writing. According to Pangram, the AI-detection tool, the op-ed was 100 percent AI-generated. That in itself was not so shocking. AI writing has regularly snuck into mainstream outlets, and especially newspaper op-ed pages, despite policies against it. Up to now, those accused of passing off a computer’s writing as their own have tended to either apologize or deny it. In April, James Taranto, the Journal’s editorial-features editor, wrote a column comparing Pangram to a “defamation machine” that was fueling unfounded accusations of AI use, including in op-eds he had overseen. “Those of us who practice writing as a professional craft have an ethical duty, and sometimes a contractual obligation, to ensure that our work is original,” he wrote. The difference this time is that Druckenmiller owned it. “Of course I used AI,” he told NOTUS on Tuesday. “I’m not embarrassed by it,” he added. “I write everything using AI now for the same reason I use a calculator when I do math problems.” And rather than rebuke him, The Wall Street Journal’s editorial-page editor, Paul Gigot, defended the practice. “AI is a fact of modern life,” he said in a statement. Last night, Gigot followed up with a full column on the subject, mocking the “media pharisees” who wag their fingers at automated writing. He clarified that the Journal’s opinion staffers must still draft their own columns and editorials but said that he doesn’t intend to police AI use by outside contributors. “Many contributors, especially prominent politicians or CEOs, employ speechwriters or hire a Beltway writing shop,” he wrote. “How different is that from using AI to streamline an essay?” It’s one thing for Druckenmiller to not be embarrassed; plenty of business and tech tycoons are bullish about AI’s utility for writing and just about everything else. “If Stan Druckenmiller isn’t embarrassed,” the venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya posted on X, “you shouldn’t be either.” Valorizing the process of unassisted human writing is “like after matches was invented, still celebrating the arduous time to rub two sticks together,” Palihapitiya added. However, one of America’s most prestigious newspapers welcoming the technology into its pages is unprecedented. Is AI writing entering its post-shame era? Gigot is not wrong that Druckenmiller’s frankness seems almost refreshing in a moment when so much of the writing world is stuck in denial. And his assertion that an AI-composed essay could reflect a human’s authentic ideas is reasonable. I won’t pretend to know enough about bond markets to assess Druckenmiller’s op-ed on its merits. But it seems to have advanced a substantive and nonobvious argument that broadly reflects his views, regardless of who—or what—strung its words together. Op-eds by public figures are rarely authorial master classes anyway. But the notion that Druckenmiller and Gigot deserve points for honesty overlooks their lack of transparency. Before this week, the one thing everyone in the AI-writing debate still seemed to agree on was the importance of disclosure. The Journal’s opinion section appears to have blown past that. Druckenmiller’s op-ed contains no indication that he used AI. In his column, Gigot scoffed at the idea that his readers deserve to know when a piece is chatbot-assisted. “Disclose what?” he asked rhetorically. “Interrogate an author on how precisely he used ChatGPT? I know some publications claim to do this, but I suspect it’s more pro forma than systematic.” (Gigot did not respond to my requests for comment, nor did a spokesperson for Dow Jones, the Journal’s parent company. Taranto told me via email that he stands by his April op-ed and believes that Gigot’s statements are consistent with what he wrote.) If the Journal’s higher-ups really believe that their readers don’t care whether an op-ed was written by AI, what would be the harm in letting them know when it is? In fact, studies have found that readers sometimes prefer ChatGPT’s prose or short stories to the human variety—but sour on them when informed about the AI’s involvement. Gigot might conclude from this that people actually like AI writing and just don’t realize it yet. Another interpretation is that people would rather spend their limited time on prose that emanated from another human mind. Perhaps outsourcing an op-ed to a chatbot isn’t materially different from outsourcing it to a ghostwriter. (Although if that’s the case, maybe we should question the practice of ghostwriting before using it to justify AI.) In any circumstance, the Journal’s leap from nuh-uh to so what? feels premature. Yes, many transformative technologies have overcome opposition on their way to broad acceptance, but that doesn’t mean the resistance is a waste of time. It’s part of how society hashes out norms, sets limits, and buys time to adapt. Publishing AI writing under a human byline without telling anyone seems more likely to erode people’s trust in the technology than build it. There’s another reason to keep up the norm of disclosure: When people let a chatbot do their writing—even if they’re guiding and carefully reviewing its work—they might not realize that it’s doing some of their thinking too. Jenna Russell, a doctoral candidate in computer science at the University of Maryland who has studied AI writing in newspapers, told me that her colleagues’ latest line of inquiry involves “argument collapse.” In a paper that has yet to be peer-reviewed, Maryland researchers found that AI-written essays are far less likely to advance novel points than those written entirely by humans. “These LLMs can start to affect our ideologies without our consciously knowing that it’s happening,” Russell said. Maybe Druckenmiller owning his AI use and receiving the Journal’s blessing heralds a new era of guilt-free mechanized writing. Or maybe it’s just another example of the rich and powerful getting away with something that others can’t. Gigot’s defense of Druckenmiller suggested that his reputation and stature obviated concerns about his use of AI. “His contribution to the public debate was still valuable, and he’s welcome in our pages any time,” Gigot wrote. In contrast, when a previously obscure writer, Mia Ballard, was accused of using AI in her horror novel Shy Girl, her publisher launched an investigation, canceled the book, and left her reputation in shreds. How this plays out for the Journal and the rest of the industry will probably depend, aptly enough, on market forces. If people really are willing to pay for opinions articulated by chatbots, other publications are likely to follow suit. They’ll have no shortage of submissions from writers eager to turn a few prompts into a published op-ed.

item.title: The Generational Difference in Southern Manners
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 2.31
This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here. It is a truth universally acknowledged that the southerner is the most mannerly person in America. Before any Yanks get defensive, I want to clarify that this does not necessarily make them the kindest group in America. As a young child in Tennessee, I learned that a “Bless your heart” to one’s face paired particularly well with a cutting remark behind closed doors. I also learned that etiquette was a pesky but persistent thing: Anytime I replied to my father with a curt “yes,” he’d look at me sideways and say, “Yes, what?” I’d sigh. “Yes sir.” My father is a seventh-generation Kentuckian, and my mother’s family has lived in the South since the 18th century. Growing up, I knew that there was a regalia to the southerner’s manners that might come as a surprise to those who cast the region as unrefined. Men are to hold doors for their dates and give up their seats to women on the bus. In some spaces, they will still stand when a lady enters or exits the room. There are also the more casual types of manners. When you pass any stranger on the street, you say, “Howdy,” or, “How are you?” You wave at pedestrians you drive by in your truck. You let neighbors borrow an egg or a cup of sugar without any expectation of repayment. Even as the identity of the South evolves, and more young people lose certain traits that are identifiably southern, manners remain one of the region’s most distinctive and steadfast qualities. The region’s attitudes toward hospitality are a natural outgrowth of these broader social graces. In the South, people like to emphasize that anyone’s cousin’s neighbor’s friend will be welcome in your home. As Walter H. Page described in The Atlantic in 1881, if a stranger comes “with a letter of introduction from some of their old friends, or if he happen to be connected, however distantly, with an old family known to them, he will at once be taken into their homes, and he will receive every hospitality.” This kindness has its limits, however. “The South is famous for its courtesy, but the highly refined concept of honor that largely produced its manners has also helped to make the region the most violent in the country,” Benjamin Schwarz noted in a 1997 Atlantic essay. “As the old saying goes, a southerner is gracious and friendly until he is mad enough to kill you.” Although plenty of southerners are motivated to adhere to codes of etiquette by a sense of selflessness and responsibility, the manners that they are so careful to keep are also an effort to protect their reputation. And a well-mannered person isn’t necessarily a mild-mannered person. One 1996 study compared the behaviors of white male University of Michigan students who grew up in the North with those who grew up in the South: When a man bumped into a student and called him an asshole, the students raised in the South were more likely to think that their masculine reputation was threatened and respond aggressively. You also cannot tell the story of southern manners without telling the story of Black southerners—specifically, the story of their enslavement and its lingering effects. “A Southerner of the upper class delighted in saying that he was taught his manners by his ‘Black Mammy,’” Jessie W. Parkhurst, the then-dean of women at the Tuskegee Institute, wrote in 1938. Many enslaved women who worked domestic roles were made to care for white children. Beginning in the antebellum era, they were caricatured as grateful and devoted caregivers, even as they were being underpaid and overworked. Long after the abolition of slavery, many white southerners, including my father, who was born into the first breaths of the civil-rights movement, were still raised by Black nannies. (This is true outside the South as well—the majority of domestic workers in America today are women of color.) My father, like many other white southerners, learned most of his manners from the nanny with whom he spent so many hours of his childhood. The courtesies shown in the region have long been “the product of the fusion of black and white attitudes,” Schwarz noted in his essay. But politeness was often forced on Black southerners because their lives depended on it: As recently as decades ago, any perceived violations of etiquette, including simply making eye contact with white people, could provoke brutal beatings and lynchings. And Black contributions to manners were rarely given equal import. After slavery was outlawed, Black women had limited employment prospects in the Jim Crow era and the years after, and they were usually severely underpaid. Today, the extent to which southerners are mannerly has evolved, as all things do. Some southerners lament what they see as a recent loss to their distinctive approach to etiquette, but this was already the case in 1897, when W. P. Trent wrote in this magazine, “We have seen that the Southerner’s basis of character is a fine one, and that he is becoming, year by year, more thoroughly nationalized.” He explained that “external manners have undoubtedly changed: there is now less suavity, less punctiliousness, less attention to small details, than of old; but this was true of the South of 1860 as compared with that of 1760, and means nothing but progress in the direction of greater freedom and individuality in conformity with the rest of the world.” Part of the reason could be that more people are moving to the South. In January, I wrote about the disappearing southern drawl, another aspect of the region’s culture that is noticeably changing. I noted that, according to the U.S. census, the South gained more residents than all other regions combined from 2023 to 2024. I also found that the proliferation of the internet has undeniably altered southern culture; young kids are exposed to different behaviors on social media, and their role models aren’t just nannies or teachers or parents—they now come in the form of content creators and online friends. These factors may be driving the shift in southern manners writ large. I’ve observed a generational difference even in my own family. My sisters still live in Tennessee, and I live in New York City, but none of us spends our days quite like our mother. She will make warm conversation with strangers whenever she possibly can. Living in a big city can often hurry me out of this habit. She’ll fill your plate a second or third time despite your saying you couldn’t possibly have another bite. I offer my guests a glass of wine and whatever nonperishable snack they can scavenge from the pantry. She will listen to a story she has heard hundreds of times with the enthusiasm of it being its first telling. My sisters and I don’t have this same patience. But time spent with my mother, who puts hours of care and kindness into daily interactions, always reminds me of the goodness to be found in doing the mannerly thing—in being inquisitive, leaving a kind note, shouting “How are ya?” at the neighbor, knowing that it may turn into a two-hour conversation. Sometimes these niceties are more than just nice. In an age of constant hurry, they’re also an excuse to slow down, if only for a moment.

item.title: The Terrible Movie That Chinese Audiences Can’t Stop Watching
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 2.21
One of the only compliments I can offer the new Chinese animated film Niu Lai is that it certainly qualifies as a film. There is sound. The pictures move. But beyond the basics of what makes a movie a movie, Niu Lai, which translates to “The Ox Comes,” contains little artistic merit. The plot, about a calf coming of age with the help of a leopard, a bird, and his mother, is thin, and the characters have been so nightmarishly rendered on a rudimentary computer program that they might as well be sleep-paralysis demons. Yet Niu Lai has become a bona fide box-office hit in China. Since a small distributor unceremoniously dumped it in theaters in early August, the film has become one of the most lucrative movies in Chinese history, making more than $7 million off a reported budget of no more than $500 and outperforming recent blockbusters such as The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Much of its success is thanks to Chinese social media, where clips of it first went viral: Some users have embraced Niu Lai as a meme, purchasing tickets so they could ridicule the baffling work with an audience. Others have championed the project as anti-AI art, arguing that it deserves to be appreciated as a purely human creation. As flawed as Niu Lai may be, to the fans, it’s at least better than AI slop. I’m not so sure about that. Watching a bootleg version of Niu Lai felt painful but apt: What better way was there to see a jankily made film than in potato quality on my computer at home? Instead, what’s distinctly human about Niu Lai comes from everything around it: how it was made, how it became a sensation, and how it has inspired further creativity in turn. Theater workers have drawn posters by hand to help advertise the movie. Businesses have made plush toys of the bovine hero. Fans have donned cow masks for screenings, and although the film isn’t available in the United States, underground viewings have popped up in major cities. As such, Niu Lai is the rare passion project that has attracted audiences not because it’s so bad that it’s good, but because it’s an occasion to celebrate the ability to have an original idea at all. Never mind that the idea was apparently underdeveloped from the start. The first-time director, Xin Yumeng, explained in an interview that he wanted to write about an ox because that’s his father’s zodiac symbol; the year he began working on it also happened to be 2021, the year of the ox. Production took five years, as the then-29-year-old Xin and his mother, Sun Lifang, wrote the screenplay together and made up the entire crew and cast: Sun sang the theme song, and Xin animated the 86-minute film frame by frame on SketchUp, an architectural-modeling program. The process was grueling, Xin said, adding that he kept going in part because he saw the story as a way to inspire viewers to not tang ping, or “lie flat,” referring to a societal trend in 2021 where young people in China rejected overworking by cheekily glorifying the act of lying down. In some ways, the movie is a deeply Chinese phenomenon: Fuzzy cartoon characters tend to become popular in the country—Zootopia 2 is the highest-grossing Hollywood film ever released there—and the words niu lai could also refer to the coming of a bull market, which has led some Chinese stock investors to purchase tickets for good luck. Plus, Niu Lai’s threadbare plot is rooted in the principle of filial piety, as the titular protagonist learns to respect and care for his mother. The Niu Lai phenomenon also seems to embody a phrase that’s gained traction lately in China: huo ren gan, which, translated literally, means “alive-human feeling.” The film expresses this quality, but not only because Xi didn’t use AI to help create it. What makes Niu Lai stand out most is its unabashed sincerity. It is an earnest attempt to tell a fable about a naive cow, and the story of its making is deeply charming: Here is a mother-son duo, total outsiders to the entertainment industry, trying their best to turn their quixotic idea into reality. Making a movie anywhere requires overcoming so many hurdles that have nothing to do with art or creativity; there are budgets to be balanced and business expectations to be met. But Niu Lai is a modest reminder that any film simply begins with an idea and an irrepressible urge to see it through.

item.title: A slow travel success story in Slovenia’s secret valley
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.25
The drive to Pedrovo is vertiginous, and each hairpin bend has me sending a silent prayer that we won’t meet a tractor coming the other way. When we near it, we abandon the car and continue on foot to the hamlet, a scattering of red-roofed, whitewashed houses high on the steep karst hillside. The air is warm and dry, scented with wild sage. We follow a hand-painted sign to Čilčevi Farmstead. Descending stone steps to a lush garden, we find a shaded table set with fresh cheeses produced at the farm’s own dairy. Below, the valley stretches in both directions, a wide flat plain hemmed in by steep mountain slopes, with the Vipava River winding lazily through fields and vineyards. If the Vipava valley gets a mention in a Slovenian guidebook, it’s usually as a wine region footnote. The area is an hour’s drive south-west of Ljubljana, meeting Italy at the cross-border city of Nova Gorica (called Gorizia on the Italian side). Most visitors skip it in favour of the Soča valley to the north, drawn to the turquoise river and opportunities for rafting on the rapids. Vipava is a landscape shaped by a strong wind, the burja, which barrels down from the Alps, keeping the red earth arid, the trees bent low, and creating the perfect terrain for dry wines and dried meats. Tourism has traditionally been less of a focus, but I’m here with my family to meet local entrepreneurs and producers, to learn how this valley is building a genuine visitor experience that works for the community. Part of the reason for the slow development of tourism has been the scarcity of accommodation, save a few nondescript business hotels and a handful of holiday cottages. One place that’s helping change that narrative is Wellba, a boutique guesthouse in the village of Planina, where an old abandoned farmstead has been converted into self-catering apartments and guest rooms by a local couple, working with traditional craftspeople and salvaged materials. Marko and Tereza Kobal grew up on this hillside and then worked in Ljubljana before deciding to return to build a family business, striving to create the kind of place they seek out when travelling. “People who travel want to experience something that is just the way it is, without embellishment, pretence, exaggeration – somewhere authentic,” says Marko. We enter Wellba through a traditional “black kitchen”, its walls darkened by generations of wood smoke. “When we came here the building needed work but it had a real soul. We want the building to stand for another 300 years, so we took the renovation slowly and carefully.” Our light, spacious accommodation wears its history lightly, with plenty of space for playing card games and reading books on the balcony, with views of the neighbouring farmyard and the valley beyond. Next door, another tumble-down farm building will be converted and opened in 2027. The couple are also working on a boutique hotel in Vipava town in the valley below. The dream is for their children to run Wellba one day, forging their futures in this valley. Across Vipava, similar small projects are emerging: small, family-run and developing slowly and thoughtfully. Tom Ločniškar and Borut Kokalj began Čilčevi Farmstead during the pandemic, having moved to Pedrovo and become interested in farming. “We started to keep animals. Now we have 150, which is too many animals for just a hobby,” laughs Tom. He recalls the mad panic to source equipment before the lockdowns began. The pandemic also brought him his first customers, people who were out walking and keen to support local businesses. Tom and Borut keep local Istrska sheep and Drežnica goats, which graze on dry karst grasslands, changing pastures across this hillside every four days. Having tasted fresh cheese straight from the chill of the dairy, including creamy goat’s cheese with fenugreek and buttery mature sheep’s cheese, we walk uphill to meet the goats. Tom says that in the early 1900s around 1,000 people lived in Pedrovo, but by the 1970s the permanent population had fallen to just two, and remained that low until the 1990s. “The village was almost abandoned because people moved to the cities,” he says. “It was the same in a lot of hill villages: life was hard and tractors didn’t work on steep slopes.” Today the population has risen to 20, with second homeowners roughly doubling that number in the holidays. Elsewhere in the village, I meet Alenka and Mark Smerajc, who were one of the first families to return, raising three children and running a business here. Today they have two small holiday cottages in what were farm outbuildings and run a relaxed courtyard restaurant for guests, opening to the public at weekends and for holidays. “People wanted food,” shrugs Alenka, as her teenage children help bring out beautiful plates of handmade pasta with local cheese and wild herbs from the kitchen. “In Vipava valley there was no tourism, so we got to decide how to build it,” says Jani Peljhan. That means GPS-guided cycling tours along roads too small to merit signposts, and experimenting with “wine trains”, carrying visitors from Nova Gorica to the vineyards with local winemakers on board to lead tasting sessions. Jani’s company, Wajdušna, also offers hiking and paragliding, both gaining in popularity here. He meets us at Wellba with some e-bikes and we pedal through Ajdovščina to spot Roman ruins, and up to Vipavski Križ, famed for being one of the smallest towns in Slovenia, before zigzagging back up the other side of the valley through vineyards. The warmth of the afternoon and the steep hillsides makes me appreciate the “sport” mode on the bikes. In other regions, wine tourism often means visitor centres and branded experiences. In Vipava it still means sitting in someone’s kitchen. At Vina Lisjak in Zalošče, I eat at a little restaurant run by two brothers. “We opened the restaurant to show the wine,” says Peter Lisjak. “It’s all from our farm.” We eat generous platters of house dried meat, aged mountain cheeses, a fennel frittata and slow-cooked celeriac steaks with celery pesto and spinach. Dishes are served family style and there’s plenty of time for stories, with samples of delicious wine straight from the barrels in the cellar. From Wellba, we walk across the village to Ferjančič vineyard, where seventh generation winemaker Matic Ferjančič talks us through his wines. His father developed the vineyard, going from five to 50,000 plants. “We work hard in the vineyard to make it easy in the cellar,” he says. As we chat, Matic keeps an ear to the baby monitor for the eighth generation sleeping upstairs. Although many of my favourite restaurant experiences are the simple ones, Vipava valley cuisine can reach loftier heights. One night we smarten up the best we can and follow a winding road uphill to Zemono Manor, to eat at Gostilna Pri Lojzetu. Chef Tomaž Kavčič is known as a Slovenian slow food pioneer, and has earned a Michelin star for his playful dishes and proud use of local ingredients. We eat delicate Vipava river trout with fermented apricots from the previous summer, and langoustine bisque from the coast. Traditional dishes such as jota, a sauerkraut and potato stew, are honoured on the menu, their humble roots celebrated not hidden. There are some theatrics, like a juniper plant producing flavoured vapour to complement a sorbet, but the restaurant atmosphere is friendly and relaxed. The server chats with my young stepson about his preferences, and brings him a generous bowl of gnocchi. It’s Kavčič’s night off so he sits with friends and a bottle of wine at the back of the restaurant, coming round all the tables frequently to chat. Vipava may not remain overlooked for ever. But talking to the people building businesses here, there is little appetite for becoming the next famous wine destination. What they seem to want instead is something rarer and more interesting: tourism that helps a place thrive without changing what made it worth visiting in the first place. The trip was provided by Vipava Valley Tourism and the Slovenian Tourist Board. Wellba Planina has doubles from £97

item.title: Check your accounts — Amex offering elevated referral bonuses of up to 45,000 points for select cardmembers
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 6.13
Check your accounts — Amex offering elevated referral bonuses of up to 45,000 points for select cardmembers If you're a current holder of the American Express Platinum Card® or the American Express® Gold Card, you may want to check your accounts. Some of us here at TPG are seeing elevated referral bonuses — as high as 45,000 points. This can let you take home a large chunk of Membership Rewards points just by referring others to your card. Here's what you need to know about these offers. Elevated Amex referral offers we're seeing In case you're not aware, American Express allows you to share referral links with your friends and family members. If they apply and are approved through those links, they can receive their own welcome bonuses (after satisfying the minimum spending requirements), while you'll receive your own one-time bonus. While these usually fall into the range of 10,000 to 15,000 points or miles, select cardholders may see significantly higher bonus amounts right now. For example, I have an offer to earn 45,000 points on my Amex Platinum for each eligible referral. I also have an offer to earn 40,000 points on my Amex Gold for each eligible referral. Applicants using those links may be eligible for the following welcome offers on those cards: - Amex Platinum: Find out your offer and see if you're eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. - Amex Gold: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 100,000 bonus points after spending $8,000 on purchases in your first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer. Your referral can apply for a different Amex card Each card allows you to earn a referral bonus up to five times per calendar year. Even better? Your friend or family member doesn't even need to get the card that you sent them a referral for. Here's the relevant FAQ from American Express' referral page: Do I have to refer my friend to the same card I have? No. A referred friend will typically be taken to a product page for the same American Express card associated with the referral link. However, they can explore other available American Express cards and choose the card that best fits their needs by navigating to the personal cards or business cards tab. As long as the referred friend remains within the referral link and gets an available American Express card, the referring card member could earn a referral bonus. The available American Express cards presented through a referral link may vary based on the referring card member's account and other eligibility considerations. For example, let's say I send my Amex Platinum referral link to a friend, but he's actually interested in a Delta cobranded card — especially since those just launched limited-time welcome offers, available now through Nov. 4. If he clicks my referral link, he'll likely land on this page: However, if he clicks on Personal Cards at the top of the page, he can now select the Delta card he wants. If he applies and is approved for that card, he'd be eligible for the Delta offer, while I would still receive the 45,000 Membership Rewards points as a referral bonus. Related: American Express Membership Rewards: How to earn, redeem and transfer points How to check your offer and generate a referral link There are two ways to generate a referral link. The easiest option is to use this link, log in to your American Express account and then navigate to the relevant card. You'll see the offer on your account, and at the right-hand side, there's the option to email a potential applicant directly or generate a link that can be copied and pasted elsewhere. Alternatively, you can log into your American Express account, navigate to the relevant card, and look for either the Refer a Friend section or the "Refer a Friend. Earn Rewards." link at the right-hand side of the page. Share your links in the comments below If you're an existing cardholder and see these elevated bonuses in your account(s), we'd love to help share the love with our audience. Please feel free to post your Gold or Platinum referral links in the comments below, but only if you're eligible for a higher-than-normal referral bonus. Then, for anyone who applies using someone's link, please give that comment a thumbs up. If you see comments with five of those, move on to someone else, as those readers have maxed out their referral bonuses. Bottom line Referring your friends and family to your existing cards can be a great way to earn extra points or miles, and right now, we're seeing elevated offers for select Amex Platinum and Amex Gold cardmembers. If you're targeted, remember that the person you refer may be able to select another eligible Amex card through your referral link while you still earn the referral bonus associated with your card. However, there's no telling how long these will be around — so if you're hoping to share these links, we strongly recommend doing so now before it's too late. To learn more, check out our full review of the Amex Platinum and full review of the Amex Gold.

item.title: Rove adds dining and in-store rewards in major platform expansion
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.68
Rove adds dining and in-store rewards in major platform expansion Rove launched in April 2025 as a loyalty program that lets you earn transferable travel rewards not tied to a credit card. So far, Rove members have been able to earn miles on flight bookings, hotel reservations, gift card purchases and online shopping. And Rove has grown its roster of transfer partners to 20 over the 16 months since its launch. But on Aug. 28, Rove announced several major enhancements, including the introduction of Rove Dining and in-store card-linked offers. Here's what you should know. Not a Rove member yet? Sign up through this link and earn a referral bonus of 1,500 miles, with the opportunity to earn an additional 5,000 miles when making your first hotel booking over $500 as a new user with the code "BRIANKELLY500." View this post on Instagram Earn miles with Rove Dining Perhaps the biggest news for Rove users is the launch of Rove Dining. This new way to earn Rove miles is available at thousands of restaurants; you can search for participating restaurants near you using the Rove website or app. Rove Dining is available at launch in select cities, but Rove has plans to expand the offering to additional cities and restaurants. To earn Rove miles when dining at participating restaurants, follow these steps: - Link an eligible payment card to your Rove account. (You likely want to use one of the best cards for dining.) - Dine at a participating restaurant. - Pay your bill at the restaurant using your linked card. Rove declined to tell TPG which network powers Rove Dining. So, it's unclear at this point whether linking a card to Rove Dining will unlink it from Rewards Network programs like AAdvantage Dining. As such, be sure to read the terms when linking a card to your Rove account, and watch for any emails that say your cards have been unlinked from other dining rewards programs. Related: The credit card checklist that saves me hundreds on date nights Earn Rove miles with in-store card-linked offers You could previously earn Rove miles when shopping online, but now you can also earn them on in-store purchases at participating retailers when you use an eligible card that's linked to your Rove account. The initial set of participating retailers is limited, but Rove says it plans to expand its in-store card-linked offers to thousands of retail locations. Likewise, Rove said in-store shopping is being rolled out on a per-account basis, so don't be alarmed if you don't see it in your account yet. Rove told TPG that users may need to activate offers for some merchants. However, according to a Rove spokesperson, this will be the exception rather than the norm; users usually won't need to activate any offers before using a linked card at a participating retailer. Rove said it also plans to launch personalized offers that members can enroll in to earn more miles per dollar spent at select merchants. Enjoy a redesigned hotel booking experience One of the easiest ways to earn Rove miles has been booking hotels. But if you've searched for hotels through Rove in the past, you know doing so has had some quirks and annoyances. Luckily, Rove has overhauled its Rove Hotels platform and says users will now enjoy: - Stronger mileage earning opportunities - Tens of thousands of additional properties - More detailed room and property information - Clearer bedding information before booking Rove said it has also significantly expanded its loyalty-eligible hotel rates, noting it now has "around 99% hotel coverage within eligible chain properties." Loyalty-eligible rates let users earn Rove miles while remaining eligible for applicable benefits through the hotel's loyalty program. And if you use Rove Hotels on the app, you can try out an artificial intelligence-powered feature to get answers to common questions about specific hotel properties. Access Rove's newly launched iOS app and Android public beta Rove is officially launching its iOS app, which had previously been in beta. Plus, an Android version of the Rove app is now also available via public beta. Rove says the app brings its "core earning and travel tools into a single mobile experience." This means you can use the Rove app to track your Rove miles, buy gift cards, find restaurants that participate in Rove Dining, book travel and more. Related: These 14 apps and websites make award redemptions easier to find Earn Rove miles instantly when buying gift cards One of the most compelling ways Rove has marketed itself is the idea of booking a nonrefundable hotel and earning enough Rove miles instantly to book your flight to that hotel. Well, now you can also earn Rove miles instantly when you buy eligible gift cards from select brands. This instant earning may be useful if you only need a few more Rove miles for a particular travel booking or transfer. For example, if you want to transfer 15,000 miles to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club to book an award but only have 14,500 Rove miles in your account, you could buy a gift card that would let you earn at least 500 miles instantly. Of course, you'll want to ensure the gift card you're buying is eligible for instant earnings and that it's for something you'll naturally use. And if you don't see any brands you like offering instant earnings, check back in the coming weeks and months, as Rove plans to add more brands to its collection of instant-earn gift cards. Use Rove's new Safari extensions and upgraded Chrome extension Finally, Rove has also debuted new Chrome and Safari browser extensions for online shopping. The Safari browser extension is new, while the Chrome one is an improvement over the previous one, as Rove says it includes "thousands of additional stores, increased earning opportunities, and thousands more coupon codes." Members can also enjoy a mobile Safari extension that's connected to the Rove iOS app. These extensions help alert members to ways they can earn Rove miles on purchases, so they can shop as usual without having to click through Rove before shopping with a specific merchant. Bottom line This expansion gives Rove members more ways to earn miles without changing how they spend, particularly through the new dining program and card-linked in-store offers. The revamped hotel platform, instant-earning gift cards and new app and browser tools should also make the program easier to use. Just pay particular attention when linking cards for dining and in-store offers, as doing so may affect your ability to use other card-linked programs. And if you aren't a Rove member yet, be sure to sign up through this link to earn a referral bonus of 1,500 miles. You can also earn an additional 5,000 miles when making your first hotel booking over $500 as a new user with the code "BRIANKELLY500."

item.title: United's Airbus A321XLR is about to make its (domestic) debut: Here are the routes
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.27
United's Airbus A321XLR is about to make its (domestic) debut: Here are the routes Who doesn't like that new-plane smell? United Airlines travelers can look forward to the scent onboard its brand-new Airbus A321XLRs when they begin flying in September. Ahead of the new aircraft's global debut in December, you can experience the new long-range narrow-body aircraft on some domestic services. United will christen the XLR on flights from its Dulles International Airport (IAD) hub to San Diego International Airport (SAN) on Sept. 9 and to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) on Oct. 1, a spokesperson confirmed Friday. Long-range aircraft goes domestic (for now) The XLRs are United's newest plane. They're designed especially for longer flights, with 20 lie-flat Polaris business-class suites up front in a 1-1 layout. There are also 12 Premium Plus (premium economy) recliners arranged in a 2-2 layout. In the back are 34 extra-legroom Economy Plus seats in a 3-3 layout — except for four seats where the middle seat is blocked — along with 84 standard economy seats. There's even a snack bar for all passengers at the back of the cabin. United has orders for 50 XLRs that will primarily fly transatlantic flights from its IAD and Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) hubs. The airline will shift the XLR to long-haul flights Dec. 1 when it begins flying daily between IAD and both Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS) and Dublin Airport (DUB). And, next summer, the XLR is headlining United's blockbuster 2027 transatlantic expansion, flying five of nine new routes, including to Ibiza, Spain; Luxembourg; and Toulouse, France. But for the next few months, the plane will operate some transcontinental service domestically — something executives had suggested this week could happen, albeit on a temporary basis. Booking United's new Airbus A321XLR For anyone looking to fly on the XLR before its international debut, MileagePlus award tickets are available on IAD-SAN for as few as 12,700 miles in economy for Sept. 9. And, if they are lucky, travelers can snag one of the new premium economy seats sold as just an extra-legroom economy option. First-class seats are available later in September, starting at 85,000 miles. Bottom line United ultimately plans to focus its new XLR on long-haul international service. But with its luxe new domestic airplane delayed and crews still adapting to this new aircraft, it's not surprising to see the new aircraft make its debut on the domestic front — at least for a few months. item.title: Frontier makes it easier to earn top-tier elite status in 2027 but cuts earning rates for basic fares and noncardholders
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.42
Frontier makes it easier to earn top-tier elite status in 2027 but cuts earning rates for basic fares and noncardholders Frontier Airlines has announced a host of changes to its Frontier Miles loyalty program that will make it easier to earn top-tier Elite Diamond status in 2027, as well as new and enhanced benefits for all elite members and bonus miles for cardholders. But there's some unpleasant news for passengers who often book basic fares and companion travelers. Effective immediately, Frontier has lowered the number of elite status points required to earn Elite Diamond status from 100,000 to 75,000. That means members who earn 75,000 points in 2026 can enjoy Elite Diamond status in 2027. The 2026 qualification requirements for Elite Silver, Elite Gold and Elite Platinum remain unchanged at 10,000, 20,000 and 50,000 points, respectively. However, beginning Jan. 1, 2027, the Elite Silver requirement will increase to 15,000 points, while the Elite Gold qualification threshold will rise to 25,000 points. Elite Platinum status will continue to require 50,000 points. There's good news for all elite members in 2027 with the following new or enhanced status benefits: - Elite Silver (requires 15,000 elite status points): Enjoy new space-available, complimentary upgrades to UpFront Plus or first class four hours before departure when you buy an Economy or Premium bundle, plus complimentary upgrades as a status holder to preferred seating when you buy an Economy bundle. - Elite Gold (requires 25,000 elite status points): Enjoy new space-available, complimentary upgrades to UpFront Plus or first class eight hours before departure when you buy an Economy or Premium bundle, plus complimentary upgrades as a status holder to premium seating when you buy an Economy bundle. - Elite Platinum (requires 50,000 elite status points): Enjoy new space-available, complimentary upgrades to UpFront Plus or first class 18 hours before departure when you buy an Economy or Premium bundle, plus complimentary upgrades for each person on your booking to premium seating when you buy an Economy bundle. The checked bag allowance for each traveler on the booking will also increase from 40 to 50 pounds. However, Elite Platinum members will lose their current unlimited companion travel benefit and instead receive two companion travel certificates. - Elite Diamond (requires 75,000 elite status points, down from 100,000): Enjoy new space-available complimentary upgrades to UpFront Plus or first class 24 hours before departure when you buy an Economy or Premium bundle. The existing allowance of two free checked bags for each traveler on the booking will also increase from 40 to 50 pounds per bag. As an additional program improvement for the 2027 program year, Frontier will add milestone rewards, where Frontier Miles elite members at each tier will be able to select additional perks and rewards on top of the elite status benefits above. The airline says details of these perks will be revealed later in 2026. Frontier Miles will also change how many miles you earn per dollar spent on both basic fares and bundles starting Sept. 1. The changes are particularly bad news for noncardholders. As for Frontier Airlines World Mastercard® cardholders, they'll earn more on bundles but less on basic fares. The information for the Frontier Airlines World Mastercard has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Here are the mileage earning rates for basic fare bookings made now and for bookings made from Sept. 1: | Frontier Miles status | Current: No cobranded credit card | From Sept. 1: No cobranded credit card | Current: Cobranded credit card member | From Sept. 1: Cobranded credit card member | |---|---|---|---|---| | Member | 10 miles per dollar spent | 1 mile per dollar spent | 15 miles per dollar spent | 9 miles per dollar spent | | Elite Silver | 12 miles per dollar spent | 3 miles per dollar spent | 17 miles per dollar spent | 11 miles per dollar spent | | Elite Gold | 14 miles per dollar spent | 5 miles per dollar spent | 19 miles per dollar spent | 13 miles per dollar spent | | Elite Platinum | 16 miles per dollar spent | 7 miles per dollar spent | 21 miles per dollar spent | 15 miles per dollar spent | | Elite Diamond | 20 miles per dollar spent | 11 miles per dollar spent | 25 miles per dollar spent | 19 miles per dollar spent | As you can see, Frontier will slash the number of miles all noncardholder members, including top-tier elite members, earn on basic fares while also reducing the number of miles cardholders will earn on this fare type from Sept. 1. For members purchasing Economy, Premium or Business bundles, the following are the earning rates now and for bookings made from Sept. 1: | Frontier Miles status | Current: No cobranded credit card | From Sept. 1: No cobranded credit card | Current: Cobranded credit card member | From Sept. 1: Cobranded credit card member | |---|---|---|---|---| | Member | 10 miles per dollar spent | 6 miles per dollar spent | 15 miles per dollar spent | 17 miles per dollar spent | | Elite Silver | 12 miles per dollar spent | 8 miles per dollar spent | 17 miles per dollar spent | 19 miles per dollar spent | | Elite Gold | 14 miles per dollar spent | 10 miles per dollar spent | 19 miles per dollar spent | 21 miles per dollar spent | | Elite Platinum | 16 miles per dollar spent | 12 miles per dollar spent | 21 miles per dollar spent | 23 miles per dollar spent | | Elite Diamond | 20 miles per dollar spent | 16 miles per dollar spent | 25 miles per dollar spent | 27 miles per dollar spent | This means members without a cobranded card will earn less on bundles, though the reduction is not as severe as with basic fares. Cardholders will see a slight increase in the number of miles they earn. Both tables include the additional 5 Frontier miles per dollar earned when eligible purchases are made with the Frontier Airlines World Mastercard. Related: Frontier Airlines' planes set for big upgrade: Starlink Wi-Fi coming in 2027 Bottom line These program changes to Frontier Miles announced by Frontier Airlines are mostly positive, especially if you have a cobranded card. There are genuine benefit improvements at every tier, and top-tier Elite Diamond status is now much easier to earn. The airline is clearly trying to incentivize members not to book the cheapest fare type, severely reducing mileage earning rates, especially for noncobranded cardholders, a growing trend among U.S. airline loyalty programs. The higher earning rates for cardholders purchasing bundles are welcome, though noncardholders are somewhat penalized, even when purchasing the most expensive fare type. If you fly Frontier regularly (especially enough to reach any elite status level and enjoy all those new perks in 2027), it's a good time to consider the Frontier Airlines World Mastercard, as you'll earn more miles than noncardholders at every status level and on every fare type when booking flights from Sept. 1 on.

item.title: Delta Amex current offers: Earn up to 200,000 SkyMiles with these offers
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.15
Delta Amex current offers: Earn up to 200,000 SkyMiles with these offers Editor's Note Delta Air Lines and American Express have launched a new round of limited-time welcome offers across their cobranded credit card lineup. Together, they offer a slate of cards for everyone from occasional flyers to frequent travelers. Depending on the card, new cardmembers can earn thousands of SkyMiles, statement credits or even round-trip Delta Comfort flight certificates, making now a potentially great time to add a Delta card to your wallet. Keep in mind that you'll have the best shot at approval if your credit score is in the good-to-excellent range. These offers run through Nov. 4, so let's break down what's available and which Delta Amex may be the best fit for you. Comparing Delta credit card welcome offers Here's an overview of the offers at first glance: | Card | Welcome offer | Annual fee | Bonus value* | |---|---|---|---| | | Earn two domestic round-trip Delta Comfort Flight Certificates (valid for travel to the U.S. 48, Puerto Rico, or the U.S. Virgin Islands) and 50,000 bonus miles after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. A 21+ day advance purchase is required; up to $80 per person in taxes and fees apply. Other restrictions apply. Offer ends Nov. 4. | | $600 in miles, plus the value of the two round-trip Delta Comfort flight certificates | | | Apply and find out if your welcome offer is as high as 90,000 bonus miles, plus earn a $300 statement credit after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. You may not be eligible for the maximum offer amount. Offer ends Nov. 4. | | Up to $1,380, including the value of the statement credit | | | Apply and find out if your welcome offer is as high as 80,000 bonus miles, plus earn a $250 statement credit after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. You may not be eligible for the maximum offer amount. Offer ends Nov. 4. | | Up to $1,210, including the value of the statement credit | | | Earn 10,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. | | $120 | | | Earn 200,000 bonus miles after spending $20,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Nov. 4. | | $2,400 | | | Earn 100,000 bonus miles after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Nov. 4. | | $1,200 | | | Earn 90,000 bonus miles after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Nov. 4. | | $1,080 | *Bonus value is based on TPG's August 2026 valuations and is not provided or reviewed by the issuer. Who is eligible for Delta American Express cards? American Express has a few eligibility rules to keep in mind before applying for one of these cards. For starters, Amex typically only allows a person to earn one welcome bonus per card in their lifetime. That means you'll want to prioritize applying when a card offers an elevated, limited-time offer, such as the ones all but one of these cards have right now. You also may not be eligible for a welcome bonus on a personal Delta Amex card if you have or previously had a higher-tier Delta Amex card. For example, if you have or previously had the Delta Reserve Amex, you may not be eligible for the welcome offers on the Delta Blue, Delta Gold or Delta Platinum. Delta's business Amex cards are not subject to this same "family rule." Amex may consider other factors when determining your eligibility, including your income, credit score and history with the issuer. Fortunately, you'll generally find out whether you're eligible for a welcome offer before accepting the card. Delta personal cards Delta offers four personal cards. The card that is right for you depends on how frequently you fly with Delta and how much you're willing to pay for an annual fee. Let's take a look at what differentiates each of the Delta SkyMiles personal cards. Delta SkyMiles Reserve Best for: Delta loyalists or those who want Sky Club access (subject to limitations) The Delta SkyMiles Reserve is ideal for hardcore Delta fans and frequent flyers. Current welcome offer: Earn two domestic round-trip Delta Comfort Flight Certificates (valid for travel to the U.S. 48, Puerto Rico, or the U.S. Virgin Islands) and 50,000 bonus miles after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. A 21+ day advance purchase is required; up to $80 per person in taxes and fees apply. Other restrictions apply. Offer ends Nov. 4. This bonus is worth $600 in miles, plus the value of the two round-trip Delta Comfort flight certificates, according to TPG's valuations. This is the first time flight certificates have been included in a welcome offer. It's somewhat difficult to compare this offer to the welcome offers we've seen for this card in recent history, since its full valuation will vary widely depending on how you redeem the two round-trip flight certificates. If you frequently fly with Delta within the U.S., now may be a great time to apply. Plus, if you can maximize them for at least $450 each, this would be considered the best-ever offer on this card. Annual fee: $650 Key benefits: Delta's premium consumer credit card offers a range of valuable perks. For loyal Delta flyers who enjoy visiting the Sky Club, this card can pay for itself through lounge access, spending boosts and other benefits. With this card, you'll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline. Plus, you'll enjoy a slew of Delta-related perks, including: - Access to complimentary upgrades (for non-Medallions) and priority boarding - Annual companion certificate upon card renewal for round-trip travel in first class, Comfort or Main Cabin within the U.S. (including Alaska and Hawaii) as well as other select destinations. (Delta Basic experiences are not eligible for this benefit.) - Complimentary access to American Express Centurion Lounges when flying on a same-day Delta flight with a ticket purchased on the card - Delta Sky Club access, plus four one-time guest passes each year (you'll receive 15 visits per year; earn an unlimited number of visits when you spend $75,000 or more between Jan. 1 and Dec. 31 of each calendar year) - Earn 1 Medallion Qualification Dollar per $10 spent on your card, plus 2,500 MQDs at the start of each Medallion qualification year - Two free checked bags, first checked bag free worldwide, second on U.S. domestic Delta flights - 15% off award redemptions for Delta flights for eligible cardmembers (when paying taxes and fees with this card and booking through delta.com or the Fly Delta app) To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Reserve. Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Reserve American Express Card Delta SkyMiles Platinum Best for: Frequent Delta flyers If you fly frequently with Delta but can't justify the pricier Delta SkyMiles Reserve, the Delta SkyMiles Platinum is worth considering. Current welcome offer: Apply and find out if your welcome offer is as high as 90,000 bonus miles, plus earn a $300 statement credit after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. You may not be eligible for the maximum offer amount. Offer ends Nov. 4. Per TPG's valuations, this bonus is worth up to $1,380, including the value of the statement credit. Thanks to the statement credit, this is one of the most valuable welcome offers we've ever seen for this card, so now is an excellent time to apply. Annual fee: $350 Key benefits: This card is a good option if you fly Delta regularly and want to earn miles on purchases and reach elite status. However, even if you aren't pursuing status, the companion certificate alone can make the annual fee for this card worth it. With this card, you'll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline. It also includes the following perks: - Annual companion certificate upon card renewal for Main Cabin round-trip flights within the U.S. (including Alaska and Hawaii), as well as destinations in Mexico, and select destinations. (Delta Basic experiences are not eligible for this benefit.) - Earn 1 MQD for every $20 spent on your card, plus a 2,500 MQD Headstart at the beginning of each Medallion qualification year - Priority boarding - Two free checked bags, first checked bag free worldwide, second on U.S. domestic Delta flights - 15% off award redemptions for Delta flights for eligible cardmembers (when paying taxes and fees with this card and booking through delta.com or the Fly Delta app) To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Platinum. Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Platinum American Express Card Delta SkyMiles Gold Best for: Occasional Delta flyers or those test-driving a Delta card If you want to take advantage of a welcome bonus but don't fly Delta frequently, the Delta SkyMiles Gold is a strong option. Current welcome offer: Apply and find out if your welcome offer is as high as 80,000 bonus miles, plus earn a $250 statement credit after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. You may not be eligible for the maximum offer amount. Offer ends Nov. 4. TPG's valuations place this bonus at up to $1,210, including the value of the statement credit. The addition of the statement credit makes this the most valuable offer we've seen on this card, so now is a great time to apply. Annual fee: $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150 Key benefits: This card is ideal for occasional Delta flyers seeking a few extra perks when flying with the airline. With this card, you'll earn 2 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline. Other perks include: - Two free checked bags, first checked bag free worldwide, second on U.S. domestic Delta flights - Priority boarding - $200 Delta flight credit annually after spending $10,000 in a calendar year - 20% inflight discount (in the form of a statement credit) - 15% off award redemptions for Delta flights for eligible cardmembers (when paying taxes and fees with this card and booking through delta.com or the Fly Delta app) To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Gold. Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Gold American Express Card Delta SkyMiles Blue Best for: Infrequent Delta flyers If you want an entry-level card to start earning SkyMiles and fly less frequently with Delta, then Delta SkyMiles Blue is the card for you. Current welcome offer: Earn 10,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. According to TPG's valuations, these miles are worth $120. The SkyMiles Blue typically doesn't receive an elevated offer, so we recommend applying whenever you're ready. Annual fee: $0 Key benefits: As a no-annual-fee card, it offers fewer benefits than the others. Still, there are some simple perks for cardmembers. With this card, you'll earn 2 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline. Other benefits include: - Pay with Miles (take up to $50 off the cost of your flight for every 5,000 miles you redeem when booking on delta.com) - 20% inflight discount (in the form of a statement credit) To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Blue. Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Blue American Express Card Delta business cards If you own a small business or have a side hustle through which you pay business expenses, one of these offers may be a great addition to your work wallet. Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business Best for: Business owners who exclusively fly with Delta As the most expensive business card Delta offers, the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business comes packed with great perks for Delta loyalists. Current welcome offer: Earn 200,000 bonus miles after spending $20,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Nov. 4. Per TPG's valuations, this bonus is worth $2,400. This is by far the highest welcome bonus we've seen on this card, topping the previous high by 75,000 miles. If the card is already a good fit for your business, we'd recommend taking advantage of this offer. Just be sure to keep the high spending requirement in mind. Annual fee: $650 Key benefits: This card offers a range of useful perks for Delta-loyal small-business owners. With this card, you'll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on purchases made directly with Delta. Its suite of Delta-related benefits includes: - Access to complimentary upgrades (when available) for non-Medallion members and priority boarding - Annual companion certificate upon card renewal for round-trip travel in first class, Comfort or Main Cabin within the U.S. (including Alaska and Hawaii) as well as other select routes, including some destinations in Mexico. (Delta Basic experiences are not eligible for this benefit.) - Complimentary access to American Express Centurion Lounges when flying on a same-day Delta flight with a ticket purchased using the card (up to two guests may also enter for a fee of $50 each) - Delta Sky Club access (you'll receive 15 visits per year; earn an unlimited number of visits when you spend $75,000 or more between Jan. 1 and Dec. 31 of each calendar year) - Earn 1 MQD per $10 spent on your card, plus 2,500 MQDs at the start of each Medallion qualification year - Two free checked bags, first checked bag free worldwide, second on U.S. domestic Delta flights - 15% off award redemptions for Delta flights for eligible cardmembers (when paying taxes and fees with this card and booking through delta.com or the Fly Delta app) To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business. Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business American Express Card Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business Best for: Business owners who fly frequently with Delta Business owners who are looking for a good mid-tier airline business card should consider the Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business for its earnings potential and benefits. Current welcome offer: Earn 100,000 bonus miles after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Nov. 4. According to TPG's valuations, this offer is worth $1,200. We've seen this 100,000-mile offer several times before, but it remains one of the highest we've seen on the card. If you've been considering the Delta Platinum Business, now could be a good time to apply. Annual fee: $350 Key benefits: This is a solid mid-tier option for business owners who travel with Delta semi-frequently. With this card, you'll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline. Other Delta-related perks include: - Annual companion certificate each year upon card renewal for Main Cabin round-trip flights within the U.S. (including Alaska and Hawaii), as well as other select routes, including some destinations in Mexico. (Delta Basic experiences are not eligible for this benefit.) - Complimentary upgrades (when available) for non-Medallion members and priority boarding - Earn 1 MQD for every $20 spent on your card, plus a 2,500 MQD Headstart at the beginning of each Medallion qualification year - Two free checked bags, first checked bag free worldwide, second on U.S. domestic Delta flights - 15% off award redemptions for Delta flights for eligible cardmembers (when paying taxes and fees with this card and booking through delta.com or the Fly Delta app) To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business. Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business American Express Card Delta SkyMiles Gold Business Best for: Business owners who fly occasionally with Delta The Delta SkyMiles Gold Business is ideal for smaller businesses or business owners who aren't Delta loyalists. Current welcome offer: Earn 90,000 bonus miles after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Nov. 4. The bonus is worth $1,080 when factoring in TPG's valuations. This offer pops up fairly frequently, but it's among the highest we've seen for this card. If you're looking to add it to your business's wallet, now may be a good time. Annual fee: $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150 Key benefits: Even if they don't fly Delta often, small-business owners can still benefit from this card's perks. With this card, you'll earn 2 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline. Other perks include: - Two free checked bags, first checked bag free worldwide, second on U.S. domestic Delta flights - Priority boarding - Up to $200 annual Delta flight credit after spending $10,000 in a calendar year - 20% inflight discount (in the form of a statement credit) - 15% off award redemptions for Delta flights for eligible cardmembers (when paying taxes and fees with this card and booking through delta.com or the Fly Delta app) To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Gold Business. Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Gold Business American Express Card Which Delta credit card is right for you? With a full lineup of Delta cards, you may wonder how to pick the best offer for your needs. While it might be tempting to go with the highest offer, you should also consider its long-term value to your wallet. The good news is that many of these offers can be a great fit, depending on your travel habits. As a round-up: - Reserve: Loyal Delta flyers who want lounge access - Platinum: Regular Delta flyers - Gold: Occasional Delta flyers - Blue: Infrequent Delta flyers Bottom line Delta and American Express offer a wide range of cobranded cards, whether you fly with the airline occasionally or are a frequent Delta loyalist. With elevated welcome offers available on nearly every card right now, there are some compelling opportunities to earn a significant stash of SkyMiles. Just remember that American Express has a once-per-card, per-lifetime rule for welcome offers. If you've had a particular Delta Amex before, or, in some cases, a higher-tier personal Delta card, you may not be eligible for that card's welcome offer. These limited-time offers end Nov. 4, so if one of the Delta Amex cards is already a good fit for your travel habits, now could be a fantastic time to apply.
