item.title: Who should (and shouldn’t) get the Capital One Venture X card?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.48
Who should (and shouldn’t) get the Capital One Venture X card? Editor's Note Since it first appeared on the scene back in 2021, the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card quickly became one of the top travel rewards credit cards. It offers tons of valuable perks, from lounge access and annual travel statement credits to anniversary bonus miles and a solid return on everyday spending. That said, the card also carries a $395 annual fee, so you'll want to make sure you'll get enough from its benefits to justify keeping it year after year. Here's how to decide whether the Venture X is right for you or whether a less-expensive option like the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card might be a better fit. Capital One Venture X decision guide — the quick version Here's a quick decision tree for whether the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card is right for you. The Venture X is probably a good fit for you if … - You travel at least a few times a year. - You can use the card's $300 annual travel credit. - You want premium travel perks without juggling numerous statement credits. - You value airport lounge access. - You like earning transferable points that you can redeem with several airlines and hotels. The Venture X is probably not a good fit for you if … - You rarely travel. - You want a credit card with a low annual fee. - You prefer earning cash back. - You want lounge access at the widest range of airports. - You don't expect to use enough of the card's benefits to justify its $395 annual fee. Related: 6 things to do when you get the Capital One Venture X card Who should get the Venture X? The Venture X works particularly well for travelers who can use its core benefits without going out of their way to do so. You travel frequently and can use the annual travel credit The single most valuable benefit of the Venture X is its up to $300 annual travel credit. Every year you have the card, starting with your first year, you get up to $300 in credits to put toward things like airfare, hotel bookings and car rentals. The only condition is that you have to book your travel through Capital One Travel. If you already spend at least $300 on travel each year and are comfortable booking through Capital One Travel, this benefit can offset a significant portion of the card's $395 annual fee. You want transferable miles Capital One miles are a very dynamic type of travel rewards currency. You can redeem them at a value of one cent apiece for bookings made through Capital One Travel, or apply them as a statement credit toward travel purchases you make with your Venture X card within 90 days. TPG's August 2026 valuations tag the value of Capital One miles at 1.85 cents apiece, largely because you can transfer them to 15+ airline and hotel partners, including Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue and Accor Live Limitless. If you're willing to learn these programs and search for award availability, the Venture X can be a strong fit. Related: Capital One airline and hotel transfer partners: How to maximize your miles You value (and can use) airport lounge access The Venture X gives the primary cardholder access to Capital One Lounges and Landings and the ability to enroll in a Priority Pass membership for access to 1,300-plus participating lounges worldwide. If you regularly travel through airports with Capital One locations, and have time to visit a lounge, this benefit can be tremendously helpful. But if you rarely fly through these specific airports and have tight connections, then you won't get much use out of it. Keep in mind that Capital One's guest-access policies have become less generous, so travelers who frequently visit lounges with family or friends should consider that when evaluating the benefit. And, like other airport lounges, Capital One's do get crowded, but at least you can join a virtual waiting list so you're not stuck queuing up for a long time before heading in. Related: A complete guide to Capital One's airport lounges: What to know in 2026 You value travel protections and expedited airport security The Venture X comes with a statement credit of up to $120 for a TSA PreCheck or Global Entry application fee once every four years. If you already receive this benefit from another card, you can use your Venture X to pay for someone else's eligible application. The Venture X also includes a suite of travel and purchase protections, including trip cancellation and interruption insurance, trip delay reimbursement, primary rental car coverage and cellphone protection. These benefits can provide meaningful value when things go wrong, particularly if you travel frequently and use the card to pay for eligible purchases. If you don't take too many trips, though, then this card might not be worth it for you. Related: 5 of the most underrated travel rewards cards You want simplicity in a premium card Part of what makes the Venture X card so attractive is how simple its rewards-earning formula is. On the earning side, the card accrues: - 10 miles per dollar spent on hotels and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel - 5 miles per dollar spent on flights and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel - 2 miles per dollar spent on all other eligible purchases The 2-miles-per-dollar earning rate on other eligible purchases also makes the Venture X an easy catch-all card. My husband and I use it for purchases that don't earn bonus rewards on our other cards, such as car repairs, dry cleaning and insurance. The straightforward travel statement credit, anniversary bonus miles and a strong base earning rate makes the Venture X appealing if you want premium travel benefits without managing numerous bonus categories or monthly and quarterly credits. Related: The best premium credit cards: A side-by-side comparison Who shouldn't get the Venture X? The Venture X is an impressive card, but paying a $395 annual fee doesn't make sense if its biggest benefits don't match your travel habits. You want a lower annual fee While the Venture X's $395 annual fee is less than those of some other premium cards, it's still substantial. If that's more than you want to pay each year, you might be better off with its younger sibling, the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card. It earns 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel and 2 miles per dollar on other eligible purchases, while carrying a $95 annual fee. What's more, the Venture card comes with the same Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fee statement credit so you could come out ahead in the first year with that benefit alone. Related: The best credit cards with no annual fee You are only loyal to a single airline or hotel While the value of Capital One miles lies in their versatility, if you devote every flight and every night to earning airline or hotel elite status, then you might be better off with a cobranded card whose earning and other benefits, such as free checked bags and priority boarding, might suit your travel habits better. Lounge access is your main attraction While Capital One's network of lounges is growing, there are still only a handful of Capital One-branded lounges (my favorite is the one at JFK thanks to its cheesemonger!). Venture X cardholders also saw their guest access privileges pared back earlier this year, and you now have to pay to bring in most guests. If lounge access, particularly when traveling with guests, is your top priority, compare the Venture X with cards that provide access to broader or different lounge networks. For example, the American Express Platinum Card® gives cardmembers access to the American Express Global Lounge Collection, which includes Amex Centurion and Priority Pass lounges (enrollment required) as well as Delta Sky Clubs (when flying Delta Air Lines; limited to 10 annual visits). Which card is better will ultimately depend on the airports and airlines you use most. Related: The best credit cards for airport lounge access You can't (or don't want to) leverage transfer partners While Capital One miles are valuable for direct redemptions through Capital One Travel at a cent apiece, they can be worth multiples more when transferring to certain airline and hotel partners. But that can be a lot of work. First, you've got to get familiar with those partner programs, then you've got to find high-value redemptions that work for you. And while I have the desire to do that sort of travel sleuthing, it's not the best use of everyone's time. If that doesn't appeal to you, a straightforward cash-back card may be a better fit. And if you still want to earn Capital One miles but don't need the Venture X's premium perks, the lower-annual-fee Venture could be a better compromise. Related: The easy route: How to redeem Capital One miles at a fixed value Bottom line The Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card can be a strong premium travel card for someone who travels regularly, can use the $300 annual travel statement credit and values benefits such as lounge access, transferable miles and travel protections. That said, to make its $395 annual fee worth it, you've actually got to use its benefits, most notably the $300 annual travel statement credit for trips booked through Capital One Travel. If you can't do that and take advantage of a few other benefits, such as lounge access and Capital One's fantastic array of airline and hotel transfer partners, you might want to consider an easier-to-use card with a lower annual fee. Ultimately, the question is simple: Will you naturally use enough of the Venture X's benefits to justify paying $395 each year? If the answer is yes, the card could deserve a spot in your wallet. To learn more, read our full review of the Venture X. For Capital One products listed on this page, some of the above benefits are provided by Visa® or Mastercard® and may vary by product. See the respective Guide to Benefits for details, as terms and exclusions apply. Deal alert: Points and miles travel deals for August 2026 Editor's Note From bonus points on your next hotel stay to sales on award tickets, we're always looking for travel deals that help you earn more points and miles and redeem them for maximum value. Plus, scroll down for a targeted Chase Offer at Under Canvas that you could stack with this sale. In other hotel news, points travelers will be excited to check out these new points properties opening in Cancun and Kyoto. And this weekend only, learn how you can save $15 and help families in need. Each week, we help our readers by rounding up promotions so they don't have to scour the internet for the best reward redemptions and offers. This includes everything from frequent flyer programs and hotel rewards programs to credit card offers and rental car deals. Here's our latest list of noteworthy new points and miles promotions for August. Below is one of the best offers we found for August. Until Sept. 30, you can earn 25 bonus miles for every dollar you give online on donations of $25 or more. You can double your bonus miles by paying with an American Airlines cobranded card. Earn bonus United miles when you rent a car Need a vehicle for your next trip? United MileagePlus is awarding extra miles on car rentals booked through the program's portal. You can earn 2,000 bonus miles on rentals of three to five days, or 2,750 bonus miles on rentals of six-plus days. That's in addition to the miles you would normally earn, which depend on your Premier status tier and whether you pay with a United card. Book and complete your rental by Oct. 31. Blackout dates apply. Earn 2 Delta Comfort Flight Certificates + 50K Miles Annual fee $650 Regular APR 19.49%-28.49% Variable Recommended credit Excellent to Good The is a must-have for frequent Delta flyers. Perks include Delta Sky Club lounge access, complimentary checked bags and an annual companion certificate. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐½ *Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG’s editors and is not influenced by the card issuer. Delta SkyMiles Reserve Amex: The basics The carries a $650 annual fee (see rates and fees), but the benefits go a long way toward offsetting that cost. The annual companion certificate alone can be worth more than the annual fee. Cardmembers also get complimentary lounge access, two free checked bags (the first bag is free worldwide and the second bag on domestic U.S. flights) and priority upgrades. These benefits make me feel valued as a cardmember and Delta flyerwhen I travel. I know I'll enjoy a speedy trip through airport security before heading to a lounge, and I often get upgraded to a premium cabin, making my flight more comfortable. The card doesn't have the highest earning rates out there, but it is still worth putting some spend on this card if you want to earn Delta elite status. TPG recommends a good-to-excellent credit score to increase the chances of approval. Let's take a closer look at the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Amex and its benefits to help you decide if it’s right for you. High spending requirement to earn unlimited Sky Club access Other Delta cobranded cards offer superior earning categories Delta SkyMiles Reserve Amex benefits The offers several useful perks for frequent Delta flyers. Lounge access Delta Reserve Amex cardmembers receive access to Delta Sky Clubs and American Express Centurion Lounges. Delta SkyMiles Reserve cardmembers receive 15 annual visits to Delta Sky Club lounges when traveling on a same-day, Delta-marketed or Delta-operated flight, with unlimited annual visits after spending $75,000 in a calendar year. It’s simple to keep track of your visits online or in the Delta app. Cardmembers can pay a $50 fee per person, per location, for Sky Club access when traveling on a Delta partner airline flight that is not marketed or operated by Delta. After a cardmember has used all 15 complimentary visits, they must pay $50 per visit to access a Sky Club. The Delta Reserve Amex will also get you unlimited complimentary visits to American Express Centurion Lounges when flying Delta with a ticket purchased on a U.S.-issued American Express card. You can bring up to two guests into the Centurion Lounge with you for a fee of $50 per person, per location (or $30 per child aged 2 to 17). We all know airport lounges can get crowded. I love that the Delta Reserve Amex provides me with options, so I still have somewhere to grab a drink and a bite to eat even if one lounge is at capacity. Cardmembers also get four one-time Sky Club guest passes upon account opening and each year upon account renewal. This is especially useful when I travel with my family. After using your guest passes, you can pay $50 per person, per location, to bring up to two guests or immediate family (spouse or domestic partner and children under 21) into the Sky Club. Guests can access Grab and Go Sky Club locations for $25 per person per visit. Annual companion certificate Cardmembers receive a companion certificate each year after their account anniversary. The companion certificate is valid for one round-trip ticket to destinations in the U.S. (including Hawaii and Alaska), Central America, Mexico and the Caribbean in first class, Delta Comfort or Main Cabin (when you purchase one adult round-trip ticket). Depending on what you redeem your companion ticket for, you could use it to save hundreds or even thousands of dollars each year, especially if you fly first class. I used my most recent companion pass to cover my son's ticket on our positioning flights before a trip to Paris. It made a huge impact on our budget and allowed us to spend on other things (mostly coffee and baguettes) during our time in Paris. Elite status qualification Delta Reserve Amex cardmembers earn 1 Medallion Qualification Dollar for every $10 spent, with no limit on how many MQDs you can earn through card spending. You’ll also receive a boost of 2,500 MQDs at the start of each Medallion Qualification Year. You only need 5,000 MQDs to reach Silver Medallion status. On average, I fly Delta fewer than 10 times per year, yet I still easily maintain my Silver Medallion status. If you fly more frequently or put significant spending on this card, reaching Gold Medallion status is realistic. Preflight and inflight benefits The offers several benefits that make your time in the airport, in the air and during your trips more comfortable: Two free checked bags for the cardmember (and up to eight companions) traveling on the same reservation (the first bag is free worldwide and the second bag on domestic U.S. flights, though it's important to note only other eligible Delta cardmembers on the same reservation will receive a second checked bag free on domestic flights) The Delta Reserve Amex also includes extensive shopping and travel protections when you use your card for certain purchases, and it includes complimentary Hertz President’s Circle status. Enrollment in the Hertz Gold+ program is required. 3 miles per dollar spent on eligible purchases made directly with Delta 1 mile per dollar spent on all other eligible purchases Based on TPG’s August 2026 valuations of Delta miles at 1.2 cents each, you’ll only get a 3.6% return on Delta purchases and a 1.2% return on everything else. As I mentioned before, this card's value doesn't come from everyday spending. I primarily use this card to earn MQDs and access its travel benefits. Despite the frustration with Delta's dynamic pricing on award flights, I find redeeming Delta SkyMiles for Delta flights pretty straightforward thanks to Delta's helpful award calendar. If your dates are flexible, you can use the calendar to price the cheapest award flights. If you have the flexibility, you’d be better off saving your Delta miles for one of the carrier’s frequent award deals. I frequently visit the Orlando theme parks, so I regularly check for available deals and often see round-trip pricing as low as 10,400 miles (plus taxes and fees) from my home airport to Orlando International Airport (MCO). You can also use your SkyMiles to fly on international SkyTeam partner airlines such as Air France and Korean Air, as well as select nonalliance partners like WestJet. You can redeem Delta SkyMiles for many things other than flights (including premium alcoholic beverages in Sky Clubs as well as hotels and rental cars), but the redemption value for these doesn't match what you get when redeeming for flights. Downsides to consider about the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Amex With an annual fee of $650, you really need to do the math on whether you will get enough value out of this card beyond the first year. It makes sense for me because I regularly fly Delta and can utilize most of the benefits and statement credits. It's also worth noting that earning 1 mile per dollar spent is not the most impressive earning rate for everyday spending. If you want a card that earns more than 1 mile or point per dollar spent across all nonbonus category purchases, consider another option. Lastly, if you don't enjoy tracking monthly statement credits, this may not be the best card for you. If you don't take advantage of the credits offered by this card, you're leaving money on the table that could otherwise help offset the cost of the hefty annual fee. For a limited time, new applicants can earn two domestic round-trip Delta Comfort flight certificates and 50,000 bonus miles after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. A 21+ day advance purchase is required; up to $80 per person in taxes and fees apply. Other restrictions apply. Offer ends Nov. 4. The miles portion of this welcome offer is worth up to $600, according to TPG's valuations. This is the first time flight certificates have been included in a welcome offer. If you can maximize them for at least $450 each, this would be the best-ever offer on this card. However, if you can't, you're better off holding out for an offer of at least 125,000 miles (offer no longer available). Here are the key terms for the flight certificates: Valid for round-trip travel to the U.S. mainland (48 states), Puerto Rico or the U.S. Virgin Islands Travel must be booked and completed by Jan. 15, 2028 Can be used for Delta Comfort or Delta Main Cabin Passengers pay up to $80 per person in taxes and fees Other cards to consider if you don't want the Delta Reserve Amex Most cardmembers carry it for two reasons: Delta Sky Club access and an extra boost toward earning Delta elite status. When it comes to these perks, the Delta Reserve Amex has three primary competitors: If you want a lower annual fee: Try the , which also offers two free checked bags (the first bag is free worldwide and the second bag on domestic U.S. flights) and priority boarding. It has a lower annual fee of $350 (see rates and fees), which may be easier to justify for some consumers. To learn more, read our full review of the Delta Platinum Amex. If you’re eligible for a business card: You might prefer the . This way, you can easily separate your personal and business expenses while still enjoying similar travel perks, such as lounge access and an annual companion certificate. To learn more, read our full review of the Delta Reserve Business Amex card. As a frequent Delta flyer, I recommend the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Amex over other cards in the cobranded Delta Amex suite. This is because of the solid lounge access, discount on award bookings, free checked bags and annual companion certificate. These benefits are especially valuable for parents who frequently travel with their children. These benefits make flying with Delta stress-free and enjoyable, especially when I receive a coveted first-class upgrade. The perks this card offers and the value I derive from them have made it the only airline card in my wallet. For rates and fees of the Delta Reserve Amex, click here. For rates and fees of the Delta Platinum Amex, click here.

item.title: Ink Business Cash vs. Amex Blue Business Cash: Which no-annual-fee business card is better?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 2.50
Ink Business Cash vs. Amex Blue Business Cash: Which no-annual-fee business card is better? The Ink Business Cash® Credit Card (see rates and fees) and the The American Express Blue Business Cash® Card are two no-annual-fee cards (see rates and fees for the Blue Business Cash) that take very different approaches to rewards. The Ink Business Cash offers elevated cash back in several business-friendly categories, while the Blue Business Cash earns a flat 2% cash back on eligible purchases up to $50,000 per calendar year (then 1% back on all purchases). The Ink Business Cash is the better choice for business owners who want to maximize rewards on common business expenses, while Blue Business Cash is a better fit for those who want simple, predictable cash back on everyday spending. Here's how the Ink Business Cash and Amex Blue Business Cash compare, including their welcome offers, benefits and earning structures. Ink Business Cash vs. Amex Blue Business Cash: At a glance | Card Features | Ink Business Cash | Amex Blue Business Cash | |---|---|---| | Annual fee | $0 | $0 | | Welcome offer | Earn $1,000 bonus cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening. | Earn a $250 statement credit after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months of card membership. | | Authorized user/employee card fee | $0 | | | Foreign transaction fee | 3% | | Quick picks by business type | Best for | Card | |---|---| | Businesses with significant office supply, internet, cable or phone expenses | Ink Business Cash | | Businesses that want to power-up their existing Ultimate Rewards business card | Ink Business Cash | | Businesses that want simple, flat-rate cash back | Amex Blue Business Cash | | Businesses with expenses that don't fit traditional bonus categories | Amex Blue Business Cash | Ink Business Cash vs. Amex Blue Business Cash: Welcome bonus New Ink Business Cash cardholders can earn $1,000 bonus cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening. New Amex Blue Business Cash cardholders, meanwhile, can earn a $250 statement credit after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months of card membership. The Ink Business Cash, therefore, offers $750 more in potential value from its welcome bonus. But you'll need to spend $5,000 more on purchases than you would with the Blue Business Cash to earn it. The Ink's larger bonus is therefore the clear winner if you can comfortably meet its spending requirement. But don't spend money you wouldn't otherwise spend simply to earn a credit card welcome offer. Before you apply, keep eligibility restrictions in mind. Chase states that the Ink Business Cash welcome bonus may not be available if you've ever had this card or another no-annual-fee Chase business card. Meanwhile, American Express generally restricts welcome offers to applicants who haven't previously had that card, commonly referred to as its once-per-lifetime rule. Winner: Ink Business Cash. Its welcome offer is substantially more valuable, and the additional spending required to earn it is reasonable for many established businesses. Related: The best credit card welcome bonuses of August 2026 Ink Business Cash vs. Amex Blue Business Cash: Benefits | Benefit | Ink Business Cash | Amex Blue Business Cash | |---|---|---| | Purchase protection | Yes; up to 120 days | Yes; up to 90 days* | | Extended warranty protection | Yes | Yes* | | Rental car coverage | Primary for eligible business rentals | Secondary** | | Expanded Buying Power | No | Yes*** | Neither card offers the premium perks you'll find on more expensive business cards, but both provide a useful collection of protections despite charging no annual fee. *Eligibility and benefit levels vary by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Policies are underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. **Eligibility and benefit level varies by card. Not all vehicle types or rentals are covered, and geographic restrictions apply. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for details. Policies are underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. ***The amount you can spend above your credit limit is flexible, so it adapts based on several factors. The amount you can spend with Expanded Buying Power is not unlimited. Purchase and rental car protections The Ink Business Cash has an advantage when it comes to purchase and rental car protections. Its purchase protection covers eligible new purchases against damage or theft for up to 120 days, compared with up to 90 days* on the Blue Business Cash. More significantly, the Ink provides primary auto rental collision damage waiver coverage on eligible rentals for business purposes, while the Blue Business Cash offers secondary coverage**. With primary coverage, you generally won't have to first file a claim with your personal auto insurance for an eligible loss. That can make the Ink Cash valuable for business owners who frequently rent cars for work. Extended warranty protection Both cards can also provide additional protection after an eligible manufacturer's warranty expires. The Ink Business Cash adds an additional year to eligible U.S. manufacturers' warranties of three years or less, while the Blue Business Cash can add up to one year to eligible warranties of five years or less*. The differences here aren't significant enough to sway me toward one card over the other, but either benefit could save your business money if an eligible purchase needs repair or replacement after its original warranty expires. Expanded buying power The Blue Business Cash has one benefit the Ink doesn't: Expanded Buying Power***. This feature can allow eligible cardmembers to spend beyond their credit limit without an over-limit fee (see rates and fees), with the amount available varying based on factors such as purchase, payment and credit history. You'll still need to pay your balance according to the card's terms. Both cards also allow businesses to add employee cards without an additional annual cost, making it easier to manage employee spending while earning rewards on their purchases. Winner: Ink Business Cash. Both cards offer useful protections for no-annual-fee products, but the Ink's longer purchase protection period and primary rental car coverage for eligible business rentals give it the edge. Related: 6 reasons to apply for the Chase Ink Business Cash card How to earn and redeem rewards with Ink Business Cash vs. Amex Blue Business Cash | Card | Earning rates | |---|---| | Ink Business Cash | | | Amex Blue Business Cash | | Earning rewards The biggest difference between these cards is the way they earn rewards: the Ink Business Cash rewards specific types of business spending, while the Blue Business Cash rewards almost everything at the same rate. If your business regularly spends money at office supply stores or pays for internet, cable and phone services, the Ink Business Cash can be significantly more rewarding. You'll earn 5% back on up to $25,000 in combined purchases in those categories each account anniversary year. That means a business that spends heavily in those categories can earn considerably more than it would with a flat-rate 2% card. The Ink also earns 2% back at gas stations and restaurants on up to $25,000 in combined purchases each account anniversary year. For example, $10,000 in eligible office supply store and telecommunications spending would earn $500 in cash back with the Ink Business Cash, compared with $200 with the Blue Business Cash. But the math changes when your expenses don't fit neatly into the Ink's bonus categories. The Blue Business Cash earns 2% back on all eligible purchases up to $50,000 per calendar year (after that, earn 1% back on all purchases). You don't need to think about whether a purchase qualifies for a bonus category, and you don't need to remember which categories have spending caps. There's also an important consideration for businesses with high annual spending. Once you've reached $25,000 in combined purchases in each of the Ink's 5% and 2% bonus-category groups, additional purchases in those categories earn 1%. The Blue Business Cash, meanwhile, continues earning 2% on eligible purchases until you've spent $50,000 during the calendar year. So while the Ink has a higher earning ceiling in its bonus categories, the Blue Business Cash can be more rewarding for a business with a broad mix of expenses. Winner: Tie. The Ink Business Cash for bonus-category spending; Amex Blue Business Cash for simplicity. Redeeming rewards With the Blue Business Cash, cash back is automatically applied to your account as a statement credit each month, making redemptions particularly simple. The Ink Business Cash offers more flexibility. Although Chase markets the card as earning cash back, rewards are issued as Chase Ultimate Rewards points worth 1 cent apiece when redeemed for cash back. You can also redeem them for options such as gift cards and travel through Chase Travel℠. The Ink's rewards can become even more valuable if you pair the card with an eligible Ultimate Rewards card, which we'll discuss below. Winner: Ink Business Cash. The Blue Business Cash makes redeeming rewards easier, but the Ink provides more redemption options. Related: 19 incredible ways to use 100K Chase Ultimate Rewards points Transferring rewards The Blue Business Cash doesn't earn transferable Membership Rewards. Its rewards are cash back, automatically issued as statement credits, so there's no option to transfer your rewards to airline or hotel partners. The Ink Business Cash has considerably more upside. On its own, the card doesn't allow you to transfer rewards to travel partners. However, if you also hold an eligible Ultimate Rewards card, such as the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees), Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (see rates and fees) or Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card (see rates and fees), you can combine your rewards and then transfer them to Chase's airline and hotel partners, such as United MileagePlus, Marriott Bonvoy and World of Hyatt. That can potentially provide significantly more value than redeeming your rewards for cash back. For example, 50,000 Ink Business Cash points would be worth $500 as cash back, but TPG values 50,000 Ultimate Rewards points at $1,025 according to our August 2026 valuations. Of course, maximizing your points this way requires more work than simply accepting cash back. You'll need to find award availability and understand how Chase's transfer partners work. For business owners who prioritize simplicity and don't want to spend time navigating award programs, the Blue Business Cash's automatic statement credits may be more appealing despite offering less potential value. Winner: Ink Business Cash. Related: Why all travelers should earn transferable credit card points Can I have both the Ink Business Cash and Amex Blue Business Cash? Yes, there's no rule preventing you from having both the Ink Business Cash and Amex Blue Business Cash. In fact, the cards can complement each other: You could use the Ink Business Cash for purchases that earn 5% or 2% cash back and the Blue Business Cash for eligible purchases that don't fall into the Ink's bonus categories. Keep in mind that the Blue Business Cash's 2% earning rate applies only to the first $50,000 in eligible purchases each calendar year (then 1%). Before opening both cards, consider whether your business spending is high enough to justify managing two cards and whether you're eligible for each card's welcome offer. If neither card fits your spending habits, consider a business card with a flat-rate earning structure, a card with transferable points or a card with bonus categories that better match your expenses. Related: How to choose the best credit card for your business expenses Should I get the Ink Business Cash or the Amex Blue Business Cash? Choose the Ink Business Cash if your business spends heavily on office supplies, internet, cable, phone services, gas or restaurants. The 5% and 2% bonus categories can produce significantly more cash back than a flat-rate card if you can maximize them. The Ink is also the better choice if you're already invested in Chase Ultimate Rewards. While you can redeem its rewards as cash back, having an eligible Chase card gives you the potential to turn those rewards into transferable points. Choose the Amex Blue Business Cash if you want to earn 2% cash back without thinking about bonus categories (earn 2% cash back on the first $50,000 in purchases you make each calendar year; then 1% back on all purchases). It's especially compelling for businesses with varied expenses that don't fit neatly into the Ink's bonus categories. It's also worth considering the Blue Business Cash if your business has substantial expenses but doesn't want to manage multiple cards. The 2% rate applies across eligible purchases, up to $50,000 per calendar year, so you can simply put most or all of your business expenses on the card and let the rewards accumulate. Ultimately, the decision comes down to whether you're willing to trade simplicity for potentially higher rewards. Related: Your guide to the Chase Ink Business credit cards Bottom line Choosing between the Ink Business Cash and Amex Blue Business Cash comes down to how much effort you want to put into maximizing your business spending. The Ink Business Cash has the higher potential upside, while the Blue Business Cash is a better fit if you value simplicity and predictable cash back. Neither card is ideal for businesses that frequently make purchases abroad because both charge foreign transaction fees. And if you're looking for premium travel benefits or transferable rewards without adding another Chase card to your wallet, you may want to consider a different business card altogether. To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Ink Business Cash Card and our full review of the American Express Blue Business Cash Card. Apply here: Ink Business Cash Credit Card Apply here: The American Express Blue Business Cash Card For rates and fees of the Amex Blue Business Cash, click here.
